- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/brushing.rs`

Turning pointer gestures into row-state changes (linked brushing).

Views translate a gesture into data terms (a rectangle in plot coordinates,
or the screen positions of drawn points) and call into this module. The
result is applied to the shared [`RowStateManager`], so every other view picks
up the new selection the next time it draws.

- `struct PlotRegion`: An axis-aligned rectangle in plot (data) coordinates.
- `fn selection_mode`: Combine modifier keys into a selection mode: alt/option subtracts, command/ctrl toggles, shift extends, none replaces.
- `fn row_number_click`: The rows and selection mode for a click on a row number in the data grid.
- `fn rows_in_region`: Rows whose points fall inside `region`, ascending and without duplicates (a plot may draw a row more than once, e.g.
- `fn chart_rows_in_region`: Rows behind the control-chart points inside `region` (sample number on the horizontal axis), ascending and without duplicates.
- `fn chart_point_visible`: Whether a control-chart point is drawn: at least one of its rows is not hidden.
- `fn chart_point_selected`: Whether a control-chart point shows as selected: any of its rows is selected.
- `fn bar_rows_in_region`: Rows counted by the bars a box selection touches: a bar is touched when the region overlaps the rectangle `[center ± width/2] × [0, count]`.
- `fn bar_at`: The bar under the plot-coordinate point `(x, y)`, if any.
- `fn selected_in_bar`: Number of a bar's rows that are selected (drawn as a highlighted portion).
- `fn box_rows_in_region`: Rows of a box plot whose values fall within the region's horizontal range (the vertical position is irrelevant: values lie on one line).
- `fn nearest_row`: The row whose drawn point is nearest to `cursor` in screen space, if within `max_distance` pixels.
- `fn brush_region`: Apply a box selection to the shared row state.
- `fn brush_click`: Apply a click: select the clicked row, or with no row hit and [`SelectionMode::Replace`], clear the selection (clicking empty space).

### `crates/app-model/src/capability_analysis.rs`

Process capability of one numeric column against specification limits
([`stat_quality::capability`]), bound to the dataset's row state.

Values are taken in row order from rows with a value that are not excluded
(order matters for the moving-range and subgroup estimates of the
short-term σ). The report gives the indices with confidence intervals, a
summary of the process, observed and expected nonconforming rates, and a
row-linked histogram with the limits and the fitted normal curve.

With a non-normal model ([`CapabilityModel`]) the report leads with the
percentile-based indices of [`stat_quality::nonnormal`] and the expected
rates under the fitted distribution, shows the distribution with its
reference percentiles, draws its density over the histogram and a
quantile plot against it, and keeps the normal-theory indices at the end
for comparison. Bootstrap percentile intervals for those indices can be
added ([`stat_quality::bootstrap_percentile_intervals`]).

The **summary page** layout gathers one study on one page, in this order:
the indices, the process summary, the location chart (X̄ or individuals,
following the σ-within method's subgrouping) and its range, standard
deviation or moving-range chart, the last subgroups' individual values
against the specification limits, the histogram, and a probability plot
against the model.

With a **by** column the study is also run on each group's rows (in row
order within the group), giving a Capability by Group table (N, mean,
overall SD, Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk and the observed share out of
specification) and a Ppk by Group chart with reference lines at 1 and
1.33, its groups in natural order or sorted by Ppk ([`GroupOrder`]). The
standard layout can add the probability plot, which carries the
specification limits as horizontal lines. The report offers an
in-specification indicator column (a formula: 1 inside the limits, 0
outside, missing without a value).

- `const CAPABILITY_LEVEL`: Confidence level of the intervals.
- `const LAST_SUBGROUPS`: Subgroups (or individual values) shown in the summary page's last-subgroups plot.
- `struct BootstrapSettings`: Resampling settings of bootstrap intervals.
- `enum GroupOrder`: Order of the groups in the Ppk by Group chart.
- `struct CapabilityRequest`: What to analyse.
- `struct CapabilityAnalysis`: A computed capability study.

### `crates/app-model/src/categorical_logistic.rs`

Ordinal and nominal logistic regression bound to a dataset
([`stat_discrete::polytomous`]).

The response is a column of categories (text or numbers). For the
**ordinal** (proportional-odds) model they are ordered — by default in
natural order (numerically when every label is a number), or in the
order the request lists — and the model is
`P(Y ≤ j) = logistic(αⱼ − xᵀβ)`, so a positive coefficient favours higher
categories. For the **nominal** (baseline-category) model each category
but a reference one gets its own equation
`ln(P(Y = j)/P(Y = reference)) = β₀ⱼ + xᵀβⱼ`.

Predictors and effects are coded as in the linear model (continuous
predictors as they are, categorical ones as indicators, interactions and
powers centred, sum-to-zero coding when a categorical predictor enters a
higher-order effect). Each effect gets a likelihood-ratio test from
refitting without its columns.

- `enum CategoricalModel`: Which model a categorical response gets.
- `struct CategoricalLogisticRequest`: Columns, effects and options of an ordinal or nominal logistic regression.
- `struct CategoricalLogisticAnalysis`: A fitted ordinal or nominal logistic regression and what its report needs.

### `crates/app-model/src/cause_effect.rs`

Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram drawn from columns of causes and
sub-causes (Ishikawa, *Guide to Quality Control*, 1976, chapter 3).

Each row is one cause path: its value in the first column names a main
branch (a category of causes), the second column a cause on that branch
and the third, if given, a sub-cause of that cause. Repeated paths are
merged (and counted); an empty cell ends the path there. Branches, causes
and sub-causes keep the order in which they first appear, so the table
controls the drawing. Every label carries the rows behind it, so clicking
it selects them in every linked view.

[`CauseEffectDiagram::layout`] places everything in page points, shared by
the screen and by figure export: a horizontal spine ending in the effect,
main branches slanting off it alternately above and below, each cause on
a short horizontal rib off its branch and each sub-cause indented under
its cause.

- `struct CauseEffectRequest`: What to draw.
- `struct CauseNode`: One branch, cause or sub-cause of a [`CauseEffectDiagram`].
- `struct CauseEffectDiagram`: A cause-and-effect diagram for display.
- `struct FishboneLine`: A line of a [`FishboneLayout`].
- `struct FishboneLabel`: A piece of text of a [`FishboneLayout`].
- `struct FishboneLayout`: Where everything of a fishbone diagram is drawn, in page points with the origin at the bottom left and y up.
- `const LINE_HEIGHT`: Height of a line of text, as a multiple of its size.
- `fn text_width`: Estimated width of `text` at `size` points (an average glyph is a little over half the size wide).
- `struct CauseEffectAnalysis`: A computed cause-and-effect diagram.

### `crates/app-model/src/censored_distribution.rs`

Censored values and detection limits in the Distribution report
(Helsel, *Statistics for Censored Environmental Data Using Minitab and R*,
2nd ed., 2012).

A value can be known exactly, known only to lie below a limit
(left-censored: a non-detect below a detection or reporting limit),
known only to lie above a limit (right-censored), or known to lie in an
interval. Two layouts say which:

* **Indicator:** a second column flags censored values (nonzero = censored);
  the analysed column holds the value or, for a censored row, its limit,
  and every flagged value is censored in one chosen direction.
* **Interval:** the analysed column holds the lower end and a second column
  the upper end; equal ends are an exact value, a missing lower end a
  left-censored value (below the upper end), a missing upper end a
  right-censored value (above the lower end).

The report then gives:

* a summary of the exact and censored values and the detection limits;
* the nonparametric estimate of the distribution function — Turnbull's
  (1976) self-consistent estimate ([`stat_reliability::turnbull`]), which
  is the Kaplan–Meier estimate for right-censored data and the
  Kaplan–Meier estimate of the flipped data ("reversed" Kaplan–Meier,
  Helsel ch. 6) for left-censored data — with its percentiles (shown as
  "< limit" when they fall below the lowest detection limit) and mean
  (the mass below the lowest limit placed at that limit, so a high-side
  estimate, as Helsel notes);
* maximum-likelihood fits of the normal, lognormal, Weibull, gamma,
  exponential, logistic and log-logistic distributions to the censored
  data ([`stat_reliability::fit_censored`]), ranked by AIC, with their
  parameters, mean and median and Wald and likelihood-ratio limits;
* a plot of the nonparametric estimate with the fitted distribution
  functions;
* when every finite end is a whole number ≥ 0, Poisson and negative
  binomial fits to the counts with their censoring
  ([`stat_reliability::censored_count`]): a count below a detection limit
  `d` lies in `0 … ⌈d⌉ − 1`, one above `d` is at least `⌊d⌋ + 1`, and an
  interval `[l, u]` includes both ends.

- `enum CensorDirection`: Which way an indicated value is censored.
- `enum Censoring`: How censored values are marked (see the module docs).
- `struct CensoredDistribution`: The censored-data part of a Distribution report.

### `crates/app-model/src/clipboard.rs`

Copying cells out as text and pasting text in.

**Copy** writes tab-separated text, one line per row, which spreadsheets
and text editors read as a block of cells. Values appear as the grid shows
them (numbers in shortest round-trip form, dates in their display format,
missing values empty); a field holding a tab, line break or quote is quoted
with doubled inner quotes (RFC 4180 style).

**Paste** reads tab- or comma-separated text ([`parse`]): tab-separated if
the text has a tab, else comma-separated if every line splits into the same
number of fields (more than one) and not every comma is followed by a
space (`Smith, John` is one value), else one value per line. The paste
summary says when the text was split at commas.

* [`paste_edit`] stores the block in the grid with its top-left corner at
  the cell cursor, as one undoable [`Edit::Batch`]. Rows and columns are
  added at the end as needed (a new column's type is inferred from its
  pasted values, as when reading a file). Each value is checked against
  its column's type; if any is wrong, nothing is pasted. A first line that
  repeats the target columns' names (as copied rows carry) is skipped.
* [`table_from_text`] makes a new table from the text. The first line is
  taken as column names when every field in it is filled in, distinct and
  not a number, and more lines follow; otherwise columns are named
  `Column 1`, `Column 2`, ….

- `fn parse`: Split clipboard text into rows of fields (see the module documentation).
- `fn splits_on_commas`: Whether [`parse`] splits `text` at commas (it has no tab and splits into columns there).
- `fn paste_text`: [`paste_edit`] of `text` as [`parse`] splits it.
- `struct PasteSummary`: What a paste will do, for the status message.
- `fn paste_edit`: The edit that pastes `cells` (rows of text fields) into `table` with the top-left value at `(row, column)`, adding rows and columns at the end as needed (see the module documentation).
- `fn table_from_text`: A new table named `name` from clipboard text (see the module documentation), with notes about how values were read.
- `fn copy_text`: Tab-separated text of the given rows and columns (with a line of column names first when `names` is set), ending in a line break.
- `fn error_text`: An error's message without its category prefix, for the status line.

### `crates/app-model/src/compare.rs`

Comparative tests bound to a dataset ([`stat_inference`]): one sample
against a hypothesized value, two or more independent groups, and paired
or repeated measurements.

Data can be laid out either way:

* **stacked** — every measurement in one column, with a second column
  naming its group (or, for paired data, its condition and subject);
* **side by side** — one column per group or condition (paired values on
  the same row).

Excluded rows and missing values are left out. For paired data in stacked
form, subjects without a value for every condition are dropped.

- `struct OneSampleRequest`: Columns and settings of a one-sample analysis.
- `struct OneSampleAnalysis`: A one-sample analysis.
- `enum GroupLayout`: Where the groups' values are.
- `struct GroupComparisonRequest`: Settings of a comparison of independent groups.
- `struct GroupComparison`: A comparison of independent groups.
- `enum PairedLayout`: Where paired or repeated measurements are.
- `struct PairedRequest`: Settings of a paired comparison.
- `struct PairedComparison`: A paired or repeated-measures comparison.

### `crates/app-model/src/comparison_report.rs`

One entry point for the comparison, proportion, rate and power reports —
and the attribute capability, principal-components chart, monitoring limits, between/within capability and acceptance
sampling reports, and the measurement-study and design-study reports
([`crate::gauge_studies`], [`crate::robust_design`],
[`crate::declared_design`], [`crate::design_evaluation`]), which work the same way — so front ends can
treat them uniformly (their settings are edited in place and the report re-run).

- `enum ComparisonReport`: A computed comparison-type report.

### `crates/app-model/src/competing_risks.rs`

Competing risks bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::competing_risks`]): Aalen–Johansen cumulative
incidence of each cause (failure mode) with limits, stacked or overlaid,
per group; Gray's test of each cause across groups; Fine–Gray
subdistribution hazards regression on covariates with predicted cumulative
incidence; and, for engineering data, a life distribution per failure mode
combined into the series system's failure probability.

**Layout:** one row per unit (or per set of identical units, with a
frequency column): the time of failure or censoring, and the cause or
failure mode, one value of which means "censored" (still running). An
optional group column compares groups; optional covariate columns
(continuous, or nominal coded by indicators of all levels but the first)
enter the regression. Excluded rows and rows without a time or cause are
left out; rows missing a covariate are left out of the regression only.

Failure-mode fits use every unit together (the group column is not used
there).

- `struct CompetingRisksRequest`: Columns and settings of a competing-risks analysis.
- `struct RegressionResult`: The Fine–Gray part of the analysis.
- `struct CompetingGroup`: One group's estimates.
- `struct CompetingRisksAnalysis`: A computed competing-risks analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/control_chart.rs`

A control-chart analysis bound to a dataset and its row state.

The chart is built from **column roles**: the measurement column, and
optionally a subgroup ID column, a phase column and a label column. Rows
are taken in table order, skipping excluded rows and rows with a missing
measurement, phase or subgroup ID (so excluding an out-of-control point
recomputes the limits without it, the usual Phase I practice).

- **Phases** are runs of consecutive rows with the same phase value; each
  gets its own center line and limits, and run rules restart at each one
  (see [`stat_quality::phased`]).
- **Subgroups**, within a phase, are the rows sharing a subgroup ID (in
  order of first appearance), so subgroup sizes may vary; without an ID
  column they are consecutive runs of `subgroup_size` rows.
- **Labels** name each plotted point: the label column's value on the
  subgroup's first row, else the subgroup ID (else, on a short-run chart,
  the part number).
- **Part numbers** (short-run charts) are the values of the part column;
  each part gets its own mean and σ within each phase.

Every plotted point records the dataset rows it summarizes, which is what
links chart brushing to the data grid: a moving range carries both
points' rows and a moving average every point it averages.

Besides the X̄/R, X̄/S and individuals charts the analysis draws the
moving-average, three-way, zone and short-run charts of
[`stat_quality::extended`].

**Options** (individuals, X̄–R and X̄–S charts): limits at `k`σ, moving
ranges over `w` values, and limits from standard (historical) values
typed in or read from a saved limits table ([`standard_from_table`]); see
[`stat_quality::phased`]. Any chart can show only its **last N
subgroups**, with limits from all subgroups (the earlier ones are only
hidden) or from those N alone. A **run chart** section plots every value
at its subgroup's position, joins the subgroup means or medians, and
draws the center line at the median (or mean) of all values.
[`saved_limits_table`] writes the limits, process center and σ of every
phase as a data table, which can later give the standard values.

- `const DEFAULT_SPAN`: Default span of a moving-average chart.
- `struct LastSubgroups`: Show only the last subgroups of a chart.
- `struct ControlChartRequest`: Which chart to draw, from which columns.
- `struct RuleSet`: A set of the eight run rules, as a bit mask (bit `k − 1` for rule `k`).
- `struct ControlChartOptions`: User-toggleable parts of a control-chart report.
- `enum RunCenter`: The subgroup summary a run chart joins, and its center line.
- `struct ControlChartAnalysis`: A computed chart pair plus the row mapping needed to report and brush it.
- `const PROCESS_CENTER`: Column of a saved limits table holding the process center.
- `const PROCESS_SIGMA`: Column of a saved limits table holding the process σ.
- `fn standard_from_table`: The standard values for measurement `name` in a limits table saved by [`ControlChartAnalysis::limits_data_table`] (or any table with "Measurement", "Process center" and "Process sigma" columns): the last row for that measurement with a finite center and a positive σ.
- `fn saved_limits_table`: The limits table of a control-chart report (`None` for any other report; an error when the chart cannot be computed).

### `crates/app-model/src/correlation_analysis.rs`

Correlations of several continuous columns, bound to the row state
([`stat_multivariate::correlations`]).

Excluded rows are left out; a missing value removes the row from the
pairs that need it (pairwise) or from every pair (listwise). The report
shows each column's summary, the Pearson matrix, a heat map of it (each
cell's value printed in the cell), every pair's r with its Fisher-z
interval and p-value, and optionally Spearman's ρₛ, the partial
correlations (from the complete rows) and the covariance matrix.

- `struct CorrelationRequest`: What to correlate and which tables to show.
- `struct CorrelationAnalysis`: A computed correlation report.

### `crates/app-model/src/counts.rs`

Proportion and event-rate comparisons bound to a dataset
([`stat_inference::proportions`], [`stat_inference::rates`]).

A proportion analysis counts the rows whose outcome equals a chosen event
level, either in one sample (against a hypothesized proportion), by the
levels of a grouping column, or for paired outcomes in two columns
(McNemar). A rate analysis sums an event-count column (and optionally an
exposure column) overall or by group.

- `enum ProportionComparison`: What the proportions are compared with.
- `struct ProportionRequest`: Settings of a proportion analysis.
- `fn column_levels`: Distinct non-empty labels of a column in natural order.
- `struct ProportionAnalysis`: A proportion analysis.
- `struct RateRequest`: Settings of an event-rate analysis.
- `struct RateAnalysis`: An event-rate analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/crossover_analysis.rs`

Two-period, two-treatment crossover trials
([`stat_inference::crossover`]): treatment, period and carryover effects,
the analysis of variance, and average equivalence of a test treatment to
a reference by two one-sided tests, on the difference or the ratio
(log) scale.

The data are stacked: one row per subject and period, with columns for
the response, the subject, the period and the treatment received. The
period and treatment columns must each have exactly two values. A
subject's sequence is the order in which it received the treatments.
Subjects without exactly one usable row in each period, or that received
the same treatment twice, are left out and counted in the report.

- `struct CrossoverRequest`: Settings of a crossover report.
- `struct CrossoverReport`: A computed crossover report.

### `crates/app-model/src/curve_templates.rs`

Assay curve templates: ready-made nonlinear regressions for common
laboratory experiments.

A template is a model formula ([`crate::nonlinear_analysis`]) written for
one kind of experiment, with its parameters named in that field's terms,
starting values computed from the data, default bounds, weighting and
sharing across data sets, and the quantities the field reads off the fit
(an inhibition constant, a half-life, a quantitation range…) with their
intervals ([`stat_linear::nonlinear::assay`]). Choosing a template fills
in an ordinary [`NonlinearRequest`]; every option of nonlinear regression
(global fits, weights, robust fitting, profile intervals, inverse
prediction) still applies, and the report adds the template's own
sections.

Templates are named by the standard model names of the cited literature:

* **Standard curves** — four- and five-parameter logistic calibration
  curves (Rodbard, "Statistical quality control and routine data
  processing for radioimmunoassays", *Clin. Chem.* 20, 1974; Gottschalk &
  Dunn, *Anal. Biochem.* 343, 2005), acceptance by ICH M10 (2022).
* **Receptor binding** — saturation, competition and kinetic binding
  (Hulme & Trevethick, "Ligand binding assays at equilibrium", *Br. J.
  Pharmacol.* 161, 2010; Cheng & Prusoff, *Biochem. Pharmacol.* 22, 1973;
  Motulsky & Mahan, *Mol. Pharmacol.* 25, 1984).
* **Enzyme kinetics** — Michaelis–Menten, substrate inhibition, Hill,
  reversible inhibition mechanisms, tight-binding inhibition (Morrison,
  *Biochim. Biophys. Acta* 185, 1969) and the integrated rate equation
  (Schnell & Mendoza, *J. Theor. Biol.* 187, 1997; Goudar, Sonnad &
  Duggleby, *Biochim. Biophys. Acta* 1429, 1999); Cornish-Bowden,
  *Fundamentals of Enzyme Kinetics*, 4th ed., 2012.
* **Pharmacological dose–response** — logistic agonist and inhibitor
  curves, bell-shaped and biphasic curves, Gaddum–Schild antagonism
  (Arunlakshana & Schild, *Br. J. Pharmacol.* 14, 1959; Lew & Angus,
  *Trends Pharmacol. Sci.* 16, 1995), the operational model of agonism
  (Black & Leff, *Proc. R. Soc. B* 220, 1983) and relative potency from
  parallel curves (Finney, *Statistical Method in Biological Assay*, 1978).
* **Growth, decay and survival** — modified Gompertz growth (Zwietering
  et al., *Appl. Environ. Microbiol.* 56, 1990), Baranyi–Roberts growth
  (*Int. J. Food Microbiol.* 23, 1994), first-order decay and association,
  linear-quadratic cell survival (Fowler, *Br. J. Radiol.* 62, 1989;
  Franken et al., *Nat. Protoc.* 1, 2006), the Boltzmann activation curve
  and the Arrhenius equation.

- `const GAS_CONSTANT`: Gas constant, J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ (CODATA 2018, exact).
- `enum TemplateGroup`: Kind of experiment a template is for.
- `enum CurveTemplate`: The templates.
- `enum SecondKind`: What the second column of a template holds.
- `struct SecondRole`: The second column a template reads besides the x column.
- `enum DataSets`: How a template uses a data-set column.
- `struct ConstantSpec`: A number the template needs that is not in the data.
- `struct ParamSpec`: One parameter of a template.
- `struct DerivedSpec`: A quantity computed from a template's parameters.
- `enum Extra`: Extra report sections of a template.
- `struct StartData`: The data starting values are computed from.
- `struct TemplateSettings`: A template applied to a table: what the report needs beyond the model.

### `crates/app-model/src/dashboard.rs`

Dashboards: reports and notes from a project's tables arranged on a grid,
with local filters shared by every tile (roadmap §10).

A [`Dashboard`] belongs to a [`ProjectFile`] and uses only that project's
tables. It holds:

* **tiles** ([`DashboardTile`]) placed on a grid of `grid_columns` columns
  and as many rows as needed; each tile covers a rectangle of whole cells
  ([`GridArea`]) and tiles never overlap. A tile is either a report — its
  own copy of a report request ([`SavedReport`], the same request a table's
  reports and [`run_report`] use) bound to one table by [`TableId`] — or a
  heading or text note ([`TileContent::Text`]);
* **local filters**: at most one [`FilterCondition`] per column name.
  Every filter applies to every report tile whose table has a column of
  that name (all conditions must hold); a table without the column is not
  filtered by it. Filters never change a table's own row states: each
  tile runs on a copy of its table's [`RowStateManager`] in which the rows
  outside the filters are also excluded and hidden ([`Dashboard::filter_rows`]).
  Row indices stay those of the table, so selecting rows in a tile is
  linked, through the table's own row states, with every other view of the
  same table, and only of that table;
* **shared column pickers** ([`SharedSwitcher`]): at most one per column
  name. A switcher names a column, the columns it can show instead, and
  the one it shows now. Every report tile that reads the switcher's
  column runs with the chosen column in its place, in every role the
  request uses it ([`Dashboard::switched_report`]). A tile is left as it
  is when its table lacks the chosen column, or when its request already
  reads the chosen column (the two would collide). Tiles keep their own
  requests unchanged, so choosing the switcher's own column again shows
  them as they were.

[`compute_dashboard`] runs every tile. Changes go through
[`DashboardEdit`]s, each of which returns its inverse when applied, so a
[`DashboardHistory`] can undo and redo them. Dashboards are saved in the
version-3 project file (see [`crate::project`] for the JSON form).

- `const DEFAULT_GRID_COLUMNS`: Grid width of a new dashboard, in columns.
- `const MAX_GRID_COLUMNS`: Widest grid allowed, in columns.
- `const MAX_GRID_ROWS`: Rows a tile may reach down to (its `row + height`): a bound that keeps saved files sane, far beyond any practical dashboard.
- `const DASHBOARD_HISTORY_LIMIT`: Most edits kept for undo by a [`DashboardHistory`].
- `struct DashboardId`: A dashboard's identifier within a project: stable across saves and independent of the dashboard's (editable) name.
- `struct TileId`: A tile's identifier within its dashboard (a positive number, stable across saves and moves).
- `struct GridArea`: The rectangle of grid cells a tile covers: its top-left cell (`column`, `row`, counted from 0) and its span (`width` columns by `height` rows, each at least 1).
- `enum TextStyle`: How a text tile's text is shown.
- `enum TileContent`: What a tile shows.
- `struct DashboardTile`: One tile of a dashboard.
- `struct SharedSwitcher`: A column picker shared by every tile of a dashboard (see the [module documentation](self)): tiles that read `column` run with `current` in its place.
- `struct SwitchedReport`: A tile's request as the dashboard's switchers make it ([`Dashboard::switched_report`]).
- `fn substitute_column`: `report` (a request on `table`) reading column `to` wherever it reads `from`; `None` when it does not read `from`, already reads `to`, or `table` lacks either.
- `struct Dashboard`: A dashboard: tiles on a grid, local filters and shared column pickers (see the [module documentation](self)).
- `struct TableFilter`: The dashboard's filters as they apply to one table.
- `enum DashboardEdit`: One reversible change to a dashboard.
- `struct DashboardHistory`: Undo and redo stacks of [`DashboardEdit`]s for one dashboard (at most [`DASHBOARD_HISTORY_LIMIT`] undo steps; applying a new edit clears redo).
- `struct FilteredTable`: A table's row states as a dashboard's tiles see them.
- `enum TileOutput`: What a tile shows once computed.
- `struct ComputedTile`: One computed tile.
- `struct DashboardResults`: Everything a dashboard shows: each table's filtered row states and each tile's output, in tile order.
- `fn filtered_table`: The filtered row states of `table` for `dashboard`, or `None` when the project has no such table.
- `fn compute_tile`: Run tile `id` of `dashboard` on its table's filtered rows (see [`compute_dashboard`]); `None` when the dashboard has no such tile.
- `fn compute_dashboard`: Run every tile of `dashboard`: each report tile's request, as the switchers make it ([`Dashboard::switched_report`]), through [`run_report`] on its table with the rows outside the dashboard's filters excluded and hidden ([`Dashboard::filter_rows`]); text tiles as stored.

### `crates/app-model/src/data_surface.rs`

Contour and surface plots of data (Visualize ▸ Contour and surface
plot…): a response column over two others, made into a surface through
the scattered observations ([`stat_viz::interpolate`]) by Delaunay
triangulation with linear interpolation, or by a thin-plate spline that
interpolates or smooths (smoothing chosen by generalized
cross-validation; Wahba 1990).

The surface is evaluated on a regular grid once, when the report runs.
The report shows a table describing the fit, a contour plot of the grid
with the observations (brushable), and — drawn by front ends from
[`DataSurfaceAnalysis::mesh`] — a rotatable 3-D surface, filled or as a
wireframe, with the observations as points.

Excluded rows are left out of the surface, as for analyses.

- `enum SurfaceFit`: How the surface is made from the observations.
- `const MAX_GRID`: Most grid divisions along each axis.
- `const MIN_GRID`: Fewest grid divisions along each axis.
- `struct DataSurfaceRequest`: Columns and method of a contour and surface plot.
- `struct DataSurfaceOptions`: How the surface is drawn (saved with the project).
- `fn data_surface_to_json`: The project-file form (`"analysis": "data-surface"`).
- `fn data_surface_from_json`: Read the project-file form.
- `struct DataSurfaceAnalysis`: A surface made from the observations, on its grid.

### `crates/app-model/src/declared_design.rs`

Declaring an existing table as a designed experiment: which columns are
factors (numeric, with their low and high settings, by default the
smallest and largest values in the data; or categorical with two levels,
coded −1 and +1 in sorted order) and which are responses.

The report describes the design the table holds: the factors and their
levels, the runs (distinct settings, replicated settings and the
pure-error degrees of freedom they give, centre runs), how correlated the
coded factor columns are (zero for an orthogonal design), and which
polynomial models the runs can estimate, with each model's D-efficiency
`100 · |XᵀX|^{1/p} / n` in coded units (−1 at the low setting, +1 at the
high; [`stat_doe::d_efficiency`]). The declaration is saved with the
project, so the design's description travels with the data.

A design run with restricted randomization (a split-plot or
split-split-plot experiment) also names its whole-plot column and, for a
split-split-plot design, its subplot column, and may record the model it
was built for. The report then lists the plots and which factors stay
fixed within them, and [`split_plot_analysis`] turns the declaration into
the mixed model that analyses it: the model's fixed effects with random
intercepts for the whole plots (and the subplots within them), fitted by
REML so that whole-plot effects are tested against whole-plot error.

- `struct DeclaredFactor`: A factor column with optional settings coded −1 and +1.
- `struct DesignDeclarationRequest`: A table declared as a design.
- `struct ModelSupport`: A model and what the runs say about it.
- `struct DeclaredDesign`: A computed design declaration.
- `fn split_plot_analysis`: The mixed model that analyses a declared split-plot design: the first response on the factors with the recorded model's terms (main effects when none is recorded or it does not parse), a random intercept for each whole plot and, for a split-split-plot design, for each subplot within its whole plo…

### `crates/app-model/src/degradation.rs`

Degradation analysis bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::degradation`]): life information from measurements
of a characteristic that drifts towards a failure threshold.

**Layouts:**
* *Repeated measures* — unit, time and response columns, several
  measurements per unit. Each unit's path (linear on transformed scales,
  asymptotic or power) is fitted by least squares and solved for its
  *pseudo failure time*, and a life distribution (or, with a stress column
  constant within each unit, a life–stress model) is fitted to those times
  with censoring for units whose path never reaches the threshold; or the
  linear path is fitted as a random-effects model and the implied
  distribution of the threshold-crossing time is computed, with parametric
  bootstrap intervals.
* *Destructive* — time and response columns, one measurement per unit
  (optionally a stress column): a location–scale regression of the
  transformed response on transformed time gives the time-to-threshold
  distribution.

Excluded rows and rows with missing values are left out.

- `const BOOTSTRAP_SEED`: Seed of the parametric bootstrap (fixed, so a report reproduces exactly).
- `enum DegradationLayout`: Where the measurements come from.
- `enum DegradationMethod`: How repeated measures are turned into life information.
- `struct DegradationRequest`: Columns and settings of a degradation analysis.
- `struct DegradationUnit`: One unit of a repeated-measures analysis.
- `struct DegradationAnalysis`: A computed degradation analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/design_augment.rs`

Augmenting a design held in a data table: an [`AugmentRequest`] names the
factor columns (with the settings coded −1 and +1, as for a declared
design), the response columns and the method, and [`augment_table`]
returns a **new** table with every original row and column, followed by
the added runs (factor settings in actual units, every other column
empty), and a nominal block column (1 for the original runs, 2 for the
added ones). The methods are those of [`stat_doe::augment`]: fold-over,
center runs, axial runs, and D-optimal augmentation for a model over the
factor names, optionally within constraints ([`stat_doe::Region::parse`]).

A numeric continuous factor is coded from its low and high settings
(by default the smallest and largest values among the rows). A
categorical factor (text, or numbers marked nominal or ordinal) must have
exactly two levels, coded −1 and +1 in sorted order; a fold-over swaps
them and the other methods keep it at one of them (center and axial runs
need continuous factors).

- `enum AugmentMethod`: How to add runs.
- `struct AugmentRequest`: A request to augment the design in a table.
- `struct AugmentOutcome`: The augmented table and what was done.
- `fn augment_table`: Augment the design held in `table` as `request` asks.
- `fn whole_plots_request_from_json`: A whole-plot augmentation from script settings (JSON): `factors` (column names, or `#{ column, low, high }`), `whole_plot` (the column naming each run's whole plot), `responses` (optional), `model` (formula over the factor names, or `"main effects"`, `"interactions"` (default), `"quadratic"`), `w…
- `fn added_type_labels`: The role of a new run, by its point type: for tests and callers.

### `crates/app-model/src/design_evaluation.rs`

Evaluating a design held in a table before its responses are collected
([`stat_doe::evaluation`]): the power of the test of each model term for
an anticipated coefficient, the relative prediction variance (profile
along each factor, maximum and average over the region, and the
fraction-of-design-space curve), the alias matrix for terms left out of the
model, the absolute correlations among model and alias terms, and the D,
A, G and I criteria. A comparison column whose two levels split the rows
into two candidate designs puts the same criteria side by side, with the
relative efficiencies of the first design to the second.

The region is the cube of coded settings unless the request gives
constraints (linear limits and disallowed combinations in actual units,
as for optimal designs; [`stat_doe::Region::parse`]): then the maximum and
average prediction variance and the fraction of design space are over
the constrained region ([`stat_doe::evaluate_design_in`]). Optimal designs
created with constraints come with this report already set up
([`crate::doe::design_project`]).

Factors are coded as in [`crate::declared_design`]: numeric factors from
their low and high settings (by default the smallest and largest values
among all rows, so both compared designs share one region), two-level
categorical factors −1 and +1 in sorted order.

- `struct DesignEvaluationRequest`: What to evaluate: the factor columns, the model and the test settings.
- `struct DesignEvaluationAnalysis`: A computed design evaluation.

### `crates/app-model/src/design_simulation.rs`

Simulated responses for the design held in a table: a [`SimulateRequest`]
names the factor columns (coded −1 and +1 as for a declared design), a
model and the prior of [`stat_doe::simulate`], and
[`simulate_design_responses`] returns new response columns, one per
simulation, and a table of the true coefficients that made them.

A numeric continuous factor is coded from its low and high settings (by
default the smallest and largest values among the rows); a categorical
factor must have exactly two levels, coded −1 and +1 in sorted order.
Rows without every factor setting get missing responses.

- `struct SimulateRequest`: What to simulate.
- `struct SimulateOutcome`: The simulated columns and their coefficients.
- `fn simulate_request_from_json`: A simulation request from script settings (JSON): `factors` (column names, or `#{ column, low, high }`), `model` (formula over the factor names, or `"main effects"`, `"interactions"` (default), `"quadratic"`), `count` (1), `seed` (1), `name` (`"Simulated Y"`), and the prior: `main`, `all_parents`…
- `fn simulate_design_responses`: Simulate responses for the design in `table`.

### `crates/app-model/src/discriminant_analysis.rs`

Discriminant analysis bound to a dataset
([`stat_multivariate::discriminant`]): linear or quadratic normal-theory
classification of a categorical response from numeric predictors, with
Fisher's canonical discriminant functions. Uses the shared
predictive-model sections and saved columns ([`crate::prediction`]).

**Rows.** Rows that are excluded, miss the response or miss a predictor
take no role. The model is fitted to the training rows; validation and
test rows (from a validation column or a random hold-out) are only
predicted, so their fit measures estimate the error on new data. With
k-fold cross-validation every row trains and each row is also predicted
by the model fitted without its fold.

**Priors.** Proportional to the training rows of each class, or equal.

**Saved columns.** Each class's posterior probability and the most likely
class (the shared prediction columns, so the model can be compared with
others under Compare models), the validation roles, and the scores on the
canonical functions.

- `enum PriorChoice`: Prior probabilities of the classes.
- `fn rule_label`: Display name of a classification rule.
- `struct DiscriminantRequest`: Columns and settings of a discriminant analysis.
- `struct DiscriminantAnalysis`: A fitted discriminant analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/distance_analysis.rs`

Distances between rows and principal coordinates analysis, bound to the
row state ([`stat_multivariate::distance`], [`stat_multivariate::pcoa`]).

**Distances** are measured between the included rows from chosen
columns with a metric: Euclidean and Manhattan (numeric columns,
optionally standardized to unit variance), Gower's coefficient for mixed
types (continuous columns range-scaled, ordinal columns by their level
ranks in natural order, nominal columns as match/mismatch; missing values
allowed pair by pair), Jaccard on presence/absence (nonzero = present),
Bray–Curtis on non-negative abundances, and Hamming and simple matching
on the values or levels. Rows with a missing value are left out except
for Gower's coefficient. The distances feed

* the **Distance matrix** table operation (Data ▸ Reshape), which makes a
  new table with one row and one column per object, the layout the
  dimension-reduction and principal-coordinates reports read as a
  "distance matrix";
* **principal coordinates analysis** (PCoA; Gower 1966): the eigenvalues
  of Gower's centred matrix with each one's share and the broken-stick
  expectation, an ordination plot of the first two axes (points keep
  their dataset rows for brushing), correlations of numeric columns with
  the axes, and saved coordinates; negative eigenvalues of non-Euclidean
  distances are reported and can be removed by the Lingoes or Cailliez
  correction (Legendre & Legendre 2012, §9.3.4);
* hierarchical clustering with any metric or a distance matrix
  ([`crate::ClusterAnalysis`]).

- `const DISTANCE_LIMIT`: Largest number of objects (the full matrix is kept).
- `struct DistanceSpec`: Columns and metric of a distance computation.
- `struct Measured`: Distances between the objects (rows) used.
- `fn measure`: Measure the distances of `spec` between the included rows.
- `fn matrix_from_columns`: Read a distance matrix stored as `columns` (row `i` and column `i` are the same object; the table has one row per column).
- `fn distance_table`: The new table of a distance matrix: an object label column (the values of `label`, or the row numbers) and one distance column per object, named by the labels.
- `enum PcoaInput`: Where a principal coordinates analysis gets its distances.
- `struct PcoaRequest`: Settings of a principal coordinates analysis.
- `struct PcoaAnalysis`: A computed principal coordinates analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/distribution.rs`

The distribution of one column: summary statistics and plots.

A column is analysed as **continuous** if it is numeric with the continuous
measurement level, and as **categorical** otherwise (text columns, or numeric
columns marked nominal/ordinal). Excluded rows and missing values are left
out; plots keep each bar's / point's dataset rows so brushing links them to
the data grid.

For continuous data the report can add a **normal fit**: the maximum
likelihood mean and the usual sample standard deviation with confidence
intervals (`x̄ ± t s/√n`; `s √((n−1)/χ²)` for σ), the fitted density drawn over
the histogram (scaled to counts: `n · bin width · φ`), Shapiro–Wilk and
Anderson–Darling tests ([`stat_core::normality`]), and a normal quantile
plot with the line `x̄ + s·z`.

Histogram bins: Sturges' rule `k = ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1` bins (Sturges 1926,
*JASA* 21), with the width rounded up to a "nice" value (1, 2, 2.5 or 5 × 10ᵐ)
and the edges aligned to multiples of the width.

- `const TRIM`: Proportion trimmed from each tail for the trimmed and winsorized means.
- `struct DistributionRequest`: Which column, and how to compute quantiles.
- `struct DistributionOptions`: User-toggleable parts of a distribution report.
- `struct DistributionAnalysis`: The computed distribution of one column.
- `fn histogram_bars`: Sturges-rule histogram with a "nice" bin width; each bar lists its rows.

### `crates/app-model/src/distribution_calculator.rs`

Distribution calculator and random data: probabilities, quantiles,
density and moments for any distribution in [`stat_core::catalog`], a
plot of the density (or probability mass) with the region of interest
marked, and seeded random columns.

The region is one of `X ≤ a`, `X ≥ a`, `a ≤ X ≤ b` or `X < a or X > b`.
For discrete families the bounds are inclusive at whole numbers, so
`P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(⌈a⌉ − 1)`. The report also inverts the
distribution at a chosen probability `p`, giving the lower and upper
quantiles `F⁻¹(p)` and `F⁻¹(1 − p)`.

- `enum ProbabilityRegion`: The region whose probability is computed.
- `struct CalculatorRequest`: Settings of a distribution-calculator report.
- `struct CalculatorReport`: A computed distribution-calculator report.
- `fn random_column`: A column of `n` seeded random draws from `family` with `params`: the same seed always gives the same values.

### `crates/app-model/src/distribution_fit_analysis.rs`

Distribution identification: maximum-likelihood fits of many continuous
distributions to one column ([`stat_core::distribution_fit`]), bound to the
dataset's row state.

The report ranks the fitted families by AIC with each one's
Anderson–Darling statistic and p-value (and, for a family with a
threshold, the likelihood-ratio test of that threshold), lists the
parameter estimates, draws the best fit over a histogram, and gives a
quantile–quantile plot (Wilk & Gnanadesikan 1968) for each of the
best-fitting families: the ordered values against the fitted
distribution's quantiles at the median-rank plotting positions
`(i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4)` (Benard & Bos-Levenbach 1953), so a good fit lies
along the line `y = x`. Optionally the Johnson and Box–Cox
transformations to normality are listed alongside, with the normality
test of the transformed values.

- `struct DistributionFitRequest`: What to fit.
- `struct DistributionFitAnalysis`: A completed identification.

### `crates/app-model/src/distribution_tests.rs`

Optional sections of a distribution report that test or bound the values
of one continuous column: tolerance intervals
([`stat_inference::tolerance`]), outlier tests
([`stat_inference::outliers`]) and runs tests for randomness in row order
([`stat_inference::runs`]).

Each is switched on from the report's options menu with its own settings;
the settings are saved with the report.

- `struct ToleranceSettings`: Settings of a tolerance interval: an interval that contains at least `proportion` of the population with the stated `confidence`.
- `enum OutlierMethod`: Which outlier test.
- `struct OutlierSettings`: Settings of an outlier test.
- `struct RunsSettings`: Settings of the runs tests for randomness.
- `fn side_label`: Name of an outlier side.

### `crates/app-model/src/doe.rs`

Creating designed experiments from the application: a [`DesignRequest`]
names the design type, the factors and the export options, and
[`create_design`] builds it with [`stat_doe`] and turns it into a data table
ready to receive results. Mixture experiments, whose components are
proportions of a blend rather than factors with low and high settings,
have their own [`MixtureDesignRequest`] and [`create_mixture_design`].

A split-plot design ([`DesignKind::SplitPlot`]) for hard-to-change
factors gets `Whole Plot` (and `Subplot`) columns; [`design_project`]
opens it with the design declared (whole-plot columns and model recorded)
and a project script that fits the mixed model analysing it.

- `enum DesignKind`: The kind of design to create.
- `struct DesignRequest`: Everything needed to create a design table.
- `fn build_design`: Build the design described by `request`.
- `fn build_split_plot`: Build the split-plot design described by `request`, with the request's factor names and settings.
- `fn create_design`: Build the design and export it as a data table named after the design.
- `fn split_plot_request_from_json`: A split-plot design request from script settings (JSON): `factors` (`[#{ name, low, high, changes }]` with `changes` `"easy"`, `"hard"` or `"very-hard"`; low and high default to −1 and +1), `model` (formula over the factor names, or `"main effects"`, `"interactions"` (default), `"quadratic"`), `r…
- `fn definitive_screening_request_from_json`: A definitive screening design request from script settings (JSON): `factors` (a count, or `[#{ name, low, high }]`), `extra_runs` (0), `center_runs` (1), and the output settings `randomize`, `units`, `response`.
- `fn categorical_screening_request_from_json`: A screening design with categorical factors from script settings (JSON): `factors` (`[#{ name, low, high }]` for continuous factors and `#{ name, levels }` for categorical ones), `runs` (default [`stat_doe::categorical_screening::default_runs`]), `model` (`"main effects"` (default) or `"interacti…
- `fn dsd_comparison_table`: Definitive screening designs for `k` factors compared across extra runs and center runs ([`stat_doe::dsd_comparison_choices`] around `chosen`), as a table with one row per choice.
- `const SPLIT_PLOT_SCRIPT`: Name of the project script that fits a split-plot design's mixed model.
- `fn design_project`: Create the design as a new document: its table and, for a split-plot design, the design declared with its whole-plot (and subplot) columns and model, and a project script ([`SPLIT_PLOT_SCRIPT`]) that fits the mixed model once the responses are entered.
- `enum MixtureKind`: The kind of mixture design.
- `struct MixtureDesignRequest`: Everything needed to create a mixture design table.
- `const MAX_MIXTURE_REPLICATES`: Most replicates of a mixture design.
- `fn build_mixture_design`: Build the mixture design described by `request` (blends in proportions, replicated, in standard order).
- `struct ModelSupport`: Whether a Scheffé model can be fitted to a design's blends, with the degrees of freedom left for error.
- `fn mixture_model_support`: Which Scheffé models `design` supports (linear, quadratic, special cubic).
- `fn create_mixture_design`: Build the mixture design and export it as a data table: a run number, the standard order (when randomized), one column per component scaled to the requested total, a nominal "Blend type" column and the empty response.

### `crates/app-model/src/dose_response_analysis.rs`

Dose–response (probit) analysis bound to the row state
([`stat_discrete::dose_response`]): the proportion responding against a
(log) dose, with effective doses such as the ED50 and their fiducial
limits.

Each row is a group of subjects (a count responding out of a number of
trials) or, without a trials column, one subject with a 0/1 response.
Excluded rows and rows missing a value are left out; rows with a zero or
negative dose on a log scale (untreated controls) are counted and left out.

- `struct DoseResponseRequest`: What to analyse.
- `struct DoseResponseAnalysis`: A computed dose–response analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/editing.rs`

Data editing with undo and redo.

Every change to a dataset's values or structure is an [`Edit`]. Applying an
edit returns its inverse — the edit that puts things back — so the
[`EditHistory`] keeps a stack of inverses: undoing applies the top inverse
and pushes *its* inverse onto the redo stack, and vice versa.

Row edits keep the [`RowStateManager`] aligned with the table: removed rows
take their selection, exclusion, hiding and color with them, and restoring
them brings those back.

Inserting or removing a column moves the columns after it. Analyses refer to
columns by position, so an applied edit reports the move as a
[`ColumnShift`], and [`ColumnShift::map`] translates an old position to the
new one (a [`Edit::Batch`] reports one shift per column it inserts or
removes, in order). Callers should not remove a column an analysis still
uses ([`Edit::removed_columns`] tells which columns an edit would remove).

- `const HISTORY_LIMIT`: Most edits kept for undo.
- `const HISTORY_BYTES`: Most memory, in bytes, the undo history of one table may hold (roughly: see [`Edit::approx_bytes`]).
- `enum Edit`: One reversible change to a dataset.
- `enum ColumnShift`: How column positions moved as a result of an edit.
- `struct Applied`: The result of applying an edit.
- `struct EditHistory`: Undo and redo stacks for one dataset, bounded by [`HISTORY_LIMIT`] edits and [`HISTORY_BYTES`] of memory.

### `crates/app-model/src/effect_size_sections.rs`

Report sections shared by several reports: ANOVA effect sizes with
noncentral-F intervals, measures of association with noncentral-χ²
intervals ([`stat_inference::effect_sizes`]), and the linear-trend
contrast across ordered groups ([`stat_inference::multiple::linear_trend`]).

- `fn anova_effect_size_section`: One row per effect: η², partial η², partial ω², Cohen's f, and intervals for the population partial η² and f.
- `fn association_section`: φ and Cramér's V with intervals.
- `fn linear_trend_section`: The linear-trend contrast across `groups` in the order of `labels`.

### `crates/app-model/src/embedding_analysis.rs`

Dimension reduction of rows into a low-dimensional map, bound to the row
state: classical and metric (SMACOF) multidimensional scaling, t-SNE and
UMAP ([`stat_multivariate::mds`], [`stat_multivariate::tsne`],
[`stat_multivariate::umap`]).

The objects are the dataset rows. Their dissimilarities are either the
Euclidean distances between their values in the chosen numeric columns
(optionally standardized), or a distance matrix stored as columns: with
`n` chosen columns the table has `n` rows, and row `i` / column `i` are
the same object. Excluded rows (and their matching columns) are left
out. The report shows the fit, the map (points keep their dataset rows
for brushing, optionally coloured and marked by a column) and, for the
scaling methods, a Shepard diagram; the coordinates can be saved as
columns. Every method is seeded and reproducible.

- `const SCALING_LIMIT`: Largest number of objects for metric scaling (it keeps the full distance matrix).
- `enum EmbeddingMethod`: Which embedding.
- `struct EmbeddingRequest`: Method, input and settings of an embedding.
- `struct EmbeddingAnalysis`: A computed embedding.

### `crates/app-model/src/external/html.rs`

Tables on web pages: the `<table>` elements of an HTML document read as
rows of text, with `colspan` and `rowspan` cells repeated into every
position they cover (as the HTML table model lays them out).

- `struct PageTable`: One `<table>` of a page as a grid of cell text.
- `enum TableChoice`: Which table of a page to read.
- `fn looks_like_html`: Whether a response looks like an HTML page rather than data.
- `fn page_tables`: Every top-level-or-nested `<table>` of `html`, in document order, and the index of the one `choice` picks (`None` when the page has no table, or a numbered or named table is not there).
- `fn column_names`: Unique, non-empty column names (`Column 3` for a blank one, `Price 2` for a second `Price`).

### `crates/app-model/src/external.rs`

Tables read from outside the application: SQL databases (SQLite built
in; PostgreSQL and MySQL through pure-Rust drivers; ODBC data sources
with the optional `odbc` feature) and data on the web (JSON or delimited
text fetched by HTTP GET).

A table read this way remembers its [`ExternalSource`] — the connection
settings and query, or the URL and headers — so it can be read again
([`refresh_edit`]) and so project files can record where it came from.
**Credentials are never stored**: passwords and the values of headers
marked secret live only in a [`Secrets`] value for the session, and are
asked for again after a project is reopened. The ODBC connection string
is stored with any `PWD=` or `Password=` setting removed, and a web
address with any password in it (`https://user:pass@host`) removed.

Values are read as text and typed exactly as delimited text files are
([`stat_data::table_from_records_with_notes`]): a column of numbers is
numeric, one of dates or times is a date-time column, anything else is
text; SQL `NULL` and JSON `null` are missing values.

Web data: a JSON document is turned into rows from an array of objects —
the document itself, the array at a dotted path such as `data.items`, or
(with no path) the only member of the top-level object that is such an
array. Nested objects become dotted column names (`address.city`); arrays
inside a row are kept as their JSON text. A web page (HTML) is read from
one of its `<table>` elements ([`html`]): the one named in the request,
else the one the address's `#section` points to, else the largest. Other
responses are read as delimited text with the delimiter detected.

- `const TIMEOUT_SECONDS`: Seconds allowed for connecting to a server or fetching a URL.
- `enum DatabaseKind`: Which kind of database.
- `enum TlsMode`: Whether to encrypt the connection to a database server.
- `struct DatabaseConnection`: How to reach a database.
- `fn strip_odbc_password`: An ODBC connection string without its `PWD=` / `Password=` settings.
- `fn is_secret_header`: Whether a header's value is a credential that must not be saved (`Authorization`, `Cookie`, and names mentioning a key, token, secret or password).
- `enum WebFormat`: How a web response is read.
- `struct WebHeader`: An HTTP header sent with a web request.
- `struct WebRequest`: A web request: HTTP GET of a URL.
- `fn strip_url_password`: A URL with any password in its user information removed (`https://ann:pw@host/x` → `https://ann@host/x`).
- `fn url_secret_parameters`: The `name=value` parameters of a URL's query whose names mark a credential ([`is_secret_header`]: `api_key`, `token`, `access_token`, `password`, `secret`, `auth`…), with their values (empty when blanked).
- `fn strip_url_secrets`: A URL without credentials: no password in its user information ([`strip_url_password`]) and the secret query parameters ([`url_secret_parameters`]) kept by name with their values blanked (`?city=Oslo&api_key=abc` → `?city=Oslo&api_key=`), so they can be asked for again.
- `fn fill_url_secrets`: `url` with blank secret query parameters filled in from `values` (`(name, value)` pairs).
- `enum ExternalSource`: Where a table came from.
- `struct Secrets`: Credentials for one source, kept for the session only.
- `fn list_tables`: The tables (and views) in a database, as names [`DatabaseKind::select_all`] accepts (`schema.table` outside the default schema).
- `fn run_query`: Run `query` and return its rows as a table named `name`.
- `fn json_document_table`: Rows of a JSON document as a table: see the [module documentation](self).
- `fn response_table`: The response to `request` (`text`, with its content type) as a table: JSON, a table on a web page, or delimited text, as [`WebRequest::format`] says; [`WebFormat::Auto`] decides from the content type and the text.
- `enum WebRead`: A response read for the Open Data dialog.
- `fn response_read`: The response to `request` as cells (a web-page table or delimited text), or as a table when it is JSON; see [`response_table`].
- `fn fetch`: Fetch a web request and read the response as a table.
- `fn fetch_cells`: Fetch a web request and read the response for the Open Data dialog (see [`response_read`]).
- `fn refresh_edit`: The edit that replaces `table`'s rows with `fresh`'s, as one undoable step: every row is replaced (row states are reset), columns with the same name are refilled in place (keeping their measurement level when their type is unchanged), new columns are added at the end, and columns the source no lo…

### `crates/app-model/src/factor_analysis.rs`

Exploratory factor analysis bound to a dataset
([`stat_multivariate::factor`]).

The rows complete in every chosen column and not excluded give the
correlation (or covariance) matrix. The number of factors is the request's,
or by default the number of eigenvalues of the correlation matrix above 1
(Kaiser's guideline; above the mean eigenvalue for a covariance matrix),
reduced if maximum likelihood would have negative degrees of freedom.

The report shows the eigenvalues and scree plot, the test of fit
(maximum likelihood), unrotated and rotated loadings (pattern and
structure, and the factor correlations, for an oblique rotation),
communalities and uniquenesses, the variance each factor accounts for and
a plot of the variables' loadings on factors 1 and 2. Factor scores
(regression or Bartlett) can be saved as columns.

- `fn extraction_label`: Display name of an extraction method.
- `fn rotation_label`: Display name of a rotation.
- `fn score_label`: Display name of a factor-score method.
- `struct FactorRequest`: Columns and settings of a factor analysis.
- `struct FactorAnalysisReport`: A computed factor analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/factorial_analysis.rs`

Analysis of a two-level factorial experiment held in a table
([`stat_doe::factorial_analysis`]): effects in coded units with `t`
tests or Lenth's method, normal and half-normal plots of the effects,
main-effect, interaction and cube plots of the data means or the fitted
model, and dispersion effects.

Factors are coded as in [`crate::declared_design`]: a numeric factor's
low and high settings (by default the data's smallest and largest values)
become −1 and +1, and a two-level categorical factor is coded −1 and +1 in
sorted order. The model is fitted at the coded settings actually run, so a
run that missed its target keeps the effects unbiased (the report says so).

A continuous response is fitted by least squares. A binary response (0/1,
or any two-level column) is fitted by logistic regression and a count by
Poisson regression ([`stat_discrete::fit_glm`]); their effects are on the
link scale (log odds, log mean) with Wald `z` tests. A saturated Poisson
model is fitted exactly, and its effects are also judged by Lenth's
method.

- `enum FactorialTerms`: Which terms the model has.
- `enum FactorialResponse`: The kind of response.
- `enum MeansSource`: Whether plots show data means or model predictions.
- `struct FactorialAnalysisRequest`: A factorial analysis.
- `struct FactorialAnalysis`: A computed factorial analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/factorial_repeated.rs`

Factorial repeated-measures ANOVA bound to a dataset
([`stat_inference::repeated::factorial_repeated_measures`]): one to three
within-subject factors, up to three between-subject factors (four factors
in all), univariate tests with Greenhouse–Geisser and Huynh–Feldt
corrections per within-subject effect, Mauchly's tests, cell means, simple
effects of one factor at each level of another, and a profile plot.

The data are stacked (long): one row per measurement, with a response
column, a subject column and one column per factor. A subject's
between-subject levels must be the same on every row; several rows in one
within-subject cell are averaged (and counted in the report); subjects
missing a cell are left out. Wide data (one column per condition) can be
stacked with Data ▸ Reshape ▸ Stack columns first.

Simple effects use a separate analysis at each level of the second factor
(the data of that level only, so each test has its own error term and
sphericity correction), as Maxwell & Delaney (2nd ed., ch. 12) recommend
for within-subject factors.

- `const MAX_FACTORS`: Most factors in one analysis.
- `struct FactorialRepeatedRequest`: Settings of a factorial repeated-measures report.
- `struct FactorialRepeatedReport`: A computed factorial repeated-measures report.

### `crates/app-model/src/fatigue_analysis.rs`

Fatigue (stress–life, S–N) curves bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::fatigue`]): cycles to failure against stress
amplitude with run-outs as right-censored observations, a Basquin,
semi-log, quadratic log–log or endurance-limit curve with lognormal,
Weibull or log-logistic scatter fitted by maximum likelihood (ASTM
E739-10; Meeker & Escobar 1998, ch. 17; Pascual & Meeker 1999).

The report gives the specimens per stress level, the fit, the curve's
coefficients with Wald and likelihood-ratio limits (and Basquin's
`S = A·N^b` form), the fatigue strength (the stress whose chosen life
quantile equals a given number of cycles), quantiles of life at chosen
stresses, the S–N plot with quantile curves (e.g. the 10% curve, B10)
and a lower confidence bound of the lowest one, standardized residuals
against stress, and a probability plot of the standardized residuals
across all stress levels (Turnbull estimate, so run-outs are handled as
censored) against the model's standard distribution.

**Layout:** a cycles column, a run-out column (nonzero = the specimen did
not fail; optional), a stress column and an optional frequency column.
Excluded rows and incomplete rows are left out.

- `struct FatigueRequest`: Columns and settings of a fatigue-curve analysis.
- `struct FatigueAnalysis`: A computed fatigue-curve analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/fdr.rs`

False-discovery-rate adjustment of many p-values (Benjamini–Hochberg,
Benjamini–Yekutieli or Storey q-values) and the interval ("forest") plot,
shared by the screening, contingency-table and model-comparison reports.

- `const STOREY_LAMBDA`: The `λ` of Storey's estimate of the proportion of true null hypotheses.
- `enum FdrMethod`: A false-discovery-rate adjustment.
- `struct IntervalRow`: One row of an interval plot: label, estimate and interval.
- `fn interval_plot`: An interval ("forest") plot: one horizontal row per item, top to bottom, with a marker at the estimate, a segment over the interval and a vertical reference line at `reference`.

### `crates/app-model/src/file_formats.rs`

Which file formats the application opens and exports, recognised by
extension, and the text-based readers and writers behind them.

| Format | Extensions | Open | Export |
|---|---|---|---|
| Project (data + row states + reports) | `.acraft` | ✓ | ✓ (save) |
| Comma-separated values | `.csv` | ✓ | ✓ |
| Tab-separated values | `.tsv`, `.tab` | ✓ | ✓ |
| Delimited text | `.txt`, `.dat` | ✓ | — |
| JSON array of row objects | `.json` | ✓ | ✓ |
| Spreadsheet workbook | `.xlsx`, `.xlsm`, `.xlsb`, `.xls`, `.ods` | ✓ | `.xlsx` |

The delimiter of every text format except tab-separated values is
detected ([`stat_data::detect_delimiter`]), so a `.csv` written with
semicolons (as spreadsheets do where the decimal mark is a comma) opens
correctly. Spreadsheets are binary formats read by [`crate::files`]; each
cell is rendered as text (date cells as ISO 8601 text, through
[`spreadsheet_date_text`]), so type inference is the same as for text
files. Text and sheets are read as a [`RawSheet`] first, and the table's
block (header row, first data row, columns) is detected or given
([`crate::open_data`]).

Exported data files carry values only. Measurement levels, row states and
reports are kept by project files.

- `enum FileKind`: A kind of file the application can open.
- `const OPEN_EXTENSIONS`: Every extension [`FileKind::from_path`] recognises, for file-picker filters.
- `enum ExportFormat`: A data export format.
- `enum Opened`: What opening a file produced.
- `fn read_text_file`: Read a text-based file of `kind` whose contents are `text`.
- `fn text_sheet`: Delimited `text` of `kind` split into a sheet: at `delimiter` when given, else at a tab for [`FileKind::Tsv`] and at the detected delimiter otherwise.
- `fn read_text_with`: Delimited `text` of `kind` read with `settings` (their delimiter, else as [`text_sheet`] picks).
- `fn spreadsheet_date_text`: ISO 8601 text for a spreadsheet date cell holding `serial` (days, with the time of day as a fraction) in the 1900 or 1904 date system (ECMA-376 Part 1 §18.17.4), so that [`table_from_cells`] reads it as a date:  * a duration cell gives an ISO 8601 duration (`PT1H30M`); * a serial from 0 up to 1 i…
- `fn table_from_cells`: A table from a grid of cell texts, as read from a spreadsheet, with the table's block detected ([`crate::open_data::detect_block`]): title rows above it are skipped, fully empty rows and columns are dropped, blank header cells are named `Column N`, and repeated names get a ` (2)`, ` (3)`, … suffix.
- `fn table_from_cells_with_notes`: [`table_from_cells`], also returning notes on how values were read (see [`stat_data::table_from_records_with_notes`]).
- `fn name_from_path`: A table name from a file path: the file name without its extension.

### `crates/app-model/src/files.rs`

Reading and writing data files, including the binary spreadsheet
formats (`calamine` to read `.xlsx`/`.xlsm`/`.xlsb`/`.xls`/`.ods`,
`rust_xlsxwriter` to write `.xlsx`). Shared by the desktop application
and scripts; recognising formats and the text readers and writers live in
[`crate::file_formats`].

- `enum RawFile`: A data file read as cells, before the Open Data dialog (or detected settings) picks the table from it.
- `fn decode_text`: Decode a text file's bytes: UTF-8 (a byte-order mark is dropped), UTF-16 with a byte-order mark or with the zero bytes of mostly-ASCII UTF-16 text, else Windows-1252 (Latin-1), with a note saying so.
- `fn read_raw`: Read the data file at `path` as cells (a delimited text file or a workbook); `None` for a project or JSON file, which has no choices to make.
- `fn open_path`: Open the file at `path`.
- `fn open_path_with`: Open the data file at `path` with settings given as a map (the script function `open_table(path, options)`): the members of [`OpenSettings::to_json`] (any left out are detected), and for a workbook `sheet` (one sheet by name), or `sheets` (a list of names; all non-empty sheets when left out) with…
- `fn sheet_table_name`: The name of the table read from sheet `sheet` of the workbook `file` when the workbook has several sheets.
- `fn read_sheets`: Every sheet of the workbook at `path` as cells, empty sheets included.
- `fn read_workbook`: Every non-empty sheet of the workbook at `path` as a table, named `name` (or `name – sheet` when there are several sheets), each read with detected settings.
- `fn read_sheet`: The sheet named `sheet` of the workbook at `path` as a table named `name – sheet`, with notes on cells that did not fit their column's type.
- `fn with_value_labels`: `table` with each column that has value labels turned into a text column of the labels (values without a label kept as they are), for an export that writes labels; `None` when no column has labels.
- `fn export_table`: Write `table` to `path` in `format`.

### `crates/app-model/src/forecasting.rs`

Shared parts of the Time Series menu's forecasting reports (exponential
smoothing and seasonal ARIMA): the sections every forecasting model
shows — the forecast plot and table, residual plot, residual
autocorrelation with white-noise limits, the Ljung–Box test with the
fitted parameters taken off its degrees of freedom, and in-sample
accuracy — plus the table "Save forecasts" adds to the project. The series
itself (rows, time stamps, seasonal period, forecast time stamps) comes
from [`crate::time_series_data`].

- `fn read_series`: Read the series of `input` ([`Series::extract`]), which a model needs at least 3 values of.
- `fn period_note`: How the seasonal period of `series` was chosen, for the model summary.
- `struct ForecastPath`: Forecasts `1..=h` steps ahead with prediction intervals, whatever the model.
- `fn level_label`: Percent label of a level, such as "95%".
- `struct ForecastSettings`: Settings common to every forecasting report.
- `struct InSampleAccuracy`: In-sample accuracy of one-step fitted values.
- `fn accuracy`: Accuracy of `fitted` one-step values against `actual`: `RMSE = √(Σd²/n)`, `MAE = Σ|d|/n`, `MAPE = 100 Σ|d/y|/n` with `d = y − ŷ`, over the observations with a fitted value (a differenced model has none for its first `d + mD`).
- `fn forecast_plot`: The forecast plot: observations (tied to rows), one-step fitted values continued by the forecasts, forecast markers, the widest interval as a band and narrower ones as thin lines, and a rule at the forecast origin.
- `fn forecast_table`: The forecast table: one row per step ahead.
- `fn residual_plot`: Residuals over time, tied to rows, with a zero line.
- `fn ljung_box_lag`: Lags pooled by the Ljung–Box test: `2m` (at most `n/5`) for a seasonal series, otherwise 10 (at most `n/5`), and always more than the fitted parameters (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: Principles and Practice*, 3rd ed., §5.4).
- `fn residual_diagnostics`: Residual autocorrelation plot (spikes with markers, ±z/√n white-noise limits) and the Ljung–Box test with `fitted_parameters` taken off its degrees of freedom.
- `fn accuracy_table`: In-sample accuracy table.
- `fn forecast_data_table`: The table "Save forecasts" adds to the project: the time, the observed value and one-step fitted value for each observation, then one row per forecast with its limits at each level.
- `fn saved_forecast_table`: The forecast table of a forecasting report (exponential smoothing or ARIMA), computed again from its request: what "Save forecasts as data table" adds to the project.

### `crates/app-model/src/forest_analysis.rs`

Random forests bound to a dataset ([`stat_predictive::forest`]): many
decision trees grown on bootstrap samples of the training rows, each
split chosen from a random subset of the predictors, their predictions
averaged. Uses the shared predictive-model sections ([`crate::prediction`]).

**Rows.** As for decision trees: excluded rows and rows missing the
response are left out; missing predictor values are routed by surrogate
splits. Training rows grow the forest; validation and test rows only
measure it (a forest has no size to tune). Out-of-bag predictions give an
honest error estimate from the training rows themselves, shown as its own
row of the fit table; with k-fold validation the table shows the
cross-validated predictions instead (one forest per fold).

**Importance.** Permutation importance (increase in out-of-bag error when
a predictor is shuffled) with its standard error, and the mean impurity
reduction per tree.

- `struct ForestRequest`: Columns and settings of a random forest.
- `struct ForestAnalysis`: A fitted random forest.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/format.rs`

Number formatting for report tables.

- `fn format_number`: Format `v` with about `sig` significant digits, switching to scientific notation for very large or very small magnitudes.
- `fn format_p_value`: Format a p-value: four decimals down to 0.0001, then two significant digits in scientific notation (so very small p-values remain informative).
- `fn format_optional`: Format an optional value, using "—" for `None`.

### `crates/app-model/src/formula.rs`

Formula columns: a column whose values are computed, row by row, from a
Rhai expression over the other columns.

#### Writing formulas

A formula is a Rhai expression (or a few statements, the last giving the
value) evaluated once per row. Inside it:

* A column whose name is a plain identifier (letters, digits and `_`, not
  starting with a digit) is a variable holding the current row's value:
  `Weight / Height ** 2`. Any column, whatever its name, can be read with
  `col("Body mass")`.
* Numbers are decimal (`/` always divides exactly, so `1 / 2` is `0.5`),
  dates and times are numbers of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 UTC, and a
  missing number is `NaN` (a missing text value is `""`).
* The result may be a number, `true`/`false` (stored as 1 / 0), text, or
  `()` / `NaN` for a missing value. A row whose evaluation fails is missing.

The function library ([`FUNCTIONS`]) covers missing values, mathematics,
probability distributions, text and regular expressions, dates, other rows
(`row()`, `lag`, `lead`), column summaries optionally by group (`col_mean`,
`col_sd`, `col_quantile`, …), cumulative sums, ranks and seeded random
numbers.

#### Recalculation

[`refresh`] recomputes the formula columns affected by a change, in
dependency order. Every [`crate::editing::Edit`] calls it, so formula
columns follow edits, undo and redo. A formula's references are found by
scanning its text ([`references`]): identifier columns, and quoted names
given to the column functions. Renaming a column rewrites the formulas that
use it ([`renamed`]); formulas may not form a cycle ([`check`]).

Cell edits, pastes, new rows, deletions and sorts report the rows they
touched ([`Changed::Partial`]). A row-wise formula ([`is_row_wise`])
recomputes only those rows; one that reads other rows recomputes them all.
While some rows are recomputed, the evaluation watches for reads beyond
the current row and falls back to every row if one happens.

- `struct FormulaError`: A formula that cannot be used, with where in its text the problem is.
- `enum FormulaValue`: One computed value.
- `struct Evaluation`: The values a formula gives on some rows.
- `const COLUMN_FUNCTIONS`: Functions whose quoted arguments name columns.
- `fn is_identifier`: `true` if `name` can be written bare in a formula.
- `fn column_reference`: How to write a reference to column `name` in a formula: bare when it is an identifier, else `col("…")`.
- `fn references`: The columns of `table` that `formula` uses, as indices (ascending).
- `fn renamed`: `formula` with references to column `old` changed to `new`.
- `fn check`: Check `formula` for column `target` of `table` (or a new column, `None`): it compiles, names only existing columns, and does not make the formulas form a cycle.
- `fn evaluate`: Evaluate `formula` on `rows` of `table` (for previews), as for column `target` (`None` for a new column).
- `fn fill`: Store `eval` in a column like `column`: numeric results keep a numeric or date-time column's type (and become text in a text column); any text result makes the column text.
- `enum Changed`: What an edit changed, for deciding which formulas to recompute.
- `struct RowChanges`: The rows an edit touched, as positions in the table after it.
- `fn is_row_wise`: Whether `formula` is row-wise: each row's value depends only on that row's values, so a change to some rows (or rows added, removed or reordered) needs only those rows recomputed.
- `fn refresh`: Recompute the formula columns affected by `changed`, in dependency order.
- `fn refresh_noting`: [`refresh`], returning one note per formula column that could not be computed (a formula on a cycle, or one that no longer compiles), naming the column and why; those columns keep their values.
- `fn refresh_all`: Recompute every formula column.
- `fn refresh_all_noting`: [`refresh_all`], returning the notes of [`refresh_noting`].
- `fn users`: The formula columns that use column `index`, by name.
- `struct ParameterFormula`: A model formula with named parameters, such as `Vmax * Conc / (Km + Conc)` with parameters `Vmax` and `Km`: compiled once for a table and evaluated on chosen rows for any parameter values (see [`crate::nonlinear_analysis`]).
- `fn compile_with_parameters`: Compile model formula `formula` with parameters `parameters` for `table`.
- `struct FunctionInfo`: One library function as the formula editor lists it.
- `const FUNCTIONS`: Every library function, by category.

### `crates/app-model/src/formula_typeset.rs`

The typeset view of a formula: a column formula written in Rhai, drawn
as mathematics (fractions stacked over a rule, powers raised, square
roots under a radical sign, sums as Σ, a row's neighbours as subscripts).

[`typeset`] reads one expression with the operator precedence of the
formula language (Rhai: `||` below `&&` below `==` `!=` below `<` `<=`
