- `enum NonlinearModel`: The model of a nonlinear regression.
- `struct ParameterSetting`: Name, starting value, bounds and sharing of one parameter.
- `enum Weighting`: Observation weights.
- `enum FitMethod`: How the parameters are estimated.
- `struct NonlinearRequest`: What to fit.
- `struct NonlinearAnalysis`: A computed nonlinear regression.

### `crates/app-model/src/notebook.rs`

Script notebooks: a document of text cells and Rhai code cells with the
outputs of their last run (printed lines, errors, the cell's value shown
as text or as tables, and the reports it added), kept in a project.

The cells are run by `stat_script::NotebookSession`, which keeps the
variables and functions of earlier cells for later ones, as a single
script would. Running is the application's business; this module is the
document and its saved form.

#### Saved form
A project's `"notebooks"` member (optional; see [`crate::project`]):

```text
"notebooks": [
  { "name": "…",
    "cells": [
      { "kind": "text", "source": "…" },
      { "kind": "code", "source": "…", "run": 3,          (run: optional)
        "outputs": [                                      (optional)
          { "kind": "printed", "text": "…" },
          { "kind": "error", "text": "…", "line": 4 },    (line: optional)
          { "kind": "value", "text": "…" },
          { "kind": "table", "title": "…", "columns": ["…"], "rows": [["…"], …] },
          { "kind": "report", "table": "…", "title": "…" },
          { "kind": "note", "text": "…" } ] },
      … ] },
  … ]
```

- `enum CellKind`: What a cell holds.
- `enum CellOutput`: One output of a code cell's last run.
- `struct NotebookCell`: One cell.
- `struct Notebook`: A notebook: named cells.
- `fn read_notebooks`: The `"notebooks"` member of a project document (empty when absent).
- `fn notebooks_json`: The JSON form of a project's notebooks.

### `crates/app-model/src/open_data.rs`

Choosing which block of a sheet becomes a table, for the Open Data dialog,
file opening, web tables, pasted text and the script `open_table` options.

A file is first read as a [`RawSheet`]: every cell as text, rows and
columns numbered from 1 as in the dialog's preview, nothing taken as a
header yet. A [`Block`] then says where the table sits:

* **Header row** — the row holding the column names, or none (the columns
  are then called `Column 1`, `Column 2`, …).
* **Header rows** — how many rows, from the header row down, hold names.
  Their texts are joined with a space (`Temperature` over `Min` gives
  `Temperature Min`). A blank cell in an upper header row takes the text to
  its left, as a merged heading cell spans the columns under it.
* **Data starts on row** / **Data ends on row** — the rows read as values;
  blank rows among them are skipped.
* **First column** / **Last column** — the columns read; columns blank in
  every header and data row are dropped.

[`detect_block`] proposes a block: the largest run of consecutive non-blank
rows (runs above or below it of similar width join it; a narrow run such
as a title or a footnote does not), started at its first row that is at
least half as wide as the table. That row is the header unless it holds
numbers and no column has text in it above numbers below. The dialog shows
this as a starting point only.

[`ValueOptions`] add a decimal comma (`1,5` read as 1.5, and `1.234,5` as
1234.5, for a column whose every value reads that way) and extra missing
markers. Names are then made unique and non-blank
([`stat_data::unique_names`]) and the values typed exactly as delimited
text is ([`stat_data::table_from_records_with_notes`]).

- `struct RawSheet`: A sheet of cells as text, before any row is taken as the header: one workbook sheet, a text file split at its delimiter, a web-page table or pasted text.
- `enum CellRole`: What a cell of the preview is, under a [`Block`].
- `struct Block`: Where the table sits in a [`RawSheet`].
- `struct ValueOptions`: How values are read, beyond the standard rules.
- `struct OpenSettings`: Everything needed to read a table from a sheet: the block, the value options and, for text, the delimiter.
- `fn split_text`: Split `text` into a sheet at `delimiter` (detected when `None`; see [`stat_data::detect_delimiter`]), returning the delimiter used.
- `fn detect_decimal_comma`: Whether the sheet's numbers look written with a decimal comma: some cells read as such (`1,5`, `-0,25`) and none has a decimal point.
- `fn detect_block`: Propose where the table sits in `sheet` (see the module documentation).
- `fn detect_settings`: The settings [`detect_block`] and [`detect_decimal_comma`] propose for a sheet split at `delimiter` (`None` for a sheet that is not text).
- `type BlockText`: What [`read_block`] returns: the column names, the rows of values (as text) and notes on how they were read.
- `fn read_block`: The column names and rows of values the settings pick from `sheet` (names not yet made unique), with notes.
- `fn table_from_sheet`: The table `settings` pick from `sheet`, named `name`, with notes on how it was read.
- `fn stack_sheets`: One table from several sheets read with their own settings, stacked: a first column named `sheet_column` holds each row's sheet name, then every column any sheet has, matched by name, in the order first met (blank where a sheet lacks one).
- `fn use_row_as_names_edit`: The edit behind Data ▸ Use row as column names: the cells of `row` (0-based) become the column names (blank or repeated ones made unique as on import), the row is removed, and text columns whose remaining values are all numbers or dates are typed again, as one undoable step.

### `crates/app-model/src/outlier_analysis.rs`

Multivariate outlier distances of each row, bound to the row state
([`stat_multivariate::outliers`]).

The rows complete in every chosen column and not excluded give the mean
and covariance; each of them gets its Mahalanobis distance, jackknifed
distance and Hotelling T². The report plots the chosen distance by row
number against its reference limit (rows above it drawn as a distinct
shape and listed), and every point keeps its dataset row for brushing.
All three distances can be saved as columns.

- `enum OutlierDistance`: Which distance the report plots.
- `struct OutlierRequest`: Columns, plotted distance and α.
- `struct OutlierAnalysis`: Computed outlier distances.

### `crates/app-model/src/pareto_chart.rs`

Pareto chart of defect categories (Juran), bound to the row state
([`stat_quality::pareto`]).

Each row names a category; bars count rows, or add up a frequency column,
ranked largest first with a cumulative-percentage line. Categories below
a threshold share can be pooled into an "Other" bar, placed last. A
grouping column draws one Pareto chart per level side by side, each
ranked on its own (Juran's stratified Pareto). Every bar carries its
dataset rows, so clicking a bar selects them in every linked view.

- `struct ParetoRequest`: What to chart.
- `struct ParetoChartOptions`: Display options of a Pareto chart.
- `struct ParetoBar`: One bar of a [`ParetoChartSpec`].
- `struct ParetoPanel`: One panel (a level of the grouping column, or the whole data).
- `struct ParetoChartSpec`: Data for drawing a Pareto chart: bars at x = 1, 2, … within each panel, panels side by side with a gap of one bar.
- `const PARETO_BAR_WIDTH`: Width of a bar (bars sit one unit apart).
- `struct ParetoAnalysis`: A computed Pareto chart.

### `crates/app-model/src/pca_chart.rs`

A multivariate control chart from a principal-components model, bound to
the row state ([`stat_quality::pca_chart`]): T² on the retained component
scores and the squared prediction error (SPE) of what the model leaves
out, with variable contributions to every signal, a parallel-coordinates
view of the signalling rows, and a change-point estimate.

Rows are taken in table order, skipping excluded rows and rows missing a
value in any measurement column. The first `reference` rows (all when
`None`) fit the model; later rows are monitored against it. Every plotted
point is one dataset row, so brushing the charts selects it.

- `const PCA_PLOT_POINTS`: Signals shown in each contribution and parallel-coordinates plot (the largest statistics).
- `struct PcaChartRequest`: What to chart.
- `struct PcaChartAnalysis`: A computed principal-components monitoring chart.

### `crates/app-model/src/permutation_analysis.rs`

Permutation tests on table columns ([`stat_inference::permutation`]): two
independent groups (difference of means or of medians), paired columns
(sign-flip test of the mean difference) and the correlation of two
columns (Pearson or Spearman). Exact enumeration when the arrangements are
few, seeded Monte Carlo otherwise.

- `const MAX_RESAMPLES`: Most random arrangements a report may request.
- `enum PermutationDesign`: What is permuted.
- `struct PermutationRequest`: A permutation test request.
- `struct PermutationAnalysis`: A computed permutation test.

### `crates/app-model/src/pk_analysis.rs`

Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics bound to a dataset
([`stat_inference::nca`]): per subject (and treatment) the peak
concentration and its time, the areas under the concentration and first
moment curves to the last sample and to infinity, the terminal rate
constant with its regression, half-life, mean residence time, and, with
a dose, clearance and volume; then each parameter summarized by
treatment (geometric mean and coefficient of variation, arithmetic mean,
standard deviation, median and range), and the profiles on linear and
semi-logarithmic axes.

**Layout:** long data, one row per sample, with subject, time and
concentration columns, an optional treatment (or period) column whose
levels give separate profiles of the same subject, and an optional dose
column (the first value of each profile is used) or a single dose.
Concentrations below the limit of quantification should be entered as
0. Excluded rows and rows with a missing time or concentration are left
out.

- `enum PkDose`: Where the dose comes from.
- `struct PkRequest`: Columns and settings of a non-compartmental analysis.
- `struct PkAnalysis`: A computed non-compartmental analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/plot_breaks.rs`

Axis breaks on report plots.

Report scatter plots ([`PlotSpec`]) take the same breaks as graph
canvases ([`stat_viz::axis_breaks`]): several stretches left out of an
axis, each piece between them on its own scale and with its own share of
the axis, and slashes or a zigzag where the axis is cut. A plot's axes
are linear in data units, so the breaks are laid out on the linear scale,
with shares over the extent of everything the plot draws on that axis
([`data_extent`]).

An axis takes breaks when it is continuous: not labelled by categories,
a probability scale or dates, and not divided into panes; contour maps
and ternary plots take none ([`breakable`]). The view draws
[`broken_plot`] (every coordinate mapped, points inside a removed
stretch left out) and labels its ticks from the same maps, so box and
click selection, the screen and exported figures agree.

- `fn breakable`: Whether each axis of `spec` (`[x, y]`) can be broken.
- `fn data_extent`: The extent of everything `spec` draws on each axis (`[x, y]`): points, curves, bands, line work and annotations.
- `fn plot_breaks`: The maps of `spec`'s broken axes under `axes` (`[x, y]`; `None` for an axis without breaks or one that cannot take them).
- `fn broken_plot`: `spec` with every coordinate drawn through the broken axes `[x, y]`: points inside a removed stretch are left out (with their group memberships), curve vertices inside one are dropped and annotations in one are not drawn.
- `fn breaks_notes`: The note under a plot with points left out by a break, or whose broken axes mix scales.

### `crates/app-model/src/plot_style.rs`

Plot styles in project files, dashboards, scripts and graph files.

A [`PlotStyle`] (see `stat_viz::plot_style`) is written as one JSON object:

```text
{
  "x": {axis}, "y": {axis}, "y2": {axis},
  "equal_scale": false, "category_labels": "automatic",
  "hover_coordinates": true, "show_key": true,
  "title": "…" | null, "show_title": true,
  "scale_ratio": 1, "print_scale": millimetres | null,
  "export": {…}, "reference_lines": {"lines": [line, …], "bands": [band, …]},
  "annotations": {…}, "key": {…}
}
line = {"orientation": "horizontal" | "vertical", "value": value, "label": "…", "show_value": true,
        "color": "#rrggbb" | "#rrggbbaa" | null, "width": 1.5,
        "pattern": "solid" | "dashed" | "dotted" | "dash-dot", "scope": "whole" | "panel" | "group"}
band = {"orientation": …, "from": value, "to": value, "label": "…", "color": … | null,
        "opacity": 0.18, "edges": true, "edge_labels": true, "scope": …}
value = number | {"stat": "mean" | "median" | "quantile" | "mean-sd" | "individuals-centre"
                           | "individuals-upper" | "individuals-lower", "parameter": p or k}
axis = {"major": "auto" | interval, "minor": "none" | "auto" | {"subdivisions": n} | {"every": interval},
        "origin": 0, "grid": "major" | "major-and-minor" | "none",
        "tick_marks": true, "tick_labels": true,
        "format": "auto" | {"decimals": n} | {"scientific": n} | {"percent": n},
        "title": "…" | null, "show_title": true, "side": "standard" | "opposite",
        "break": [from, to] | null,
        "breaks": {"at": [[from, to], …], "mark": "slashes" | "zigzag",
                   "segments": [{"scale": "log10" | null, "share": percent | null}, …]},
        "tick_direction": "inside" | "outside" | "both",
        "major_mark": {"length": 5, "width": 1}, "minor_mark": {"length": 3, "width": 1},
        "offset": points, "extend_to_ticks": false,
        "custom_ticks": [{"value": v, "label": "\\pi"}, …], "range": [min, max] | null}
```

Every settings member is written, so a style read back is the style
written whatever the plot's own defaults are; members left out of a file
keep the value they have in the style the file is read onto. The four
formatting parts are written only when they differ from their defaults.
Graph canvases keep their titles and breaks in their own `"axes"` member,
so their style is written without them ([`StyleTitles::Without`]).

`"break"` is an axis's first break, kept for files read by earlier
versions; `"breaks"` (written when anything beyond one plain break is set)
holds every break, each piece's scale (`null`: the axis's own) and share
of the axis in percent (`null`: automatic), and the break-mark style, and
wins when both are present.

- `enum StyleTitles`: Whether titles and axis breaks are part of a written style.
- `fn plot_style_to_json`: The JSON form of `style` (see the module documentation).
- `fn plot_style_from_json`: Read [`plot_style_to_json`] onto `style`: members left out keep their value in `style`.
- `fn reference_to_json`: The JSON form of a plot's reference lines and bands.
- `fn reference_from_json`: Read [`reference_to_json`].

### `crates/app-model/src/plot_view.rs`

Plot view limits and the axis-drag gestures that change them.

Each axis behaves like a ruler the user can grab:

* **Near either end** (the outer [`END_HANDLE_FRACTION`] of its length) the
  axis is a *handle* for that limit: dragging moves only that limit while the
  opposite limit stays fixed, and the value that was under the pointer when
  the drag began stays under the pointer — so the axis stretches or
  compresses to follow it.
* **Anywhere else** dragging *shifts* the whole axis: both limits move
  together and the visible span is unchanged, again keeping the grabbed value
  under the pointer.

Positions are measured along the axis in screen units, from the end with the
smaller value: left-to-right for a horizontal axis and bottom-to-top for a
vertical one (callers convert from screen coordinates, whose y grows
downward).

- `const END_HANDLE_FRACTION`: Fraction of an axis's length, at each end, that acts as a limit handle.
- `const MIN_HANDLE_DISTANCE`: Closest the pointer may come to the fixed end while dragging a handle, in screen units; prevents division by (near) zero.
- `struct ViewBounds`: Visible data ranges of a plot.
- `enum Axis`: Which axis.
- `enum AxisHandle`: What dragging at a position on an axis does.
- `fn handle_at`: The handle under a position `along` an axis of screen length `length` (measured from the smaller-value end).
- `struct AxisDrag`: An axis drag in progress: the state captured when it began.
- `fn drag_range`: New `(lower, upper)` limits of one axis after a drag from `start_along` to `along`, for an axis of screen length `length` showing `[lower, upper]`.

### `crates/app-model/src/pls_analysis.rs`

Partial least squares regression bound to a dataset
([`stat_predictive::pls`]), with the shared predictive-model sections
([`crate::prediction`]).

**Responses.** A continuous response gives PLS regression. A categorical
response gives PLS discriminant analysis (PLS-DA): one 0/1 indicator per
class is modelled together, and a row is assigned the class with the
largest predicted indicator. For the fit measures, the predicted
indicators are clipped to [0, 1] and rescaled to sum to 1; they rank rows
like probabilities but are not calibrated.

**Rows.** Predictors must be numeric. Rows that are excluded, miss the
response or miss any predictor are left out (PLS has no rule for missing
values); their predictions are missing.

**Number of factors.** The fewest factors whose held-out mean squared
error is within one standard error of the smallest
([`stat_predictive::choose_factors`]): held out on the validation rows
when there are any, otherwise by k-fold cross-validation on the training
rows (the k-fold method's folds, or 10 folds). The predicted residual
sum of squares (PRESS) is shown factor by factor. A fixed number may be
set instead.

- `struct PlsRequest`: Columns and settings of a PLS model.
- `struct PlsAnalysis`: A fitted PLS model.
- `fn request_members_to_json`: The request's members after `response` and `predictors`, for project files.
- `fn request_from_json`: Read a request from a project file's report entry (missing members take their defaults).

### `crates/app-model/src/pooling.rs`

Reports pooled across multiply imputed data sets.

A stacked imputation table ([`crate::multiple_imputation`]) holds the
original rows (imputation 0) and `m` completed copies. A report on it
whose scope pools by the imputation column ([`ReportScope::pool`]) is
fitted to each completed copy separately and the results are combined
by Rubin's rules ([`stat_inference::pooling`]): pooled estimates with
Barnard–Rubin degrees of freedom and their within/between variance
split, multi-parameter tests (D₁; for linear models also D₃), pooled R²
for linear models, and each imputation's own estimates. The report's
usual sections follow, computed from the original rows only
(imputation 0), which is the complete-case analysis.

Supported reports and what is pooled:

* linear models: coefficients (with one design, so centred terms and
  category levels mean the same in every imputation), D₁ and D₃ tests of
  each effect and of the whole model, R² and adjusted R² on Fisher's z
  scale (Harel 2009); complete-data degrees of freedom `n − p`;
* generalized linear and mixed models: coefficients and D₁ tests of each
  term, with `ν_com = n − p` (as R mice uses for these models);
* one-sample tests: the mean (`ν_com = n − 1`); two independent groups:
  the difference in means with the pooled variance (`ν_com = n₁ + n₂ − 2`),
  and with more groups each group's mean; two paired columns: the mean
  difference (`ν_com = n − 1`);
* correlations: each Pearson correlation on Fisher's z scale.

[`ReportScope::pool`]: crate::report_scope::ReportScope::pool

- `const TERMS_BY_IMPUTATION`: Most terms listed by imputation in the drill-down table.
- `fn can_pool`: Whether reports like `saved` can be pooled across imputations.
- `fn pooled_sections`: The pooled sections for `report` on `table`, whose column `column` numbers the imputations; `rows` are the table's row states narrowed by the report's own row filter.
- `fn imputation_count`: How many imputations a pooled report on `table` combines.

### `crates/app-model/src/power_analysis.rs`

Power and sample-size reports ([`stat_inference::power`]). These reports
do not read the data table: they describe a planned study.

One of three quantities is solved for, given the others: the power for a
sample size, the sample size for a target power, or the smallest effect
detectable with a sample size and target power. The report shows the
inputs, the answer, power against sample size, and power against the size
of the effect.

Besides tests of means, proportions, rates, standard deviations and
equivalence, the designs include margins of error (the answer is the
probability that the interval's half-width is at most a chosen `E`),
tolerance intervals (the probability that the interval's content stays
below a chosen limit), and two-level, screening and general factorial
experiments, where the sample size is the number of replicates.

- `enum PowerSolve`: What to solve for.
- `struct PowerRequest`: A power or sample-size question.
- `struct PowerAnalysis`: The answer to a [`PowerRequest`].
- `fn effect_name`: Name of the effect parameter of a design.
- `fn power_name`: Name of the probability a design reports: the power of a test, or for estimation designs the probability of the planned precision.
- `fn design_rows`: Labelled parameters of a design.

### `crates/app-model/src/prediction.rs`

The shared framework for predictive models (decision trees now; forests,
boosting and the others of the roadmap later): which rows train, tune and
test a model ([`ValidationMethod`], [`RoleAssignment`]), the response as a
model sees it ([`Response`]), predictions for every row
([`Predictions`]), and the report sections and saved columns every
predictive model shares ([`fit_measures_section`],
[`confusion_section`], [`prediction_columns`]) through the [`Predictor`]
interface. Fitted predictors also implement
[`crate::surface_profiler::SurfaceModel`], so they get the Response
Explorer, the 3-D profiler and several-responses desirability.

Fit measures are those of [`stat_predictive::measures`], reported for
each role: training rows show how well the model fits the data it learned
from (optimistic), validation rows the data that chose its size, and test
rows (used for neither) an honest estimate for new data.

- `enum ValidationMethod`: How rows are divided between training, validation and test.
- `enum Response`: The response as a predictive model sees it, for every table row.
- `struct PredictorInfo`: One predictor of a tree-based model.
- `struct FeatureSet`: The predictors of a tree-based model and their values for every row.
- `fn setting_value`: A profiler setting as a predictor value (missing when it does not fit the predictor).
- `struct RoleAssignment`: The role of every table row.
- `enum Predictions`: Predictions for every table row (NaN where the model cannot predict).
- `trait Predictor`: A fitted predictive model, as shared report sections see it.
- `fn fit_measures_section`: "Fit by Role": the fit measures of `model` on its training, validation and test rows, and from cross-validation when used.
- `fn confusion_section`: Confusion matrices (actual by predicted counts) of a categorical response, one block per role; `None` for a continuous response.
- `struct PredictionFormulas`: Formulas computing a model's predictions, for formula columns.
- `fn prediction_columns`: Columns a predictive model can save: predicted values (continuous), or each class's probability and the most probable class (categorical), as formula columns when `formulas` gives them; and the validation roles.

### `crates/app-model/src/prediction_formula.rs`

A fitted model's prediction equation written as a formula column
(see [`crate::formula`]), so the predictions follow later edits to the
data and can be computed for new rows.

The linear predictor `η = b₀ + Σ bⱼ xⱼ` is written effect by effect, the
way [`ModelDesign`] codes the design columns:

* a continuous main effect is `b * x`;
* a continuous factor inside an interaction or power is centred at its
  mean over the rows the model was fitted to: `b * (x - x̄) ** 2`;
* a spline term is one `natural_spline(x, [knots], k)` or
  `bspline(x, [knots], degree, k)` per basis column (boundary knots first
  and last; see [`crate::formula`]);
* an effect with categorical factors becomes a `switch` on the level (or,
  for several factors, on the levels joined by a tab), giving each level
  combination its effective coefficient `Σ bⱼ cⱼ` under the design's
  coding (reference or sum-to-zero), times the effect's continuous part.
  A level the model was not fitted to falls to `0.0 / 0.0` (NaN), which
  makes that row's prediction missing without an evaluation error.

Effects whose coefficients are all exactly zero (e.g. predictors a lasso
dropped) are left out. The mean is the inverse link of `η`: `logistic(η)`
for the logit link, `exp(η)` for the log link. Coefficients are written
with every digit needed to read back the same `f64`, so the formula
reproduces the model's predictions to rounding.

- `enum Link`: How the model maps its linear predictor `η` to the predicted mean.
- `struct FactorColumn`: A predictor column as the formula reads it.
- `fn factor_columns`: The predictor columns `indices` of `table`, in order (skipping unknown indices, which a fit would already have refused).
- `fn prediction_formula`: The formula predicting the response of a model with design `design` (predictors read from `factors`, one per design term), intercept `intercept`, one coefficient per design column in `slopes`, and link `link`.

### `crates/app-model/src/project/folders.rs`

Folders the user makes in a project's tree, to group its tables,
reports (graph canvases included), dashboards and notebooks.

A folder has a name, folders of its own and a set of items. Each item is
in at most one folder; items in no folder stay at the top of the project.
Folders change nothing about the items themselves: a report in a folder
still belongs to its table and re-runs with it.

Folders are saved in the version-3 form as the optional member
`"folders"`:

```text
"folders": [
  { "name": "…",
    "items": [ {"table": "table-1"}
             | {"table": "table-1", "report": index}   (index in that table's "reports")
             | {"dashboard": "dashboard-1"}
             | {"notebook": "…"}, … ],                 (optional)
    "folders": [ … ] },                                (optional; folders inside)
  …
]
```

On reading, items that name a table, report, dashboard or notebook the
project does not have are left out, as is a second mention of an item
already placed; report indices follow reports left out on reading.

- `const MAX_FOLDER_DEPTH`: Deepest nesting of folders read from a file (deeper ones are an error, so a malformed file cannot exhaust the stack).
- `enum FolderItem`: Something a folder can hold.
- `struct ProjectFolder`: A folder of a project's tree.

### `crates/app-model/src/project/tables.rs`

Project files holding several tables, with derived-table lineage and a
window layout (format version 3; see the parent module for the
JSON form).

A [`ProjectFile`] is a list of [`ProjectTable`]s, each with a stable
[`TableId`], plus the project's scripts and an optional
[`ProjectLayout`]. A table made by a table operation keeps a
[`TableLineage`]: the operation ([`TableOrigin`]), the ids of its source
tables within the project, and a [`DataFingerprint`] of each source as it
was when the table was made. Comparing those fingerprints with the
sources' current data ([`ProjectFile::origin_is_stale`]) tells whether a
source changed since; [`ProjectFile::rerun_origin`] re-runs the stored
operation on the current sources through [`TableOperation::run`].

[`save_project_file`] writes a project with exactly one table, an empty
layout and no dashboards in the single-table form of [`save_project`] (byte for byte), so
builds that predate version 3 still open it; anything else is written in
the version-3 form. [`load_project_file`] reads both.

- `const PROJECT_FILE_VERSION`: Version written for project files in the several-table form.
- `struct TableId`: A table's identifier within a project file: stable across saves and independent of the table's (editable) name.
- `struct DataFingerprint`: A 64-bit FNV-1a hash of a source table's contents, with the row states the operation reads (see [`DataFingerprint::of_source`]).
- `struct SourceSnapshot`: One source of a derived table, as it was when the table was made.
- `struct TableLineage`: How a table in a project was made: the operation and, for each of its sources, where that source is in the project and what it held.
- `struct ProjectTable`: One table in a project file, with everything kept alongside it.
- `enum ViewMode`: How a table's document is shown.
- `struct TableView`: A table's view mode in the layout.
- `enum WindowContent`: What a popped-out window shows.
- `struct PoppedOutWindow`: A window popped out of the main window.
- `struct DashboardWindow`: A dashboard shown in a window of its own.
- `struct ProjectLayout`: Plain data describing how the application had the project laid out.
- `struct ProjectFile`: A project: several tables, their scripts, dashboards and layout.
- `struct Rerun`: The result of [`ProjectFile::rerun_origin`].
- `fn save_project_file`: Serialize a project file to JSON text.
- `fn load_project_file`: Parse a project file in either form: a version 1 or 2 single-table project (which becomes a one-table [`ProjectFile`] whose table has the id `table-1`), or a version-3 file written by [`save_project_file`].
- `fn load_project_file_noting`: [`load_project_file`], also returning notes on what could not be restored: reports and dashboard tiles that cannot be read are left out, and formula columns on a cycle or that no longer compile keep their saved values, each with a note naming it and why (see [`load_project_noting`](super::load_pr…

### `crates/app-model/src/project.rs`

Project files: a dataset together with its row states and the analyses run
on it, so that reopening the file brings every report back.

#### Format
A project is a UTF-8 JSON document (extension `.acraft`):

```text
{
  "format": "statistical-engine-project",
  "version": 1 | 2,
  "table": {
    "name": "…",
    "columns": [ {"name": "…", "type": "numeric" | "text" | "datetime",
                  "level": "continuous" | "nominal" | "ordinal",
                  "value_labels": [["1", "Treatment"], …],     (optional)
                  "hover": true,                                (optional)
                  "values": [ … ]}, … ]
  },
  "rows": { "excluded": [row, …], "hidden": [row, …], "selected": [row, …],
            "colors": [[row, "#rrggbb"], …],
            "markers": [[row, "square"], …],                   (optional)
            "style_column": "…",                               (optional)
            "subsets": [{"name": "…", "rows": [row, …]}, …],   (optional)
            "active_subset": "…" },                            (optional)
  "reports": [ {"analysis": "linear-model", "response": "y", …,
                "options": {…}}, … ],
  "origin": {"operation": "stack", "sources": ["…"], …}   (optional)
  "scripts": [ {"name": "…", "source": "…", "run_on_open": true}, … ]
                                                          (optional)
}
```

Numbers are written in shortest round-trip form and missing numeric values
as `null`, so the data reload bit for bit.

A `"datetime"` column (version 2) stores its values as numbers of seconds
since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 UTC (`null` when missing), exactly like a numeric
column, plus how they are shown: `"format"` (`"date"`, `"datetime"`,
`"time"` or `"duration"`), `"fraction_digits"` (0–6) and `"offset_minutes"`
(the display offset from UTC). A project is written as version 1 unless it
has a date-time column, so files without dates still open in builds that
predate version 2; version 1 files always load. Reports store what was asked for
(columns by name, settings, display options), not results: on loading, each
analysis is re-run on the restored data and row states, which reproduces the
report exactly because every analysis is deterministic.

`"origin"`, present only for a table made by a table operation, records
the operation and its options ([`crate::table_ops::TableOrigin`]). It is
optional, so it does not change the format version.

`"external_source"`, present only for a table read from a database or the
web, records the connection and query, or the URL and headers, so the
table can be refreshed ([`crate::external::ExternalSource`]). It never
holds a password or a secret header value. Also optional.

`"scripts"`, present only when the project carries scripts, holds Rhai
scripts ([`ProjectScript`]) kept with the data. Those marked
`"run_on_open"` are offered to run when the project is opened; the
application asks before running them. Also optional.

#### Several tables (version 3)
A project holding more than one table, dashboards or a window layout is written by
[`save_project_file`] in a second form, version 3:

```text
{
  "format": "statistical-engine-project",
  "version": 3,
  "tables": [
    { "id": "table-1",
      "table": {…}, "rows": {…}, "reports": [ … ],   (as in the single-table form)
      "origin": {…},                                 (optional, as above)
      "source_tables": [ {"id": "table-2", "fingerprint": "89ab…"} | null, … ],
                                                     (with "origin" only)
      "external_source": {…} },                      (optional, as above)
    …
  ],
  "scripts": [ … ],                                  (optional, as above)
  "name": "…",                                       (optional: the name the user gave the
                                                     project, shown instead of the file's)
  "notebooks": [                                     (optional; crate::notebook)
    { "name": "…",
      "cells": [ {"kind": "text" | "code", "source": "…",
                  "run": n,                          (optional: run number)
                  "outputs": [ {"kind": "printed" | "value" | "note", "text": "…"}
                             | {"kind": "error", "text": "…", "line": n}
                             | {"kind": "table", "title": "…", "columns": […], "rows": [[…], …]}
                             | {"kind": "report", "table": "…", "title": "…"}, … ]}, … ]},
    … ],
  "folders": [                                       (optional; folders::ProjectFolder)
    { "name": "…",
      "items": [ {"table": "table-1"} | {"table": "table-1", "report": index}
               | {"dashboard": "dashboard-1"} | {"notebook": "…"}, … ],
      "folders": [ … ] }, … ],                       (both optional)
  "dashboards": [                                    (optional)
    { "id": "dashboard-1", "name": "…",
      "grid_columns": 12,                            (optional; default 12)
      "filters": [ {"column": "…", "levels": ["…", …]}
                 | {"column": "…", "min": x, "max": y}, … ],   (optional)
      "tiles": [                                     (optional)
        { "id": 1, "column": 0, "row": 0, "width": 6, "height": 4,
          "table": "table-1", "report": {…} },        (a report tile)
        { "id": 2, "column": 6, "row": 0, "width": 6, "height": 1,
          "text": "…", "style": "heading" | "body" }, (a text tile; style optional)
        … ] },
    …
  ],
  "layout": {                                        (optional; every member optional)
    "active_table": "table-1",
    "views": [ {"table": "table-1", "mode": "data" | "results" | "side-by-side"}, … ],
    "windows": [ {"table": "table-2", "view": "data" | "results" | {"report": index},
                  "position": [x, y], "size": [width, height]}, … ],
    "active_dashboard": "dashboard-1",
    "dashboard_windows": [ {"dashboard": "dashboard-1",
                            "position": [x, y], "size": [width, height]}, … ]
  }
}
```

Each table's `"id"` is unique within the file, non-empty, and stays the
same across saves (names can change). Date-time columns are allowed in
every table (version 3 includes version 2).

`"source_tables"` has one entry per name in the origin's `"sources"`, in
the same order: the id of that source table within the project and a
fingerprint (16 hexadecimal digits of a 64-bit FNV-1a hash; see
[`DataFingerprint::of_source`]) of its data when the derived table was
made, or `null` when that source is not in the project. Comparing the
fingerprints with the sources' current data tells that a source changed
since ([`ProjectFile::origin_is_stale`]); [`ProjectFile::rerun_origin`]
makes the table again from the current sources.

`"dashboards"` ([`crate::dashboard`]) arranges report and text tiles on a
grid `"grid_columns"` wide (1–48 columns, rows as needed). Each dashboard
`"id"` is unique and non-empty; each tile `"id"` is a positive whole number
unique within its dashboard. A tile covers `"width"` × `"height"` cells
(each at least 1) from its top-left cell (`"column"`, `"row"`, counted from
0), stays within the grid's columns and never overlaps another tile. A
report tile holds its own copy of a report request, in the form of a
`"reports"` entry with columns named in its `"table"` (the id of one of
the file's tables; a tile naming another table makes the file invalid).
`"filters"` holds at most one condition per column name: a list of
accepted levels (cell text) or an inclusive range with finite limits. A
filter applies to every report tile whose table has a column of that name
and is skipped for tables without one; it never changes the tables' own
row states. Like reports, tiles store requests, not results: they are
computed again when shown ([`crate::dashboard::compute_dashboard`]).

`"layout"` is plain data for the application: which table is shown, each
table's view mode, windows popped out of the main window (positions and
sizes in points, outer frame), the dashboard shown in the main window in
place of a table (`"active_dashboard"`) and dashboards in windows of
their own (`"dashboard_windows"`). Layout entries naming a table not in
the file, a report the table does not have, or a dashboard the file does
not have, are ignored on loading.

A project with exactly one table, no layout and no dashboards is always
written in the single-table form (version 1 or 2, byte for byte what
[`save_project`] writes), so builds that predate version 3 still open it.
[`load_project_file`] reads both forms; a single-table file becomes a
one-table [`ProjectFile`] whose table has the id `table-1`.
[`load_project`] also reads a version-3 file holding exactly one table
(its dashboards and layout are not part of a [`Project`] and are left out).

- `const PROJECT_FORMAT`: Value of the `format` member identifying a project file.
- `const PROJECT_VERSION`: Newest version of the single-table project form ([`save_project`]).
- `const PROJECT_EXTENSION`: Project file extension (without the dot).
- `enum SavedReport`: One saved analysis: what to compute and how to display it.
- `struct Project`: A dataset, its row states and its saved reports.
- `struct ProjectScript`: A Rhai script kept in a project file.
- `fn save_project`: Serialize a project to JSON text.
- `fn load_project`: Parse a project written by [`save_project`] (or a version-3 project file holding exactly one table; its layout and source links are ignored).
- `fn load_project_noting`: [`load_project`], also returning notes on what could not be restored: a report that cannot be read (for example one naming a column the table does not have) is left out, and a formula column whose formula is on a cycle or no longer compiles keeps its saved values; each gets a note naming it and w…
- `fn column_to_json`: A column in the project-file form: `name`, `type` (`"numeric"`, `"text"` or `"datetime"` with its display settings), `level` and `values` (missing numbers as `null`).
- `fn column_from_json`: Parse a column written by [`column_to_json`].
- `fn read_value_labels`: Value labels saved as `[[code, label], …]` pairs (none when absent).
- `fn checked_report_to_json`: [`report_to_json`], refusing a report that refers to a column index the table does not have (which [`report_to_json`] would write as an empty name that no table can resolve).
- `fn report_to_json`: The JSON form of one report request, as stored in a project's `"reports"` array: `{"analysis": key, …settings, "options": {…}}`, columns by name.
- `fn report_from_json`: Read one report request written by [`report_to_json`], resolving column names against `table`.
- `fn chart_name`: The project-file name of a control chart type.
- `fn level_name`: The project-file name of a measurement level.
- `fn parse_color`: A row colour from `"#rrggbb"` text.

### `crates/app-model/src/project_template.rs`

Project templates: a project's reports, graph canvases, dashboards,
scripts and plot styles without its data, to build again on new data.

"Save project as template…" writes [`template_text`]; "New project from
template…" reads it ([`ProjectTemplate::parse`]), maps each template
table's columns onto a new table ([`ColumnMapping`], as for
"Duplicate on another table…" in [`crate::report_transfer`]) and builds
the project ([`ProjectTemplate::apply`]). Several data files can each take
the template of a one-table project ([`merge_projects`] puts them in one
project).

The file is the project file with every table emptied:

```text
{"format": "statistical-engine-template", "version": 1,
 "tables": [{"name": "…", "needs": ["Load", "Strain", …]}, …],
 "project": {…a project file whose columns hold no values and whose
             row states are empty…}}
```

`needs` lists, per table and in the order of the project's tables, the
data columns the reports, dashboards and formula columns read; the
table's columns in `project` are those columns (their names, kinds and
measurement levels, to show when mapping) and the formula columns they
use, which are computed again on the new data. Derived tables (made by a
table operation) are left out, as are row states and the window layout.

- `const TEMPLATE_FORMAT`: The `format` member of a template file.
- `const TEMPLATE_EXTENSION`: The file extension of templates.
- `fn template_text`: The template of project `file` (see the [module documentation](self)), with a note for each table left out.
- `struct TemplateTable`: One table of a template.
- `struct ProjectTemplate`: A template read from its file (see the [module documentation](self)).
- `fn merge_projects`: One project holding every table of `files` (each usually one table built from the same template), with table and dashboard identifiers made unique and each dashboard named after its table when there are several.

### `crates/app-model/src/proportional_hazards_analysis.rs`

Proportional hazards (Cox) regression bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::proportional_hazards`]).

**Layout:** a time column, an optional numeric censor column (coded as in
survival curves: by default a non-zero value marks a unit still running
at its time) and predictors, continuous or categorical, with effects
(interactions and powers) coded as in the linear model; an optional
strata column gives each of its levels its own baseline hazard. Excluded
rows and rows missing any value are left out.

The report gives the model summary with the likelihood-ratio, Wald and
score tests of all effects, the Effect Pareto and likelihood-ratio test of
each effect (a refit without its columns), coefficients and hazard ratios
with Wald and profile-likelihood limits, the Grambsch–Therneau tests of
proportional hazards with a plot of scaled Schoenfeld residuals per
coefficient, predicted survival curves with pointwise limits at chosen
covariate settings, survival at chosen times, the Breslow baseline, and
deviance residuals. The profiler shows the hazard ratio against the
average unit, or the survival probability at a chosen time.

- `enum HazardProfile`: What the profiler of a proportional hazards report predicts.
- `struct ProportionalHazardsRequest`: Columns, effects and options of a proportional hazards regression.
- `struct ProportionalHazardsAnalysis`: A fitted proportional hazards model and what its report needs.

### `crates/app-model/src/pvalue_analysis.rs`

Adjusting a column of p-values for multiple testing and combining them
([`stat_inference::pvalues`]).

Each usable row (not excluded, with a p-value) is one test. The report
lists every row's p-value with its Bonferroni, Šidák, Holm, Hochberg,
Benjamini–Hochberg and Benjamini–Yekutieli adjustments and Storey
q-value, counts the rejections of each method at the chosen `α`, plots
the ordered p-values against the Benjamini–Hochberg line, and combines
them by Fisher's and Stouffer's (optionally weighted) methods. Every
adjustment can be saved as a new column.

- `struct PValueRequest`: Settings of a p-value adjustment report.
- `struct PValueAnalysis`: A computed p-value adjustment report.

### `crates/app-model/src/recode.rs`

Recoding a column: mapping each distinct value to a new one, for the data
grid's Recode dialog.

The values are listed as the grid shows them ([`stat_data::Column::cell_text`]).
Giving several values the same new text merges them into one category;
blank new text makes the value missing. The result either replaces the
column's values in place (one undoable step) or becomes a new column whose
type is the original's when every new value fits it, else numbers when
every new value is a number, else text.

- `struct ValueCount`: One distinct value of a column, with how many rows hold it.
- `fn distinct_values`: The distinct values of column `column` with their counts: numbers (and dates) in increasing order, text in alphabetical order ignoring case, the missing value (if any) last.
- `enum RecodeTarget`: Where the recoded values go.
- `fn recode_edit`: The edit that recodes column `column` by `mapping` (old text → new text; values not in the mapping stay as they are), and how many cells change.
- `mod helpers`: Text helpers offered by the Recode dialog for the new values.

### `crates/app-model/src/recording.rs`

Recording what a person does in the application as a Rhai script that
replays it.

The [`Recorder`] keeps, for every table it follows, the state a script
would have reached by running the lines written so far (the *replay
state*). The application tells it about data edits as they happen and
shows it each table's current row states and reports; it writes an
[`Action`] for every difference and applies the action to the replay
state, using the same code scripts use. So whatever the application did,
the script ends in the same place: same data, row states and reports.

- `enum OpenedFrom`: How a table being recorded was opened.
- `struct Recorder`: Writes a script while the person works.

### `crates/app-model/src/recovery.rs`

Crash reports and recovery saves for the desktop application.

**Crash reports.** When the program panics, the panic hook writes the
message, where it happened and a backtrace to a text file in the log
folder ([`log_dir`]):

| System | Folder |
|---|---|
| macOS | `~/Library/Logs/AnovaCraft` |
| Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AnovaCraft\Logs` |
| Linux and others | `$XDG_STATE_HOME/anovacraft/logs` (default `~/.local/state/…`) |

Only the newest [`MAX_REPORTS`] reports are kept.

**Recovery saves.** Each run of the application is a *session* with a
folder of its own under [`recovery_root`] (the `Recovery` folder next to
the settings file). While it runs, projects with changes since they were
opened or saved are written there as ordinary project files every couple
of minutes, and the session's heartbeat file is touched every half
minute. Saving a project removes its recovery copy, and a normal exit
removes the whole folder. A folder whose heartbeat has stopped therefore
belongs to a run that ended abnormally (a crash, a forced quit, a power
cut), and the next launch offers to restore its projects
([`orphaned_sessions`]).

Recovery copies leave out row selections and the window layout, which
are not counted as unsaved changes either.

- `const MAX_REPORTS`: Crash reports kept in the log folder; older ones are deleted.
- `const STALE_AFTER_SECS`: Seconds without a heartbeat after which a session is taken to have ended abnormally.
- `fn log_dir`: The folder crash reports are written to on this computer.
- `fn log_dir_for`: The crash-report folder for operating system `os` (as in `std::env::consts::OS`) with environment lookup `env`.
- `fn recovery_root`: The folder holding recovery sessions on this computer.
- `fn recovery_root_for`: The recovery folder for operating system `os` with environment lookup `env`: `Recovery` beside the settings file.
- `fn now_secs`: Seconds since 1970 now.
- `struct CrashReport`: What a crash report says.
- `fn write_crash_report`: Write `report` to a new file in `dir` (created if needed), named from `stamp` (a file-name-safe time such as `2026-10-21-041502`), and delete all but the newest [`MAX_REPORTS`] reports there.
- `struct RecoveryInfo`: How a recovered project is described when it is offered back.
- `struct RecoverySession`: This run's recovery folder and what it holds.
- `fn note_crash`: Note in session folder `dir` that it ended with the crash report at `report` (called from the panic hook).
- `struct RecoveredProject`: A project saved for recovery by a run that ended abnormally.
- `struct OrphanedSession`: A run that ended abnormally: its recovered projects and crash report.
- `fn orphaned_sessions`: Sessions under `root` other than `own` whose heartbeat stopped more than [`STALE_AFTER_SECS`] before `now`, oldest first.

### `crates/app-model/src/recurrence.rs`

Repairable systems (recurrent events) bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::repairable`]): Nelson's mean cumulative function with
confidence limits, per population, the difference between two
populations, constant-rate and power-law process fits, and the Laplace
and military handbook trend tests.

**Layout:** one row per repair, with the system's identifier and its age
at the repair. An optional event column marks rows that are not repairs
(value 0): such a row gives the system's age at the end of observation.
A system without one is taken to be observed up to its last repair. An
optional population column splits the systems into groups (each system
in one group); with exactly two, their difference is shown.

Excluded rows and rows missing a value are left out. Repairs are drawn on
the estimate as filled markers and ends of observation as hollow ones,
each linked to its row.

- `struct RecurrenceRequest`: Columns and settings of a repairable-systems analysis.
- `struct RecurrenceGroup`: One population's systems and estimates.
- `struct RecurrenceAnalysis`: A computed repairable-systems analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/regularized.rs`

Penalized (regularized) regression analysis bound to a dataset: lasso,
ridge or elastic net ([`stat_predictive::elastic_net`]), with the penalty
chosen by cross-validation. Categorical predictors are indicator coded.

- `struct RegularizedRequest`: Columns and settings for a penalized regression.
- `struct RegularizedAnalysis`: A fitted penalty path with cross-validation.

### `crates/app-model/src/reliability_growth.rs`

Reliability growth analysis bound to a dataset
([`stat_reliability::growth`]): the power-law (Crow–AMSAA) process fitted
to the cumulative failure times of one system under development, per
phase, with cumulative-failure, intensity and MTBF plots and the
Cramér–von Mises goodness-of-fit test.

**Layout:** one row per failure, with its cumulative test time. An
optional event column marks rows that are not failures (value 0): such a
row records the end of the test (or of its phase) without a failure, so
that phase is time-terminated there. A phase without one ends at its last
failure (failure-terminated), unless it is the last phase and an end time
is given. An optional phase column splits the test where the design
changed; phases follow each other in time on the same cumulative clock,
each starting where the one before ended.

Excluded rows and rows missing the time, event or phase are left out.
Each failure is drawn as a point linked to its row.

- `struct GrowthRequest`: Columns and settings of a reliability growth analysis.
- `struct GrowthPhase`: One fitted phase with its failure rows.
- `struct GrowthAnalysis`: A computed reliability growth analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/reliability_json.rs`

Project-file (JSON) form of the reliability growth, repairable-systems
and test-plan reports (see [`crate::project`]). Columns are stored by
name; a missing setting keeps its default, so older files stay readable
when settings are added.

```text
{"analysis": "reliability-growth", "time": "Hours", "event": "Failure",
 "phase": "Phase", "end_time": 4000, "beta": "unbiased", "confidence": 0.95}
{"analysis": "repairable-systems", "system": "Unit", "time": "Age",
 "event": "Repair", "group": "Design", "variance": "robust",
 "limits": "normal", "confidence": 0.95}
{"analysis": "life-distributions", "layout": "intervals", "start": "From",
 "end": "To", "frequency": "Units", "group": "Supplier",
 "families": ["weibull", "lognormal"], "detail": "weibull",
 "confidence": 0.95, "probabilities": [0.1, 0.5], "times": [1000],
 "known_shape": 2}            (or "layout": "times", "time": "Hours",
                               "censor": "Censored", "censor_coding": "nonzero-censored")
{"analysis": "proportional-hazards", "time": "Weeks", "censor": "Relapse",
 "censor_coding": "nonzero-event", "predictors": ["Treatment", "log WBC"],
 "strata": "Sex", "ties": "efron", "ph_transform": "km", …}
     (see crate::proportional_hazards_analysis::to_json)
{"analysis": "survival-regression", "layout": "intervals", "start": "From",
 "end": "To", "frequency": "Units", "predictors": ["Temperature"],
 "distribution": "weibull", …}      (see crate::survival_regression_analysis::to_json)
{"analysis": "reliability-test-plan", "plan": "demonstration",
 "reliability": 0.9, "time": 1000, "confidence": 0.9, "shape": 1.5,
 "failures": 0, "test_time": 1000}            (or "units": 20)
{"analysis": "reliability-test-plan", "plan": "estimation",
 "distribution": "weibull", "spread": 2, "fraction_failing": 0.3,
 "percentile": 0.1, "confidence": 0.95, "precision": 1.5}
{"analysis": "reliability-test-plan", "plan": "accelerated",
 "distribution": "weibull", "spread": 2, "relationship": "arrhenius",
 "use_stress": 50, "high_stress": 120, "p_use": 0.001, "p_high": 0.9,
 "percentile": 0.1, "confidence": 0.95, "precision": 2,
 "levels": [[80, 0.5], [120, 0.5]]}
```

### `crates/app-model/src/report.rs`

Report content: what a result section shows, independent of how it is drawn.

The GUI renders [`ReportSection`]s as collapsible sections. Tables arrive
already formatted as text; plots arrive as data series in plot coordinates,
each point tagged with its dataset row so views can apply shared row state.

- `struct TextTable`: A table of pre-formatted cells.
- `struct RowPoint`: One plotted observation, tagged with its dataset row.
- `type Polyline`: A polyline in plot coordinates.
- `struct PlotSpec`: Data for a scatter plot with optional overlay curves.
- `struct ContourMap`: A surface drawn as a contour map under a plot: the sampled surface, the plot's own number of levels, the quantity's name (the colour bar's title) and how it is drawn (from the report's Plot settings).
- `enum LinePattern`: How a fitted curve is drawn, so curves stay distinguishable without color.
- `struct SurvivalPlotSpec`: A survival plot: step-function estimates with optional confidence bands and fitted parametric curves, one curve per group, plus a marker for every analysed row (filled for events, hollow for censored observations) placed on its group's curve so it can be brushed.
- `struct RiskTable`: Data of a number-at-risk table: every curve's exit times (event or censoring), so a view can count those still at risk at whatever time ticks its axis shows.
- `struct SurvivalCurveSpec`: One group's curves in a [`SurvivalPlotSpec`].
- `struct Annotations`: Labelled markers in plot coordinates, in groups with legend names.
- `struct PlotPane`: One labelled pane of a faceted plot, spanning `[x_min, x_max]`.
- `struct PointGroups`: Assignment of plotted points to named groups.
- `struct ChartPoint`: One plotted point of a control chart.
- `struct LimitStep`: Limits holding over a stretch of samples of a control chart.
- `struct PhaseMark`: The start of a phase on a control chart.
- `struct ControlChartSpec`: Data for drawing one control chart.
- `struct BarItem`: One bar: an interval on the horizontal axis whose height is the number of dataset rows it counts.
- `struct BarChartSpec`: Data for a bar chart: a histogram, or frequencies of categorical levels.
- `struct BoxPlotSpec`: Data for a horizontal box plot of one variable (Tukey 1977): box from the first to the third quartile, median line, whiskers to the most extreme values within 1.5 IQR of the box, and the points beyond plotted individually.
- `enum SectionContent`: What a section shows.
- `struct TreeDiagram`: A decision tree for display: nodes with their rule, counts and rows.
- `struct TreeDiagramNode`: One node of a [`TreeDiagram`].
- `struct EffectSource`: One model effect and its test's p-value.
- `struct EffectPareto`: Model effects sorted from most to least significant, for a Pareto chart of `−log₁₀ p` (Juran's Pareto ordering applied to significance; the `−log₁₀ p` scale is the one of genome-wide association "Manhattan" plots) with the p-values alongside.
- `enum SectionKind`: Stable identifier of a section within a report, used for view state such as which sections are open.
- `struct ReportSection`: One collapsible section of a report.
- `struct ReportOptions`: User-toggleable parts of a linear-model report.
- `fn hierarchy_note`: A note when `effects` (products of predictors, with `names`) break the hierarchy principle: an interaction or power without the lower-order effects it is built from ([`stat_linear::hierarchy`]).
- `const SIGNIFICANCE_LEVEL`: The level below which report tables can mark a p-value as significant.
- `fn is_p_value_heading`: Whether a report table heading names a p-value column ("p", "p-value", "p-value (…)").
- `fn is_significant`: Whether a p-value cell, as reports format it ("0.0123", "3.1e-6", "<0.0001"), is below `level`.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_columns.rs`

Columns a report can add to its table: predicted values and residuals of
models, principal component scores, cluster numbers, a Box–Cox
transformed column. The report's options menu and scripts
(`report.save_columns(...)`) both offer exactly these.

- `struct ReportColumn`: A column a report offers to add to its table.
- `fn report_columns`: The columns report `saved` offers on `table` with row states `rows` (empty for reports that offer none).

### `crates/app-model/src/report_export/docx.rs`

Reports as Word documents (Office Open XML WordprocessingML,
ECMA-376), written as XML parts in a zip container.

The document uses Word's built-in style names (Title, Heading 1–3, so the
navigation pane and a table of contents pick the headings up) plus a few
of its own: "Report Meta" for the line under the title, "Report Note",
"Report Formula" (monospace, shaded) and the table style "Report Table"
(rules above and below and under the header row). Tables mark their
header row to repeat on every page, numeric columns are right-aligned,
and plots are inline pictures: a 300 ppi PNG, with the SVG alongside
through the `asvg:svgBlip` extension, which Word 2016 and later draw
instead of the PNG. The page size is Letter or A4 with 0.75 in margins,
and the footer shows "Page n of N".

- `fn write`: `doc` as a `.docx` file.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_export/markdown.rs`

Reports as Markdown text (GitHub-flavoured: pipe tables with numeric
columns right-aligned), with each plot saved as a 300 ppi PNG in a
folder beside the file and linked from the text.

- `fn write`: `doc` as Markdown, and its plots as PNG files under `folder` (named `plot-01.png`, …), which the text links to by relative path.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_export/pdf.rs`

Reports as PDF documents, paged on Letter or A4.

The document is laid out first (pages of positioned lines, rules and
figures) and then written with `krilla`:

* text in the bundled Inter, numbers in JetBrains Mono, both embedded as
  subsets, with DejaVu Sans for characters they lack (Greek letters,
  arrows, combining marks); lines are shaped with `rustybuzz`, so the
  widths used for wrapping and right-aligning are the widths drawn;
  bold is the regular face filled and outlined;
* headings kept with what follows them; tables in rules with their
  header row repeated on every page they run onto, numeric columns
  right-aligned in the monospace font; tables too wide for the page are
  set smaller (down to 6.5 pt), then their text columns wrap, then they
  are split into column groups that each repeat the first column;
* plots drawn from their SVG as vector graphics (`krilla-svg`), scaled
  to the text width;
* a footer with the title and "Page n of N", a bookmark for every report
  and section heading, and the title in the document information.

- `fn write`: `doc` as a PDF file.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_export/pptx.rs`

Reports as PowerPoint presentations (Office Open XML PresentationML,
ECMA-376), 16:9 slides written as XML parts in a zip container.

The first slide carries the title and the line naming the table, its
rows and the export date. When several reports are exported each starts
with a slide of its title. Every open section then gets slides of its
own, titled with the section title (a real title placeholder, so the
outline view and screen readers find it):

* a plot as a picture fitted to the slide (a 300 ppi PNG with the SVG
  alongside, which PowerPoint 2016 and later draw instead);
* a table as a native table, set smaller as it gets wider, its rows
  spread over as many slides as they need (titled "… (continued)") and
  very wide tables split into column groups that each repeat the first
  column; numeric columns are right-aligned;
* notes and formulas as text, spread over slides the same way.

- `fn write`: `doc` as a `.pptx` file.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_export/xlsx.rs`

Reports as Excel workbooks: one sheet per report, its open sections in
order down the sheet. Section titles are bold, tables have a bold
header row, and a cell showing a plain number (`0.0312`, `−2.5`,
`4.3e-6`, `1,234.5`, `12.5%`) is stored as that number with a number
format that shows it in the same precision, so it can be computed with;
anything else (`< 0.0001`, `7.25 ▲`, labels) stays text. Plots are
inserted as 300 ppi PNG pictures at their document size.

- `fn cell_number`: A cell's number and the number format that shows it as the report did, or `None` when the cell is not a plain number.
- `fn write`: `doc` as an `.xlsx` file: one sheet per report.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_export.rs`

Reports exported as documents: PDF, Word (`.docx`), PowerPoint
(`.pptx`), HTML, Markdown and Excel workbooks.

Every format is written from the same [`ReportDocument`], built from the
reports as an export sees them ([`HtmlReport`]: the open sections, in
report order) and the data they were run on ([`HtmlSource`]):

* a title (the report's, or `"<table> reports"` for every report of a
  table), with a line naming the table, its row counts and the export
  date;
* for each report (when there are several) a heading, then each open
  section as a heading with its body: tables (numeric columns
  right-aligned), notes, formulas, and plots drawn by
  [`crate::report_figure`] (graph canvases by [`crate::graph_figure`]),
  the same figures the right-click "Save plot as…" items write.

The formats:

| Format | Plots | Writer |
|---|---|---|
| PDF | vector, from the figure's SVG | [`pdf`]: paged on Letter or A4, bundled fonts embedded (subset), bookmarks per heading, page numbers |
| Word | 300 ppi PNG with the SVG alongside (Word 2016 and later show the SVG) | [`docx`]: Office Open XML (ECMA-376) with heading styles, header rows that repeat on each page, page numbers |
| PowerPoint | 300 ppi PNG with the SVG alongside | [`pptx`]: 16:9 slides, one or more per section, long tables continued over slides |
| HTML | inline SVG | [`crate::html_export`] |
| Markdown | PNG files in a `<name>_files` folder beside the `.md` file | [`markdown`]: GitHub-flavoured tables |
| Excel | PNG pictures | [`xlsx`]: one sheet per report; numbers stored as numbers in the precision shown |

- `enum ReportFormat`: A document format reports can be exported to.
- `enum PaperSize`: Paper size of paged formats.
- `struct ExportOptions`: Settings of an export.
- `enum ExportScope`: What to export: one report, or several under one title.
- `struct Heading`: A document heading: the title, a report (when several are exported) or a section.
- `enum Block`: One piece of a [`ReportDocument`].
- `struct DocTable`: A report table with its columns classified for alignment.
- `struct DocFigure`: A plot of a report, drawn on demand in the format a writer needs.
- `struct ReportDocument`: Reports laid out as a document, ready for any writer.
- `type ExportFile`: One file of an export: its path relative to the chosen file's folder (the chosen file itself first) and its contents.
- `fn render`: The files of `scope` exported as `format`: one file for every format but Markdown, which adds its plots as PNG files in a `<name>_files` folder.
- `fn with_extension`: `path` with `format`'s extension, unless it already has it (or, for HTML and Markdown, a common alternative such as `.htm`).
- `fn export`: Export `scope` as `format` to `path` (its extension added when missing), writing any extra files beside it.
- `fn svg_size`: Width and height (in points) of an SVG figure written by [`stat_viz::export`], read from its `width`/`height` attributes (`540pt`) or, failing that, its view box.
- `fn png_size`: Width and height in pixels of a PNG image, from its header.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_figure.rs`

Report plots drawn as vector figures (SVG, PDF, EPS) with
[`stat_viz::export::export_chart`], for saving from scripts.

Each plot kind is drawn from the same data the report view draws:
scatter plots with their fits, bands, groups and labels; control charts
with centre line, limits and flagged points; histograms and frequency
charts; box plots; survival curves; and effect Pareto charts. Groups
carry a marker shape as well as a color, and excluded rows are drawn as
hollow gray markers, as on screen. Figures use the light palette.

- `fn is_plot`: Whether a section is drawn as a plot (and so can be saved as a figure).
- `struct FigureLayout`: Page size and view of a figure.
- `fn section_figure`: The section's plot as a vector figure titled with the section's title, or `None` for tables and notes.
- `fn section_figure_with`: [`section_figure`] with a chosen page size and view (the view replaces the fitted axis ranges).
- `fn section_figure_styled`: [`section_figure_with`] with the plot's reference lines and bands (`reference`, from its plot style): bands behind the marks, lines over them, their key entries added, and the fitted ranges widened to show them (a view from `layout` is kept as it is).
- `fn chart_kind`: `Some(true)` for plot sections drawn as one x–y panel, which can carry reference lines; `Some(false)` for other plots; `None` for tables and notes.
- `fn reference_values`: The plotted values of a report plot that its reference statistics are computed from, rows in order: an x–y plot's points (horizontal and vertical), a control chart's plotted statistics (vertical, in sample order), a box plot's values (horizontal) and a survival plot's rows.
- `fn reference_layers`: The reference lines and bands of a report plot showing `content`.
- `fn profile_figure`: The Response Explorer as a figure: one panel per factor, side by side (wrapping after `columns`), each showing the predicted response with its confidence band as that factor varies, the factor's setting (vertical line or diamond) and the current prediction (dashed).
- `fn linked_profile_figure`: Linked Response Explorer rows as one figure: a row of panels per profile (every profile over the same factors), each row on its own vertical range, as on screen.
- `const PANE_HEADROOM`: Headroom (fraction of the fitted vertical range) added above a paned scatter plot for its pane headings, as the report view adds.
- `fn fishbone_figure`: A cause-and-effect diagram as a figure, laid out as on screen ([`CauseEffectDiagram::layout`]).
- `fn tree_figure`: A decision tree as a figure: one box per node shown (nodes for which `collapsed` is true hide their branches, as on screen) holding the rule leading to it, its count and prediction and, for a classification tree, a bar of class shares whose colours the key names.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_run.rs`

Run a saved report request: the one place that turns a [`SavedReport`]
into its title and sections, shared by the desktop application, project
reloading, scripts (`stat-script`) and the headless runner.

A report request is what a dialog produces and what a project file stores
(see [`crate::project`] for the JSON form). Running it is deterministic, so
the same request on the same data and row states gives identical sections
whether it came from a dialog, a project file or a script.

- `struct ComputedReport`: A report request together with what running it produced.
- `fn run_report`: Run `saved` on `table` with row states `rows`.
- `fn analysis_key`: The identifier of a report's analysis in project files and scripts, e.g.
- `fn graph_title`: Title of a graph report: "Y by X", with any panel split.
- `fn graph_page_size`: Page size of an exported graph, in points: 7.5 × 5 inches per panel row, up to a letter-size page.
- `fn graph_figure`: A graph canvas drawn as a vector figure (SVG, PDF or EPS) at its default view (every axis fitted to its data), titled with [`graph_title`] (or the graph's own title), with its right axis and axis breaks.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_scope.rs`

A report's own row filter and column picker.

Any report can carry a **row filter**: conditions on columns (ticked
levels of a categorical column, an interval of a continuous one) that a
row must all pass to enter the analysis. The filter never changes the
table's row states: the report is computed from a copy of them in which
rows outside the filter are also excluded and hidden
([`ReportScope::apply`]), so the data grid and every other report still
use those rows. Conditions name their columns, so they survive columns
being inserted or removed, and follow renames.

Reports with one response or process column (see
[`SavedReport::switch_slot`]) can also carry a **column picker**: a list
of columns to step the report through, one at a time, without opening its
dialog again. Switching changes the request's column and recomputes the
report; everything else in the request stays. A capability study's
specification limits belong to its column, so the scope keeps the limits
set for each column it has visited ([`ReportScope::spec_limits`]).

On a stacked table of multiple imputations
([`crate::multiple_imputation`]) a report can also be **pooled across
imputations** ([`ReportScope::pool`]): its usual sections are computed
from the original rows (imputation 0) only, and pooled sections
([`crate::pooling`]) computed from the completed copies come first.

All of these are kept with the request as [`SavedReport::Scoped`] and
stored in a project file as members of the report object: `"row_filter"`
(a list of conditions, each `{"column", "levels"}` or `{"column", "min",
"max"}`), `"column_switcher"` (column names), `"switcher_limits"`
(`[{"column", "lower", "upper", "target"}]`) and `"pool_imputations"`
(the name of the column numbering the imputations).

- `struct ReportScope`: A report's row filter and column picker.
- `fn plot_style_key`: The key of the `nth` plot (counting from 0) of the sections of kind `kind` in a report, under which [`ReportScope::plot_styles`] keeps its style, e.g.
- `fn contour_style_to_json`: The project-file form of a contour style: `fill`, `lines`, `labels`, `scale` (`"sequential"`, `"heat"`, `"spectrum"`, `"diverging"`, `"grey"`), `reverse`, `opacity`, and when set `levels`, `min` and `max` (a fixed range) and `centre`.
- `fn contour_style_from_json`: Read [`contour_style_to_json`]; members left out keep their defaults.
- `fn apply_mask`: A copy of `rows` with the rows where `keep` is `false` also excluded and hidden.
- `struct SwitchSlot`: The column a column picker changes in a report request.

### `crates/app-model/src/report_transfer.rs`

Running a report on another table.

"Duplicate on another table…" copies a report (or graph canvas) with its
display options and plot styles onto a different table. Reports refer to
columns by position or by name, so the copy is made through the
project-file form, which names every column: the report is written
against its own table ([`checked_report_to_json`]) and read back against
the target table with the target's columns renamed, for the moment, to
the names they stand in for ([`stage`]); name references are then turned
back into the target's own names ([`rename_back`]). Positions never
change, so the result refers to the target table exactly.

Which target column stands in for which source column is a
[`ColumnMapping`]: columns with the same name match by themselves, a
name differing only in case or spacing is offered, and the rest are
chosen by the user. Project templates ([`crate::project_template`])
use the same mapping.

- `enum ValueKind`: The kind of values a column holds, as a mapping describes it.
- `struct ColumnNeed`: A column a report or template reads, as it was on its own table.
- `fn report_needs`: Every column `report` reads on `table`, in table order.
- `struct ColumnMapping`: Which column of a target table stands in for each needed column.
- `fn duplicate_report`: `report`, written against `source`, read against `target` with each (source name, target name) pair of `pairs` standing in for each other.

### `crates/app-model/src/resampling.rs`

Bootstrap of any statistic a report shows (Efron & Tibshirani, *An
Introduction to the Bootstrap*, 1993): the report's request is re-run on
row-resampled copies of the data, and chosen numeric cells of one of its
tables are collected from each replicate.

The resampling is [`stat_inference::bootstrap`]'s: `B` resamples, each of
the `n` rows the report uses drawn with replacement (within each level of
an optional stratum column, keeping the levels' sizes), seeded per
replicate and run in parallel, so a seed reproduces the report exactly.
The rows used are the non-excluded rows with a value in every column the
report refers to. The BCa acceleration comes from the jackknife (the
report re-run `n` times with one row left out), computed only for up to
[`JACKKNIFE_LIMIT`] rows; above that the report gives percentile
intervals only.

Cells are read as the report shows them (the typographic minus and a
trailing `%` are understood), so the values carry the report's displayed
precision — typically five or six significant digits. A replicate whose
report fails, or whose cell is missing or not a number, is counted as
failed for that statistic and left out; the counts are reported.

- `const JACKKNIFE_LIMIT`: Largest number of rows for which the jackknife (and so the BCa interval) is computed: the jackknife re-runs the report once per row.
- `const MAX_REPLICATES`: Most replicates a bootstrap report may request.
- `struct BootstrapRequest`: A bootstrap of cells of one table of a report.
- `fn cell_value`: A report cell read as a number: the typographic minus becomes `-`, a trailing `%` is dropped; anything else that is not a finite number (a dash, `∞`, text) gives `None`.
- `fn numeric_cells`: Statistics that can be bootstrapped: `(row label, column heading)` of every numeric cell of `table` outside its first column, in table order.
- `fn can_bootstrap`: `true` when a report of this kind can be bootstrapped (it has tables computed from rows: not a graph, not a bootstrap itself, and not a report that uses no columns).
- `struct BootstrapStatistic`: One bootstrapped statistic.
- `struct BootstrapAnalysis`: A computed bootstrap report.

### `crates/app-model/src/robust_design.rs`

Robust (parameter) design with orthogonal arrays
([`stat_doe::orthogonal`]): creating an inner × outer array experiment as
a data table, and analysing it by signal-to-noise ratios.

The created table has one row per inner-array run (control-factor
settings) and one response column per outer-array run (noise conditions,
named in the column heading) or per replicate. The analysis takes any
table laid out that way: factor columns, and the columns holding each
run's repeated responses.

- `struct ArrayFactor`: A factor assigned to an array column: its name and level labels (their number must match the column's levels).
- `struct RobustDesignRequest`: Everything needed to create a robust-design table.
- `fn create_robust_design`: Build the robust-design table and a one-line description.
- `struct SignalToNoiseRequest`: A signal-to-noise analysis: each row is a run, with factor settings and repeated responses.
- `struct SignalToNoiseAnalysis`: A computed signal-to-noise analysis.

### `crates/app-model/src/scatter3d.rs`

The 3-D scatter plot (Visualize ▸ 3-D scatter plot…): rows placed by three
continuous columns in a rotatable box, with optional colour, size and
marker-shape channels and drop lines to the floor.

This module holds the GUI-independent part: which rows are plotted, their
positions and channel values, the axis ranges and the summary table. The
projection is [`crate::surface_profiler::Camera`]; the desktop view draws
the points back to front and handles rotation and brushing.

Rows with a missing position or channel value are left out. Excluded rows
are kept (front ends draw them hollow); hidden rows are for the front end
to leave out, as on the graph canvas.

- `struct Scatter3dRequest`: Columns of a 3-D scatter plot.
- `struct Scatter3dOptions`: Display options of a 3-D scatter plot (saved with the project).
- `fn scatter3d_to_json`: The project-file form (`"analysis": "scatter-3d"`).
- `fn scatter3d_from_json`: Read the project-file form.
- `enum ColorChannel`: What a point's colour shows.
- `enum ColorValue`: A point's value on the colour channel.
- `struct Scatter3dPoint`: One plotted row.
- `struct Scatter3dAnalysis`: The rows of a 3-D scatter plot and their channels.

### `crates/app-model/src/screening.rs`

Screening many responses: the same model fitted to each of many response
columns against the same factors, with every effect's p-values adjusted
across the responses for the false discovery rate ([`crate::fdr`]).

Each response uses the rows (not excluded) that have it and every factor.
The models, all with main effects only, are:

* **linear model** (least squares): each effect's partial F test (the
  increase in the residual sum of squares when its columns are dropped);
* **Poisson regression** (log link): each effect's likelihood-ratio test
  (drop in deviance, χ² on the effect's columns);
* **negative binomial regression** (log link, shape `θ` estimated, as
  MASS `glm.nb`): each effect's likelihood-ratio test with `θ` refitted
  in the reduced model;
* **Kruskal–Wallis** (one categorical factor): the tie-corrected `H` test.
