  estimates are `γ̂ = x₍₁₎`, `θ̂ = x̄ − x₍₁₎`; because the fitted
  distribution then gives the smallest value probability zero, the reported
  parameters are the unbiased estimates `θ* = n(x̄ − x₍₁₎)/(n − 1)`,
  `γ* = x₍₁₎ − θ*/n` (Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan, vol. 1, §19.4), while
  the log-likelihood (for AIC and the threshold test) is the maximum.
* Three-parameter forms: the profile log-likelihood
  `ℓ_p(γ) = max_{μ,σ} ℓ(γ, μ, σ)` is searched over `γ = x₍₁₎ − d`,
  `d = r·e^t` (`r` the sample range) on a grid of `t`, then refined by
  golden-section search. The likelihood of these families can grow without
  bound as `γ → x₍₁₎` (Weibull or gamma shape below one; Hill 1963 for the
  lognormal); the estimate is the largest **interior** local maximum
  (Cohen & Whitten 1980), and a fit with none is reported as failing.

#### Goodness of fit
The Anderson–Darling statistic with estimated parameters is
`A² = −n − (1/n) Σ (2i − 1)[ln F(x₍ᵢ₎) + ln(1 − F(x₍ₙ₊₁₋ᵢ₎))]`
(D'Agostino & Stephens, *Goodness-of-Fit Techniques*, 1986, ch. 4).
Its null distribution depends on the family and on which parameters were
estimated, so p-values come from:
* the normal: the published formula for the modified statistic
  `A*  = A²(1 + 0.75/n + 2.25/n²)` ([`crate::normality::anderson_darling`]);
* every other family: Monte Carlo simulation (a parametric bootstrap).
  For the location–scale and exponential families the statistic's null
  distribution does not depend on the parameter values, so it is simulated
  from the standard distribution once per family and sample size and
  cached; for the gamma and three-parameter families it depends on the
  shape, and samples are drawn from the fitted distribution. Samples are
  simulated at size `min(n, 250)`; beyond that the percentage points change
  by `O(1/n)` (Stephens 1974, *JASA* 69) and the published modifications
  for the normal, exponential, logistic and extreme-value families are
  applied to both sides of the comparison. The p-value is
  `(1 + #{A²_sim ≥ A²})/(B + 1)`.

The likelihood-ratio test of a threshold compares each three-parameter
form with its two-parameter form: `2(ℓ₃ − ℓ₂)` against χ²₁.

[`johnson_transformation`] chooses and fits a Johnson system transformation
to normality by the percentile method (Slifker & Shapiro 1980,
*Technometrics* 22; selection over the percentile spacing as in Chou,
Polansky & Mason 1998, *J. Quality Technology* 30).

- `enum FitFamily`: A family of continuous distributions that can be fitted to a sample.
- `struct FittedDistribution`: A fitted distribution.
- `struct NamedParameter`: One named parameter of a fitted distribution.
- `fn fit_distribution`: Fit `family` to `x` by maximum likelihood (see the module docs).
- `fn anderson_darling_statistic`: The Anderson–Darling statistic `A²` of sorted data against `dist` (`+∞` when a value lies outside the fitted support).
- `enum PValueMethod`: How an Anderson–Darling p-value was obtained.
- `struct AndersonDarling`: An Anderson–Darling goodness-of-fit test.
- `struct ThresholdTest`: A likelihood-ratio test of a threshold.
- `struct IdentifyOptions`: Options for [`identify_distribution`].
- `struct FamilyFit`: One family's fit and goodness of fit.
- `fn identify_distribution`: Fit each of `families` to `x` with its Anderson–Darling test and, for threshold forms, the likelihood-ratio test of the threshold.
- `enum JohnsonFamily`: A member of the Johnson system.
- `struct JohnsonTransformation`: A fitted Johnson transformation to normality.
- `fn johnson_transformation`: Choose and fit a Johnson transformation to normality: for each percentile spacing `z = 0.25, 0.26, …, 1.25` the Slifker–Shapiro percentile estimates pick the SB, SL or SU member from the quantile ratio `mn/p²` and fit it; among the fits that transform every value, the one whose transformed values…

### `crates/stat-core/src/distributions.rs`

Continuous sampling distributions used for inference.

All functions are written from their canonical definitions in terms of the
regularized incomplete beta function `I_x(a, b)` (DLMF §8.17; Abramowitz &
Stegun 26.5.27 and 26.6.2):

* Student's t with ν degrees of freedom, for `t ≥ 0`:
  `P(T > t) = ½ I_{ν/(ν+t²)}(ν/2, ½)`.
* Fisher–Snedecor F with (d₁, d₂) degrees of freedom:
  `P(F > f) = I_{d₂/(d₂+d₁f)}(d₂/2, d₁/2)`.

* Chi-square with k degrees of freedom:
  `P(X > x) = Q(k/2, x/2)`, the regularized upper incomplete gamma function.
* Normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ:
  `P(X > x) = ½ erfc((x − μ)/(σ√2))` (DLMF 7.18 / A&S 26.2.29).

Upper-tail probabilities are computed directly (never as `1 − cdf`) so that
small p-values keep full relative precision.

- `trait ContinuousDistribution`: Common interface for univariate continuous distributions.
- `struct StudentsT`: Student's t distribution with `ν > 0` degrees of freedom.
- `struct FisherSnedecor`: Fisher–Snedecor F distribution with `(d₁, d₂)` degrees of freedom.
- `struct Normal`: Normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean `μ` and standard deviation `σ > 0`.
- `struct ChiSquared`: Chi-square distribution with `k > 0` degrees of freedom.

### `crates/stat-core/src/eigen.rs`

Eigen-decompositions of small dense symmetric matrices (a few hundred
rows at most): covariance, correlation and SSCP matrices, and the
symmetric-definite generalized problems of multivariate analysis.

* [`symmetric_eigen`]: `A = V Λ Vᵀ` by cyclic Jacobi rotations (Golub &
  Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., §8.5). Jacobi is slower than
  tridiagonal QR but delivers small eigenvalues to high relative accuracy,
  which matters for nearly singular covariance matrices.
* [`generalized_symmetric_eigen`]: `A v = λ B v` with `A` symmetric and
  `B` symmetric positive definite, reduced to a standard problem through
  the Cholesky factor `B = L Lᵀ`: `(L⁻¹ A L⁻ᵀ) w = λ w`, `v = L⁻ᵀ w`
  (Golub & Van Loan §8.7.2). The eigenvectors are `B`-orthonormal:
  `Vᵀ B V = I`. This is the eigen-analysis of `E⁻¹H` in MANOVA and of
  `W⁻¹B` in canonical discriminant analysis.

Matrices are row vectors (`Vec<Vec<f64>>`, each inner vector a row).

- `fn symmetric_eigen`: Eigenvalues (largest first) and unit eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix.
- `fn generalized_symmetric_eigen`: Eigenvalues (largest first) and `B`-orthonormal eigenvectors of the symmetric-definite problem `A v = λ B v`.
- `fn cholesky`: Lower Cholesky factor `L` of a symmetric positive-definite matrix (`A = L Lᵀ`), or `None` when a pivot is at or below `1e-12` of the largest diagonal element.

### `crates/stat-core/src/error.rs`

Error type shared by every crate in the engine.

The variants are hand-written rather than derived with `thiserror` because the
build environment this was first written in had no access to crates.io. The
shape (one enum, `Display` + `std::error::Error`) is exactly what `thiserror`
would generate, so swapping it in later is a mechanical change.

- `enum StatError`: Every failure mode a statistical routine in this workspace can report.
- `type Result`: Convenience alias used throughout the workspace.

### `crates/stat-core/src/interrupt.rs`

Stopping a long computation from outside, and reporting its progress.

The application runs some analyses on background threads and lets the
user cancel them. It installs an [`Interrupt`] for the thread doing the
work with [`with`]; routines with long loops (trees of a forest, rounds of
boosting, sampler draws, resampling replicates) call [`check`] once per
iteration, which returns [`StatError::Cancelled`] once the interrupt is
set, and [`Interrupt::step`] to count progress. Without an installed
interrupt both cost one thread-local read and never stop anything, so the
routines behave exactly as before when called directly.

Loops that run on other threads (rayon) read the interrupt with
[`current`] before spreading out and check it themselves.

- `struct Interrupt`: A cancel flag and a progress count shared between a computation and the code that started it.
- `fn with`: Run `f` with `interrupt` installed for this thread (the previous one, if any, is put back afterwards, also when `f` panics).
- `fn current`: The interrupt installed for this thread, if any.
- `fn check`: `Err(Cancelled)` if this thread's computation was cancelled.
- `fn begin`: Start counting a stage of `total` steps on this thread's interrupt.
- `fn step`: Count one step on this thread's interrupt.

### `crates/stat-core/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-core

Numerical foundation of the statistical engine. Everything here is implemented
from published mathematical definitions (references are given in each module):

* [`matrix`] — a small column-major dense matrix used as the interchange type.
* [`summation`] — compensated sums and dot products (error-free transformations).
* [`qr`] — Householder QR with column pivoting, the basis of least squares.
* [`eigen`] — symmetric and symmetric-definite generalized eigenproblems (Jacobi).
* `svd` — singular value decomposition by one-sided Jacobi rotations.
* [`special`] — log-gamma, incomplete beta and gamma functions, `erfc`.
* [`box_cox`] — Box–Cox power transformation: profile likelihood, λ̂ and its confidence interval.
* [`distributions`] — normal, Student's t, chi-square and Fisher–Snedecor F.
* [`noncentral`] — noncentral t, chi-square and F (power calculations).
* [`studentized_range`] — the studentized range (multiple comparisons).
* [`discrete`] — binomial, Poisson and hypergeometric probabilities.
* [`catalog`] — every distribution above under one interface (density,
  probabilities, quantiles, moments, seeded random draws).
* [`quadrature`] — Gauss–Legendre integration rules.
* [`descriptive`] — moments, quantiles (Hyndman–Fan types 1–9), robust
  estimators, lag-1 autocorrelation.
* [`normality`] — Shapiro–Wilk and Anderson–Darling tests of normality.
* [`distribution_fit`] — maximum-likelihood fits of fourteen continuous
  families (with and without thresholds), Anderson–Darling goodness of fit
  with simulated p-values, and Johnson transformations to normality.
* [`ode`] — Dormand–Prince 5(4) adaptive Runge–Kutta solver with dense
  output for initial value problems (models defined by differential equations).
* [`rng`] — a seedable SplitMix64 generator (designs, random samples,
  normal and triangular draws for simulation).
* [`optimize`] — Nelder–Mead inside a box, Latin hypercube starts, and
  Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least squares.
* [`correlation`] — Pearson and Spearman correlation with inference.
* [`error`] — the [`StatError`] type shared by the workspace.

### `crates/stat-core/src/matrix.rs`

A minimal dense, column-major `f64` matrix.

Column-major storage is chosen because the dominant workloads (Householder QR,
least squares, per-variable statistics) walk down columns. The type is
deliberately small: it is the interchange format between crates, not a
general linear-algebra library. When a full backend such as `faer` is adopted,
conversion to and from this type is a single contiguous copy.

- `struct Matrix`: Dense matrix of `f64` stored in column-major order.

### `crates/stat-core/src/noncentral.rs`

Noncentral t, chi-square and F distributions, used for the power of t, F
and chi-square tests.

Each is evaluated as a Poisson mixture of central distributions, summed
outward from the largest Poisson weight until the remaining terms are
negligible (Johnson, Kotz & Balakrishnan, *Continuous Univariate
Distributions*, vol. 2, chs. 29–31):

* **Noncentral χ²** with `k` df and noncentrality `λ`:
  `P(X ≤ x) = Σⱼ e^{−λ/2}(λ/2)ʲ/j! · P(k/2 + j, x/2)` (regularized gamma).
* **Noncentral F** with `(d₁, d₂)` df and noncentrality `λ`:
  `P(F ≤ f) = Σⱼ e^{−λ/2}(λ/2)ʲ/j! · I_x(d₁/2 + j, d₂/2)`,
  `x = d₁f/(d₁f + d₂)`.
* **Noncentral t** with `ν` df and noncentrality `δ` (Lenth 1989, *Applied
  Statistics* 38, AS 243): for `t ≥ 0`, with `x = t²/(t² + ν)`,
  `P(T ≤ t) = Φ(−δ) + ½ Σⱼ [pⱼ I_x(j + ½, ν/2) + qⱼ I_x(j + 1, ν/2)]`,
  `pⱼ = e^{−δ²/2}(δ²/2)ʲ/j!`, `qⱼ = δ e^{−δ²/2}(δ²/2)ʲ / (√2 Γ(j + 3/2))`;
  for `t < 0`, `P(T ≤ t; δ) = 1 − P(T ≤ −t; −δ)`.

Upper tails are summed directly from upper-tail central probabilities where
the mixture allows it (χ², F), so small tail probabilities keep relative
precision.

- `struct NoncentralChiSquared`: Noncentral chi-square distribution.
- `struct NoncentralF`: Noncentral F distribution.
- `struct NoncentralT`: Noncentral t distribution.

### `crates/stat-core/src/normality.rs`

Tests of normality.

* **Shapiro–Wilk W** for `3 ≤ n ≤ 5000`, with the coefficient
  approximations and p-value transformation of Royston (1995), "Remark AS
  R94: A remark on algorithm AS 181: The W-test for normality", *Applied
  Statistics* 44(4), 547–551:
  * `mᵢ = Φ⁻¹((i − 3/8)/(n + 1/4))`, `u = 1/√n`;
  * `a_n = m_n/‖m‖ + 0.221157u − 0.147981u² − 2.071190u³ + 4.434685u⁴ − 2.706056u⁵`,
    and for `n > 5` also
    `a_{n−1} = m_{n−1}/‖m‖ + 0.042981u − 0.293762u² − 1.752461u³ + 5.682633u⁴ − 3.582633u⁵`;
    the remaining `aᵢ = mᵢ/√φ` with `φ` chosen so that `‖a‖ = 1`;
    antisymmetry `a_{n+1−i} = −aᵢ`;
  * `W = (Σ aᵢ x₍ᵢ₎)² / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²`;
  * p-value: for `n = 3` exactly `p = (6/π)(asin √W − asin √¾)`; for
    `4 ≤ n ≤ 11`, `z = (−ln(γ − ln(1 − W)) − μ)/σ` with `γ = 0.459n − 2.273`,
    `μ = 0.5440 − 0.39978n + 0.025054n² − 0.0006714n³`,
    `ln σ = 1.3822 − 0.77857n + 0.062767n² − 0.0020322n³`; for `n ≥ 12`,
    `z = (ln(1 − W) − μ)/σ` with `L = ln n`,
    `μ = −1.5861 − 0.31082L − 0.083751L² + 0.0038915L³`,
    `ln σ = −0.4803 − 0.082676L + 0.0030302L²`; `p = 1 − Φ(z)`.
* **Anderson–Darling A²** with mean and variance estimated from the sample
  (Stephens' "case 3"): `A² = −n − (1/n) Σ (2i − 1)[ln Φ(z₍ᵢ₎) + ln(1 − Φ(z₍ₙ₊₁₋ᵢ₎))]`,
  `zᵢ = (xᵢ − x̄)/s`. The p-value uses the modified statistic
  `A* = A²(1 + 0.75/n + 2.25/n²)` and the piecewise approximation of
  D'Agostino & Stephens (1986), *Goodness-of-Fit Techniques*, Table 4.9.

Small p-values are evidence against normality.

- `const SHAPIRO_WILK_MAX_N`: Largest sample size accepted by [`shapiro_wilk`] (the range over which Royston's approximations were fitted).
- `struct NormalityTest`: A normality test result.
- `fn shapiro_wilk`: Shapiro–Wilk test (Royston 1995).
- `fn anderson_darling`: Anderson–Darling test for normality with estimated mean and variance.

### `crates/stat-core/src/ode.rs`

Initial value problems for ordinary differential equations.

[`solve_initial_value`] solves `y' = g(x, y)`, `y(x₀) = y₀`, `y ∈ ℝᵐ`, at a
list of output points. It is used to fit models defined by differential
equations: the model is solved once per evaluation of the objective, at the
observed `x` values.

#### Method

The explicit Runge–Kutta pair of order 5(4) of Dormand & Prince (1980),
"A family of embedded Runge–Kutta formulae", *J. Comput. Appl. Math.*
6:19–26, implemented as described for the code DOPRI5 by Hairer, Nørsett &
Wanner, *Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I* (2nd ed., 1993), §II.4
and §II.5:

* **Local extrapolation and FSAL.** The step is advanced with the
  fifth-order solution; the embedded fourth-order solution only estimates
  the error. The last stage is evaluated at the new point, so it is the
  first stage of the next step ("first same as last"): six evaluations of
  `g` per accepted step.
* **Error norm.** With the error estimate `errᵢ = h Σⱼ eⱼ kⱼ,ᵢ` (`e = b − b̂`)
  and scale `scᵢ = atol + rtol · max(|y₀ᵢ|, |y₁ᵢ|)`, the step is accepted
  when `‖err‖ = √(m⁻¹ Σ (errᵢ/scᵢ)²) ≤ 1` (Hairer et al. eq. II.4.11).
* **Step-size control.** The PI (proportional–integral) controller of
  DOPRI5 (Hairer et al. §IV.2, eq. 2.43c, after Gustafsson 1991):
  `h_new = h · min(facmax, max(facmin, 0.9 · ‖err‖^{−α} · ‖err_old‖^{β}))`
  with `α = 1/5 − 0.75 β`, `β = 0.04`, safety factor 0.9, `facmin = 0.2`,
  `facmax = 10`, and `‖err_old‖` the norm of the previous accepted step
  (at least 10⁻⁴). After a rejection the step shrinks by
  `max(facmin, 0.9 ‖err‖^{−α})` and the following accepted step may not
  grow.
* **Initial step.** Unless one is given, the starting step comes from the
  algorithm of Hairer et al. §II.4 ("Starting step size", steps (a)–(f)):
  an explicit Euler step of size `h₀ = 0.01 ‖y₀‖/‖g(x₀, y₀)‖` estimates the
  second derivative, and `h₁ = (0.01 / max(‖y′‖, ‖y″‖))^{1/5}`;
  the start is `min(100 h₀, h₁)`.
* **Dense output.** Outputs that fall inside a step are interpolated with
  the continuous extension of order 4 of Hairer et al. §II.6 (the
  coefficients of Shampine 1986 used by DOPRI5), so output points never
  shorten the steps: asking for a thousand outputs costs the same number
  of steps as asking for the last one.

Outputs on both sides of `x₀` are allowed: the solver integrates forward
from `x₀` through the outputs above it and, separately, backward from `x₀`
through those below it.

The method is explicit, so it is meant for non-stiff problems. On a stiff
problem the step size collapses and the routine stops with a step-limit or
step-size error rather than returning an inaccurate answer.

- `struct OdeOptions`: Accuracy and work limits for [`solve_initial_value`].
- `type RightHandSide`: The right-hand side `g` of `y' = g(x, y)`: `rhs(x, y, dydx)` writes `g(x, y)` into `dydx` and returns `false` where `g` cannot be computed.
- `struct OdeSolution`: The solution of an initial value problem at the requested outputs.
- `fn solve_initial_value`: Solve the initial value problem `y' = g(x, y)`, `y(x₀) = y₀` at the points `outputs`, by the Dormand–Prince 5(4) method with adaptive steps and dense output (see the [module documentation](self) for the method and its references).

### `crates/stat-core/src/optimize/least_squares.rs`

Nonlinear least squares by Levenberg–Marquardt with Gauss–Newton steps.

#### Problem
Minimise `S(θ) = Σᵢ rᵢ(θ)²` over parameters `θ` (length `p`) inside an
optional box `lower ≤ θ ≤ upper`, for a residual vector `r(θ)` of length
`n ≥ p` with Jacobian `J = ∂r/∂θ` (`n × p`).

#### Method
Each iteration solves the damped linearised problem

```text
min_δ ‖ [ J ; √λ D ] δ + [ r ; 0 ] ‖²
```

by pivoted Householder QR of the augmented matrix (never forming `JᵀJ`).
`D` is diagonal with `Dⱼⱼ` the largest column norm `‖J·ⱼ‖` seen so far,
which makes the step invariant to the units of each parameter (Moré, "The
Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm: implementation and theory", *Lecture Notes
in Mathematics* 630, 1978). `λ = 0` is the Gauss–Newton step. A step that
lowers `S` is accepted and `λ` divided by 10 (down to exactly zero, so the
iterations end in pure Gauss–Newton steps and keep its quadratic rate on
small-residual problems); a step that does not is rejected and `λ`
multiplied by 10 (Marquardt, "An algorithm for least-squares estimation of
nonlinear parameters", *J. SIAM* 11, 1963).

The iterations start cautiously: `λ = 100` and steps no longer than the
scaled parameter vector, `‖Dδ‖ ≤ ‖Dθ‖` (a fixed trust region in the
spirit of Moré's step bound), which keeps a poor start from jumping into a
region where the model is flat in some parameter. If that run does not
converge, the iterations are repeated from the start with `λ = 10⁻³` and
unbounded steps, and the better result is kept.

#### Bounds
Trial points are projected onto the box. A parameter sitting on a bound
whose gradient component pushes it outward is held fixed for the step
(an active-set projected Gauss–Newton step); at the solution such
parameters are reported in [`LeastSquaresResult::at_bound`].

#### Convergence
The primary criterion is Bates & Watts' relative offset ("A relative
offset orthogonality convergence criterion for nonlinear least squares",
*Technometrics* 23, 1981): with `QᵀR` the QR of the Jacobian over the
free parameters and `k` their number,

```text
relative offset = √( ‖Q₁ᵀ r‖² / k ) / √( (‖r‖² − ‖Q₁ᵀ r‖²) / (n − k) )
```

— the length of the remaining Gauss–Newton increment in the expectation
plane relative to the residual standard error. It is scale free and
measures the distance from the minimum in statistical units rather than
the change between iterations. Two further criteria cover cases where it
is undefined: an exactly zero residual sum of squares, and (when `n = k`)
a relative parameter change below [`LeastSquaresOptions::step_tolerance`].
Very close to the minimum the decrease of `S` a step achieves can fall
below the rounding error of `S` itself; when no damped step then lowers
`S` and the offset is already below 10⁻³, plain Gauss–Newton steps are
taken while `S` stays within its rounding error and the offset keeps
halving, and a final offset below 10⁻⁵ counts as converged.

#### Derivatives
[`LeastSquaresProblem::jacobian`] may supply analytic derivatives; when it
returns `None` they are computed by central differences with step
`hⱼ = ε^{1/3}·max(|θⱼ|, 10⁻⁸)` (one-sided with step `ε^{1/2}·max(|θⱼ|, 10⁻⁸)`
next to a bound or where the residuals are undefined on one side), see
[`numeric_jacobian`].

- `trait LeastSquaresProblem`: A residual vector and (optionally) its Jacobian, the input of [`levenberg_marquardt`].
- `struct ResidualFn`: A [`LeastSquaresProblem`] from a residual closure (numeric derivatives).
- `struct LeastSquaresOptions`: Settings of [`levenberg_marquardt`].
- `enum Termination`: Why [`levenberg_marquardt`] stopped.
- `enum BoundState`: Which bound, if any, a parameter ends on.
- `struct LeastSquaresResult`: The result of [`levenberg_marquardt`].
- `fn numeric_jacobian`: Central-difference Jacobian of `problem`'s residuals at `theta` into `out` (`n × p`), respecting the box (`lower`/`upper`, empty for none); `r0` are the residuals at `theta`.
- `fn levenberg_marquardt`: Minimise `Σ rᵢ(θ)²` from `start` by Levenberg–Marquardt with Gauss–Newton steps (see the module documentation for the method, bounds and convergence criteria).

### `crates/stat-core/src/optimize.rs`

Derivative-free minimisation inside a box, and space-filling start points.

* [`minimize_in_box`]: Nelder–Mead (Nelder & Mead, "A simplex method for
  function minimization", *Computer Journal* 7, 1965) with the standard
  coefficients (reflection 1, expansion 2, contraction ½, shrink ½),
  every trial point projected onto the box, and restarts from the best
  point found until a restart no longer improves it (a common remedy for a
  simplex that collapses early; Kelley, *Iterative Methods for
  Optimization*, 1999, §8.1).
* [`latin_hypercube`]: a random Latin hypercube sample of the unit cube
  (McKay, Beckman & Conover, *Technometrics* 21, 1979): each coordinate's
  `n` values fall one in each of `n` equal strata, so a few starts already
  spread across every factor's range.
* [`levenberg_marquardt`]: nonlinear least squares (Levenberg–Marquardt
  with Gauss–Newton steps, bounds, Bates & Watts' relative offset
  convergence criterion, analytic or central-difference derivatives); see
  [`least_squares`].

- `struct BoxMinimum`: The best point a search found.
- `fn minimize_in_box`: Minimise `f` over the box `lower ≤ x ≤ upper`, starting from `x0`, with at most `max_evaluations` evaluations of `f`.
- `fn latin_hypercube`: `n` points of a random Latin hypercube in `[0, 1)^dims`, from `rng`: for each coordinate the points take one value in each interval `[k/n, (k+1)/n)`, in random order and at a random place inside it.

### `crates/stat-core/src/qr.rs`

Householder QR factorization with column pivoting.

#### Method
For an `n × p` matrix `A` with `n ≥ p`, the factorization is

```text
A P = Q R
```

where `P` is a column permutation, `Q` is orthogonal (`n × n`, stored implicitly
as `p` Householder reflectors `Hₖ = I − τₖ vₖ vₖᵀ`) and `R` is `p × p` upper
triangular with non-increasing `|Rₖₖ|`. At each step the remaining column with
the largest trailing 2-norm is moved into position (Businger & Golub, 1965,
"Linear least squares solutions by Householder transformations",
Numer. Math. 7). Trailing norms are recomputed rather than down-dated, which
costs the same asymptotic `O(n p²)` as the factorization and avoids the
cancellation that makes norm down-dating unreliable.

Householder QR is backward stable: the computed factors are the exact factors
of `A + δA` with `‖δA‖ ≤ c·n·p·ε‖A‖` (Higham, *Accuracy and Stability of
Numerical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., §19). Least-squares solutions computed from it
avoid the squaring of the condition number incurred by the normal equations.

#### Numerical rank
The pivoting makes the diagonal of `R` rank-revealing in practice: the numerical
rank is the number of `|Rₖₖ|` exceeding `tol · |R₀₀|`. Callers should scale the
columns of `A` to comparable norms first, otherwise a column that is merely
measured in small units can be mistaken for a linearly dependent one.

- `fn norm2`: Euclidean norm computed with scaling to avoid spurious overflow/underflow.
- `struct QrDecomposition`: The result of factoring `A P = Q R`.

### `crates/stat-core/src/quadrature.rs`

Gauss–Legendre and Gauss–Hermite quadrature.

The `n`-point rule integrates polynomials of degree `2n − 1` exactly on
`[−1, 1]`. Nodes are the roots of the Legendre polynomial `Pₙ`, found by
Newton's method from the Chebyshev-like starting values
`cos(π(i − ¼)/(n + ½))`, with weights `2 / ((1 − x²) Pₙ'(x)²)`
(Abramowitz & Stegun 25.4.29; Davis & Rabinowitz, *Methods of Numerical
Integration*, §2.7). Composite rules split `[a, b]` into equal panels.

- `fn gauss_legendre`: Nodes and weights of the `n`-point Gauss–Legendre rule on `[−1, 1]`, nodes in increasing order.
- `fn gauss_hermite`: Nodes and weights of the `n`-point Gauss–Hermite rule for `∫ f(x) e^{−x²} dx` over the real line, nodes in increasing order.
- `struct CompositeRule`: A composite Gauss–Legendre rule: `panels` equal sub-intervals, each with the same `n`-point rule.

### `crates/stat-core/src/ranking.rs`

Ranks with a choice of rule for tied values.

The values are put in ascending order (missing values, NaN, get no rank)
and numbered 1, 2, …, n. A run of equal values spanning positions
`i + 1, …, j + 1` is ranked by the [`TieRule`]:

| rule | rank of every value in the run |
|---|---|
| average | `(i + j)/2 + 1`, the mean of the positions |
| minimum | `i + 1` (competition ranking, "1 2 2 4") |
| maximum | `j + 1` ("1 3 3 4") |
| dense | one more than the number of distinct smaller values ("1 2 2 3") |
| first | the positions themselves, in row order ("1 2 3 4") |

These are the standard definitions (Kendall & Gibbons, *Rank Correlation
Methods*, 5th ed., §3.1, for mid-ranks; the others as in common
statistical software).

- `enum TieRule`: How tied values are ranked (see the module documentation).
- `fn ranks_with_ties`: Ranks of `x` from 1 under `rule`; NaN values get NaN and are not counted.

### `crates/stat-core/src/rng.rs`

A seedable pseudo-random generator: SplitMix64 (Steele, Lea & Flood 2014,
"Fast splittable pseudorandom number generators", *OOPSLA*), shared by
experimental designs (run-order randomization, exchange starts) and
random sampling of table rows.

- `struct Rng`: A small, fast, seedable generator (SplitMix64; Steele, Lea & Flood 2014), so designs, randomizations and random samples are reproducible from their seed.
- `fn triangular_quantile`: Quantile `u ∈ [0, 1]` of the triangular distribution on `[low, high]` with mode `mode`: `low + √(u (high − low)(mode − low))` below `F(mode) = (mode − low)/(high − low)`, `high − √((1 − u)(high − low)(high − mode))` above.

### `crates/stat-core/src/special.rs`

Special functions needed by the probability distributions.

* [`ln_gamma`] — Lanczos approximation (Lanczos 1964, SIAM J. Numer. Anal. B 1)
  with the widely published `g = 7`, nine-term coefficient set; relative error
  about 1e-15 for `x > 0`. The reflection formula covers `x < 0.5`.
* [`ln_beta`] — `ln Γ(a) + ln Γ(b) − ln Γ(a + b)`.
* [`stirling_error`], [`saddle_deviance`] — the pieces of Loader's (2000)
  saddle-point form of `ln Γ`, "Fast and accurate computation of binomial
  probabilities". Writing `ln Γ(x + 1) = (x + ½) ln x − x + ½ ln 2π + δ(x)`
  keeps the large, cancelling terms of order `x ln x` out of densities and
  of the incomplete gamma and beta prefactors, which the incomplete
  functions, [`gamma_prefactor`], [`beta_prefactor`] and
  [`ln_gamma_difference`] use for parameters of 10 or more. Plain `ln Γ`
  differences lose about `x · 10⁻¹⁶` absolutely, so relative accuracy fell
  to 1e-10 at `x ≈ 10⁶` and 1e-6 at `x ≈ 10¹⁰`.
* [`regularized_incomplete_beta`] — `I_x(a, b)` evaluated with the continued
  fraction of DLMF §8.17(v), eq. 8.17.22, using the modified Lentz algorithm
  (Thompson & Barnett 1986, J. Comput. Phys. 64), and the symmetry
  `I_x(a, b) = 1 − I_{1−x}(b, a)` to stay in the rapidly converging region
  `x < (a + 1)/(a + b + 2)`.
* [`regularized_gamma_p`] / [`regularized_gamma_q`] — the regularized incomplete
  gamma functions, by the power series of DLMF 8.11.4 for `x < a + 1` and the
  continued fraction of DLMF 8.9.2 (modified Lentz) otherwise, so that the
  smaller of `P` and `Q` is always computed directly, without cancellation.
* [`erfc`] — the complementary error function, `erfc(x) = Q(1/2, x²)` for
  `x ≥ 0` (DLMF 7.11.2).
* [`digamma`] / [`trigamma`] — `ψ(x) = d ln Γ(x)/dx` and `ψ′(x)`, by the
  recurrences `ψ(x) = ψ(x + 1) − 1/x`, `ψ′(x) = ψ′(x + 1) + 1/x²` up to
  `x ≥ 10` (20 for `ψ′`) and then the asymptotic series of DLMF 5.15.8 and 5.11.2.

- `fn ln_gamma`: Natural logarithm of `|Γ(x)|`.
- `fn ln_beta`: `ln B(a, b) = ln Γ(a) + ln Γ(b) − ln Γ(a + b)` for `a, b > 0`.
- `fn stirling_error`: Remainder of Stirling's approximation, `δ(x) = ln Γ(x + 1) − [(x + ½) ln x − x + ½ ln 2π]`, for `x > 0`.
- `fn saddle_deviance`: Deviance term `D(x; m) = x ln(x/m) + m − x ≥ 0` of a Poisson count `x` against mean `m` (Loader 2000, `bd0`), for `x ≥ 0`, `m > 0`.
- `fn ln_gamma_difference`: `ln Γ(x + d) − ln Γ(x)` for `x > 0`, `x + d > 0`, without the cancellation of two large `ln Γ` values.
- `fn poisson_probability`: Poisson probability `mᵏ e⁻ᵐ / Γ(k + 1)` for real `k ≥ 0` and `m > 0`.
- `fn gamma_prefactor`: `xᵃ e⁻ˣ / Γ(a)`, the factor in front of the incomplete gamma series and continued fraction, for `a > 0`, `x > 0`: `a` times [`poisson_probability`]`(a, x)`.
- `fn beta_prefactor`: `xᵃ yᵇ / B(a, b)` with `y = 1 − x`, the factor in front of the incomplete beta continued fraction, for `a, b > 0` and `0 < x < 1`.
- `fn regularized_incomplete_beta`: Regularized incomplete beta function `I_x(a, b) = (1 / B(a, b)) ∫₀ˣ t^{a−1} (1 − t)^{b−1} dt`.
- `fn regularized_incomplete_beta_pair`: [`regularized_incomplete_beta`] with `y = 1 − x` supplied by the caller.
- `fn regularized_gamma_p`: Regularized lower incomplete gamma function `P(a, x) = γ(a, x) / Γ(a)`.
- `fn regularized_gamma_q`: Regularized upper incomplete gamma function `Q(a, x) = Γ(a, x) / Γ(a) = 1 − P(a, x)`.
- `fn erfc`: Complementary error function `erfc(x) = (2/√π) ∫ₓ^∞ e^{−t²} dt`.
- `fn digamma`: Digamma function `ψ(x) = Γ′(x)/Γ(x)` for `x > 0` (NaN otherwise).
- `fn trigamma`: Trigamma function `ψ′(x)` for `x > 0` (NaN otherwise).
- `fn lambert_w`: Lambert W function, principal branch `W₀(x)`: the solution `w ≥ −1` of `w·eʷ = x` for `x ≥ −1/e` (NaN below −1/e and for NaN).
- `fn wright_omega`: Wright omega function `ω(z) = W₀(eᶻ)`: the solution `w > 0` of `w + ln w = z` for real `z`.

### `crates/stat-core/src/studentized_range.rs`

The studentized range distribution, used for Tukey–Kramer and Games–Howell
multiple comparisons.

For `k` independent standard normal variables with range `R` and an
independent `S = √(χ²_ν / ν)`, `Q = R / S`. The range distribution is

```text
W(w; k) = P(R ≤ w) = k ∫ φ(z) [Φ(z) − Φ(z − w)]^{k−1} dz,
```

and `P(Q ≤ q) = ∫₀^∞ f_S(s) W(qs; k) ds` with
`f_S(s) = 2 (ν/2)^{ν/2} s^{ν−1} e^{−νs²/2} / Γ(ν/2)` (Hartley 1942;
Copenhaver & Holland 1988, *J. Statist. Comput. Simul.* 30). Both integrals
are evaluated by composite Gauss–Legendre quadrature; the outer one over the
central `1 − 2·10⁻¹⁴` of `S`, in the variable `u = ln s` (density
`s·f_S(s)`), so that for few degrees of freedom the far tail of `Q`, which
comes from very small `s`, is resolved as well as the centre. For
`ν > 10⁶` the factor `S` is taken as 1. Inside the outer integral the
range distribution `W` is evaluated by barycentric interpolation at
Chebyshev–Lobatto points on `[0, w₁]`, where `2k·Φ(−w₁/2) = 10⁻¹⁷` bounds
`1 − W(w₁)`; `W` is entire, so the interpolant is accurate to rounding
and each CDF costs a few hundred interpolations instead of tens of
thousands of normal probabilities.
Quantiles are found by safeguarded secant iteration on the CDF.

- `struct StudentizedRange`: Studentized range distribution with `k` means and `ν` error degrees of freedom.

### `crates/stat-core/src/summation.rs`

Accurate floating-point summation and dot products.

Statistical results such as residual sums of squares are sums of many terms of
mixed magnitude, where naive accumulation can lose most significant digits.
These routines use error-free transformations so the result is as accurate as
if it had been computed in roughly twice the working precision and then rounded.

* `two_sum` — Knuth's error-free addition: `a + b = s + e` exactly.
* `two_prod` — error-free multiplication via fused multiply-add:
  `a · b = p + e` exactly.
* [`sum`] — Neumaier's improved Kahan–Babuška summation.
* [`dot`] — the `Dot2` algorithm of Ogita, Rump & Oishi (2005),
  "Accurate sum and dot product", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 26(6).

- `fn sum`: Compensated sum of `values` (Neumaier's algorithm).
- `fn sum_iter`: Compensated sum of an iterator of values.
- `fn dot`: Compensated dot product `Σ aᵢ bᵢ` (`Dot2`).
- `fn mean`: Compensated arithmetic mean.

### `crates/stat-core/src/svd.rs`

Singular value decomposition by one-sided Jacobi rotations.

For an `m × n` matrix `A` the thin SVD is `A = U Σ Vᵀ` with `U` (`m × r`)
and `V` (`n × r`) having orthonormal columns, `r = min(m, n)`, and singular
values `σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ σᵣ ≥ 0`.

#### Method
Hestenes' one-sided Jacobi method (Hestenes 1958; Demmel & Veselić 1992,
"Jacobi's method is more accurate than QR", *SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl.* 13):
plane rotations are applied to pairs of columns of `A` until every pair is
orthogonal to working precision (`|aᵢᵀaⱼ| ≤ ε √(aᵢᵀaᵢ · aⱼᵀaⱼ)`); the rotations
accumulate into `V`, the final column norms are the singular values, and the
normalized columns form `U`. The method computes small singular values to
high relative accuracy and is simple to verify. For `m < n` the transpose is
decomposed. Cost is `O(m n² · sweeps)`, with typically 6–10 sweeps.

- `struct Svd`: Thin singular value decomposition `A = U Σ Vᵀ`.
- `fn svd`: Compute the thin SVD of `a`.

### `crates/stat-core/src/text.rs`

Small helpers for writing mathematical notation in report text.

- `fn superscript`: `text` in superscript characters (digits, signs, parentheses and `n`), for exponents such as `2⁽⁵⁻¹⁾` or `x²`.

Test files: `distribution_fit/tests.rs`.

Integration tests: `extreme_arguments.rs`, `large_parameters.rs`.

## Crate `stat-data` (`crates/stat-data`)

Tabular data and shared row state (selection, exclusion, hiding, color) for the statistical engine.

Dependencies: `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-data/src/delimited.rs`

Delimited text (CSV, tab-separated, semicolon- or pipe-separated): reading
with delimiter detection and column type inference, and writing.

#### Reading
* The first record is the header.
* Fields may be quoted with `"`; a doubled `""` inside quotes is a literal
  quote, and quoted fields may contain delimiters and line breaks (RFC 4180).
* Line endings may be `\n` or `\r\n`; a leading byte-order mark is ignored.
* A field is *blank* if it is empty or a missing marker such as `NA`,
  `N/A`, `NaN` or `null` ([`crate::table::MISSING_MARKERS`], the defaults
  of pandas' `read_csv`). A column is numeric if every non-blank field
  parses as a number; blank fields in a numeric column become `NaN`
  (missing). Otherwise it is a date-time column if every non-blank field
  reads as a date, a time of day or an ISO 8601 duration
  ([`crate::temporal::detect_column`]); otherwise it is text, and keeps
  every field (markers included) as written.
* [`detect_delimiter`] picks the candidate (comma, tab, semicolon, pipe) that
  splits the first lines into the same number of fields (more than one).

#### Writing
Fields that contain the delimiter, a quote or a line break are quoted; numbers
are written in Rust's shortest round-trip form, so reading the file back
reproduces every value exactly. Date-time values are written as ISO 8601
text ([`crate::temporal::TemporalDisplay::iso_text`]). Missing values are
written as empty fields.

- `const CANDIDATE_DELIMITERS`: Delimiters tried by [`detect_delimiter`], in order of preference on ties.
- `fn read_csv`: Parse CSV (comma-separated) text into a [`DataTable`] named `name`.
- `fn read_delimited`: Parse delimited text into a [`DataTable`].
- `fn read_delimited_with_notes`: [`read_delimited`], also returning notes about how values were read (see [`table_from_records_with_notes`]).
- `fn table_from_records`: Build a table from a header and rows of text fields, inferring each column's type as described in the module documentation.
- `fn table_from_records_with_notes`: [`table_from_records`], also returning one note per column whose slash dates (such as `03/04/2026`) could be read either way round and were read month first, one per number or date column in which missing markers such as `NA` were read as missing, and one listing renamed header names.
- `fn unique_names`: Column names made usable: surrounding spaces are trimmed, a blank name becomes `Column N` (its 1-based position) and a repeated name gets a ` (2)`, ` (3)`, … suffix, so every name is non-empty and unique.
- `fn renamed_note`: The note shown when [`unique_names`] had to rename blank or repeated names (`None` when every name was kept, apart from trimming).
- `fn month_first_note`: The note shown when a column's slash dates were read month first because the values allowed either order.
- `fn missing_markers_note`: The note shown when `count` missing markers in `column` were read as missing values.
- `fn detect_delimiter`: The delimiter that splits the first lines of `text` most consistently: every record has the same number of fields, more than one, preferring more fields and then the order of [`CANDIDATE_DELIMITERS`].
- `fn write_delimited`: Render `table` as delimited text with a header row, `\n` line endings, and a trailing newline.
- `fn parse_records`: Split delimited text into records of fields, following the quoting rules in the module documentation.

### `crates/stat-data/src/json.rs`

A small JSON (RFC 8259) value model, parser and writer, plus conversion
between [`DataTable`]s and JSON arrays of row objects.

#### Values
[`JsonValue`] keeps object members in document order (a `Vec` of pairs), so
a file that is read and written again keeps its layout. Numbers are `f64`.

#### Tables as JSON
A table is written as an array with one object per row, keyed by column
name in column order: `[{"x": 1.5, "group": "a"}, …]`. Missing numeric and
date-time values are written as `null`; date-time values as ISO 8601
strings. On reading, the columns are the union of the keys in first-seen
order; a key absent from a row is a missing value. A column is numeric if
every non-null value is a number; date-time if every non-null value is a
string that reads as a date, time of day or duration
([`crate::temporal::detect_column`]); otherwise text (numbers, booleans and
nested values are rendered as text).

#### Numbers
Numbers are written in the shortest form that reads back to the same
`f64` ([`format_number`]), so a write–read round trip is exact.
Non-finite numbers have no JSON form and are written as `null`.

- `enum JsonValue`: A JSON value.
- `fn parse_json`: Parse JSON text into a [`JsonValue`].
- `fn write_json_table`: Write `table` as a JSON array of row objects (see the module documentation), one row per line.
- `fn read_json_table`: Read a table written as a JSON array of row objects.
- `fn table_from_json_rows`: A table from JSON row objects, typed as [`read_json_table`] types them.
- `fn flatten_object`: An object with nested objects flattened into dotted member names: `{"a": {"b": 1, "c": {"d": 2}}, "e": 3}` becomes `{"a.b": 1, "a.c.d": 2, "e": 3}`.

### `crates/stat-data/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-data

Data shared by every view of the application:

* [`table`] — a columnar [`DataTable`] with measurement levels.
* [`row_state`] — the [`RowStateManager`] that owns selection, exclusion,
  hiding and color for every row, the single source of truth for linked
  brushing across views.
* [`delimited`] — delimited text (CSV, tab, semicolon, pipe) reading with
  delimiter detection and type inference, and writing.
* [`json`] — a small JSON value model with a parser and writer, and
  conversion between tables and JSON arrays of row objects.
* [`table_ops`] — sort, remove duplicates, subset and sample, combine
  rows, join, stack, unstack, transpose and summarize by group.
* [`temporal`] — dates, times of day and durations: calendar arithmetic,
  ISO 8601 parsing and formatting, spreadsheet serial dates.

### `crates/stat-data/src/row_state.rs`

Shared per-row state: selection, exclusion, hiding and display color.

Every view of a dataset (data grid, plots, reports) reads row state from one
[`RowStateManager`], and every interaction that changes it writes back to the
same manager. Views redraw from the manager each frame, so a selection made in
one place is immediately visible everywhere — the linked-brushing model of
Becker & Cleveland (1987), "Brushing Scatterplots", *Technometrics* 29(2).

The three boolean states are independent:

* **Selected** — highlighted in every view; the target of row commands.
* **Excluded** — omitted from analyses (models are refit without the row), but
  still shown in the data grid and drawn in plots with a distinct marker.
* **Hidden** — not drawn in plots, but still shown in the data grid and still
  used by analyses unless also excluded.

Rows can also belong to **named subsets** (up to [`MAX_SUBSETS`]), saved
groups of rows to switch between. While a subset is active, the rows
outside it count as excluded and hidden ([`RowStateManager::is_excluded`],
[`RowStateManager::is_hidden`]), so every analysis and plot follows the
subset; the rows' own exclusion and hiding are kept underneath
([`RowState`], [`RowStateManager::is_excluded_flag`]) and come back when
the subset is switched off.

- `struct RowColor`: An sRGB display color assigned to a row.
- `enum RowMarker`: A marker shape assigned to a row, so rows coloured by a column's levels are told apart without colour too.
- `enum SelectionMode`: How a new selection combines with the current one.
- `struct RowState`: Snapshot of one row's state.
- `struct RowCounts`: Row totals for status displays.
- `const MAX_SUBSETS`: Most named subsets a table can have.
- `struct RowStateManager`: Owner of the selection, exclusion, hidden and color state of every row.

### `crates/stat-data/src/table.rs`

In-memory columnar data table.

Each column is stored contiguously and carries a measurement level (Stevens
1946, "On the theory of scales of measurement", *Science* 103). Missing
numeric and date-time values are `NaN`; missing text values are empty
strings. Date-time columns hold seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 UTC (see
[`crate::temporal`]), so they read as numbers wherever an analysis needs
one and show as dates wherever a value is displayed.

This is a deliberately small, dependency-free store. `CLAUDE.md` names Polars /
Arrow as the long-term backing; the public API here (named columns, typed
column slices, row count) is shaped so that a Polars-backed implementation can
replace it without changing callers.

- `enum MeasurementLevel`: Level of measurement of a column, which determines the analyses it can enter.
- `enum ColumnData`: Column storage.
- `const MISSING_MARKERS`: Text that marks a missing value in number and date columns: the default missing-value markers of pandas' `read_csv` (`na_values`), matched exactly after trimming surrounding spaces.
- `fn is_missing_marker`: `true` if `text` (trimmed) is one of [`MISSING_MARKERS`].
- `fn format_number`: Shortest text that reads back as exactly `x`: plain decimal notation for magnitudes in `[1e-5, 1e16)` (and zero), scientific notation otherwise, so that neither `1e300` nor `2.5e-300` expands to hundreds of digits.
- `enum CellValue`: One cell's value, as stored: a number (`NaN` for missing) or text (empty for missing).
- `enum ColumnKind`: The storage type of a column.
- `struct Column`: A named column with its measurement level.
- `struct DataTable`: A rectangular table of named columns.
- `fn is_permutation`: `true` if `order` holds each of `0..n` exactly once.

### `crates/stat-data/src/table_ops.rs`

Table operations: each takes one or more tables and builds a new one,
leaving the sources untouched.

* **Rows** — [`sorted`] (several keys, stable, missing values last),
  [`without_duplicates`], [`subset`] (rows and columns) and [`sample_rows`]
  (simple or stratified random samples, seeded).
* **Merge** — [`combine_rows`] (concatenate tables, matching columns by
  name) and [`join`] (inner, left, right and full outer joins on key
  columns).
* **Reshape** — [`stack`] (wide → long), [`unstack`] (long → wide) and
  [`transpose`].
* **Summaries** — [`summarize`]: statistics of columns by group.

Joins, selection and projection follow the relational algebra of Codd
(1970), "A relational model of data for large shared data banks",
*Communications of the ACM* 13(6), with the SQL (ISO/IEC 9075) rules for
outer joins: a missing key never matches anything, and rows without a
partner are padded with missing values. Stacking and unstacking follow the
long/wide reshaping of Wickham (2014), "Tidy data", *Journal of Statistical
Software* 59(10). Random samples use selection sampling (Knuth, *The Art of
Computer Programming* vol. 2, 3rd ed., §3.4.2, Algorithm S), which keeps
the rows in their original order; stratified samples allocate the total in
proportion to stratum size (Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., ch. 5)
with largest-remainder rounding so the stratum counts add up exactly.

Every operation returns a [`Derived`] table that records, for each result
row, the single source row it came from when there is exactly one (so row
states can follow), and notes about anything the caller should be told
(type changes, rows left out, renamed columns).

Values are compared as follows everywhere: numbers and date-times by value
(`-0` equals `0`), text exactly; a missing value is `NaN` or blank text.
For grouping and duplicate detection two missing values are equal; for
join keys they never are.

- `fn natural_order`: Order labels numerically when both are numbers, otherwise as text; numbers come before text.
- `struct RowOrigin`: The source row a result row was copied from.
- `struct Derived`: A table built by an operation.
- `struct SortKey`: One sort key.
- `fn sort_order`: The row order that sorts `table` by `keys`: entry `i` is the source row that goes to position `i`.
- `fn sorted`: `table` sorted by `keys` (see [`sort_order`]).
- `fn duplicate_rows`: Rows that repeat an earlier row on `columns` (all columns when empty), ascending.
- `fn without_duplicates`: `table` without the rows [`duplicate_rows`] finds.
- `fn subset`: The given `rows` (in that order) and `columns` (in that order) of `table`.
- `enum SampleSize`: How many rows a random sample takes.
- `fn sample_rows`: A random sample of the `eligible` rows of `table`, ascending.
- `fn combine_rows`: The rows of `tables` one after another, matching columns by name.
- `enum JoinKind`: Which rows a join keeps.
- `enum Relationship`: What the join expects of its keys; a violation stops the join.
- `fn join`: Join `left` and `right` on pairs of key columns `(left, right)`.
- `fn stack`: Wide → long: the chosen `columns` become two columns, `label_name` (the column each value came from, as text) and `value_name` (the value).
- `fn unstack`: Long → wide: one row per combination of the `ids` columns (in order of first appearance; two missing values match) and, for each `values` column, one column per level of `label` (levels in natural order).
- `fn transpose`: Rows ↔ columns: each chosen column becomes a row and each row a column.
- `enum Statistic`: A statistic [`summarize`] can compute for each group.
- `struct SummarizeOptions`: What [`summarize`] computes.
- `fn summarize`: Statistics of `columns` for each group of `rows` (the rows to use, e.g.

### `crates/stat-data/src/temporal.rs`

Dates, times of day and durations.

A date-time column stores `f64` seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 UTC (the
POSIX epoch; IEEE Std 1003.1, "Seconds Since the Epoch"), with `NaN` for a
missing value. Like POSIX time, the scale has no leap seconds: every day is
86 400 s long, so `23:59:60` is rejected. Whole seconds are exact for
±2⁵³ s (about ±285 million years); near the present the resolution is about
0.24 µs. Storing seconds as `f64` keeps date columns on the same numeric
path as every other continuous column (fits, smoothers, axes).

Calendar arithmetic is the proleptic Gregorian calendar of ISO 8601,
implemented with the public-domain `days_from_civil` / `civil_from_days`
algorithms of H. Hinnant, "chrono-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms".

Text forms follow ISO 8601-1:2019 and its RFC 3339 profile; spreadsheet
serial dates follow ECMA-376 Part 1 §18.17.4 (the 1900 and 1904 date
systems).

Each column has a [`TemporalDisplay`]: what the values are (calendar date,
date-time, time of day, duration), how many fractional-second digits to
show, and a fixed offset from UTC in minutes at which dates and times are
shown. Values are always stored in UTC; the offset changes only display.

- `const SECONDS_PER_DAY`: Seconds in a day.
- `const MAX_FRACTION_DIGITS`: Largest number of fractional-second digits shown or written.
- `const MAX_OFFSET_MINUTES`: Largest offset from UTC accepted, in minutes (±18:00).
- `enum TemporalFormat`: What the values of a date-time column represent.
- `struct TemporalDisplay`: How a date-time column shows its values.
- `fn days_from_civil`: Days from 1970-01-01 to the proleptic Gregorian date `year-month-day` (negative before 1970).
- `fn civil_from_days`: The proleptic Gregorian date `(year, month, day)` that is `days` days after 1970-01-01.
- `fn is_leap_year`: `true` for a Gregorian leap year.
- `fn days_in_month`: Number of days in `month` (1–12) of `year`.
- `fn is_valid_date`: `true` if `year-month-day` is a real calendar date.
- `fn seconds_from_civil`: Seconds since the epoch of the date-time `year-month-day hh:mm:ss` in UTC.
- `fn swap_day_month`: The same instant with its month and day exchanged, keeping the time of day, as seen at `offset_minutes` from UTC: 2026-03-04 10:00 becomes 2026-04-03 10:00.
- `fn from_spreadsheet_serial`: Seconds since the epoch for a spreadsheet serial date-time (whole days plus a fraction of a day), or `None` if it names no real date.
- `fn to_spreadsheet_serial`: The 1900-system spreadsheet serial for `seconds` since the epoch, or `None` before 1900-01-01 (which the system cannot represent).
- `enum DateOrder`: Which of the first two numbers of a slash date such as `03/04/2026` is the month.
- `struct DetectedColumn`: A date-time column read from text by [`detect_column`].
- `fn detect_column`: Read a column of text as dates, times of day or durations.

Integration tests: `table_ops_reference.rs`, `temporal_reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-discrete` (`crates/stat-discrete`)

Categorical data analysis: contingency tables and tests of independence.

Dependencies: `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/dose_response.rs`

Dose–response (quantal response) analysis: probit, logit or
complementary log-log regression of the proportion responding on a
(usually log-transformed) dose, with effective doses and their fiducial
limits.

#### Model
At dose `d` with `x = h(d)` (`h` the identity, `log₁₀` or `ln`), each of
`nᵢ` subjects responds independently with probability
`P = F(α + βx)`, where `F` is the standard normal cdf (probit), the
logistic cdf (logit) or `1 − exp(−e^η)` (complementary log-log). The model
is the binomial GLM of [`crate::glm`] with the trials as prior weights,
fitted by maximum likelihood. Rows with the same dose are pooled first, so
one-row-per-subject (0/1) data and grouped data give the same fit.

#### Goodness of fit and heterogeneity
Pearson's `χ² = Σ (rᵢ − nᵢP̂ᵢ)² / (nᵢP̂ᵢ(1 − P̂ᵢ))` on `k − 2` df (`k` dose
groups) tests the model. When it is significant at the chosen level the
variation between groups exceeds binomial variation, and Finney (*Probit
Analysis*, 3rd ed., 1971, §4.4) multiplies the variances by the
heterogeneity factor `h = χ²/(k − 2)` and uses Student's t on `k − 2` df in
place of the normal deviate.

#### Effective doses and fiducial limits
The dose giving response probability `p` is `m = (F⁻¹(p) − α̂)/β̂` on the
`x` scale (ED50, the median effective dose, at `p = ½`). Its fiducial
limits (Finney 1971, §4.3; Fieller's theorem, Fieller 1954, *JRSS B* 16)
are the values of `x` with

`(α̂ + β̂x − F⁻¹(p))² ≤ t² (v₁₁ + 2x v₁₂ + x² v₂₂)`,

`vᵢⱼ` the (heterogeneity-scaled) covariances of `(α̂, β̂)` and `t` the normal
(or t) quantile: the roots of
`(β̂² − t²v₂₂)x² + 2(β̂(α̂ − ξ) − t²v₁₂)x + (α̂ − ξ)² − t²v₁₁ = 0`, `ξ = F⁻¹(p)`.
They exist only when `g = t²v₂₂/β̂² < 1` (the slope is significantly
non-zero); otherwise the limits are unbounded and are not reported. They
are asymmetric about `m`, unlike the delta-method interval, which is also
given (`se(m) = √(v₁₁ + 2m v₁₂ + m²v₂₂)/|β̂|`). Limits on the `x` scale are
transformed back to doses.

- `enum DoseScale`: Scale on which the dose enters the model.
- `struct DoseResponseOptions`: Options for [`fit_dose_response`].
- `struct DoseGroup`: One dose group after pooling rows with the same dose.
- `struct EffectiveDose`: An effective dose with its limits.
- `struct DoseResponseFit`: A fitted dose–response model.
- `fn fit_dose_response`: Fit a quantal dose–response model.

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/exact_rxc.rs`

Fisher's exact test of independence for `r × c` tables (the
Freeman–Halton extension of Fisher's test), computed with the network
algorithm of Mehta & Patel (1983), with a seeded Monte Carlo estimate when
the exact computation would be too large.

#### Method
Conditional on the row totals `Rᵢ` and column totals `Cⱼ`, a table with
cells `nᵢⱼ` has the multiple hypergeometric probability

```text
P(n) = Πᵢ Rᵢ! Πⱼ Cⱼ! / (N! Πᵢⱼ nᵢⱼ!)
```

and the two-sided p-value is the total probability of every table with
the same margins whose probability does not exceed the observed table's,
`p = Σ { P(t) : P(t) ≤ P(n_obs) }` (with a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁷ on
the comparison, so that tables equal to the observed one in exact
arithmetic count).

**Network algorithm** (Mehta & Patel 1983, *JASA* 78, 427–434). Tables are
built one column at a time. After `k` columns the only thing that matters
for the remaining columns is the multiset of remaining row totals, so the
partial tables collapse onto *nodes* (the remaining row totals, sorted).
Each node keeps the distinct "past" values `Σ ln nᵢⱼ!` of the paths that
reach it, with their multiplicities. Before a past value is stored, the
node's bounds on the remaining part of `Σ ln nᵢⱼ!` are checked:

* if even the most probable completion is no more probable than the
  observed table, every completion counts and the node's whole remaining
  mass — known in closed form, `N′! / (Π R′ᵢ! Π C′ⱼ!)` — is added at once;
* if even the least probable completion is more probable than the
  observed table, no completion counts and the path is dropped;
* otherwise the path is kept and expanded at the next column.

The bounds come from two relaxations, each solved exactly by majorization
(`ln x!` is convex): dropping the row-total constraints (each remaining
column split as evenly / as unevenly as the row totals allow) and dropping
the column-total constraints (each row split across the remaining
columns); the tighter of the two is used. Mehta & Patel's own bounds are
sharper but these are valid, which is all exactness needs.

**Monte Carlo** (used when the network exceeds the work budget, or when
asked): tables with the observed margins are drawn from their null
distribution (the multiple hypergeometric) by Patefield's (1981)
algorithm (*Applied Statistics* 30, 91–97, AS 159): row by row, each
row's counts are a draw without replacement from the column totals still
unallocated, so each cell given the cells before it is hypergeometric —
`nᵢⱼ ~ H(population Σₖ≥ⱼ C′ₖ, successes C′ⱼ, draws R′ᵢ)` with `C′` and `R′`
what remains — and is drawn by inversion searching outward from the mode
when its variance is small, otherwise by Stadlober's (1989) ratio-of-uniforms
rejection method. The work per table grows with the number of cells, not
with `N`; `ln n!` is evaluated on demand, and a random table is compared
with the observed one through cell-by-cell differences `ln x! − ln o!`
(from Stirling's series for large counts), which stay accurate when
`Σ ln n!` itself is beyond `f64` precision. The estimate is
`(b + 1)/(B + 1)` where `b` of the `B` tables are no more probable than
the observed one. Totals up to 2⁵³ are accepted.

The 2 × 2 special case is the two-sided test in
`stat_inference::proportions` (the same definition of "as or more
extreme"); the two agree, which the tests check.

- `const DEFAULT_WORK_LIMIT`: Default bound on the network algorithm's work (arcs examined plus past values stored) before it gives way to Monte Carlo.
- `const MAX_TOTAL`: Largest total count accepted, 2⁵³ (counts above it are not exact in `f64`).
- `struct ExactOptions`: Settings of [`fisher_exact_rxc`].
- `enum ExactMethod`: How an exact p-value was obtained.
- `struct ExactTest`: Result of Fisher's exact test of an `r × c` table.
- `fn fisher_exact_rxc`: Fisher's exact test of independence for a table of counts (rows of equal length).

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/glm.rs`

Generalized linear models fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares.

#### Model
`g(E[y]) = η = β₀ + xᵀβ` with a response distribution (family) and a link
function `g` ([`Link`]):

| Family | Links (default first) | Variance `V(μ)` | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| binomial | logit, probit, complementary log-log | `μ(1−μ)` | yes/no outcomes, dose–response |
| Poisson | log, identity | `μ` | counts |
| Gaussian | identity, log | `1` | continuous (identity equals OLS) |
| Gamma | inverse, log, identity | `μ²` | positive, skewed, constant CV |

Optional prior weights `wᵢ` multiply each observation's contribution to
the likelihood. For the binomial family they are the numbers of trials,
with the response the observed proportion `yᵢ = rᵢ/nᵢ` (grouped binary
data, as in probit analysis).

#### Fitting
Fisher scoring as iteratively reweighted least squares (Nelder & Wedderburn
1972, *JRSS A* 135; McCullagh & Nelder, *Generalized Linear Models*, 2nd ed.,
§2.5): with working weights `w = wᵢ (dμ/dη)² / V(μ)` and working response
`z = η + (y − μ)/(dμ/dη)`, each step solves the weighted least-squares
problem `min Σ w (z − xᵀβ)²` by Householder QR of `√w·X` (never forming
`XᵀWX`). A step that gives a non-finite deviance (e.g. a negative mean
under the inverse link) is halved. Iteration stops when the deviance
changes by less than `10⁻¹⁰ (|D| + 0.1)` and every estimate by less than
`10⁻¹⁰ (|β| + 10⁻⁶)` (non-canonical links converge only linearly);
estimates still drifting after five flat steps, as under separation, stop.

#### Inference
`Cov(β̂) = φ (XᵀWX)⁻¹` with dispersion `φ = 1` (binomial, Poisson) or the
Pearson estimate `φ = Σ wᵢ(yᵢ − μ̂ᵢ)²/V(μ̂ᵢ) / (n − p)` (Gaussian, Gamma; for
the Gaussian family with identity link this is `RSS/(n − p)`). Wald tests
use `z = β̂/se` against the normal distribution (t on `n − p` df when `φ` is
estimated). [`likelihood_ratio_test`] compares nested fits by the change in
deviance against χ². With the logit link `exp(β)` is an odds ratio; with
the log link, a rate (or mean) ratio.

Deviance `D = 2(ℓ_saturated − ℓ)`; `AIC = −2ℓ + 2k`, `BIC = −2ℓ + k ln n`,
with `k` coefficients (plus one for an estimated dispersion). For the Gamma
family `ℓ` is evaluated at the shape `1/φ̃` with `φ̃ = D / Σwᵢ` (the
convention of R's `Gamma()$aic`).

- `enum Family`: Response distribution.
- `enum Link`: Link function `g` with `g(μ) = η`.
- `struct GlmOptions`: Options for [`fit_glm`].
- `struct GlmCoefficient`: One coefficient with Wald inference.
- `struct GlmFit`: A fitted generalized linear model.
- `struct LikelihoodRatioTest`: A likelihood-ratio (deviance) test.
- `fn fit_glm`: Fit a generalized linear model of `y` on the columns of `x`.
- `fn likelihood_ratio_test`: Likelihood-ratio test of a reduced model nested in a full one (same data).

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-discrete

Categorical data analysis: two-way contingency tables with the classical
tests of independence (below), generalized linear models — logistic, probit,
complementary log-log, Poisson, normal and Gamma regression — in [`glm`], and
dose–response (probit) analysis with fiducial limits in [`dose_response`],
and ordinal (proportional-odds) and nominal (baseline-category) logistic
regression for responses with more than two categories in [`polytomous`].
Multi-way tables (counts, percentages and summary statistics by nested
classifications) are in [`tabulation`]; stratified tables
(Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel tests, the Mantel–Haenszel common odds ratio,
Breslow–Day homogeneity) in [`stratified`]; Fisher's exact test for
`r × c` tables (network algorithm) in [`exact_rxc`].

For an `r × c` table of counts `nᵢⱼ` with row totals `nᵢ.`, column totals
`n.ⱼ` and grand total `n`, the expected counts under independence are
`Eᵢⱼ = nᵢ. n.ⱼ / n`, and

* Pearson's statistic `X² = Σ (nᵢⱼ − Eᵢⱼ)² / Eᵢⱼ` (Pearson 1900),
* the likelihood-ratio statistic `G² = 2 Σ nᵢⱼ ln(nᵢⱼ / Eᵢⱼ)` (cells with
  `nᵢⱼ = 0` contribute 0),

are both referred to χ² with `(r − 1)(c − 1)` degrees of freedom (Agresti,
*Categorical Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., 2013, §3.2). Cramér's
`V = √(X² / (n · (min(r, c) − 1)))` measures strength of association.

The χ² approximation is doubtful when expected counts are small; the result
reports the smallest expected count and the share of cells below 5 so callers
can warn (Cochran's guideline: no more than 20% of cells below 5, none below 1).

- `struct ContingencyTable`: A two-way table of counts with labelled rows and columns.
- `struct IndependenceTest`: Result of testing a two-way table for independence.
- `fn adjusted_residuals`: Adjusted (standardized) residuals of each cell under independence, `(O − E) / √(E (1 − rᵢ/N)(1 − cⱼ/N))`, approximately standard normal when the rows and columns are independent (Haberman, *Biometrics* 29, 1973; Agresti, *Categorical Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., §2.4.5).
- `fn test_independence`: Test a contingency table for independence of its rows and columns.

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/multiple_response.rs`

Multiple-response (check-all-that-apply) questions: each case may pick
any number of `I` items, recorded as a cases × items matrix of picks.

**Frequencies.** With `n` respondents (cases that picked at least one
item) and `cᵢ` the number of cases picking item `i`, the report gives
`cᵢ`, the percentage of cases `100 cᵢ / n` (these add to more than 100%
when cases pick several items) and the percentage of responses
`100 cᵢ / Σⱼ cⱼ` (these add to 100%). Cases with no pick are counted
separately and left out of the percentages, as is usual for these tables.

**Cross-tabulation by a group.** For each group `g` with `n_g`
respondents, `c_{gi}` cases picking item `i` and the percentage of the
group's cases `100 c_{gi} / n_g`.

**Tests of marginal independence.** A case can count under several items,
so the items × groups table of counts is not a contingency table and the
ordinary χ² test does not apply to it (Agresti & Liu 1999). Each item on
its own is a 2 × G table (picked or not, by group), tested with Pearson's
χ² on `G − 1` degrees of freedom; the overall hypothesis of simultaneous
marginal independence of every item from the group is tested with the
Bonferroni-adjusted smallest p-value, `min(1, I · minᵢ pᵢ)` (Bilder &
Loughin 2004, *Biometrics* 60).

References: Agresti, A. & Liu, I.-M. (1999), "Modeling a categorical
variable allowing arbitrarily many category choices", *Biometrics* 55;
Bilder, C. R. & Loughin, T. M. (2004), "Testing for marginal independence
between two categorical variables with multiple responses", *Biometrics* 60.

- `struct ItemFrequency`: Frequency of one item.
- `struct GroupCounts`: One group's counts in a cross-tabulation.
- `struct ItemTest`: Test of one item's independence from the group.
- `struct MultipleResponseTable`: Frequencies of a multiple-response question.
- `struct MultipleResponseCrossTab`: Cross-tabulation of a multiple-response question by a group.
- `fn multiple_response_frequencies`: Frequencies of items picked: `picks[case][item]`.
- `fn multiple_response_crosstab`: Cross-tabulate picks by `group` (one label per case; `None` leaves the case out), with each item's test of independence from the group.

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/negative_binomial.rs`

Negative binomial regression for overdispersed counts: a log-linear model
`ln μᵢ = xᵢᵀβ` with `Var(Yᵢ) = μᵢ + μᵢ²/θ`, fitted by maximum likelihood
over `β` and the shape `θ` together (Lawless, "Negative binomial and mixed
Poisson regression", *Can. J. Stat.* 15, 1987; Venables & Ripley,
*Modern Applied Statistics with S*, 4th ed., §7.4).

The fit alternates the two maximizations until the log-likelihood
settles: for fixed `θ`, iteratively reweighted least squares with
working weights `wᵢ = μᵢθ/(θ + μᵢ)` and working response
`zᵢ = ηᵢ + (yᵢ − μᵢ)/μᵢ`; for fixed `μ`, Newton's method on the score
`Σ[ψ(θ + yᵢ) − ψ(θ) + ln θ + 1 − ln(θ + μᵢ) − (yᵢ + θ)/(θ + μᵢ)]`
started from the moment estimate `n / Σ(yᵢ/μᵢ − 1)²`. The first `μ` is
the Poisson fit's. Coefficient standard errors come from `(XᵀWX)⁻¹`
(θ treated as known, as is standard; `β̂` and `θ̂` are asymptotically
independent), with z tests; `θ`'s from its observed information.

The log-likelihood is
`ℓ = Σ[ln Γ(θ + yᵢ) − ln Γ(θ) − ln Γ(yᵢ + 1) + θ ln θ + yᵢ ln μᵢ
     − (θ + yᵢ) ln(θ + μᵢ)]`, `AIC = −2ℓ + 2(p + 1)`, and the deviance
`2Σ[yᵢ ln(yᵢ/μᵢ) − (yᵢ + θ) ln((yᵢ + θ)/(μᵢ + θ))]` at the fitted `θ`.

- `struct NegativeBinomialOptions`: Settings of [`fit_negative_binomial`].
- `struct NegativeBinomialCoefficient`: One coefficient with its Wald z test.
- `struct NegativeBinomialFit`: A fitted negative binomial regression.
- `fn fit_negative_binomial`: Fit `ln μ = Xβ` (plus an intercept) to non-negative counts `y`.
- `fn negative_binomial_lr_test`: Likelihood-ratio test of a reduced model against a fuller one (each with its own θ): `χ² = 2(ℓ_full − ℓ_reduced)` on the difference in the number of coefficients.

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/polytomous.rs`

Logistic regression for a response with more than two categories:
the proportional-odds (cumulative logit) model for ordered categories and
the baseline-category (multinomial) logit model for unordered ones.

#### Proportional odds (ordered response)
With categories `1 < 2 < … < J` and predictors `x` (no intercept column),

`P(Y ≤ j | x) = F(αⱼ − xᵀβ)`,  `j = 1, …, J − 1`,  `F(t) = 1/(1 + e^(−t))`,

with increasing thresholds (cut-points) `α₁ < … < α_{J−1}` and one slope
vector `β` shared by every cumulative split (McCullagh 1980, "Regression
models for ordinal data", *JRSS B* 42; Agresti, *Categorical Data
Analysis*, 3rd ed., 2013, §8.2). `exp(βₖ)` is the factor by which a unit
increase in `xₖ` multiplies the odds of a *higher* category,
`P(Y > j)/P(Y ≤ j)`, the same for every `j`. Category probabilities are
`P(Y = j) = F(αⱼ − η) − F(α_{j−1} − η)` (`α₀ = −∞`, `α_J = +∞`), computed
as `σ(u) σ(−l) (1 − e^(l−u))` to avoid cancellation.

**Parallel-lines test.** The score test of the proportional-odds
assumption (Peterson & Harrell 1990, "Partial proportional odds models for
ordinal response variables", *Applied Statistics* 39) compares the model
with the general cumulative logit model `P(Y ≤ j) = F(αⱼ − xᵀβⱼ)`, a
separate slope vector per split. At the proportional-odds estimates
(`βⱼ = β̂` for all `j`) the general model's score `U` and expected (Fisher)
information `I = Σᵢ wᵢ Σⱼ (∂πᵢⱼ/∂θ)(∂πᵢⱼ/∂θ)ᵀ / πᵢⱼ` give
`S = Uᵀ I⁻¹ U`, referred to χ² with `p (J − 2)` degrees of freedom. Only
the restricted fit is needed, so the test exists even when the general
model would give crossing cumulative curves.

#### Baseline-category logits (unordered response)
With a reference category `r`,

`ln(P(Y = j)/P(Y = r)) = β₀ⱼ + xᵀβⱼ`,  `j ≠ r`,

so `P(Y = j) = e^(ηⱼ) / (1 + Σ_{k≠r} e^(ηₖ))` (Agresti 2013, §8.1).
`exp(βⱼₖ)` multiplies the odds of category `j` against the reference per
unit of `xₖ`.

#### Fitting
Newton–Raphson on the log-likelihood `ℓ = Σᵢ wᵢ ln πᵢ,yᵢ` with analytic
gradient and Hessian, halving a step that does not increase `ℓ` (or, for
the ordinal model, that would put the thresholds out of order). Both
log-likelihoods are concave (Pratt 1981, *JASA* 76, for the cumulative
logit), so the maximum is unique when it exists. For the multinomial
model the observed and expected information coincide (canonical link), so
this is also Fisher scoring. Start: thresholds at the logits of the
cumulative sample proportions (ordinal) or intercepts at the log ratios of
the category totals (nominal), slopes 0. Iteration stops when `ℓ` changes
by less than `10⁻¹²(|ℓ| + 1)` and every parameter by less than
`10⁻⁹(|θ| + 1)`; if the classes are separated by the predictors the
estimates drift without converging, and the fit says so.

#### Inference
`Cov(θ̂)` is the inverse observed information at the estimates. Wald
statistics `z = θ̂/se` against the standard normal, intervals
`θ̂ ± z_{1−α/2} se`. The null model has the thresholds (intercepts) only;
its log-likelihood is `Σⱼ Wⱼ ln(Wⱼ/W)` (`Wⱼ` the weight of category `j`).
The whole-model likelihood-ratio test is `2(ℓ − ℓ₀)` on the number of
slope parameters. `AIC = −2ℓ + 2k`, `BIC = −2ℓ + k ln W` (`k` all
parameters, thresholds or intercepts included); McFadden's pseudo-R²
`1 − ℓ/ℓ₀` and Nagelkerke's `(1 − e^{2(ℓ₀−ℓ)/W}) / (1 − e^{2ℓ₀/W})`.

Weights are frequency weights: a row of weight 3 counts as three
identical observations (so `W`, not the number of rows, enters the BIC).

- `struct PolytomousOptions`: Options shared by [`fit_ordinal_logistic`] and [`fit_nominal_logistic`].
- `struct PolytomousStatistics`: Fit statistics common to both models.
- `struct ScoreTest`: A score (Lagrange multiplier) test.
- `struct OrdinalLogitFit`: A fitted proportional-odds (cumulative logit) model.
- `struct NominalEquation`: The equation of one non-reference category of a baseline-category model.
- `struct NominalLogitFit`: A fitted baseline-category (multinomial) logit model.
- `fn fit_ordinal_logistic`: Fit the proportional-odds (cumulative logit) model of the ordered response `y` (category codes `0 … J−1`, lowest first, named by `levels`) on the columns of `x` (no intercept column; the thresholds play its part), with the score test of parallel lines.
- `fn fit_nominal_logistic`: Fit the baseline-category (multinomial) logit model of the response `y` (category codes `0 … J−1`, named by `levels`) on the columns of `x` (an intercept is added to every equation), against the category `reference`.

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/stratified.rs`

Stratified analysis of contingency tables: a set of `K` tables (one per
stratum) cross-classifying the same row and column variables.

#### 2 × 2 × K tables
Write stratum `k`'s table as `[[a, b], [c, d]]` with `n = a + b + c + d`,
row totals `n₁ = a + b`, `n₂ = c + d` and column totals `m₁ = a + c`,
`m₂ = b + d`.

* **Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test** of conditional independence (Mantel &
  Haenszel 1959; Cochran 1954; Agresti, *Categorical Data Analysis*, 3rd ed., 2013):
  with `E(a) = n₁m₁/n` and the hypergeometric variance
  `Var(a) = n₁n₂m₁m₂ / (n²(n − 1))`,
  `CMH = (Σ(a − E(a)))² / Σ Var(a)` on 1 degree of freedom, and the
  continuity-corrected form `(max(0, |Σ(a − E(a))| − ½))² / Σ Var(a)`.
  Strata with `n < 2` carry no information and are skipped.
* **Mantel–Haenszel common odds ratio** `ψ̂ = Σ(ad/n) / Σ(bc/n)` with the
  Robins, Breslow & Greenland (1986) variance of `ln ψ̂`: with
  `P = (a + d)/n`, `Q = (b + c)/n`, `R = ad/n`, `S = bc/n`,
  `Var = ΣPR/(2R₊²) + Σ(PS + QR)/(2R₊S₊) + ΣQS/(2S₊²)`, and the interval
  `exp(ln ψ̂ ± z √Var)`.
* **Breslow–Day test** of a common odds ratio (Breslow & Day 1980, §4.4):
  in each stratum, `ã` solves `ã(n₂ − m₁ + ã) = ψ̂ (n₁ − ã)(m₁ − ã)` within
  the margins' bounds, `Var(ã) = (1/ã + 1/(n₁ − ã) + 1/(m₁ − ã) +
  1/(n₂ − m₁ + ã))⁻¹`, and `BD = Σ(a − ã)²/Var(ã)` on `K − 1` degrees of
  freedom (strata with a zero margin are left out). Tarone's (1985)
  correction subtracts `(Σ(a − ã))² / ΣVar(ã)`.

#### r × c × K tables: generalized CMH statistics
Landis, Heyman & Koch (1978), as presented by Agresti (2013). In stratum `h`, with
`nₕ` observations, row proportions `p = Rₕ/nₕ` and column proportions
`q = Cₕ/nₕ`, the cell counts `Nₕ` (vectorized by rows) have null mean
`mₕ = nₕ (p ⊗ q)` and covariance
`Vₕ = nₕ²/(nₕ − 1) (Dₚ − ppᵀ) ⊗ (D_q − qqᵀ)`. For a contrast matrix
`B = A_r ⊗ A_c`, `Q = gᵀ (B ΣVₕ Bᵀ)⁻¹ g` with `g = Σ B(Nₕ − mₕ)`:

* **general association** (rows and columns both nominal):
  `A_r = [I, 0]`, `A_c = [I, 0]`, `(r − 1)(c − 1)` degrees of freedom;
* **row mean scores differ** (ordinal columns with scores `a`):
  `A_r = [I, 0]`, `A_c = aᵀ`, `r − 1` degrees of freedom;
* **nonzero correlation** (both ordinal, row scores `u`):
  `A_r = uᵀ`, `A_c = aᵀ`, 1 degree of freedom.

For 2 × 2 × K tables all three equal the uncorrected CMH statistic.

- `struct ChiSquareTest`: A chi-square statistic with its degrees of freedom and upper-tail p-value.
- `type TwoByTwo`: One stratum's 2 × 2 table `[[a, b], [c, d]]`.
- `struct MantelHaenszel`: Mantel–Haenszel analysis of a set of 2 × 2 tables.
- `fn mantel_haenszel`: Mantel–Haenszel analysis of 2 × 2 × K tables (see the module notes).
- `struct GeneralizedCmh`: Generalized Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel statistics of an r × c × K table.
- `fn generalized_cmh`: Generalized CMH statistics (see the module notes).

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/tabulation.rs`

Multi-way tables: counts, percentages and summary statistics of
continuous measures, cross-classified by several nested row
classifications and several nested column classifications.

#### Layout
The row classifications are nested in the order given: the rows of the
table are the combinations of their levels that occur in the data, in
lexicographic order of the levels (outermost first). The column
classifications are nested the same way. Optionally,

* **subtotals** add, after each group of rows sharing an outer level, a
  row for that outer level over all inner levels (likewise for columns);
* **margins** add a grand-total row and column ("all levels").

A row or column group is written as a [`GroupKey`]: one entry per
classification, `None` where the group spans every level.

#### Cell statistics
Each observation carries a frequency weight `w ≥ 0` (1 when none is
given). For a cell, the **count** is `Σ w`; the **row percentage** is
`100 · count / (count of the cell's row group over all columns)`, the
**column percentage** the same over all rows, and the **total
percentage** `100 · count / grand total` — the denominators do not depend
on whether margins are shown. For each measure, missing values (NaN) are
left out, and with `W = Σ w` over the cell's non-missing values:
`N = W`, sum `Σ w x`, mean `Σ w x / W`, standard deviation
`√(Σ w (x − x̄)² / (W − 1))` (frequency weights: as if each value were
repeated `w` times), median (the first value whose cumulative weight
passes `W/2`, or the average of it and the next value when the cumulative
weight equals `W/2` exactly; for whole-number weights, the middle of the
values repeated by their weights), minimum
and maximum. Statistics that need more data than the cell has are NaN.

- `struct Classification`: A classification of the observations.
- `struct Measure`: A continuous measure summarized in the cells.
- `struct TabulationInput`: What a multi-way table classifies and summarizes.
- `struct TabulationOptions`: Which totals a multi-way table adds.
- `struct GroupKey`: A row or column group: one entry per classification, `None` where the group spans every level of that classification.
- `struct MeasureSummary`: Summary statistics of one measure in one cell.
- `struct MultiwayTable`: A computed multi-way table.
- `fn tabulate`: Build a multi-way table (see the module notes).

### `crates/stat-discrete/src/treatment_effects.rs`

Treatment effects from observational data: propensity scores, covariate
balance, nearest-neighbour matching, inverse-probability weighting and
augmented (doubly robust) weighting.

#### Setting
Each row has a two-level treatment `tᵢ ∈ {0, 1}`, an outcome `yᵢ` and
covariates `xᵢ` measured before treatment. Under no unmeasured
confounding and overlap (`0 < e(x) < 1`), the potential-outcome means
`μ₁ = E[Y(1)]`, `μ₀ = E[Y(0)]` (or their means among the treated) can be
estimated from the propensity score `e(x) = P(t = 1 | x)` (Rosenbaum &
Rubin 1983, *Biometrika* 70).

#### Propensity score
A logistic regression of `t` on the covariates ([`fit_glm`], binomial
family, logit link), `êᵢ` its fitted probabilities.

#### Estimands
* **ATE**, the average treatment effect over everyone: `E[Y(1)] − E[Y(0)]`.
* **ATT**, the average effect among the treated: `E[Y(1) − Y(0) | t = 1]`.

Effects are reported as the difference `μ₁ − μ₀`, and for binary and
count outcomes also as the ratio `μ₁/μ₀` (risk or rate ratio), and for
binary outcomes the odds ratio `[μ₁/(1−μ₁)]/[μ₀/(1−μ₀)]`. Ratios get
their intervals on the log scale by the delta method.

#### Methods
* **Inverse-probability weighting** (normalized, or Hájek, form;
  Lunceford & Davidian 2004, *Statistics in Medicine* 23, estimator
  `Δ̂₂`): ATE weights `t/ê + (1−t)/(1−ê)`, ATT weights `t + (1−t)ê/(1−ê)`,
  and `μ̂_g` the weighted mean of the outcome in group `g`. Stabilized
  weights multiply the treated weights by `P̂(t = 1)` and the control
  weights by `P̂(t = 0)` (ATE), or the control weights by
  `P̂(t = 0)/P̂(t = 1)` (ATT); this changes the saved weights, not the
  estimate.
* **Augmented IPW** (doubly robust; Lunceford & Davidian 2004, `Δ̂_DR`;
  Hernán & Robins 2020, *Causal Inference: What If*, §13): outcome models
  `m₁(x)`, `m₀(x)` fitted in each group (normal linear, logistic or
  Poisson regression for continuous, binary or count outcomes), and for
  the ATE `μ̂₁ = n⁻¹ Σ [tᵢyᵢ/êᵢ − (tᵢ − êᵢ) m₁(xᵢ)/êᵢ]`,
  `μ̂₀ = n⁻¹ Σ [(1−tᵢ)yᵢ/(1−êᵢ) + (tᵢ − êᵢ) m₀(xᵢ)/(1−êᵢ)]`; for the ATT
  `μ̂₁` is the treated mean and
  `μ̂₀ = Σ [tᵢ m₀(xᵢ) + (1−tᵢ) êᵢ/(1−êᵢ) (yᵢ − m₀(xᵢ))] / Σ tᵢ`. The
  estimate is consistent when either the propensity model or the outcome
  models are correct.
* **Nearest-neighbour matching** on the logit of the propensity score
  (Rosenbaum & Rubin 1985; Austin 2011, *Multivariate Behavioral Research*
  46). For the ATT each treated row, in decreasing order of its score, is
  given its `k` nearest controls; without replacement every treated row
  receives its first match before any receives a second, and a matched
  control is not used again. A caliper (in standard deviations of the
  logit over all rows) leaves treated rows with no control close enough
  unmatched. For the ATE (with replacement only) every row is also
  matched to its `k` nearest rows of the other group (Abadie & Imbens
  2006, *Econometrica* 74). Matched rows get weights — 1 for each row
