  matched in its own right and, for a matched row of the other group,
  the sum over the rows it serves of `1/(their number of matches)`,
  rescaled to sum to the number of such rows — and `μ̂_g` is the
  weighted group mean.

Trimming (Crump et al. 2009, *Biometrika* 96) leaves out rows whose
score lies outside `[α, 1 − α]`; the propensity model is not refitted.

#### Intervals
* **Sandwich** (weighting and doubly robust): the propensity model's
  score equations, the outcome models' score equations and the equations
  for `μ₁`, `μ₀` are stacked as one M-estimator `Σ ψᵢ(θ) = 0`, and
  `cov θ̂ = A⁻¹ B A⁻ᵀ` with `A = Σ ∂ψᵢ/∂θ` (central differences) and
  `B = Σ ψᵢψᵢᵀ` (Stefanski & Boos 2002, *The American Statistician* 56;
  Lunceford & Davidian 2004 §3). This accounts for estimating the
  propensity score.
* **Robust, matched data** (matching): the weighted means' sandwich with
  matched sets as clusters (without replacement) or rows as clusters
  (with replacement), with the small-sample factor
  `G/(G−1) · (N−1)/(N−2)` (`G` clusters, `N` matched rows), as
  `sandwich::vcovCL(type = "HC1")` on the weighted regression
  `y ~ treatment` that matching software recommends (Austin & Small 2014,
  *Statistics in Medicine* 33).
* **Bootstrap**: rows resampled with replacement within each treatment
  group and the whole analysis (propensity model, matching or weights,
  outcome models) repeated; percentile intervals, and the replicates'
  standard deviation as the standard error.

#### Covariate balance
Standardized mean differences `(x̄₁ − x̄₀)/s` with `s` from the unadjusted
sample — `√((s₁² + s₀²)/2)` for the ATE, `s₁` for the ATT, with
`s² = p(1−p)` for a 0/1 variable — before and after adjustment (weighted
means), and variance ratios `s₁²/s₀²` of continuous variables, with
weighted variances `Σw/((Σw)² − Σw²) · Σ w(x − x̄_w)²` (Austin 2009,
*Statistics in Medicine* 28; Austin & Stuart 2015, *Statistics in
Medicine* 34).

#### Failure modes
Treatment values other than 0/1, a group with fewer than two rows,
propensity scores of 0 or 1 (separation) among the rows kept, an outcome
outside the range of its kind, no matches within the caliper, and a
singular outcome model are errors.

- `enum OutcomeKind`: Kind of outcome, which sets the outcome models and the effect scales.
- `enum Estimand`: Which population the effect averages over.
- `struct MatchingOptions`: Nearest-neighbour matching settings.
- `enum EffectMethod`: How the effect is estimated.
- `enum IntervalMethod`: How intervals are computed.
- `struct TreatmentEffectOptions`: Options for [`estimate_treatment_effect`].
- `struct PropensityModel`: A fitted propensity-score model.
- `fn fit_propensity`: Fit the propensity score: logistic regression of `t` (0/1) on the columns of `x` (an intercept is added), named `names`.
- `enum EffectScale`: Scale on which an effect is reported.
- `struct EffectEstimate`: One effect estimate.
- `struct TreatmentEffectFit`: A treatment-effect estimate with what produced it.
- `fn estimate_treatment_effect`: Estimate the treatment effect: `x` the covariates (one row per observation, no intercept column), `names` their names, `t` the treatment (0/1), `y` the outcome.
- `fn ipw_weights`: Inverse-probability weights (0 for rows not kept).
- `struct BalanceRow`: Balance of one variable before and after adjustment.
- `fn covariate_balance`: Covariate balance of `variables` (name, value per row) between the treatment groups `t`, unweighted and with `weights` (rows with weight 0 left out).
- `fn heterogeneity_test`: Test of equal effects across independent subgroups: Cochran's `Q = Σ (θ̂_g − θ̄)²/v_g` with `θ̄` the inverse-variance weighted mean, referred to χ² on `G − 1` df (the subgroup-by-treatment interaction).

Test files: `glm/tests.rs`, `polytomous/tests.rs`, `treatment_effects/tests.rs`.

Integration tests: `negative_binomial_reference.rs`, `polytomous_reference.rs`, `stratified_reference.rs`, `treatment_effects_reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-doe` (`crates/stat-doe`)

Design of experiments: factorial, fractional factorial, screening, response surface and D-optimal designs.

Dependencies: `stat-core`, `stat-data`.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/augment.rs`

Augmenting an existing design with more runs, keeping the runs already
made.

Every function takes the existing runs in coded units (−1 at a factor's
low setting, +1 at its high setting) and returns an [`Augmented`] design:
the existing runs (block 1) followed by the new ones (block 2), with notes.
A second block is usually run later than the first, so an analysis can
include the block as a factor to absorb a shift between the two.

* [`fold_over`] — for a two-level design, the **full fold-over** repeats
  every run with all signs reversed; the combined design has no main
  effect aliased with any two-factor interaction (a resolution III
  fraction becomes resolution IV). The **fold-over on one factor**
  reverses that factor only; the factor and all its two-factor
  interactions become clear of main effects and of the other two-factor
  interactions. (Box, Hunter & Hunter, *Statistics for Experimenters*,
  2nd ed., §6.8; Montgomery, *Design and Analysis of Experiments*, §8.6.)
* [`add_center_runs`] — center runs (all factors at coded 0) give a
  pure-error estimate and a test for curvature.
* [`add_axial_runs`] — axial ("star") runs at `±α` on each factor axis,
  with optional center runs, turn a two-level factorial into a central
  composite design (α = 1 is face-centerd; a rotatable design uses
  `α = n_f^{1/4}` for `n_f` factorial runs; Box & Wilson 1951).
* [`augment_optimal`] — **D-optimal augmentation**: the existing runs stay
  fixed and `m` runs are added to maximize `det(XᵀX)` of all runs for a
  (possibly larger) model, by the same coordinate exchange as
  [`crate::optimal::d_optimal_in`] (only the new runs move; the fixed runs
  enter the information matrix), honouring a [`Region`]. Atkinson, Donev
  & Tobias, *Optimum Experimental Designs, with SAS*, §19.

- `struct Augmented`: An augmented design.
- `fn fold_over`: Fold over a two-level design: every run that is not a center run is repeated with all signs reversed (`factor = None`) or with the sign of one factor reversed.
- `fn add_center_runs`: Add `count` center runs (every factor at coded 0).
- `fn add_axial_runs`: Add axial runs at `±alpha` on each factor axis (factor order, −α before +α), then `centers` center runs: a two-level factorial becomes a central composite design.
- `fn augment_optimal`: D-optimal augmentation: add `options.runs` runs to the fixed coded runs `existing`, maximizing `det(XᵀX)` of all runs for `formula`, with the new runs inside `region` (see the module documentation).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/categorical_screening.rs`

Screening designs that mix two-level continuous factors with categorical
factors of any number of levels, built by D-optimal coordinate exchange.

#### Model and coding
A categorical factor with `L` levels enters the model through `L − 1`
**normalized Helmert contrasts**: contrast `j = 1, …, L − 1` is −1 at the
levels before `j`, `j` at level `j` and 0 after it, scaled by
`√(L / (j(j + 1)))`. The contrasts are mutually orthogonal and, over a
design that uses every level equally often, each has mean 0 and mean
square 1, like a balanced ±1 column. The model is the intercept, a column
per continuous factor and the contrasts of each categorical factor (main
effects), optionally with every two-factor interaction (the products of
the columns of two different factors). With this coding an orthogonal
array has `XᵀX = nI`, so its D-efficiency `100 · det(XᵀX)^{1/p} / n` is
100%, and every other design scores below it (Goos & Jones 2011, *Optimal
Design of Experiments: A Case Study Approach*, ch. 2–3; D-efficiency is
invariant to the choice of contrasts up to that scale).

#### Search
Coordinate exchange (Meyer & Nachtsheim 1995): from a random design, each
coordinate of each run is replaced in turn by the candidate that most
increases `det(XᵀX)`: −1 and +1 for a continuous factor, each level for a
categorical one. The determinant ratio of replacing model row `f` by `g`
is `(1 + gᵀM⁻¹g)(1 − fᵀM⁻¹f) + (fᵀM⁻¹g)²` (the determinant lemma applied
twice), so a candidate costs `O(p²)`. Passes repeat until no coordinate
improves; the best of several seeded starts is kept. A singular start is
improved for `det(XᵀX + δI)` with a small ridge `δ` until it becomes
non-singular.

Runs are stored in coded units: a continuous factor at −1 or +1, and a
categorical factor's level `ℓ = 0, …, L − 1` at `−1 + 2ℓ/(L − 1)`, its
[`Factor`] running from 1 to `L` so that actual units give the level
number (see [`level_of`]).

- `enum ScreeningFactor`: One factor of a mixed screening design.
- `const MAX_LEVELS`: Most levels of a categorical factor.
- `fn level_code`: Coded value of level `level` (0-based) of a factor with `levels` levels.
- `fn level_of`: The 0-based level whose code is nearest `code` for a factor with `levels` levels.
- `fn helmert_row`: The normalized Helmert contrasts of level `level` of `levels` levels.
- `fn model_row`: Model row of coded run `x` for factors `kinds`: intercept, main-effect columns, and with `interactions` the products of every two factors' columns.
- `fn model_terms`: Number of model terms for `kinds`.
- `fn screening_log_det`: `ln det(XᵀX)` of coded `runs` (−∞ if singular).
- `fn screening_d_efficiency`: D-efficiency `100 · det(XᵀX)^{1/p} / n` of coded `runs` (0 if singular).
- `struct CategoricalScreeningOptions`: Options for [`categorical_screening`].
- `struct CategoricalScreening`: A mixed screening design and its quality.
- `fn default_runs`: The default number of runs for `kinds`: the model terms rounded up to a multiple of the levels' least common multiple when that adds at most half again, otherwise the terms plus 4 (Goos & Jones 2011, ch.
- `fn categorical_screening`: Build a D-optimal screening design for continuous and categorical factors (see the module documentation).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/constraints.rs`

Constrained design regions for optimal designs.

A [`Region`] is the coded cube `[−1, 1]^k` cut by

* **linear inequality constraints** `Σⱼ aⱼ xⱼ ≤ b` (a `≥` constraint is
  stored with its signs reversed), for example a combined limit on two
  settings that cannot both be high, and
* **disallowed combinations**, each a conjunction of per-factor
  conditions (`<`, `≤`, `>`, `≥`, `=`): a point is excluded when it meets
  every condition of one combination, for example "temperature above 180
  together with time above 25".

A factor can also be restricted to its two coded settings −1 and +1 (a
two-level categorical factor), see [`Region::restrict_to_two_levels`].

[`Region::parse`] reads constraints written in the factors' actual units,
one per line:

```text
2*Temp + Time <= 400
Temp - Time >= 10
exclude Temp > 180 and Time > 25
```

and converts them to coded units through each factor's low and high
settings: `x_actual = m + h·x_coded` with `m = (low + high)/2` and
`h = (high − low)/2`, so `Σ aⱼ x_actual,ⱼ ≤ b` becomes
`Σ (aⱼ hⱼ) xⱼ ≤ b − Σ aⱼ mⱼ`.

The coordinate-exchange search ([`crate::optimal`]) asks the region for the
**feasible set of one coordinate** given the others
([`Region::feasible_set`]): the interval left by the cube and the linear
constraints, minus the values that would complete a disallowed
combination. Points on a constraint boundary are allowed; a point exactly
on the boundary of a strict condition (`<`, `>`) in a disallowed
combination is allowed, one on a non-strict condition (`≤`, `≥`, `=`) is
excluded. Comparisons allow a tolerance of 10⁻⁹ in coded units in favour
of the allowed region.

Following the constrained coordinate-exchange idea of Meyer & Nachtsheim
(1995, §5), each run can also slide along an active linear constraint
([`Region::slide_directions`]), which a coordinate move alone cannot do
(on a slanted boundary every coordinate move leaves it).

- `const TOLERANCE`: Tolerance of the comparisons, in coded units.
- `enum Comparison`: A comparison in a condition of a disallowed combination.
- `struct LinearConstraint`: `Σⱼ coefficients[j] · xⱼ ≤ bound` in coded units.
- `struct Condition`: One condition of a disallowed combination, in coded units.
- `struct Exclusion`: A disallowed combination: points meeting every condition are excluded.
- `struct Interval`: An interval of one coordinate, with open or closed ends.
- `struct Slide`: A direction to slide a run along an active linear constraint: the run may move to `x + t·direction` for `t` in `[t_min, t_max]` without leaving the cube or breaking a linear constraint.
- `struct Region`: The coded cube `[−1, 1]^k` cut by linear constraints and disallowed combinations (see the module documentation).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/design.rs`

The [`Design`] type shared by every generator, and its export to a
[`DataTable`].

Runs are stored in **coded units**: for two-level factors the low and high
settings are −1 and +1, the centre is 0, and axial points of a central
composite design lie at ±α. Each factor carries its low and high settings in
actual units; the linear map `actual = centre + coded · half-range` (with
`centre = (low + high)/2`, `half-range = (high − low)/2`) converts between the
two.

Runs are generated in **standard order** (for factorial designs, Yates order:
the first factor alternates fastest). [`Design::to_table`] can randomize the
run order with a seeded shuffle and records the standard order in a column, so
the experiment can be run in random order and analysed in either.

- `struct Factor`: One experimental factor.
- `fn default_factor_names`: Default factor names: `A, B, …, H, J, …, Z` (the letter I is skipped, a convention that avoids confusion with the identity in defining relations), then `X27, X28, …`.
- `enum PointType`: The role of a run within its design.
- `struct Design`: A generated design: factors, runs in coded units, and a description.
- `enum Units`: Units for exported factor columns.
- `struct TableOptions`: Options for [`Design::to_table`].

### `crates/stat-doe/src/desirability.rs`

Desirability functions for optimizing several responses at once
(Derringer & Suich, "Simultaneous optimization of several response
variables", *Journal of Quality Technology* 12(4), 1980).

Each response `ŷ` is mapped to a desirability `d ∈ [0, 1]`:

* **maximize** with lower limit `L` and upper limit `U`:
  `d = 0` for `ŷ ≤ L`, `((ŷ − L)/(U − L))^s` between, `1` for `ŷ ≥ U`;
* **minimize**: `d = 1` for `ŷ ≤ L`, `((U − ŷ)/(U − L))^s` between, `0`
  for `ŷ ≥ U`;
* **hit a target** `T` with `L < T < U`: `((ŷ − L)/(T − L))^s` from `L`
  to `T`, `((U − ŷ)/(U − T))^t` from `T` to `U`, `0` outside `[L, U]`.

The exponents (`s`, `t` > 0) shape the curve: 1 is linear, larger values
demand values close to the best, smaller ones accept values near the
limit. The overall desirability is the weighted geometric mean
`D = (Π dᵢ^wᵢ)^(1/Σwᵢ)` over the responses with a goal (importance `wᵢ`);
it is 0 as soon as any one response is unacceptable.

- `enum Goal`: What is wanted of a response.
- `struct Desirability`: A response's desirability function.
- `fn overall_desirability`: Overall desirability `D = (Π dᵢ^wᵢ)^(1/Σwᵢ)` of individual desirabilities `d` with importances `weights`, skipping NaN entries (responses without a goal).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/evaluation.rs`

Design evaluation: what a design can do for a model before any data are
collected.

Everything here depends only on the coded runs `x₁ … xₙ` (in `[−1, 1]^k`)
and the [`ModelFormula`], through the model matrix `X` (one row `f(xᵢ)ᵀ`
per run) and `(XᵀX)⁻¹`, so it serves both a planned design and one already
run. The response's error variance `σ²` is unknown before the experiment,
so variances are *relative* (in units of `σ²`) and anticipated effects are
given in units of `σ`.

#### Power of the test of each term
For term `j` with anticipated coefficient `β` (in units of `σ`) the
two-sided `t` test at level `α` rejects when `t² = β̂²/(s² cⱼⱼ)` exceeds
`F_{1−α}(1, n − p)`, with `cⱼⱼ = [(XᵀX)⁻¹]ⱼⱼ`. Under the alternative `t²`
follows a noncentral `F(1, n − p; λ)` with `λ = β²/cⱼⱼ`, so
`power = P(F(1, n − p; λ) > F_{1−α}(1, n − p))` (e.g. Montgomery,
*Design and Analysis of Experiments*, §2.4 and §13; Ryan, *Sample Size
Determination and Power*, §6). Power needs error degrees of freedom: a
saturated design (`n = p`) has none.

The relative standard error of a coefficient is `√cⱼⱼ`, and its variance
inflation factor is the `j`th diagonal element of the inverse correlation
matrix of the non-intercept model columns, `1/(1 − R²ⱼ)` (Marquardt 1970,
*Technometrics* 12(3)); 1 when the column is orthogonal to the others.

#### Prediction variance
The relative variance of the predicted mean at `x` is
`d(x) = f(x)ᵀ (XᵀX)⁻¹ f(x)`. The report gives its profile along each factor
(the others at 0), its maximum over the region (searched over a grid
containing the vertices, a uniform random sample, and a local refinement
of the best points) and its average over the region, `I = tr(M (XᵀX)⁻¹)`
with the exact moment matrix `M` of `[−1, 1]^k`
([`crate::optimal::region_moments`]).

#### Constrained regions
[`evaluate_design_in`] evaluates over a [`Region`]: the cube cut by
linear constraints and disallowed combinations, with two-level
categorical factors at ±1 only. The largest `d(x)` is then searched over
the grid points inside the region and the sample points, and the local
refinement stays inside it; the average variance uses the region's moment
matrix, estimated from quasi-random (Halton) points of the region
([`crate::optimal::region_moments_in`]); and the fraction-of-design-space
sample is the first `samples` Halton points that fall in the region
([`Region::quasi_random_points`]) instead of uniform random points of the
cube. Without constraints everything is as for the cube.

#### Fraction of design space
Zahran, Anderson-Cook & Myers (2003), "Fraction of design space to assess
prediction capability of response surface designs", *Journal of Quality
Technology* 35(4): for a seeded uniform sample of points of the region,
the sorted values of `d(x)` plotted against the fraction of the region at
or below each value. A flatter, lower curve predicts more uniformly well.

#### Alias matrix
When the true model also contains terms `X₂` that the fitted model `X₁`
omits, `E(β̂₁) = β₁ + A β₂` with the alias matrix
`A = (X₁ᵀX₁)⁻¹ X₁ᵀ X₂` (Montgomery, §8.6 and §10; Box, Hunter & Hunter,
*Statistics for Experimenters*, 2nd ed., §6). The default alias terms are
the two-factor interactions not in the model, or the three-factor
interactions when the model holds every two-factor interaction.

#### Efficiencies
Atkinson, Donev & Tobias, *Optimum Experimental Designs, with SAS* (2007),
§10–11, for `n` runs and `p` terms:
`D = 100 |XᵀX|^{1/p}/n`, `A = 100 p/(n tr (XᵀX)⁻¹)`,
`G = 100 p/(n max d(x))`. Each is 100% for an orthogonal two-level
design whose model matrix has entries ±1 (such as a full factorial for
its interaction model); `G` uses the largest `d(x)` found by the search,
so it is an upper bound when the search misses the true maximum.

- `struct EvaluationOptions`: Settings of [`evaluate_design`].
- `struct TermPower`: One model term's estimability and power.
- `struct FractionOfDesignSpace`: The fraction-of-design-space curve.
- `struct DesignEvaluation`: The evaluation of a design for a model.
- `fn default_alias_terms`: The default alias terms of `formula`: the two-factor interactions it does not contain; when it contains all of them, the three-factor interactions it does not contain (empty with fewer factors).
- `fn evaluate_design`: Evaluate coded `runs` for `formula` over the whole cube `[−1, 1]^k` (see the [module](self) documentation).
- `fn evaluate_design_in`: Evaluate coded `runs` for `formula` over `region`: the maximum and average prediction variance, G- and I-criteria and the fraction-of-design-space curve refer to the points of the region (see the [module](self) documentation).
- `struct DesignComparison`: Two designs compared for the same model: each ratio is design 1's value relative to design 2's (above 1 when design 1 is better), and the run-adjusted ratios compare information per run (the ratios of the efficiencies).
- `fn compare_designs`: Compare two evaluations of the same model.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/factorial.rs`

Full and fractional factorial designs.

#### Full factorials
[`full_factorial`] crosses every level of every factor, with `L` levels coded
as `L` equally spaced values from −1 to +1 (two levels: −1, +1; three levels:
−1, 0, +1). Runs are in Yates standard order: the first factor changes
fastest.

#### Two-level fractional factorials `2^(k−p)`
The first `k − p` ("base") factors form a full `2^(k−p)` factorial and each
of the remaining `p` factors is set to the product of a subset of the base
columns, its **generator** (e.g. `E = ABCD`). Each generator gives a word of
the **defining relation** (`I = ABCDE`); all `2^p − 1` products of these words
form the complete defining relation. The **resolution** is the length of its
shortest word: in a resolution III design main effects are aliased with
two-factor interactions, in IV two-factor interactions are aliased with each
other, in V and above no main effect or two-factor interaction is aliased with
another (Box, Hunter & Hunter, *Statistics for Experimenters*, 2nd ed., ch. 6;
Montgomery, *Design and Analysis of Experiments*, ch. 8).

[`fractional_factorial`] uses a table of minimum-aberration generators for
`k ≤ 11` (the generators tabulated in Montgomery, Table 8.14), and
[`fractional_factorial_with_generators`] accepts any generators. Factors are
named `A, B, …` (skipping `I`) in generator words.

- `fn full_factorial`: A full factorial design with `levels[j]` levels for factor `j`.
- `fn two_level_factorial`: `2^k` full factorial.
- `fn three_level_factorial`: `3^k` full factorial (levels −1, 0, +1).
- `fn tabulated_fractions`: The `(k, p)` pairs with tabulated generators.
- `struct FractionalFactorial`: A two-level fractional factorial with its aliasing information.
- `fn parse_word`: Factor bit mask from letters such as `"ABD"` (letters as in [`default_factor_names`]).
- `fn word_letters`: Letters of a bit-mask word, e.g.
- `fn resolution_label`: Roman numeral for a resolution.
- `fn fractional_factorial`: `2^(k−p)` fractional factorial from the generator table.
- `fn smallest_fraction`: The smallest fraction (largest `p`) of `2^k` with at least the given resolution among the tabulated designs, or `0` (the full factorial).
- `fn fractional_factorial_with_generators`: `2^(k−p)` fractional factorial with the given generators: `generators[i]` is the word (over the first `k − p` letters) defining factor `k − p + i`.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/factorial_analysis.rs`

Analysis of two-level factorial experiments in coded units.

#### Effects
With every factor coded −1 (low) and +1 (high), the model
`y = β₀ + Σ βₜ xₜ + ε` over product terms `xₜ = Πⱼ∈ₜ xⱼ` (main effects and
interactions, [`ModelFormula::interactions_up_to`]) is fitted by least
squares (pivoted Householder QR). The **effect** of a term is `2βₜ`: the
change in the mean response from its low to its high setting (for an
orthogonal design, the difference of the two half-means). The fit uses the
coded settings actually run, so a run that missed its target (a coded
value that is not exactly −1, 0 or +1) keeps the estimates unbiased; the
design is then no longer exactly orthogonal and the effects' standard
errors differ slightly ([`OffTarget`]).

#### Normal and half-normal plots
Daniel (1959), "Use of half-normal plots in interpreting factorial two-level
experiments", *Technometrics* 1(4): the `m` ordered effects plotted against
normal scores `Φ⁻¹((i − ½)/m)`, or their absolute values against
half-normal scores `Φ⁻¹(½ + ½(i − ½)/m)` ([`normal_scores`],
[`half_normal_scores`]). Inert effects fall on a line through the origin
with slope equal to their standard error; active effects stand off it.

#### Lenth's method
Lenth (1989), "Quick and easy analysis of unreplicated factorials",
*Technometrics* 31(4): with effects `c₁ … c_m` and no error degrees of
freedom, `s₀ = 1.5 · median|cᵢ|` and the pseudo standard error
`PSE = 1.5 · median{|cᵢ| : |cᵢ| < 2.5 s₀}`. Treating `PSE` like a standard
error on `d = m/3` degrees of freedom, the margin of error is
`ME = t_{1−α/2; d} · PSE` and the simultaneous margin of error
`SME = t_{γ; d} · PSE` with `γ = (1 + (1 − α)^{1/m})/2`. Effects beyond `ME`
are individually active; beyond `SME`, active allowing for all `m`
comparisons ([`lenth`]). The method assumes effects of equal variance (an
orthogonal design) and effect sparsity (most effects inert); with fewer
than about seven effects it has little power.

When the model leaves error degrees of freedom (replicates, centre runs or
terms left out), each effect gets an ordinary `t` test instead:
`se(2β̂) = 2 √(s² [(XᵀX)⁻¹]ₜₜ)` with `s² = RSS/(n − p)`.

#### Dispersion effects
* **Replicated designs** — Box & Meyer (1986), "Dispersion effects from
  fractional designs", *Technometrics* 28(1); Box, Hunter & Hunter,
  *Statistics for Experimenters* (2nd ed.): the log standard
  deviation `ln sᵢ` of the replicates at each distinct setting is modelled
  on the factors like a response, and its effects judged with the same
  normal plot and Lenth machinery ([`replicated_dispersion`]).
* **Unreplicated designs** — Bergman & Hynén (1997), "Dispersion effects
  from unreplicated designs in the 2^(k−p) series", *Technometrics* 39(2):
  for factor `j`, the location model is fitted separately within the runs
  at `xⱼ = +1` and at `xⱼ = −1` (equivalently, `xⱼ`'s interactions with every
  location term are added), and `Dⱼ = (RSS₊/df₊)/(RSS₋/df₋)` is compared with
  `F(df₊, df₋)` (two-sided). Box & Meyer's statistic
  `ln(Σr²₊ / Σr²₋)` from the location model's residuals is reported
  alongside ([`unreplicated_dispersion`]). Both need a location model that
  leaves residual degrees of freedom: usually the active effects only.

#### Means
[`level_means`], [`interaction_means`] and [`cube_means`] average the
response over the runs at each sign of the coded settings (centre runs,
coded 0, are left out); [`FactorialFit::predict`] gives the model's
prediction instead, with factors not shown held at their centre.

- `const TARGET_TOLERANCE`: Tolerance for a coded value to count as on target (−1, 0 or +1).
- `enum Activity`: How strongly an effect stands out.
- `struct LenthResult`: Lenth's pseudo standard error and margins of error for `m` effects.
- `fn lenth`: Lenth's method for effects `c` at significance level `alpha`.
- `fn normal_scores`: Normal scores `Φ⁻¹((i − ½)/m)`, `i = 1 … m` (increasing).
- `fn half_normal_scores`: Half-normal scores `Φ⁻¹(½ + ½(i − ½)/m)`, `i = 1 … m` (increasing).
- `fn normal_plot_positions`: The normal score of each effect, in the effects' own order (ties keep their order).
- `fn half_normal_plot_positions`: The half-normal score of each effect's absolute value, in the effects' own order.
- `enum EffectTest`: The reference distribution of the effects' tests.
- `struct EffectEstimate`: One estimated effect.
- `struct EffectSet`: A set of effects with the inference that applies to them.
- `struct OffTarget`: Runs whose coded settings missed −1, 0 and +1.
- `fn off_target`: Check coded runs against the targets −1, 0 and +1.
- `fn check_two_level`: Check that `formula` holds only products of distinct factors.
- `struct FactorialFit`: A two-level factorial model fitted by least squares.
- `fn fit_factorial`: Fit `formula` to coded `runs` and response `y`, with effects judged at level `alpha` (`t` tests with error df, Lenth's method without).
- `fn term_labels`: `(label, order)` of each non-intercept term.
- `struct CellMean`: Mean and count of the runs at one setting.
- `fn level_means`: Mean response at the low (`[0]`) and high (`[1]`) setting of each factor, by the sign of the coded value (centre runs are left out).
- `fn interaction_means`: Mean response in the four cells of factors `a` and `b`: `[level of a][level of b]`.
- `fn cube_means`: Mean response at each corner of the factors `factors` (two or three): `(corner signs, mean)` in standard order (first factor fastest).
- `fn corners`: The `2^d` corners of `[−1, 1]^d` in standard order.
- `struct ReplicatedSetting`: One distinct setting of a replicated design.
- `struct ReplicatedDispersion`: Dispersion effects of a replicated design: effects of `ln s`.
- `fn replicated_dispersion`: Box & Meyer's dispersion analysis of a replicated design: `ln s` at each distinct setting with two or more runs, modelled by `formula` when the settings can estimate it, else by the main effects.
- `struct DispersionTest`: Bergman–Hynén and Box–Meyer statistics for one factor.
- `fn unreplicated_dispersion`: Dispersion tests for an unreplicated design (one per factor) given the location model `location`.
- `fn estimable_terms`: The terms of `formula` the runs can estimate, chosen in model order: a term whose column lies in the span of the columns already kept (aliased with lower-order or earlier terms, as in a fractional factorial) is left out, and so is every term once the model is saturated (as many terms as runs).
- `fn saturated_poisson`: A saturated Poisson log-linear model (as many terms as runs): the fit is exact, `η = ln y`, so the coefficients solve `Xβ = ln y`; Wald standard errors come from `Cov(β̂) = (XᵀWX)⁻¹` with `W = diag(μ̂) = diag(y)` (McCullagh & Nelder, §6.2).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-doe

Design of experiments. Every generator returns a [`Design`]: factors with
low/high settings, runs in coded units in standard order, the role of each
run, and notes (aliasing, efficiency). [`Design::to_table`] exports a design
as a [`stat_data::DataTable`] in coded or actual units, optionally in
randomized run order, with empty response columns ready for results.

* [`factorial`] — full factorials (`2^k`, `3^k`, mixed levels) and two-level
  fractional factorials `2^(k−p)` with defining relation, resolution and
  aliases.
* [`factorial_analysis`] — effects, normal and half-normal plots, Lenth's method, dispersion
  effects and means of two-level factorial experiments.
* [`screening`] — Plackett–Burman designs and definitive screening designs
  built from conference matrices (with extra runs and center runs).
* [`categorical_screening`] — D-optimal screening designs mixing two-level
  continuous factors with categorical factors of any number of levels.
* [`simulate`] — simulated responses from random coefficients with effect
  sparsity, hierarchy and heredity.
* [`response_surface`] — central composite (circumscribed, inscribed,
  face-centred) and Box–Behnken designs.
* [`optimal`] — model formulas and D- and I-optimal designs by coordinate exchange.
* [`augment`] — fold-over, centre and axial runs, and D-optimal augmentation of an existing design.
* [`constraints`] — design regions cut by linear constraints and disallowed combinations.
* [`split_plot`] — D-optimal split-plot and split-split-plot designs for hard-to-change factors.
* [`mixture`] — simplex-lattice, simplex-centroid and extreme-vertices mixture designs and Scheffé models.
* [`orthogonal`] — standard orthogonal arrays (L4 … L27), signal-to-noise ratios and response tables.
* [`design`] — the design type, factor coding, export, seeded randomization.
* [`evaluation`] — design evaluation before data collection: power of each
  term, prediction variance (profile, maximum, average, fraction of design
  space), alias matrix, correlations, D/A/G/I efficiencies, comparing two
  designs.
* [`desirability`] — Derringer–Suich desirability functions for optimizing
  several responses at once.
* [`space_filling`] — space-filling designs for computer experiments:
  maximin Latin hypercubes, maximin and minimax distance designs, uniform designs.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/mixture.rs`

Mixture experiments: designs on the simplex `x₁ + … + x_q = 1, xᵢ ≥ 0` and
the Scheffé canonical polynomials fitted to them (Scheffé 1958, 1963;
Cornell, *Experiments with Mixtures*, 3rd ed., ch. 2; NIST/SEMATECH
e-Handbook §5.5.4).

* **Simplex-lattice `{q, m}`** — every blend whose proportions are multiples
  of `1/m`: `C(q + m − 1, m)` points. It supports the Scheffé polynomial of
  degree `m`.
* **Simplex-centroid** — the `2^q − 1` blends with equal proportions of a
  non-empty subset of components (pure blends, 50:50 binaries, …, the overall
  centroid). It supports the special cubic and, in general, the full
  `q`-component Scheffé polynomial with all products.
* **Axial check blends** (optional) — `(1 + q)/(2q)` of one component and
  `1/(2q)` of each other, half-way between the centroid and each vertex;
  interior points for checking model fit.

* **Extreme vertices** — when components have lower and upper bounds
  `Lᵢ ≤ xᵢ ≤ Uᵢ`, the region is a convex polytope inside the simplex. Its
  vertices are found by the method of McLean & Anderson (1966),
  "Extreme vertices design of mixture experiments", *Technometrics* 8(3),
  447–454: set all but one component at a bound in every combination,
  give the remaining component `1 − Σ others`, and keep the blend when that
  is within its own bounds. Bounds implied by the others
  (`Lᵢ' = max(Lᵢ, 1 − Σ_{j≠i} Uⱼ)`, `Uᵢ' = min(Uᵢ, 1 − Σ_{j≠i} Lⱼ)`) are
  applied first. Centroids of the edges and two-dimensional faces (the
  averages of their vertices) and the overall centroid (the average of all
  vertices) can be added as interior points (Cornell, ch. 4).

Because the proportions sum to one, the Scheffé models have no intercept:

```text
linear          E(y) = Σ βᵢxᵢ
quadratic       E(y) = Σ βᵢxᵢ + Σ_{i<j} βᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ
special cubic   E(y) = … + Σ_{i<j<k} βᵢⱼₖxᵢxⱼxₖ
```

- `const MAX_COMPONENTS`: Most components accepted.
- `enum BlendType`: The role of a blend in a mixture design.
- `struct MixtureDesign`: A mixture design: proportions of each component (each run sums to one).
- `enum ScheffeModel`: Scheffé canonical mixture model.
- `fn simplex_lattice`: Simplex-lattice `{q, m}` design, optionally with the overall centroid and axial check blends added (each only if not already present).
- `fn simplex_centroid`: Simplex-centroid design for `q` components, optionally with axial check blends.
- `const MAX_VERTICES_FOR_FACES`: Most vertices for which two-dimensional face centroids are found.
- `fn extreme_vertices`: Extreme-vertices design for components with bounds `lower[i] ≤ xᵢ ≤ upper[i]` (McLean & Anderson 1966): the vertices of the constrained region, then — up to `centroid_dimension` (0 none, 1 edges, 2 edges and two-dimensional faces) — the centroids of its faces, then the overall centroid if `overal…

### `crates/stat-doe/src/optimal.rs`

Model formulas and D- and I-optimal designs by coordinate exchange.

#### Model formulas
A [`ModelFormula`] is a polynomial in the coded factors: an intercept plus
terms such as `A`, `A*B` and `A^2`. [`ModelFormula::parse`] reads text like
`"A + B + C + A*B + A^2"` (factor names as given; `*` or `:` joins factors,
`^n` raises a factor to a power, and `A*A` equals `A^2`). The presets
[`ModelFormula::main_effects`], [`ModelFormula::interactions`] (main effects
and all two-factor interactions) and [`ModelFormula::quadratic`] (the full
second-order response-surface model) cover the usual cases.

#### D-optimality
For `n` runs and model matrix `X` (one row `f(x)ᵀ` per run), a D-optimal
design maximizes `det(XᵀX)`, which minimizes the volume of the joint
confidence region of the coefficients. The reported **D-efficiency** is
`100 · det(XᵀX)^{1/p} / n` for `p` model terms, which is 100% for an
orthogonal two-level design (e.g. a full factorial for a model with main
effects and interactions).

#### I-optimality
An I-optimal design minimizes the average variance of the predicted mean
over the cuboidal region `[−1, 1]^k`, `I = tr(M (XᵀX)⁻¹)` in units of `σ²`,
where `M = 2^{−k} ∫ f(x) f(x)ᵀ dx` is the region's moment matrix (Box &
Draper 1959; Atkinson, Donev & Tobias, *Optimum Experimental Designs*, §10.6).
For monomials the moments are exact: `2^{−1}∫₋₁¹ xᵃ dx = 1/(a + 1)` for even
`a` and 0 for odd `a`. I-optimal designs suit response-surface work, where
the aim is prediction rather than estimating each coefficient. Each start
is first improved for D (which also makes it non-singular), then for I,
where replacing row `x` by `y` updates the trace by two Sherman–Morrison
steps in `O(p²)`.

#### Coordinate exchange
Meyer & Nachtsheim (1995), "The coordinate-exchange algorithm for
constructing exact optimal experimental designs", *Technometrics* 37(1):
starting from a random design, each coordinate (run `i`, factor `j`) in turn is
replaced by the candidate level that most increases `det(XᵀX)`; passes over all
coordinates repeat until none improves, and the best of several random starts
is kept. It is a heuristic: more starts make finding the global optimum
more likely. Candidate levels for a factor whose highest power in the model is
`d` are `d + 1` equally spaced values from −1 to +1 (−1, +1 for linear terms;
−1, 0, +1 for quadratic ones).

Replacing row `x` by `y` multiplies the determinant by
`(1 + yᵀA⁻¹y)(1 − xᵀA⁻¹x) + (xᵀA⁻¹y)²` with `A = XᵀX` (Fedorov 1972,
*Theory of Optimal Experiments*), so each candidate costs `O(p²)`; `A⁻¹` is
recomputed by Cholesky factorization after every accepted change. A singular
starting design is handled by maximizing `det(XᵀX + δI)` with a small `δ`
until the design becomes non-singular.

- `struct Term`: One model term: the power of each factor (all zero for the intercept).
- `struct ModelFormula`: A polynomial model in `k` coded factors, always with an intercept.
- `struct OptimalOptions`: Options for [`d_optimal`].
- `struct OptimalDesign`: A D-optimal design and its quality.
- `fn log_det_information`: `ln det(XᵀX)` of `runs` for `formula` (−∞ if singular).
- `fn d_efficiency`: D-efficiency `100 · det(XᵀX)^{1/p} / n` of `runs` for `formula`.
- `fn d_optimal`: Build a D-optimal design for `formula` by coordinate exchange over the whole cube `[−1, 1]^k` (see [`d_optimal_in`] for a constrained region).
- `fn d_optimal_in`: Build a D-optimal design for `formula` inside `region` by coordinate exchange.
- `const MOMENT_SAMPLE`: Number of Halton points used to estimate the moments of a constrained region ([`region_moments_in`]).
- `fn region_moments`: Moment matrix `M` of `formula` over `[−1, 1]^k` with uniform weight.
- `fn region_moments_in`: Moment matrix `M = E[f(x) f(x)ᵀ]` of `formula` for `x` uniform over `region`, and the number of sample points used (`None` when exact).
- `fn average_prediction_variance`: Average prediction variance `tr(M (XᵀX)⁻¹)` of `runs` for `formula` over `[−1, 1]^k` (∞ if `XᵀX` is singular).
- `fn i_optimal`: Build an I-optimal design for `formula` by coordinate exchange over the whole cube (see [`i_optimal_in`] for a constrained region).
- `fn i_optimal_in`: Build an I-optimal design for `formula` inside `region`: as [`d_optimal_in`], with each start improved for D and then for the average prediction variance over the region, whose moment matrix is exact for the cube and estimated from quasi-random points of a constrained region ([`region_moments_in`]).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/orthogonal.rs`

Standard orthogonal arrays and robust (parameter) design.

#### Orthogonal arrays
An orthogonal array of strength 2 is a table of factor levels in which,
for every pair of columns, each combination of levels appears equally
often, so main effects are estimated independently of one another. The
standard arrays catalogued by Taguchi and reproduced in Phadke, *Quality
Engineering Using Robust Design* (Prentice Hall 1989, appendix C), are
built here from their published constructions:

* **L4 (2³), L8 (2⁷), L16 (2¹⁵)** — the `2^m − 1` columns of a `2^m`
  two-level array are the non-zero linear combinations over GF(2) of `m`
  basic columns. With rows numbered `r = 0 … 2^m − 1`, basic column `i`
  takes bit `m − 1 − i` of `r`, and column `c` (1-based) adds the basic
  columns named by the bits of `c`: column 3 is columns 1 + 2, column 5 is
  1 + 4, and so on — the standard column order, in which the interaction
  of columns `a` and `b` appears in column `a XOR b`.
* **L9 (3⁴), L27 (3¹³)** — likewise over GF(3): the columns are one
  representative of each projective point (`a`, `b`, `a + b`, `2a + b` for
  L9; for L27 also `c`, `a + c`, `2a + c`, `b + c`, `a + b + c`,
  `2a + b + c`, `2b + c`, `a + 2b + c`, `2a + 2b + c`), so that the
  interaction of columns 1 and 2 is carried by columns 3 and 4.
* **L12 (2¹¹)** — the 12-run Plackett–Burman design (cyclic generator,
  Plackett & Burman 1946), arranged with the all-low run first.
  Interactions are spread over the columns rather than confounded with one.
* **L18 (2¹ × 3⁷)** — the standard mixed array as tabulated by Taguchi.

Levels are numbered 1, 2, 3 as in the published tables.

#### Robust design and signal-to-noise ratios
Control factors are assigned to the columns of an **inner array**; each
inner run is repeated under the conditions of an **outer array** of noise
factors (or simply replicated). For each inner run the `n` responses give
a signal-to-noise ratio (Phadke 1989, ch. 5–6), in decibels, to be
maximized:

```text
smaller the better   η = −10 log₁₀( Σ y² / n )
larger the better    η = −10 log₁₀( Σ (1/y²) / n )
nominal the best     η =  10 log₁₀( ȳ² / s² )      (scale adjustable)
nominal, variance    η = −10 log₁₀( s² )           (location adjustable)
```

The analysis of means of the array then tabulates, for each factor, the
mean of η (and of the response) at each level; the range of those means
ranks the factors' influence, and the additive model predicts η at any
combination of levels as `η̄ + Σ_factors (η̄_level − η̄)`.

- `enum StandardArray`: The standard orthogonal arrays offered.
- `fn is_orthogonal`: `true` when every pair of columns of `rows` (1-based levels, `levels[j]` for column `j`) shows each level combination equally often (strength 2).
- `enum SignalToNoise`: A signal-to-noise ratio (Phadke 1989, ch.
- `struct LevelMeans`: The mean of a run summary at each level of one factor.
- `fn level_means`: The response table of an orthogonal-array experiment: for each factor the mean of `values` (one per run) at each of its levels.
- `fn best_levels`: The best level of each factor (largest mean) and the additive-model prediction there: `overall + Σ (best mean − overall)`.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/response_surface.rs`

Response surface designs for fitting second-order (quadratic) models.

#### Central composite designs
A two-level factorial portion (full, or a resolution V fraction so that all
two-factor interactions remain estimable), `2k` axial points at distance `α`
on each axis, and centre points (Box & Wilson 1951, *JRSS B* 13; Montgomery,
*Design and Analysis of Experiments*, §11.4). With `F` factorial runs:

* **rotatable** `α = F^{1/4}`, which makes the prediction variance depend only
  on the distance from the centre (`Σxᵢ⁴ = 3Σxᵢ²xⱼ²`);
* **spherical** `α = √k`, putting every non-centre point on one sphere;
* **face-centred** `α = 1`, so every factor uses only three levels;
* or any `α > 0`.

The usual (circumscribed) design has its axial points outside the factorial
cube; an **inscribed** design divides every coordinate by `α` so the axial
points sit at the factor limits ±1.

Default numbers of centre points: for rotatable designs, the
uniform-precision number of Box & Hunter (1957), *Ann. Math. Statist.* 28,
computed for the factorial portion used (see [`uniform_precision_centers`];
it reproduces their table: k = 2…7: 5, 6, 7, 6, 9, 14 with half fractions
for k ≥ 5; 10, 15 and 21 for full 2⁵, 2⁶ and 2⁷ portions; 20 for 2⁸⁻¹),
otherwise 3 for face-centred designs and 6 for the rest.

#### Box–Behnken designs
Three-level designs that combine two-level factorials on subsets of factors
with the remaining factors at their centre, never using the corners of the
cube (Box & Behnken 1960, *Technometrics* 2). For `k = 3, 4, 5` every pair of
factors gets a `2²` factorial; for `k = 6` and `k = 7` the published
arrangements of factor triples with `2³` factorials are used.

- `enum AxialDistance`: How far the axial points of a central composite design are from the centre.
- `struct CcdOptions`: Options for [`central_composite`].
- `fn central_composite`: Central composite design for `k ≥ 2` factors.
- `fn uniform_precision_centers`: Number of centre runs that gives a rotatable central composite design (factorial portion of `f_runs` runs, resolution V or more, `2k` axial runs at `α = F^{1/4}`) uniform precision: the scaled prediction variance `N f(x)′(X′X)⁻¹f(x)` of the full quadratic model as nearly equal at the centre and a…
- `fn box_behnken`: Box–Behnken design for `3 ≤ k ≤ 7` factors with `center_points` centre runs (`None`: 3 for `k ≤ 4`, 6 otherwise).

### `crates/stat-doe/src/screening.rs`

Screening designs.

#### Plackett–Burman
Two-level orthogonal main-effect designs in `N` runs (`N` a multiple of 4)
for up to `N − 1` factors (Plackett & Burman 1946, "The design of optimum
multifactorial experiments", *Biometrika* 33). For `N = 12, 20, 24` the rows
are the cyclic shifts of the published first row followed by a row of all
−1; for `N = 8, 16, 32, 64` the Sylvester Hadamard matrix is used (these are
the corresponding resolution III fractional factorials). Each design uses the
smallest supported `N > k`.

#### Definitive screening designs
Three-level designs in which main effects are orthogonal to each other and to
every second-order effect, and quadratic effects are estimable (Jones &
Nachtsheim 2011, "A class of three-level designs for definitive screening in
the presence of second-order effects", *J. Quality Technology* 43; built from
conference matrices as in Xiao, Lin & Bai 2012, *J. Quality Technology* 44).
For a conference matrix `C` of order `m` (zero diagonal, ±1 elsewhere,
`CᵀC = (m − 1)I`) the design is `[C; −C; 0]` with `2m + 1` runs. `m` is the
smallest available even order of at least `max(k, 6)`; extra columns are
dropped. Conference matrices come from Paley's construction over the finite
field `GF(q)`, `q = m − 1` a prime power: with `χ` the quadratic character,
`Q = [χ(j − i)]`, and `C = [[0, 1ᵀ], [±1, Q]]` (symmetric when
`q ≡ 1 mod 4`, antisymmetric when `q ≡ 3 mod 4`).

- `const PLACKETT_BURMAN_SIZES`: Run sizes supported by [`plackett_burman`].
- `fn plackett_burman`: Plackett–Burman design for `k` factors in the smallest supported run size greater than `k`.
- `fn plackett_burman_runs`: Plackett–Burman design for `k` factors in `n` runs.
- `fn conference_orders`: Orders `m` for which [`conference_matrix`] can build a matrix.
- `fn conference_matrix`: A conference matrix of order `m` by Paley's construction.
- `fn definitive_screening`: Definitive screening design for `k` continuous factors (`k ≥ 3`): the smallest conference matrix and one center run.
- `struct DsdOptions`: Choices for a definitive screening design beyond the factor count.
- `const MAX_DSD_CENTER_RUNS`: Most center runs of a definitive screening design.
- `fn dsd_order`: The conference-matrix order of the definitive screening design for `k` factors with `options`.
- `fn definitive_screening_with`: Definitive screening design for `k` continuous factors with extra runs and center runs (see [`DsdOptions`]).
- `struct DsdSummary`: Properties of one definitive screening design, for comparing choices of extra runs and center runs ([`compare_definitive_screening`]).
- `fn compare_definitive_screening`: Compare definitive screening designs for `k` factors across choices of extra runs and center runs: one [`DsdSummary`] per choice, in the order given.
- `fn dsd_comparison_choices`: The standard choices to compare with `chosen`: no extra runs and the next two conference-matrix orders up, each with one center run and with the chosen number, plus `chosen` itself; duplicates removed, by run count.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/simulate.rs`

Simulated responses for a design from random coefficients, with effect
sparsity, hierarchy and heredity.

Before an experiment is run, simulating plausible responses shows how
well its analysis would find the effects that matter. The coefficients
follow the hierarchical prior of Chipman, Hamada & Wu (1997), "A Bayesian
variable-selection approach for analyzing designed experiments with
complex aliasing", *Technometrics* 39(4), in its generative form:

* **Effect sparsity:** each main effect is active with probability `p`.
* **Heredity:** a higher-order term (an interaction, or a squared factor)
  is active with probability `p₁₁` when all its parent main effects are
  active (strong heredity), `p₀₁` when only some are (weak heredity) and
  `p₀₀` when none is. A squared factor has one parent, so only `p₁₁` and
  `p₀₀` apply to it ([`SparsityPrior::quadratic`] may give its own pair).
* **Hierarchy:** the defaults make higher-order terms rarer than main
  effects (`p₁₁ ≤ p`), the effect-hierarchy principle.
* **Sizes:** an active coefficient is drawn from `N(0, τ²)`, an inactive
  one from `N(0, (τ/c)²)` with `c` large (CHW's mixture prior), or is
  exactly zero when `inactive_sd` is 0.

Each simulated response is `y = β₀ + Σ βₜ fₜ(x) + ε` over the design's
coded runs, with `ε ~ N(0, σ²)`. Draws come from one seeded generator, so a
simulation is reproducible.

- `struct SparsityPrior`: Probabilities and sizes of the random coefficients.
- `struct SimulatedDesignResponse`: One simulated response and the coefficients that made it.
- `const MAX_SIMULATIONS`: Most simulated responses at once.
- `fn simulate_responses`: Simulate `count` responses at coded `runs` for `formula` (see the module documentation), from `seed`.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/space_filling.rs`

Space-filling designs for computer experiments.

A deterministic computer model has no random error, so replicates and
centre points tell nothing and the classical designs, which put runs at
the corners of the region, waste most of them. Space-filling designs
spread the runs evenly over the whole region instead, so that a flexible
surrogate (a Gaussian process, a spline, a polynomial) can be fitted
anywhere (Santner, Williams & Notz, *The Design and Analysis of Computer
Experiments*, 2nd ed., 2018, ch. 5).

Every design here is built in the unit cube `[0, 1]^k` and returned as a
[`Design`] in coded units `[−1, 1]^k` (coded = 2u − 1), so each factor's
low and high settings map to the ends of its range. All criteria are
measured in the unit cube.

#### Criteria
* **Minimum distance** `d_min = min_{i<j} ‖x_i − x_j‖` (Euclidean): a
  *maximin* design makes it as large as possible (Johnson, Moore &
  Ylvisaker 1990, "Minimax and maximin distance designs", *Journal of
  Statistical Planning and Inference* 26).
* **φ_p** `= (Σ_{i<j} d_ij^{−p})^{1/p}` (Morris & Mitchell 1995,
  "Exploratory designs for computational experiments", *J. Statist. Plann.
  Inference* 43): a smooth stand-in for `1/d_min` that also counts how many
  pairs are close; smaller is better, and as `p → ∞` minimizing φ_p
  maximizes `d_min`. [`phi_p`] evaluates it.
* **Fill distance** `h = sup_{x ∈ [0,1]^k} min_i ‖x − x_i‖`, the radius of
  the largest empty ball centred in the region: a *minimax* design makes it
  as small as possible, so no point of the region is far from a run.
  [`fill_distance`] measures it over a finite set of points; with
  [`evaluation_points`] (a regular grid that includes the corners when it
  fits, plus a Halton sequence) the result is an approximation from below.
* **Centered L2 discrepancy** (Hickernell 1998, "A generalized discrepancy
  and quadrature error bound", *Mathematics of Computation* 67), for `n`
  points with `z = x − ½`:
  `CD² = (13/12)^k − (2/n) Σ_i Π_j (1 + ½|z_ij| − ½z_ij²) +
  (1/n²) Σ_i Σ_l Π_j (1 + ½|z_ij| + ½|z_lj| − ½|x_ij − x_lj|)`.
  It measures how far the points' empirical distribution is from uniform
  over every corner-anchored box; [`centered_l2_discrepancy`] returns `CD`
  (the square root).

#### Designs
* [`maximin_latin_hypercube`]: a Latin hypercube (each column a permutation
  of the levels `(i − ½)/n`, so every factor is sampled once in each of `n`
  equal slices) minimizing φ_p (p = 50) by simulated annealing over swaps
  of two entries of a column (Morris & Mitchell 1995). Schedule: the
  starting temperature accepts the average worsening of `ln φ_p` among 100
  sampled swaps with probability ½; the temperature falls geometrically
  through 100 levels to 10⁻³ of its start, with an equal share of the swap
  budget at each level; the best design seen is kept.
* [`maximin_distance`]: maximin design not restricted to a lattice. Runs
  are chosen from a dense candidate set (regular grids with 2, 3, 4, …
  levels per factor while they fit, plus uniform random points) by greedy
  farthest-point selection, then improved by exchange: a point of the
  closest pair is replaced by the candidate farthest from the other points
  whenever that increases `d_min` or reduces the number of pairs at `d_min`.
  Finally the points move continuously by projected gradient descent on
  `ln φ_p` with `p` rising from 20 to 5000; the refined design is kept only
  if its `d_min` is larger.
* [`minimax_distance`]: the clustering method of Mak & Joseph (2018),
  "Minimax and minimax projection designs using clustering", *Journal of
  Computational and Graphical Statistics* 27(1): the region is represented
  by [`evaluation_points`]; k-means (k-means++ starts, Lloyd iterations)
  gives an initial partition; then each run is moved to the centre of the
  smallest ball enclosing its cluster (Frank–Wolfe iterations of Yildirim
  2008, *SIAM J. Optim.* 19) and the points are reassigned, repeating while
  the fill distance over the evaluation points falls. The design minimizes
  the fill distance *over those points*, an approximation to the region.
* [`uniform_design`]: a U-type design (columns permutations of the levels
  `(2i − 1)/(2n)`) minimizing the centered L2 discrepancy by threshold
  accepting with swaps of two entries of a column (Fang, Lin, Winker & Zhang
  2000, "Uniform design: theory and application", *Technometrics* 42).
  Thresholds fall linearly through 50 levels from the 10th percentile of
  `|ΔCD²|` among 200 sampled swaps to zero.

Every search is seeded, so the same seed gives the same design, and its
work is budgeted by the size of the problem so that designs up to
[`MAX_RUNS`] runs and [`MAX_FACTORS`] factors finish quickly; they are
heuristics, and another seed may give a slightly better design.

#### Failure modes
[`StatError::InvalidArgument`] for fewer than 2 runs, no factors, or more
than [`MAX_RUNS`] runs or [`MAX_FACTORS`] factors.

- `const MAX_RUNS`: Most runs of a space-filling design.
- `const MAX_FACTORS`: Most factors of a space-filling design.
- `const DEFAULT_P`: The exponent `p` of the φ_p criterion used by the maximin Latin hypercube.
- `enum SpaceFillingKind`: The space-filling designs offered.
- `struct SpaceFillingCriteria`: The space-filling criteria of a set of points in `[0, 1]^k`.
- `fn space_filling_design`: Build the space-filling design `kind` with `runs` runs and `factors` factors (named `A, B, …`, coded −1 to +1), searching from `seed`.
- `fn maximin_latin_hypercube`: A Latin hypercube minimizing φ₅₀ by simulated annealing (Morris & Mitchell 1995); see the [module documentation](self).
- `fn maximin_distance`: A maximin distance design (Johnson, Moore & Ylvisaker 1990) by point exchange over a dense candidate set and continuous refinement; see the [module documentation](self).
- `fn minimax_distance`: A minimax distance design by clustering (Mak & Joseph 2018); see the [module documentation](self).
- `fn uniform_design`: A uniform design minimizing the centered L2 discrepancy by threshold accepting (Fang, Lin, Winker & Zhang 2000); see the [module documentation](self).
- `fn criteria`: All space-filling criteria of `points` (in `[0, 1]^k`).
- `fn min_distance`: The smallest Euclidean distance between two of `points` (`∞` for fewer than two points).
- `fn phi_p`: The Morris–Mitchell criterion `φ_p = (Σ_{i<j} d_ij^{−p})^{1/p}`, evaluated as `(1/d_min)(Σ (d_min/d_ij)^p)^{1/p}` so large `p` neither overflows nor underflows.
- `fn centered_l2_discrepancy`: Hickernell's (1998) centered L2 discrepancy `CD` of `points` in `[0, 1]^k` (the square root of the formula in the [module documentation](self)); 0 for no points.
- `fn fill_distance`: The fill distance of `design` over `region`: the largest distance from a point of `region` to its nearest design point.
- `fn evaluation_points`: Points representing the region `[0, 1]^k` for measuring fill distance for a design of `runs` runs: a regular grid with as many levels per factor as fit in half the budget (including the corners whenever `2^k` fits), then a Halton sequence (bases 2, 3, 5, …; indices from 1) up to `clamp(20·runs, 4…

### `crates/stat-doe/src/split_plot.rs`

D-optimal split-plot and split-split-plot designs by coordinate exchange.

#### Restricted randomization
When some factors are hard to change (a furnace temperature, a batch of raw
material), an experiment groups the runs into **whole plots** within
which those factors stay fixed: the hard-to-change factors are reset once
per whole plot, the easy-to-change factors on every run. Very hard-to-change
factors add a third stratum: they stay fixed within whole plots, hard ones
within **subplots** nested in the whole plots, and easy ones vary from run
to run (a split-split-plot design).

Runs in the same whole plot share a random whole-plot effect, so the
responses follow the mixed model `y = Xβ + Z_w γ + Z_s δ + ε` with
`γ ~ N(0, σ²_w I)`, `δ ~ N(0, σ²_s I)` and `ε ~ N(0, σ²_ε I)`, and
`Var(y) = σ²_ε V`, `V = I + η_w Z_w Z_wᵀ + η_s Z_s Z_sᵀ` with the variance
ratios `η_w = σ²_w / σ²_ε` and `η_s = σ²_s / σ²_ε` (`Z_w`, `Z_s` the
whole-plot and subplot indicator matrices). The generalized least-squares
estimator has covariance `σ²_ε (XᵀV⁻¹X)⁻¹`, so a **D-optimal** split-plot
design maximizes `det(XᵀV⁻¹X)` (Goos & Vandebroek 2003, "D-optimal
split-plot designs with given numbers and sizes of whole plots",
*Technometrics* 45(3); Jones & Goos 2009, "D-optimal design of
split-split-plot experiments", *Biometrika* 96(1)). `V` is block-diagonal
with one block per whole plot, so `XᵀV⁻¹X = Σᵢ XᵢᵀVᵢ⁻¹Xᵢ`.

#### Coordinate exchange without a candidate set
Jones & Goos (2007), "A candidate-set-free algorithm for generating
D-optimal split-plot designs", *Applied Statistics* 56(3): starting from a
random design that respects the restrictions, each coordinate is replaced
by the candidate level that most increases `det(XᵀV⁻¹X)`. The coordinate
of a whole-plot factor is its setting in one whole plot (all its runs move
together), of a subplot factor its setting in one subplot, and of an easy
factor its setting in one run. A change touches one whole plot `i` only, so
the information is updated by replacing that plot's contribution
`XᵢᵀVᵢ⁻¹Xᵢ`. Passes repeat until no coordinate improves; the best of
several random starts is kept. Candidate levels are those of
[`crate::optimal`] (−1, +1 for linear terms; −1, 0, +1 for a squared
factor). A singular start is improved for `det(XᵀV⁻¹X + δI)` with a small
`δ` until it becomes non-singular.

#### Plot sizes
The `n` runs are divided as evenly as possible among the whole plots (for
a split-split-plot design: among the subplots, which are themselves
divided as evenly as possible among the whole plots), the larger plots
first.

#### Efficiency and prediction variance
With `σ²_ε = 1` the reported **D-criterion** is `ln det(XᵀV⁻¹X)`. The
**D-efficiency** `100 · det(XᵀV*⁻¹X)^{1/p} / n` uses `V* = V / (1 + η_w + η_s)`,
the covariance in units of the total variance of a run; it is 100% for an
orthogonal completely randomized design with that variance and can exceed
100% because comparisons within whole plots are free of the whole-plot
variance. Prediction variances `f(x)ᵀ(XᵀV*⁻¹X)⁻¹f(x)` are in the same
units (the variance of the estimated mean response relative to a run's
total variance).

- `enum ChangeLevel`: How hard a factor is to change, which decides the stratum where it varies.
- `struct SplitPlotOptions`: Options for [`split_plot_design`].
- `struct PlotStructure`: Which plot each run belongs to: runs are numbered in standard order, whole plot by whole plot (and subplot by subplot within them).
- `struct SplitPlotDesign`: A D-optimal split-plot or split-split-plot design and its quality.
- `const WHOLE_PLOT_COLUMN`: Name of the whole-plot column of an exported design.
- `const SUBPLOT_COLUMN`: Name of the subplot column of an exported split-split-plot design.
- `fn split_plot_log_det`: `ln det(XᵀV⁻¹X)` (with `σ²_ε = 1`) of coded `runs` for `formula` with the given plots and variance ratios; −∞ if singular.
- `fn split_plot_design`: Build a D-optimal split-plot design for `formula` (factors `A, B, …` in coded units) by coordinate exchange.
- `struct SplitPlotAugmentOptions`: Options for [`augment_split_plot`].
- `struct AugmentedSplitPlot`: A split-plot design with new whole plots added.
- `fn augment_split_plot`: Add whole plots to an existing split-plot design, keeping its runs: D-optimal by coordinate exchange over the new whole plots only (Goos & Jones 2011, *Optimal Design of Experiments: A Case Study Approach*, ch.

### `crates/stat-doe/src/surface.rs`

Analysis of a fitted second-order response surface (Box & Draper,
*Response Surfaces, Mixtures, and Ridge Analyses*, 2nd ed., ch. 10–11;
Myers, Montgomery & Anderson-Cook, *Response Surface Methodology*, ch. 6).

In coded factors `x` the fitted model is

```text
ŷ(x) = b₀ + xᵀb + xᵀBx,
```

with `b` the first-order coefficients and `B` symmetric, holding the pure
quadratic coefficients on its diagonal and half of each two-factor
interaction coefficient off it.

* **Stationary point** — where the gradient `b + 2Bx` vanishes:
  `xₛ = −½ B⁻¹ b`, with `ŷₛ = b₀ + ½ xₛᵀb`.
* **Canonical analysis** — with `B = VΛVᵀ` (eigenvalues λᵢ, orthonormal
  eigenvectors in the columns of `V`) and `w = Vᵀ(x − xₛ)`, the surface is
  `ŷ = ŷₛ + Σ λᵢ wᵢ²`: all λᵢ < 0 is a maximum, all > 0 a minimum, mixed
  signs a saddle; a λᵢ near zero means the response hardly changes along
  that axis (a ridge).
* **Ridge analysis** (Hoerl 1959; Draper 1963) — the point of greatest (or
  least) predicted response on the sphere `‖x‖ = R`, by Lagrange
  multipliers `(B − μI)x = −½ b`, with `μ > λ_max` for the maximum and
  `μ < λ_min` for the minimum. `‖x(μ)‖` is monotone in `μ` on each branch,
  so `μ` is found by bisection. When `b` has no component along the extreme
  eigenvector, the path reaches a finite radius as `μ → λ`; beyond it the
  path continues along that eigenvector (the "hard case").

- `struct QuadraticSurface`: A second-order polynomial `b₀ + xᵀb + xᵀBx` in `k` coded factors.
- `enum StationaryKind`: Shape of the surface at its stationary point.
- `struct CanonicalAnalysis`: Result of [`QuadraticSurface::canonical_analysis`].
- `enum RidgeDirection`: Direction of a ridge path.
- `struct RidgePoint`: One point of a ridge path.
- `fn symmetric_eigen`: Eigenvalues (largest first) and unit eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, by cyclic Jacobi rotations (Golub & Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, §8.5).

Integration tests: `split_plot.rs`.

## Crate `stat-functional` (`crates/stat-functional`)

Functional data analysis: curves from long data smoothed by B-spline, penalized-spline or Fourier bases with the roughness penalty chosen by GCV; landmark and continuous registration; functional principal components.

Dependencies: `rayon`, `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-functional/src/basis.rs`

Basis systems for curves: B-splines and Fourier series.

A curve is represented as `x(t) = Σⱼ cⱼ φⱼ(t)` on a closed interval
`[a, b]`. Smoothing, registration and principal components only need
the basis values and derivatives at given times and two matrices:

* the **Gram matrix** `Wⱼₖ = ∫ φⱼ φₖ dt`, the inner products of the basis
  functions, so `∫ x y dt = cₓᵀ W c_y`;
* the **roughness penalty** `Rⱼₖ = ∫ (Lφⱼ)(Lφₖ) dt` of a linear
  differential operator `L = Σₘ aₘ Dᵐ`, so `∫ (Lx)² dt = cᵀ R c`. The usual
  choice is `L = D²` (curvature); for periodic data the harmonic
  acceleration operator `L = ω²D + D³`, `ω = 2π/T`, annihilates constants
  and the first harmonic, so a heavily penalized fit tends to a sinusoid
  of period `T` instead of a constant (Ramsay & Silverman 2005, §5.2.4).

Both integrals are evaluated by Gauss–Legendre quadrature. For B-splines
the panels are the knot intervals, inside which the integrands are
polynomials of degree at most `2(k − 1)`, so an `(k + 1)`-point rule is
exact; for Fourier bases `8(M + 1)` equal panels of 12 points each give
full double precision.

#### B-splines
Order `k` (degree `k − 1`) B-splines on the knot vector
`a = … = a < τ₁ < … < τ_q < b = … = b` (each end repeated `k` times),
`n = q + k` functions, evaluated with their derivatives by the
Cox–de Boor recursion in the form of Piegl & Tiller, *The NURBS Book*,
2nd ed., Algorithm A2.3. Order 4 (cubic) is the default. The basis is a
partition of unity: `Σⱼ φⱼ(t) = 1`.

#### Fourier series
For period `T` and `n = 2M + 1` functions:
`φ₀ = 1/√T`, `φ₂ₘ₋₁ = sin(mω(t − a))/√(T/2)`, `φ₂ₘ = cos(mω(t − a))/√(T/2)`,
orthonormal over one period.

- `enum Roughness`: The roughness a smoothing penalty measures.
- `struct BSplineBasis`: B-spline basis of a given order on a knot sequence.
- `struct FourierBasis`: Fourier basis of odd size on `[a, b]` with a given period.
- `enum Basis`: A basis system for curves.

### `crates/stat-functional/src/fdata.rs`

A sample of curves stored as coefficients in a common basis.

- `struct FunctionalData`: Curves `xᵢ(t) = Σⱼ cᵢⱼ φⱼ(t)` sharing one basis.

### `crates/stat-functional/src/fpca.rs`

Functional principal component analysis.

For curves `xᵢ = Σⱼ cᵢⱼ φⱼ` with mean `x̄`, the sample covariance operator
`v(s, t) = N⁻¹ Σᵢ (xᵢ(s) − x̄(s))(xᵢ(t) − x̄(t))` has eigenfunctions `ξₖ`
solving `∫ v(s, t) ξ(t) dt = ρ ξ(s)`. In a basis with centred
coefficient matrix `C` (rows `cᵢ − c̄`), Gram matrix `W = LLᵀ` and
`V = N⁻¹CᵀC`, an eigenfunction `ξ = φᵀb` satisfies `VWb = ρb`; with
`u = Lᵀb` this is the symmetric problem `LᵀVL u = ρu`, so
`b = L⁻ᵀu` and the eigenfunctions are orthonormal, `∫ ξₖ ξₗ = δₖₗ`
(Ramsay & Silverman 2005, §8.4.2; the computation of `pca.fd` in the
fda package). The divisor is `N`, as there.

The **scores** are `sᵢₖ = ∫ (xᵢ − x̄) ξₖ dt = (cᵢ − c̄)ᵀWbₖ`; the
eigenvalue `ρₖ` is the variance (divisor `N`) of the k-th scores and
`ρₖ / Σρ` the proportion of total variation `Σᵢ ∫(xᵢ − x̄)²/N` it
explains. Truncating at `K` components gives the reconstruction
`x̂ᵢ = x̄ + Σₖ sᵢₖ ξₖ`, the best `K`-term approximation in squared
integrated error.

Eigenfunction signs are arbitrary; each is oriented so that its
integral is positive (or, if the integral is nearly zero, so that its
largest-magnitude coefficient is positive).

- `struct Fpca`: A functional principal component analysis.
- `fn functional_pca`: Principal components of the curves in `data`, keeping `n_components`.

### `crates/stat-functional/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-functional

Functional data analysis (Ramsay & Silverman, *Functional Data Analysis*,
2nd ed., Springer 2005): each observational unit is a curve `xᵢ(t)`
sampled at discrete times, possibly different for every curve.

* [`basis`] — B-spline and Fourier basis systems: values and derivatives,
  inner-product (Gram) and roughness-penalty matrices.
* [`smooth`] — curves from discrete observations by penalized least
  squares in a basis, the smoothing parameter fixed or chosen by
  generalized cross-validation (GCV).
* [`fdata`] — a sample of curves as basis coefficients: evaluation,
  mean and pointwise standard deviation.
* [`fpca`] — functional principal components: eigenfunctions of the
  sample covariance operator, scores and reconstructions.
* [`register`] — registration (alignment of curves in time): landmark
  registration with monotone cubic warping functions, and continuous
  registration by the minimum-eigenvalue criterion of Ramsay & Li (1998).

### `crates/stat-functional/src/linalg.rs`

Small dense helpers for matrices stored as rows.

### `crates/stat-functional/src/register.rs`

Registration: aligning curves in time before they are averaged or
analysed, so that variation in timing (phase) is separated from
variation in size (amplitude).

A **warping function** `hᵢ` is a strictly increasing map of `[a, b]` onto
itself; the registered curve is `xᵢ*(t) = xᵢ(hᵢ(t))`, so the feature of
`xᵢ` at time `hᵢ(t)` appears at `t` (Ramsay & Silverman 2005, ch. 7).

#### Landmark registration
Landmarks are times of recognisable features, here the time of each
curve's maximum or minimum inside a window. With `tᵢₗ` the landmarks of
curve `i` and `t₀ₗ` their mean over the curves, `hᵢ` interpolates
`hᵢ(a) = a`, `hᵢ(t₀ₗ) = tᵢₗ`, `hᵢ(b) = b` by the monotone piecewise cubic
Hermite interpolant of Fritsch & Carlson (1980), with the derivative
choices of Fritsch & Butland (1984) as implemented by SciPy's
`PchipInterpolator` ([`Pchip`]); a monotone interpolant of increasing
points is increasing, so `hᵢ` is a valid warp. Each registered curve has
its landmarks exactly at the mean landmark times. This is the warping of
scikit-fda's `landmark_elastic_registration_warping`.

#### Continuous registration
Ramsay & Li (1998, *JRSS B* 60, 351–363) align each curve to a target
`x₀` by minimizing the smallest eigenvalue of

`T(h) = [ ∫x₀²      ∫x₀ xᵢ∘h ]`
`       [ ∫x₀ xᵢ∘h  ∫(xᵢ∘h)² ]`,

which is zero exactly when `xᵢ∘h` is proportional to `x₀`, so curves are
matched in shape whatever their amplitude. The warp is
`h(t) = a + (b − a) ∫ₐᵗ exp W / ∫ₐᵇ exp W` with `W` a cubic B-spline
(`n_basis` functions, the constant direction removed since it does not
change `h`), which is strictly increasing for any `W`. The criterion is
scaled by `∫x₀²` and a roughness penalty `κ (b − a)³ ∫(W″)²` (scale free)
keeps warps smooth. Each curve's `W` is found by the Nelder–Mead method
from the previous solution. The target starts as the mean curve and is
replaced by the mean of the registered curves after each pass (a
Procrustes iteration, Ramsay & Silverman §7.6), until the warps stop
changing or the passes run out. Integrals use Simpson's rule on 401
equally spaced points; curves are evaluated at warped times by cubic
Hermite interpolation on 2001 points.

- `const WARP_GRID`: Points on which warping functions are stored.
- `enum LandmarkKind`: Which feature marks a landmark.
- `struct LandmarkSpec`: One landmark: a feature searched for in a window of time.
- `fn find_landmarks`: The landmark times of every curve (`out[i][l]`), each located on a grid of 1001 points in its window and refined to a zero of the derivative by bisection when it is inside the window.
- `struct Pchip`: A monotone piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant (Fritsch–Carlson, with SciPy's `PchipInterpolator` derivative rules).
- `struct Warp`: A warping function stored on [`WARP_GRID`] equally spaced times.
- `fn landmark_warps`: Landmark warps on `range`: `hᵢ(location_l) = landmarks[i][l]`, with the locations the landmarks' means unless given.
- `fn apply_warps`: The registered curves `xᵢ(hᵢ(t))`, re-expressed in the same basis by least squares on 501 equally spaced times.
- `struct ContinuousOptions`: Options of [`register_continuous`].
- `struct ContinuousRegistration`: The result of [`register_continuous`].
- `fn register_continuous`: Align every curve to the (iterated) mean curve by the minimum-eigenvalue criterion.

### `crates/stat-functional/src/smooth.rs`

Curves from discrete observations by penalized least squares.

Each curve `i` observed as `(tᵢⱼ, yᵢⱼ)`, `j = 1 … nᵢ`, gets the
coefficients minimizing

`PENSSE_λ(c) = Σⱼ (yᵢⱼ − φ(tᵢⱼ)ᵀc)² + λ cᵀRc`,

where `R` is the roughness-penalty matrix of the basis
([`Basis::penalty_matrix`]); the solution is `ĉ = (ΦᵀΦ + λR)⁻¹Φᵀy`
(Ramsay & Silverman 2005, §5.2). `λ = 0` is ordinary regression on the
basis (a regression spline or truncated Fourier series). The fit's
degrees of freedom are the trace of the hat matrix,
`df(λ) = tr[(ΦᵀΦ + λR)⁻¹ΦᵀΦ]`.

#### Choosing λ
One `λ` serves every curve, so the curves are smoothed alike. It
minimizes the summed generalized cross-validation criterion of Craven &
Wahba (1979),

`GCV(λ) = Σᵢ nᵢ SSEᵢ(λ) / (nᵢ − dfᵢ(λ))²`,

over `log₁₀ λ`: a grid in steps of 0.25 decades, then a golden-section
search in the best grid cell. The grid is placed relative to
`s = tr(ΦᵀΦ)/tr(R)`, from `10⁻¹⁰ s` to `10⁶ s`, so it does not depend on
the units of time. With a common set of times the summed criterion is
the pooled `N n SSE / (n − df)²` used for a sample of curves by
scikit-fda and the fda package.

- `struct CurveData`: One curve's observations.
- `enum Smoothing`: How the smoothing parameter is set.
- `struct SmoothOptions`: Options of [`smooth_curves`].
- `struct SmoothResult`: Smoothed curves and the fit of each.
- `fn smooth_curves`: Smooth every curve in `basis`.

Integration tests: `reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-inference` (`crates/stat-inference`)

Comparative inference: one-sample, paired and two-sample tests (parametric, rank-based, equivalence), variance, proportion and rate tests, multiple comparisons, repeated measures, and power and sample-size calculations.

Dependencies: `rayon`, `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-inference/src/anom.rs`

Analysis of means (ANOM): each group's mean, proportion or rate plotted
against decision limits around the overall value, so that a group outside
the limits differs significantly from the overall average (Ott 1967,
"Analysis of means — a graphical procedure", *Industrial Quality Control*
24; Nelson 1982, "Exact critical points for the analysis of means",
*Communications in Statistics — Theory and Methods* 11; Nelson, Wludyka &
Copeland, *The Analysis of Means*, SIAM 2005).

#### Critical values

With group sizes `nᵢ`, `N = Σnᵢ` and the weighted grand mean `ȳ`, the
deviations `dᵢ = ȳᵢ − ȳ` have variances `σ²(1/nᵢ − 1/N)` and covariances
`−σ²/N`, so the standardized deviations `Xᵢ = dᵢ / (σ√(1/nᵢ − 1/N))` are
multivariate normal with the negative product correlation
`ρᵢⱼ = −λᵢλⱼ`, `λᵢ = √(nᵢ/(N − nᵢ))` (equicorrelated, `ρ = −1/(k − 1)`, for
equal sizes). The decision limits are `ȳ ± h·s·√(1/nᵢ − 1/N)`, where the
exact critical value `h` solves `P(maxᵢ |Xᵢ|/S ≤ h) = 1 − α` with
`S = √(χ²_ν/ν)` independent of `X` (multivariate t; `S = 1` for a known
variance, as for proportions and rates).

Negative product correlation cannot be written through one real common
factor, as Dunnett's positive correlation can ([`crate::control`]); the
standard device (Nelson 1982; Soong & Hsu 1997, "Using complex integration
to compute multivariate normal probabilities", *Technometrics* 39) is an
imaginary common factor, which gives the one-dimensional integral

```text
P(max |Xᵢ| ≤ x) = ∫ φ(τ) Πᵢ [Φ(bᵢ − iωᵢτ) − Φ(−bᵢ − iωᵢτ)] dτ,
ωᵢ = √(nᵢ/N),  bᵢ = x√(1 − ωᵢ²).
```

Each factor, multiplied by `e^{−ωᵢ²τ²/2}` (the product of these is
`√(2π)·φ(τ)`), is the real function
`Hᵢ(τ) = (2π)^{−½} ∫_{−bᵢ}^{bᵢ} e^{−u²/2} cos(ωᵢτu) du
       = e^{−qᵢ²/2} − e^{−bᵢ²/2} Re[e^{ibᵢqᵢ} w((qᵢ + ibᵢ)/√2)]`,
`qᵢ = ωᵢτ`, with `w` the Faddeeva function, evaluated by Weideman's (1994)
rational approximation ("Computation of the complex error function", *SIAM
J. Numer. Anal.* 31) with 32 terms. So
`P = √(2/π) ∫₀^∞ Πᵢ Hᵢ(τ) dτ`, integrated by composite 16-point
Gauss–Legendre panels of unit width. The integrand decays like `τ^{−k}`
while oscillating, so the range is 400 for three groups, 300 for four and
200 (at least `12/minᵢ ωᵢ + 50`) otherwise, which keeps the truncation
error below about 10⁻⁸. Two groups are perfectly negatively correlated,
so `P = P(|X₁| ≤ x)` exactly.

For a finite `ν`, `P(x)` is interpolated (barycentric Chebyshev, 81 nodes)
on `[0, x₉]`, where the Bonferroni bound `2kΦ(−x₉) = 10⁻¹⁶` makes it one
beyond, and integrated against the density of `S` with the nodes of
Dunnett's distribution.

#### Two-way layouts

For a balanced `a × b` layout with `r` replicates per cell, the main-effect
means `ȳᵢ..` are charted with `ȳ ± h(α; a, ν)·s·√((a − 1)/(abr))` (and
likewise for the second factor), where `s² = MSE` on `ν = ab(r − 1)`
degrees of freedom; with one observation per cell the interaction mean
square is the error (`ν = (a − 1)(b − 1)`) and no interaction chart is
drawn. Interaction effects `ȳᵢⱼ. − ȳᵢ.. − ȳ.ⱼ. + ȳ...` are charted around
zero with limits `±h*·s·√((a − 1)(b − 1)/(abr))`; for a 2 × 2 layout the
four effects have equal size and `h* = t_{1−α/2, ν}` exactly, otherwise `h*`
is the studentized-maximum-modulus value for `ab` comparisons, which by
Šidák's (1967) inequality gives conservative limits (Nelson, Wludyka &
Copeland 2005, §6).

#### Failure modes

Fewer than two groups, an empty group, non-finite values, no error degrees
of freedom, zero variation, a level outside (0, 1), a proportion or rate of
zero (or a proportion of one), or an unbalanced two-way layout are errors.

- `struct AnomDistribution`: Distribution of the largest absolute standardized deviation of group means from their weighted grand mean, `maxᵢ |Xᵢ|/S` (see the module notes): the reference distribution of the analysis of means.
- `fn maximum_modulus_quantile`: The studentized-maximum-modulus critical value: the `c` with `∫ f_S(s) (2Φ(cs) − 1)^m ds = level`, which by Šidák's inequality bounds the maximum of `m` correlated standardized effects (used for two-way interaction effects).
- `enum AnomSide`: Which decision limit a group crosses.
- `struct AnomGroup`: One plotted group of an analysis of means.
- `struct AnomChart`: An analysis-of-means chart.
- `fn anom_means`: Analysis of means for normal data: group means against `ȳ ± h(α; n₁…n_k, ν)·s·√(1/nᵢ − 1/N)`, `s² = MSE` on `ν = N − k` df.
- `fn anom_proportions`: Analysis of means for binomial proportions `pᵢ = xᵢ/nᵢ`: limits `p̄ ± h(α; n₁…n_k, ∞)·√(p̄(1 − p̄))·√(1/nᵢ − 1/N)` (normal approximation), kept within [0, 1].
- `fn anom_rates`: Analysis of means for Poisson rates `uᵢ = cᵢ/nᵢ` (counts per unit of exposure): limits `ū ± h(α; n₁…n_k, ∞)·√ū·√(1/nᵢ − 1/N)`, lower limits kept at or above zero.
- `struct AnomTwoWay`: A two-way analysis of means: both main effects and, with replication, the interaction.
- `fn anom_two_way`: Two-way analysis of means of a balanced layout: `cells[i][j]` holds the `r` observations at level `i` of the first factor and level `j` of the second (see the module notes for the limits).

### `crates/stat-inference/src/area.rs`

Area under a sampled curve by the trapezoid rule, above a baseline, with
its standard error from replicate measurements.

The curve joins the mean response `ȳⱼ` at each distinct `xⱼ`
(`x₁ < … < x_m`) with straight lines. Its area is `Σ cⱼ ȳⱼ` with
trapezoid weights `c₁ = (x₂ − x₁)/2`, `cⱼ = (xⱼ₊₁ − xⱼ₋₁)/2`,
`c_m = (x_m − x_{m−1})/2`. Above a baseline `b` the net area is
`Σ cⱼ ȳⱼ − b (x_m − x₁)`. When the baseline is the mean of the first `k`
points it is itself a linear combination of the `ȳⱼ`, so the net area is
`Σ wⱼ ȳⱼ` with `wⱼ = cⱼ − (x_m − x₁)/k` for `j ≤ k`.

With independent replicates at each `x` (for example a different animal
at each time, as in destructive sampling), Bailer (1988, *J.
Pharmacokinet. Biopharm.* 16, 303–309) gives `Var = Σ wⱼ² sⱼ² / nⱼ` from
each point's sample variance `sⱼ²` and count `nⱼ`, and a normal
confidence interval `area ± z sd`. It needs at least two replicates at
every point.

Where a segment crosses the baseline it is split at the crossing, so the
area above and the area below the baseline are reported separately (their
difference is the net area). A peak is a run of the curve above the
baseline between crossings (or the ends of the data).
