likelihood slope (Deming 1943, *Statistical Adjustment of Data*; Cornbleet
& Gochman 1979, *Clin. Chem.* 25) is

`β̂ = [S_yy − λS_xx + √((S_yy − λS_xx)² + 4λS_xy²)] / (2S_xy)`,

`α̂ = ȳ − β̂x̄`, with `S` the centred sums of squares and products. With
`λ = 1` this is orthogonal regression (the first principal axis); as
`λ → ∞` it tends to ordinary least squares of y on x. Standard errors and
confidence intervals come from the jackknife (Linnet 1990, *Clin. Chem.*
36; Linnet 1993, *Clin. Chem.* 39): with the leave-one-out estimates
`θ₍₋ᵢ₎`, `se = √((n − 1)/n · Σ(θ₍₋ᵢ₎ − θ̄₍.₎)²)` and the interval
`θ̂ ± t_{1−α/2, n−2} · se`.

#### Passing–Bablok regression
A non-parametric, outlier-resistant estimate (Passing & Bablok 1983,
*J. Clin. Chem. Clin. Biochem.* 21). The slopes `Sᵢⱼ = (yⱼ − yᵢ)/(xⱼ − xᵢ)`
of all pairs `i < j` are formed, leaving out pairs with both differences
zero and slopes of exactly −1 (a tied `x` gives ±∞ by the sign of the `y`
difference). With `N` slopes sorted and `K` of them below −1, the slope is
the median shifted by `K`: `S₍(N+1)/2+K₎` for odd `N`, otherwise the mean
of `S₍N/2+K₎` and `S₍N/2+1+K₎`. Its confidence limits are `S₍M₁+K₎` and
`S₍M₂+K₎` with `C = z_{1−α/2} √(n(n − 1)(2n + 5)/18)`,
`M₁ = round((N − C)/2)` and `M₂ = N − M₁ + 1`. The intercept is
`median(yᵢ − β̂xᵢ)`, with limits `median(yᵢ − β̂_U xᵢ)` and
`median(yᵢ − β̂_L xᵢ)`. The method assumes the two measurements are
linearly related; Passing & Bablok's cumulative-sum test checks it: with
`l` points above and `L` below the line, points above score `√(L/l)`,
points below `−√(l/L)`, points on it 0; ordered by their projection
`Dᵢ = (yᵢ + xᵢ/β̂ − α̂/β̂)/√(1 + 1/β̂²)` onto the line, the largest absolute
cumulative sum divided by `√(l + L)` is compared with the Kolmogorov
distribution (critical value 1.36 at α = 0.05). With these scores the
cumulative sum after `k` points is `√(lL)·(F₊(k) − F₋(k))`, where `F₊` and
`F₋` are the empirical distribution functions of the points above and below
the line, so the statistic is Smirnov's two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov
statistic `√(lL/(l + L))·D`. (The divisor is often printed `√(L + 1)`; that
form rejects a linear relation far more often than the nominal level, about
19% at α = 0.05 for 20 points on each side.)

- `struct ComparisonEstimate`: An estimate with its standard error (when one exists) and confidence limits.
- `struct DemingFit`: A Deming regression fit.
- `fn deming_regression`: Deming regression of `y` (test method) on `x` (comparison method) with error-variance ratio `variance_ratio = Var(error of y)/Var(error of x)` (1 for orthogonal regression), with jackknife standard errors and t-based confidence limits on `n − 2` df.
- `struct LinearityTest`: Passing–Bablok's cumulative-sum test of linearity.
- `struct PassingBablokFit`: A Passing–Bablok fit.
- `fn passing_bablok`: Passing–Bablok regression of `y` (test method) on `x` (comparison method), with the cumulative-sum linearity test.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/assay.rs`

Derived quantities and acceptance checks for assay curves.

The assay curve templates (receptor binding, enzyme kinetics,
pharmacological dose–response, immunoassay standard curves, growth and
survival) are ordinary nonlinear regressions ([`super::fit_nonlinear`]);
this module holds what they report beyond the parameter estimates.

#### Derived quantities
A quantity `q = g(θ)` of the fitted parameters has the delta-method
standard error `se(q̂) = √(∇gᵀ Σ ∇g)`, `Σ` the covariance of the estimates
and `∇g` the gradient at `θ̂` (central differences), and the Wald interval
`q̂ ± t·se` ([`delta_method`]; Seber & Wild, *Nonlinear Regression*, Wiley
1989, §5.1). When `q` is a monotone function of a single parameter its
interval is that parameter's interval mapped through `g`
([`map_interval`]), which keeps the asymmetry of a profile interval and
never leaves the quantity's range (for example a dissociation constant
from a log concentration stays positive). The standard formulas:

* inhibition constant from a competition curve (Cheng & Prusoff,
  *Biochem. Pharmacol.* 22, 1973): `Ki = IC50 / (1 + [L]/Kd)`, `[L]` the
  labelled ligand's concentration and `Kd` its dissociation constant
  ([`cheng_prusoff_ki`]);
* the concentration giving `F`% of the maximal effect of a logistic curve
  with slope `h`: `EC_F = EC50·(F/(100 − F))^{1/h}` ([`ec_f`]);
* half-life of a first-order process with rate constant `k`:
  `t½ = ln 2 / k` ([`half_life`]);
* equilibrium dissociation constant from binding kinetics:
  `Kd = koff / kon` ([`kinetic_kd`]);
* relative potency of a test preparation against a standard from
  parallel log-dose curves (Finney, *Statistical Method in Biological
  Assay*, 3rd ed., Griffin 1978, ch. 4): `ρ = 10^(log EC50_S − log EC50_T)`,
  its interval `10^` of the t interval of the difference
  ([`relative_potency`]).

#### Standard curves (ligand-binding assays)
* **Back-calculation:** each calibration standard's response is read off
  the fitted curve and compared with its nominal concentration,
  `recovery = 100·x̂/x`. ICH M10 *Bioanalytical Method Validation and Study
  Sample Analysis* (2022), §7.2.1 (ligand-binding assays): back-calculated
  standards within ±20% of nominal (±25% at the lowest and highest
  standards, the LLOQ and ULOQ), at least 75% of them, and at least six
  concentration levels, meeting it ([`standard_curve_acceptance`]; the
  limits are settings, so the chromatographic ±15%/±20% can be used).
* **Precision profile:** the coefficient of variation of a concentration
  read off the curve from one response, `CV(c) = 100·sd(x̂)/c` with
  `sd(x̂) = √(s²/w(c) + se(f(c))²) / |f′(c)|` (Ekins, "The precision
  profile: its use in assay design, assessment and quality control", in
  *Immunoassays for Clinical Chemistry*, 1983; Findlay & Dillard,
  *AAPS J.* 9, 2007). The working (quantitation) range is the widest
  stretch of concentrations, within the standards, where `CV ≤` a limit
  (20% by default) ([`quantitation_range`]).

#### Failure modes
A quantity that cannot be computed at the estimates (a division by zero,
a logarithm of a negative value) or whose gradient cannot be formed is
returned as NaN with a NaN standard error; callers show it as missing.

- `struct DerivedValue`: A quantity computed from the estimates, with its uncertainty.
- `fn delta_method`: Delta-method standard error and Wald interval `q̂ ± t·se` of `q = g(θ)` at `theta` with covariance `covariance` (`P × P`; NaN rows and columns for parameters held at a bound are treated as zero variance).
- `fn map_interval`: The interval of a monotone function `g` of one parameter: `g` applied to each limit, ordered (an open limit, NaN, stays NaN).
- `fn cheng_prusoff_ki`: Inhibition constant `Ki = IC50 / (1 + [L]/Kd)` (Cheng & Prusoff 1973), for a competitor's `ic50` against a labelled ligand at concentration `ligand` with dissociation constant `kd` (same units).
- `fn ec_f`: `EC_F = EC50·(F/(100 − F))^{1/h}`: the concentration giving `f_percent` of the way from the bottom to the top of a logistic curve with Hill slope `hill` (`0 < F < 100`, `h ≠ 0`; NaN otherwise).
- `fn half_life`: Half-life `ln 2 / k` of a first-order rate constant `k` (NaN for `k ≤ 0`).
- `fn kinetic_kd`: Equilibrium dissociation constant `koff / kon` (NaN for `kon ≤ 0`).
- `fn relative_potency`: Relative potency `ρ = 10^(d)`, `d = log EC50_standard − log EC50_test`, with its interval `10^(d ± t·se(d))`, `se(d)² = Var_S + Var_T − 2·Cov_ST` (Finney 1978, ch.
- `struct AcceptanceLimits`: Limits of [`standard_curve_acceptance`].
- `struct BackCalculated`: One calibration standard read back off the curve.
- `struct Acceptance`: Verdict of [`standard_curve_acceptance`].
- `fn standard_curve_acceptance`: Back-calculated standards checked against `limits`.
- `fn quantitation_range`: The widest stretch of a precision profile where `CV ≤ limit`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/compare.rs`

Comparing two least-squares fits of the same data.

#### Extra sum-of-squares F test (Bates & Watts 1988, §3.10; Draper & Smith,
*Applied Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., §24.3)
For a simpler model nested in a more complex one (the simpler is the
complex model with some parameters fixed or set equal), with residual sums
of squares `S₀ > S₁` on `ν₀ > ν₁` residual degrees of freedom,
`F = ((S₀ − S₁)/(ν₀ − ν₁)) / (S₁/ν₁)` on `(ν₀ − ν₁, ν₁)` df; a small p
says the extra parameters reduce the sum of squares by more than chance.
For nonlinear models the F distribution is approximate (exact when the
models are linear). It is not valid for models that are not nested.

#### AICc (Burnham & Anderson, *Model Selection and Multimodel Inference*,
2nd ed., Springer 2002, §2.4 and §2.9)
For a least-squares fit with `P` estimated parameters to `n` observations,
`K = P + 1` (the error variance counts) and
`AICc = n·ln(S/n) + 2K + 2K(K + 1)/(n − K − 1)`. The model with the lower
AICc is better supported; with `Δ = AICc₀ − AICc₁`, the probability that
model 1 is the better of the two is `e^{Δ/2} / (1 + e^{Δ/2})` (Akaike
weights). Unlike the F test it does not need nested models, but both fits
must use the same observations (and the same weights).

- `struct FitScore`: One fit's summary for a comparison.
- `struct ExtraSumOfSquares`: An extra sum-of-squares F test.
- `fn extra_sum_of_squares`: The extra sum-of-squares F test of `simple` against `complex` (module documentation).
- `fn aicc_probability`: Probability (Akaike weight) that model `b` is the better of `a` and `b` by AICc; `NaN` when either AICc is undefined.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/forms.rs`

A library of common one-predictor nonlinear model forms, each with
analytic derivatives and automatic starting values.

| Form | `f(x; θ)` |
|---|---|
| Exponential | `Scale·exp(Rate·x)` |
| Exponential with asymptote | `Asymptote + Scale·exp(Rate·x)` |
| Logistic (3 parameters) | `Asymptote / (1 + exp(−Rate·(x − Midpoint)))` |
| Logistic (4 parameters) | `Lower + (Upper − Lower) / (1 + exp(−Rate·(x − Midpoint)))` |
| Gompertz | `Asymptote·exp(−exp(−Rate·(x − Inflection)))` |
| Michaelis–Menten | `Vmax·x / (Km + x)` |
| Power | `Scale·x^Exponent` |
| Rational (linear / linear) | `(a + b·x) / (1 + c·x)` |
| Straight line | `Intercept + Slope·x` |
| Dose–response, log dose | `Bottom + (Top − Bottom) / (1 + 10^((LogEC50 − x)·HillSlope))` |
| Dose–response, dose | `Bottom + (Top − Bottom) / (1 + (EC50 / x)^HillSlope)`, `x ≥ 0` |
| Asymmetric logistic (5 parameters) | `Bottom + (Top − Bottom) / (1 + 10^((LogC − x)·HillSlope))^Asymmetry` |
| Weibull growth | `Asymptote − (Asymptote − Initial)·exp(−(Rate·x)^Shape)`, `x ≥ 0` |
| Beta growth | `Ymax·(1 + (End − m)/(End − Peak))·(m/End)^(End/(End − Peak))`, `m = min(x, End)`, `x ≥ 0` |
| Segmented line | `Intercept + Slope1·x + (Slope2 − Slope1)·max(x − Breakpoint, 0)` |
| Sum of two exponentials | `Plateau + Span1·exp(−Rate1·x) + Span2·exp(−Rate2·x)` |
| Gaussian peak | `Baseline + Height·exp(−(x − Center)² / (2·Width²))` |
| Lorentzian peak | `Baseline + Height / (1 + ((x − Center) / HalfWidth)²)` |

The dose–response forms are the four-parameter Hill (log-logistic) curve,
on the log₁₀ dose scale or the dose scale; a negative `HillSlope` gives a
falling (inhibition) curve, whose midpoint is then an IC50. The
asymmetric logistic is the five-parameter logistic of Gottschalk & Dunn
("The five-parameter logistic: a characterization and comparison with the
four-parameter logistic", *Anal. Biochem.* 343, 2005) on the log-dose
scale; `Asymmetry = 1` gives the four-parameter curve. Weibull growth is
from Ratkowsky (*Handbook of Nonlinear Regression Models*, 1990); the beta
growth function, rising from 0 at `x = 0` to its maximum `Ymax` at
`x = End` with its fastest growth at `x = Peak` (`0 ≤ Peak < End`) and
constant after `End`, is from Yin, Goudriaan, Lantinga, Vos & Spiertz ("A
flexible sigmoid function of determinate growth", *Annals of Botany* 91,
2003). The segmented line is continuous at its breakpoint (Muggeo,
"Estimating regression models with unknown break-points", *Stat. Med.* 22,
2003); its derivative in `Breakpoint` is `−(Slope2 − Slope1)` for
`x > Breakpoint` and 0 otherwise.

#### Starting values
Every form is conditionally linear: given its nonlinear parameters (a rate,
midpoint, Km, exponent or `c`) the others enter linearly and follow from a
small linear least-squares problem. The starting values are the best point
of a grid over the nonlinear parameters, scaled to the data (rates
`±k / range(x)` for `k` on a log grid from 0.01 to 30, midpoints at
quantiles of `x`, Km from 0.01 to 10 times the largest `x`, exponents from
−3 to 3; Hill slopes `±rate / ln 10` for the log-dose forms, ±0.2 to 8 on
the dose scale with EC50 on a geometric grid over the positive `x`;
asymmetries 0.2 to 5; Weibull shapes 0.3 to 8; beta-growth ends at upper
quantiles of `x` and up to three times its maximum, with peaks at 0 to 95%
of the end; breakpoints between each pair of adjacent distinct `x` values
that leave two values on each side; rate pairs `Rate1 > Rate2 > 0`; peak
centers at quantiles of `x` and widths 0.01 to 1 times its range), each
with its conditionally optimal linear parameters — the
idea of separable (variable projection) least squares (Golub & Pereyra,
"The differentiation of pseudo-inverses and nonlinear least squares
problems whose variables separate", *SIAM J. Numer. Anal.* 10, 1973),
used here only to start the full fit.

- `enum CurveForm`: One of the library forms.
- `struct FormModel`: A library form evaluated at fixed predictor values, as a [`ModelFunction`] with analytic derivatives.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/global.rs`

Global (shared-parameter) fitting: several data sets fitted together, each
with its own copy of some parameters and one common value of the others
(Motulsky & Christopoulos, *Fitting Models to Biological Data Using Linear
and Nonlinear Regression*, Oxford University Press 2004, ch. 37–38).

#### Model
Data set `g` has `n_g` observations and a model `f_g(x; φ_g)` with the
same `K` parameters. The global parameter vector `θ` holds each shared
parameter once and each unshared one once per data set; `φ_g = M_g θ`
picks data set `g`'s values (`map[g][k]` is the index in `θ` of its
`k`-th parameter). The data sets are stacked, so the fit minimises
`Σ_g Σ_i (y_gi − f_g(x_gi; M_g θ))²` and every statistic of
`fit_nonlinear` — standard errors, profile
intervals, bands — refers to `θ`, with one residual variance for all
data sets. The Jacobian is `∂f_g/∂θ = (∂f_g/∂φ_g) M_g`: analytic when
every data set's model has analytic derivatives.

Sharing every parameter fits one curve to all the data; sharing none fits
the data sets separately but with a pooled variance (the same estimates as
separate fits).

- `struct GlobalModel`: Several data sets' models over one global parameter vector.
- `type Owner`: The parameter a global position belongs to, and its data set (`None` when shared).
- `fn layout`: The global parameter layout for `n_groups` data sets of a model with `shared.len()` parameters: `(map, owner)` where `map[g][k]` is the global index of data set `g`'s parameter `k`, and `owner[i]` is `(k, None)` for a shared global parameter `i` or `(k, Some(g))` for data set `g`'s copy.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/implicit.rs`

Implicit models `F(x, y; θ) = 0` fitted by orthogonal distance.

#### Model
The observations `(xᵢ, yᵢ)` lie on the curve `F(x, y; θ) = 0` up to
independent errors of equal variance in both coordinates. The estimates
minimise the sum of squared orthogonal (geometric) distances
`Σ dᵢ(θ)²`, `dᵢ` the distance from `(xᵢ, yᵢ)` to the nearest point of the
curve (Boggs, Byrd & Schnabel, "A stable and efficient algorithm for
nonlinear orthogonal distance regression", *SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput.*
8, 1987; Ahn, Rauh & Warnecke, "Least-squares orthogonal distances fitting
of circle, sphere, ellipse, hyperbola, and parabola", *Pattern
Recognition* 34, 2001). The model is passed to
`fit_nonlinear` as a [`ModelFunction`] whose value
for observation `i` is the signed distance `dᵢ` (the sign of
`F(xᵢ, yᵢ)`), fitted to a response of zeros. The error of an observation
normal to the curve has the variance `σ²` of each coordinate, so
`s² = Σdᵢ²/(n − P)` estimates `σ²`, and the standard errors follow from
the Jacobian of the distances.

#### Foot points
The nearest point `q` of the curve to `p = (xᵢ, yᵢ)` starts as the Newton
projection of `p` onto the curve (`z ← z − F(z)∇F(z)/‖∇F(z)‖²` until
`|F|/‖∇F‖ ≤ 10⁻¹²·scale`). It then moves along the tangent `t` by the
tangential part of `p − q`, `(p − q)·t`, and is projected back onto the
curve; the move is halved until the distance falls, and the steps stop
when the tangential part is below `10⁻¹⁰·scale`. At the end `F(q) = 0`
and `p − q ∥ ∇F(q)`, the conditions for a stationary distance.
The gradient `∇F` is a central difference with step `ε^{1/3}·max(|q|,
scale)`, `scale` the spread of the data.

#### Failure modes
`F` undefined near an observation, a vanishing gradient (a singular point
of the curve), or a projection that does not converge make the model
uncomputable at that `θ` (the solver then shortens its step).

- `type ImplicitFunction`: `F(x, y; θ)` for observation `i` at the point `(x, y)`, or `None` where undefined.
- `struct ImplicitModel`: Signed orthogonal distances to the curve `F = 0` as a [`ModelFunction`].

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/inverse.rs`

Inverse prediction (calibration): reading an unknown predictor value off a
fitted curve from an observed response (Draper & Smith, *Applied
Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., Wiley 1998, §3.2; Eisenhart, "The
interpretation of certain regression methods and their use in biological
and industrial research", *Ann. Math. Statist.* 10, 1939; Seber & Wild,
*Nonlinear Regression*, Wiley 1989, §5.12).

#### Method
For an observed response `y₀`, the estimate `x̂₀` solves `f(x̂₀; θ̂) = y₀`
within the calibration range `[a, b]` (normally the range of the
standards). The interval is the set of `x` whose prediction interval for
one new observation contains `y₀`:
`{x : |y₀ − f(x; θ̂)| ≤ t·√(se(x)² + s²/w₀)}`, with `se(x)` the
delta-method standard error of the fitted mean and `w₀` the weight of the
new observation (for a straight line this is the classical
Fieller-type interval of Draper & Smith eq. 3.2.6, exactly). The limits
are the crossings nearest `x̂₀` on each side.

Roots are bracketed on a grid of 400 intervals over `[a, b]` and refined
by bisection to `10⁻¹²·(b − a)`.

#### Failure modes
* `y₀` not reached by the curve within `[a, b]`: no estimate.
* More than one solution (a curve that is not monotone): the one nearest
  `a` is reported and [`InversePrediction::several_solutions`] is set.
* A limit beyond `[a, b]` (a flat curve or a response near an asymptote):
  that side of the interval is open (`None`).

- `struct InversePrediction`: One inverse prediction.
- `fn inverse_predict`: Inverse prediction of `y0` on `[a, b]`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear/robust.rs`

Robust nonlinear fitting and outlier identification (Motulsky & Brown,
"Detecting outliers when fitting data with nonlinear regression – a new
method based on robust nonlinear regression and the false discovery rate",
*BMC Bioinformatics* 7:123, 2006).

#### Robust scale
The robust standard deviation of the residuals is
`RSDR = P₆₈ · N/(N − K)`, where `P₆₈` is the 68.27th percentile of the
absolute (weighted) residuals (linear interpolation between order
statistics) — for normal errors about one standard deviation — and the
factor corrects for the `K` fitted parameters.

#### Robust fit (Cauchy / Lorentzian loss)
The estimates minimise `Σ ln(1 + (rᵢ/RSDR)²)`, the negative
log-likelihood of Cauchy-distributed errors, so a point far from the curve
has bounded influence. The minimum is found by iteratively reweighted
least squares: at a fixed scale the normal equations of the loss are
those of weighted least squares with `wᵢ = 1/(1 + (rᵢ/RSDR)²)`, so each
step refits with these weights (times any given weights) and recomputes
`RSDR` from the new residuals, as the paper does, until the estimates
stop changing (relative change below 10⁻⁷). Standard errors from the last
weighted fit treat the robust weights as known, so they are approximate.

#### Outliers (the paper's false-discovery-rate rule)
With the absolute residuals of the robust fit sorted from smallest to
largest (`i = 1..N`), each of the largest 30% (from `i = ⌊0.7N⌋`) is
given `tᵢ = |rᵢ|/RSDR` and a two-sided p-value `Pᵢ` from the t
distribution on `N − K` df. Moving up from the smallest of these, the
first `i` with `Pᵢ < αᵢ = Q(N − (i − 1))/N` marks that point and every
point further from the curve as outliers (a Benjamini–Hochberg threshold:
the largest residual is tested at `Q/N`). `Q` (1% recommended) bounds the
expected fraction of identified outliers that are false discoveries. The
paper then removes the outliers and refits by ordinary (or weighted)
least squares.

- `fn robust_sd`: `RSDR = P₆₈ · N/(N − K)` of residuals `r` with `k` fitted parameters (module documentation); `NaN` when `N ≤ K`.
- `fn outliers`: Indices of the outliers among residuals `r` of a fit with `k` parameters, by the false-discovery-rate rule at level `q` (module documentation), most extreme last.
- `struct RobustFit`: A robust fit.
- `fn fit_robust`: Fit `y = f(x; θ)` with the Cauchy loss (module documentation), from `start`, with the settings of `options` (its weights, if any, multiply the robust ones).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/nonlinear.rs`

Nonlinear least-squares regression with inference.

#### Model
`yᵢ = f(xᵢ; θ) + εᵢ`, `εᵢ` independent `N(0, σ²)`, for a model function
`f` with `P` parameters `θ`. The estimates minimise
`S(θ) = Σ (yᵢ − f(xᵢ; θ))²` ([`stat_core::optimize::levenberg_marquardt`]).
The model is given as a [`ModelFunction`]: either one of the library
forms in [`forms`] (analytic derivatives and automatic starting values),
or any function of the parameters (central-difference derivatives).

#### Inference (Bates & Watts, *Nonlinear Regression Analysis and Its
Applications*, Wiley 1988, ch. 2 and 6)
With `V = ∂f/∂θ` (`n × P`) at `θ̂`, `s² = S(θ̂)/(n − P)` and
`(VᵀV)⁻¹` from the QR decomposition of `V`. Here `P` counts the
*estimated* parameters: one fixed by equal lower and upper bounds is a
known constant of the model, not estimated, so it uses no degree of
freedom (the fit equals the fit of the model with that constant written
in):

* standard errors `se(θ̂ⱼ) = s·√[(VᵀV)⁻¹]ⱼⱼ`, `t = θ̂ⱼ / se`, two-sided
  p-values on `n − P` df, and linearisation (Wald) intervals
  `θ̂ⱼ ± t(n − P; α/2)·se`;
* the correlation of the estimates from `(VᵀV)⁻¹`;
* profile t intervals (§6.1): with `S̃(θⱼ)` the least sum of squares when
  `θⱼ` is held fixed and the other parameters re-estimated,
  `τ(θⱼ) = sign(θⱼ − θ̂ⱼ)·√(S̃(θⱼ) − S(θ̂))/s`, and the interval is
  `{θⱼ : |τ(θⱼ)| ≤ t(n − P; α/2)}`. This is the likelihood-ratio (F-test)
  interval `S̃(θⱼ) − S(θ̂) ≤ s²·F(1, n − P; α)`; unlike the Wald interval it
  follows the curvature of the model and need not be symmetric;
* the fitted mean at a point with gradient `g = ∂f/∂θ` has delta-method
  standard error `s·√(gᵀ(VᵀV)⁻¹g)`; confidence limits for the mean are
  `f ± t·se`, prediction limits for a new observation
  `f ± t·√(se² + s²)` ([`NonlinearFit::mean_interval`],
  [`NonlinearFit::prediction_interval`]).

#### Weights
With weights `wᵢ > 0` ([`NonlinearOptions::weights`]) the estimates
minimise `S(θ) = Σ wᵢ (yᵢ − f(xᵢ; θ))²`: the problem is solved for the
scaled residuals `√wᵢ (f − yᵢ)` and every statistic above uses the scaled
Jacobian `W^{1/2}V` (Bates & Watts §1.3.2 / Seber & Wild, *Nonlinear
Regression*, Wiley 1989, §2.2.2), so `s²` estimates the variance of an
observation of weight 1, `Var(yᵢ) = σ²/wᵢ`. Prediction limits for a new
observation of weight `w₀` are `f ± t·√(se² + s²/w₀)`
([`NonlinearFit::prediction_interval_weighted`]).

#### Curvature diagnostic (Hougaard 1985)
The asymptotic skewness of each estimate (Hougaard, "The appropriateness of
the asymptotic distribution in a nonlinear regression model in relation to
curvature", *J. R. Statist. Soc. B* 47, 1985; in the form of Ratkowsky,
*Handbook of Nonlinear Regression Models*, Dekker 1990, §2.5): with
`L = (VᵀV)⁻¹`, `Hₖₗ = ∂²f/∂θₖ∂θₗ` and `Wⱼₖₗ = Σᵤ Vᵤⱼ Hᵤₖₗ`,
`E(θ̂ᵢ − θᵢ)³ ≈ −s⁴ Σⱼₖₗ Lᵢⱼ Lᵢₖ Lᵢₗ (Wⱼₖₗ + Wₖⱼₗ + Wₗⱼₖ)` and the
standardised skewness is `g₁ᵢ = E(θ̂ᵢ − θᵢ)³ / (s² Lᵢᵢ)^{3/2}`. Ratkowsky's
guide: `|g₁| < 0.1` the estimator is very close to linear, `0.1–0.25`
reasonably close, above `0.25` the nonlinearity is apparent, and above 1
it is considerable. Second derivatives are central differences of the
model values (step `ε^{1/4}·max(|θ|, 10⁻⁸)`), whatever the first
derivatives.

#### Failure modes
* **No convergence** — the iteration limit is reached or no step lowers
  `S`: the fit is still returned, with [`NonlinearFit::termination`] saying
  why and a warning; its estimates and statistics are those of the last
  iterate and should not be relied on. Try other starting values.
* **Singular Jacobian** at the solution (parameters not separately
  identifiable, e.g. a redundant parameter or a rate whose curve is flat
  over the data): [`StatError::RankDeficient`].
* **Parameter at a bound** — it is reported as such, held fixed for the
  inference (no standard error; the residual df still count it, since it
  was estimated and the data put it there), and a warning says so.
* **Parameter fixed by equal bounds** — not estimated: no standard error,
  not counted in `P`, and a warning says so.
* Fewer observations than estimated parameters + 1, or non-finite responses:
  [`StatError::InsufficientData`] / [`StatError::NonFiniteInput`].

- `trait ModelFunction`: A model function `f(xᵢ; θ)` evaluated at every observation.
- `struct NonlinearOptions`: Settings of [`fit_nonlinear`].
- `struct ProfileInterval`: A profile t interval; a side is `None` when `|τ|` did not reach the critical value inside the parameter's bounds and the search range (the interval is open on that side).
- `struct NonlinearParameter`: One estimated parameter.
- `struct NonlinearFit`: A fitted nonlinear regression.
- `fn fit_nonlinear`: Fit `y = f(x; θ) + ε` by least squares from `start` and compute the inference described in the module documentation.
- `fn numeric_gradient`: Central-difference gradient `∂f/∂θ` of a scalar model value at `theta` (used for bands of models without analytic derivatives).

### `crates/stat-linear/src/ols.rs`

Ordinary least squares multiple regression.

#### Model
```text
y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + β_p x_p + ε,     ε ~ N(0, σ² I)
```
(the intercept β₀ is optional). The estimate `β̂ = argmin ‖y − Xβ‖²` and every
derived statistic follow the standard textbook definitions, e.g. Draper & Smith,
*Applied Regression Analysis* (3rd ed., 1998), chs. 4–5, and the NIST/SEMATECH
e-Handbook of Statistical Methods §4.4.

#### Numerical method
Accuracy is the priority, so the normal equations `XᵀX β = Xᵀy` are never
formed (that would square the condition number). Instead:

1. **Centering.** With an intercept, each predictor and the response are
   centered at their (compensated) means. The slopes are invariant to this
   shift, and removing the constant direction is the single largest
   improvement in conditioning for typical data (e.g. calendar years).
2. **Power-of-two column scaling.** Each centered column is divided by the
   power of two nearest its Euclidean norm. Scaling by powers of two is exact
   in binary floating point, yet equilibrates the columns so the pivoted QR's
   rank test is scale-invariant.
3. **Householder QR with column pivoting** of the scaled, centered design.
4. **Iterative refinement.** The residual `r = y − Xβ̂` is recomputed with
   compensated dot products and the correction `δ = argmin ‖r − Xδ‖` is added
   to `β̂` (Björck, *Numerical Methods for Least Squares Problems*, 1996, §2.9).
5. **Inference without cancellation.** Standard errors come from row norms of
   `R⁻¹`, and the intercept variance from `‖R⁻ᵀ x̄‖²`, both sums of squares.

#### Conventions
* **R² without an intercept** is the *uncentered* R² = Σŷ² / Σy², with the
  ANOVA sums of squares likewise uncentered. This matches the convention of the
  NIST StRD certified values (datasets NoInt1/NoInt2).
* **Information criteria** use the Gaussian maximum log-likelihood
  `ℓ = −(n/2)(ln 2π + ln(RSS/n) + 1)` and count σ² as a parameter, so with `k`
  coefficients `AIC = −2ℓ + 2(k+1)`, `BIC = −2ℓ + (k+1) ln n` and
  `AICc = AIC + 2(k+1)(k+2)/(n−k−2)` (Hurvich & Tsai 1989, Biometrika 76).

- `const INTERCEPT_NAME`: Name used for the intercept term in [`ParameterEstimate::name`].
- `struct OlsOptions`: Options controlling [`fit_linear_model`].
- `struct ParameterEstimate`: Estimate and inference for one model coefficient.
- `struct AnovaRow`: One row of an analysis-of-variance table.
- `struct AnovaTable`: Regression analysis-of-variance table.
- `struct FitSummary`: Overall goodness-of-fit summary.
- `struct ResidualDiagnostics`: Per-observation regression diagnostics.
- `struct Prediction`: Predicted mean response with confidence and prediction intervals.
- `struct LinearModelFit`: A fitted ordinary-least-squares model.
- `fn fit_linear_model`: Fit `y = Xβ (+ β₀) + ε` by ordinary least squares.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/spline.rs`

Regression spline bases: a continuous predictor expanded into the columns
of a B-spline or natural cubic spline basis, so a model can fit a smooth
curve in it with ordinary least squares or a GLM.

#### B-splines
For degree `d` (order `d + 1`), boundary knots `a < b` and interior knots
`a < t₁ < … < t_m < b`, the knot sequence repeats each boundary knot
`d + 1` times. The `m + d + 1` B-spline functions follow the Cox–de Boor
recursion (de Boor, *A Practical Guide to Splines*, 1978, ch. IX):

`B_{j,0}(x) = 1` on `[u_j, u_{j+1})`, and
`B_{j,q}(x) = (x − u_j)/(u_{j+q} − u_j) B_{j,q−1}(x)
           + (u_{j+q+1} − x)/(u_{j+q+1} − u_{j+1}) B_{j+1,q−1}(x)`.

The first function is dropped (the model's intercept takes its place), so
the basis has `m + d` columns. Outside `[a, b]` each function continues
the polynomial of the nearest interval. With these conventions the columns
are exactly those of R's `splines::bs(x, knots, degree, Boundary.knots)`.

#### Natural cubic splines
A natural cubic spline is cubic between knots and linear beyond the
boundary knots (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, *Elements of Statistical
Learning*, 2nd ed., §5.2.1; Harrell, *Regression Modeling Strategies*,
2nd ed., §2.4.5). Its basis is built from the cubic B-splines (without
the first) by removing the two directions in which the second derivative
at `a` or `b` is not zero: with `C` the `2 × (m + 3)` matrix of second
derivatives at the boundary knots and `Q` the orthogonal factor of the
Householder QR of `Cᵀ`, the basis is `B Q` without its first two columns,
`m + 1` columns. Beyond the boundary knots each column continues linearly
(value and slope at the knot). The Householder convention is LINPACK's,
so the columns equal those of R's `splines::ns`.

#### Default knots
[`SplineSpec::Count`] places `m` interior knots at the quantiles
`k/(m + 1)`, `k = 1…m`, of the values (linear interpolation, Hyndman–Fan
type 7), as R's `bs(x, df)` and `ns(x, df)` do; the boundary knots are
the smallest and largest value.

- `const MAX_KNOTS`: Most interior knots accepted.
- `const MAX_DEGREE`: Highest B-spline degree accepted.
- `enum SplineKind`: The kind of spline basis.
- `enum SplineKnots`: Where the interior knots go.
- `struct SplineSpec`: A spline term as requested: its kind and knots.
- `struct SplineBasis`: A spline basis with fixed knots: evaluates the columns at any `x`.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/stability.rs`

Shelf-life estimation from stability data of several batches (ICH Q1E,
*Evaluation for Stability Data*, 2003; Chow, *Statistical Design and
Analysis of Stability Studies*, 2007, ch. 3).

#### Batch poolability
The response (e.g. assay, % of label claim) of batch `j` at time `t` is
modelled by analysis of covariance, `yᵢⱼ = αⱼ + βⱼtᵢⱼ + εᵢⱼ`, fitted by
[`fit_linear_model`] with batch indicators and batch-by-time products. Two
extra-sum-of-squares F tests decide how far the batches can be pooled,
each at the significance level 0.25 that ICH Q1E sets (a high level, so
that a real batch difference is not pooled away):

1. equal slopes: `F = [(RSS_c − RSS_s)/(k − 1)] / [RSS_s/(n − 2k)]`, the
   separate-lines model `s` against the common-slope model `c`;
2. if slopes are not rejected, equal intercepts:
   `F = [(RSS_p − RSS_c)/(k − 1)] / [RSS_c/(n − k − 1)]` against the single
   pooled line `p`.

Rejecting equal slopes gives separate lines (the error variance still
pooled from the full model); rejecting only equal intercepts gives
parallel lines; otherwise one line for all batches.

When the separate-lines model leaves no residual degrees of freedom
(`n = 2k`, e.g. every batch measured at only two times) the slope test is
impossible: the slopes are assumed common, with a note, and the intercept
test decides between parallel lines and one line. An F test whose extra
sum of squares is negligible (below 10⁻¹² of the total) gives F = 0 and
p = 1, even when the larger model fits exactly; a real extra sum of squares
over an exact fit gives F = ∞ and p = 0.

#### Shelf life
For an attribute with a lower acceptance limit the shelf life is the
earliest time at which the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound for the
mean, `ŷ(t) − t_{0.95, df} · se(ŷ(t))`, falls to the limit (an upper limit
uses the upper bound); with both limits the two-sided 95% bounds are
compared with both (ICH Q1E §2.4). With separate or parallel lines the
shortest batch shelf life applies. The search runs from time 0 to a
horizon (default twice the longest time observed).

#### Extrapolation limit
ICH Q1E (Appendix A, for long-term data analysed statistically with no
significant change at accelerated conditions) allows a proposed shelf life
of at most twice the period covered by long-term data, `X`, and no more
than 12 months beyond it: `min(2X, X + 12 months)`. The 12-month part needs
the unit of the time column, [`ShelfLifeOptions::time_unit`]; without one
only the `2X` part is applied. [`ShelfLifeResult::supported_shelf_life`]
is the estimated shelf life cut back to that limit.

- `struct ShelfLifeOptions`: Options for [`shelf_life`].
- `enum StabilityTimeUnit`: Unit of the time values in a stability study.
- `enum ExtrapolationRule`: Which rule sets [`ShelfLifeResult::extrapolation_limit`].
- `enum PoolingModel`: The model chosen by the poolability tests.
- `struct PoolingTest`: One extra-sum-of-squares F test.
- `struct BatchLine`: A batch's fitted line and shelf life under the chosen model.
- `struct ShelfLifeResult`: Result of [`shelf_life`].
- `fn shelf_life`: Estimate the shelf life from stability data.

### `crates/stat-linear/src/stepwise.rs`

Stepwise selection of model effects (Efroymson 1960; Draper & Smith,
*Applied Regression Analysis*, 3rd ed., ch. 15; Venables & Ripley, *Modern
Applied Statistics with S*, §6.8).

Effects are blocks of design columns (all of a categorical effect's columns
enter or leave together); the intercept is always in the model.

* **p-value criterion** — an effect enters when its partial F-test against
  the current model has `p < α_enter` (the smallest such p first) and leaves
  when its test within the current model has `p > α_remove` (the largest
  first). `F = [(RSS_without − RSS_with)/df] / [RSS_with/(n − p_with)]`.
* **AIC / BIC** — `n·ln(RSS/n) + k·p`, with `p` the number of coefficients
  (intercept included) and `k = 2` (AIC) or `ln n` (BIC), as in R's
  `extractAIC`; each step takes the move that lowers the criterion most.

Directions: **forward** from the empty model, **backward** from the full
model, **mixed** from the empty model, checking after every entry whether an
effect should leave (p-values) or considering entries and removals together
(AIC/BIC). Selection is a heuristic search; the final model's p-values do not
account for the selection.

Only estimable models are visited: a move is skipped when the model it leads
to is rank deficient (the effect is aliased with effects already in it) or
leaves no residual degrees of freedom. So forward and mixed searches work
with more candidates than observations, or with aliased candidates. A
backward search needs a starting model: when the full model is not
estimable, it starts from the largest estimable model built by adding the
effects in order (list main effects first), and reports the rest as set aside.

**Heredity** ([`stepwise_selection_with_parents`]): with *strong* heredity
an interaction or power may enter only when all its parents are in the
model, and an effect may not leave while an effect built on it remains;
with *weak* heredity one parent in the model suffices (Chipman 1996; see
[`crate::hierarchy`]). Backward searches remove higher-order effects before
the effects they are built from.

- `enum StepDirection`: Search direction.
- `enum StepCriterion`: Selection criterion.
- `enum Heredity`: Which parent effects an interaction or power needs in the model.
- `struct StepwiseOptions`: Options for [`stepwise_selection`].
- `enum StepAction`: Entering or leaving.
- `struct StepRecord`: One step of the search.
- `struct StepwiseResult`: Result of [`stepwise_selection`].
- `fn stepwise_selection`: Select effects for `y` from the columns of `x`, where effect `i` occupies columns `effects[i]`.
- `fn stepwise_selection_with_parents`: [`stepwise_selection`] where effect `i`'s parent effects are `parents[i]` (indices into `effects`), restricted by `options.heredity`.

Test files: `method_comparison/tests.rs`, `stability/tests.rs`.

Integration tests: `curve_fitting_reference.rs`, `curve_forms.rs`, `manova_reference.rs`, `marginal_reference.rs`, `nonlinear_reference.rs`, `spline_reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-mixed` (`crates/stat-mixed`)

Linear and generalized linear mixed models: random intercepts and slopes, REML/ML, Laplace and adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature.

Dependencies: `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/dense.rs`

Small dense linear algebra on square matrices stored row-major: Cholesky
factorisation, triangular solves, inverses and a symmetric eigensolver.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/family.rs`

Response distributions of a mixed model, each with its link.

- `enum MixedFamily`: Response distribution and link of a mixed model.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/fit.rs`

Fitting: REML or ML for the normal family; Laplace or adaptive
Gauss–Hermite approximations to the likelihood for the others.

- `struct RandomTerm`: One random-effects term: a grouping column, and the effects that vary by its levels (an intercept and/or slopes).
- `struct MixedModel`: A mixed model's data: response, fixed-effects design, prior weights, offset and random-effects terms.
- `struct ResidualGroups`: Levels of the grouping whose residual variances differ.
- `enum DfMethod`: Denominator degrees of freedom of the normal family's t and F tests.
- `struct MixedOptions`: Fitting options.
- `struct VarianceTest`: A likelihood-ratio test of equal residual variances.
- `struct RobustSummary`: Cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors of the fixed effects.
- `struct FixedEffect`: A fixed effect with its test and interval.
- `struct VarianceComponent`: A variance of a random effect (or the residual variance).
- `struct RandomCorrelation`: A correlation between two random effects of one term.
- `struct ConditionalModes`: Conditional modes (BLUPs for the normal family) of one term's random effects, with their conditional standard deviations.
- `struct ScaleParameter`: The family's extra scale parameter (Gamma dispersion, negative binomial shape).
- `struct ContrastTest`: A test of a linear hypothesis `Lβ = 0` on the fixed effects.
- `struct MixedFit`: A fitted mixed model.
- `fn fit_mixed`: Fit a linear (normal family) or generalized linear mixed model.
- `fn satterthwaite_limits`: Satterthwaite (1946) confidence limits of a variance `v` with large-sample standard error `se`: treating `ν·v̂/v` as χ² with `ν = 2(v/se)²` degrees of freedom gives `[ν·v / χ²₁₋α/₂(ν), ν·v / χ²α/₂(ν)]` (Burdick & Graybill 1992, §2; Milliken & Johnson 2009, ch.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-mixed

Linear and generalized linear mixed models: fixed effects plus random
intercepts and slopes for one or more grouping columns (crossed or
nested), for normal, binomial, Poisson, Gamma and negative binomial
responses.

* **Normal** responses are fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML,
  the default) or maximum likelihood, profiling the fixed effects and the
  residual variance out of the likelihood and minimising over the
  covariance parameters θ (Bates et al. 2015, *J. Stat. Softw.* 67(1)).
  Fixed effects get t and F tests with Satterthwaite's denominator degrees
  of freedom (Satterthwaite 1946; Kuznetsova et al. 2017).
* **Other families** maximise the Laplace approximation to the marginal
  likelihood, or, with a single random intercept, adaptive Gauss–Hermite
  quadrature (Pinheiro & Bates, *J. Comput. Graph. Stat.* 4, 1995). The
  conditional modes come from penalized iteratively reweighted least
  squares. A first pass optimises θ with β solved alongside the random
  effects; a second optimises θ and β together. Fixed effects get Wald z
  tests from the curvature of the approximate likelihood.

The numerical core eliminates the random-effects term with
the most effects level by level, so a model with thousands of levels of
one grouping column stays cheap.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/nested.rs`

Nested comparison of groups: subjects nested in groups, replicate
measurements on each subject (a two-level hierarchical design).

The model is `y_gsr = μ + α_g + b_gs + e_gsr` with subject effects
`b_gs ~ N(0, σ²_s)` and residuals `e_gsr ~ N(0, σ²)`. It is fitted by REML
([`fit_mixed`]); the test of equal group means is an F test with
Satterthwaite's denominator degrees of freedom, and group means and
pairwise differences get t tests and intervals on Satterthwaite degrees
of freedom (Kuznetsova, Brockhoff & Christensen 2017). Treating the
replicates as independent observations would understate every standard
error; the subjects, not the measurements, are the experimental units.

With equal replicates per subject and equal subjects per group the
classical nested ANOVA (Sokal & Rohlf, *Biometry*, 4th ed., ch. 10) gives
the same group test, `F = MS_groups / MS_subjects(groups)` on
`(a − 1, S − a)` degrees of freedom whenever the REML estimate of `σ²_s`
is positive; it is reported alongside for such balanced data.

- `struct NestedEstimate`: An estimate with its standard error, Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, t test against zero and confidence interval.
- `struct NestedAnova`: The classical nested ANOVA table (balanced data).
- `struct NestedComparison`: Result of a nested comparison.
- `fn nested_comparison`: Compare groups with subjects nested in groups.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/optimize.rs`

Derivative-free and quasi-Newton minimisation with lower bounds, and
finite-difference Hessians.

* Nelder–Mead (Nelder & Mead, *Computer Journal* 7, 1965) with vertices
  projected onto the bounds and restarts from the best point (a common
  remedy for premature collapse, Kelley, *Iterative Methods for
  Optimization*, 1999, §8.1).
* BFGS on finite-difference gradients with projection onto the bounds and
  an Armijo backtracking line search; variables held at a bound by the
  gradient are frozen for the step (Nocedal & Wright, *Numerical
  Optimization*, 2nd ed., 2006, §6.1 and §16.7).

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/ordinal.rs`

Ordinal responses: the cumulative logit (proportional odds) mixed model

```text
logit P(Yᵢ ≤ k | b) = αₖ − ηᵢ,   ηᵢ = offsetᵢ + xᵢᵀβ + zᵢᵀb,   k = 1 … K−1,
```

with thresholds `α₁ < … < α_{K−1}` in place of an intercept (Hedeker &
Gibbons, "A random-effects ordinal regression model for multilevel
analysis", *Biometrics* 50, 1994; Agresti, *Analysis of Ordinal
Categorical Data*, 2nd ed., 2010, ch. 10). A positive coefficient moves
the response towards higher categories; `exp(β)` is the odds ratio of a
higher rather than a lower category.

The likelihood integrates over the random effects as for the other
families: the Laplace approximation at the conditional mode of the
spherical effects u (found by Newton's method, which is penalized
iteratively reweighted least squares with the observed information
`−∂²ℓᵢ/∂ηᵢ²` as weights; the cumulative logit log-likelihood is concave in
η), or adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature for a single random intercept.
θ, the thresholds (as `α₁` and the logs of the gaps, so that they stay
ordered) and β are optimised together by quasi-Newton steps polished by
Nelder–Mead; standard errors come from the Hessian of the approximate
deviance in (θ, α, β).

- `fn category_probabilities`: Category probabilities at linear predictor `eta`.

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/shelf_life.rs`

Shelf life with batch as a random effect (Chow & Shao, "Estimating drug
shelf-life with random batches", *Biometrics* 47, 1991; ICH Q1E, 2003).

Batches in a stability study are a sample of the batches that will be
made. Treating them as random, the response of batch `j` at time `t` is

```text
yᵢⱼ = (β₀ + b₀ⱼ) + (β₁ + b₁ⱼ) tᵢⱼ + εᵢⱼ,   (b₀ⱼ, b₁ⱼ) ~ N(0, G),   ε ~ N(0, σ²),
```

fitted by REML with a correlated random intercept and slope. Two bounds
can set the shelf life, each the earliest time at which it meets an
acceptance limit (one-sided at the confidence level with one limit,
two-sided with both):

* the **population mean** `β₀ + β₁t`: `x̂ ∓ t_ν · √(xᵀ Cov(β̂) x)`;
* a **future batch**'s mean `β₀ + b₀ + (β₁ + b₁)t`, whose prediction
  variance adds the batch-to-batch variation:
  `x̂ ∓ t_ν · √(xᵀ Cov(β̂) x + xᵀ Ĝ x)`, with `x = (1, t)`.

`ν` is Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom of the variance in the bound
(see [`MixedFit::prediction_variance`]). The future-batch bound is the
conservative one ICH Q1E's batch-to-batch concern points to; the
population-mean bound describes the average batch.

- `struct RandomBatchOptions`: Options for [`random_batch_shelf_life`].
- `struct RandomBatchShelfLife`: Result of [`random_batch_shelf_life`].
- `fn random_batch_shelf_life`: Estimate the shelf life with batches as random (see the module notes).

### `crates/stat-mixed/src/system.rs`

The random-effects structure and the penalized least-squares system at the
heart of every fit.

The model for the linear predictor is `η = offset + Xβ + ZΛ(θ)u` with
spherical random effects `u ~ N(0, I)` (times σ² for the normal family),
so `b = Λu` has covariance `ΛΛᵀ` (Bates, Mächler, Bolker & Walker,
"Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4", *J. Stat. Softw.* 67(1),
2015, §3). `Λ` is block diagonal: for random-effects term `k` with `qₖ`
effects (intercept, slopes) it repeats one lower-triangular `qₖ × qₖ`
factor `Tₖ` for every level of the term's grouping column.

Each evaluation solves the penalized weighted least-squares problem

```text
min ‖W^½(v − Xβ − ZΛu)‖² + ‖u‖²
```

whose normal equations have the block matrix
`[ΛᵀZᵀWZΛ + I, ΛᵀZᵀWX; XᵀWZΛ, XᵀWX]`. The term with the most effects
(levels × `qₖ`) is eliminated first: its block is itself block diagonal
(one small `qₖ × qₖ` block per level), so its Schur complement onto the
remaining random effects and β is formed level by level and only that
smaller dense matrix is factorised. Its Cholesky factor gives
`log|ΛᵀZᵀWZΛ + I|` and `log|R_X|²` (the REML adjustment) directly.

Integration tests: `edge_cases.rs`, `extensions.rs`, `independent.rs`, `reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-multivariate` (`crates/stat-multivariate`)

Multivariate methods: correlations, outlier distances, item analysis, principal components, clustering, Gaussian mixtures, latent class analysis, multidimensional scaling, t-SNE and UMAP.

Dependencies: `rayon`, `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/cluster_number.rs`

Choosing the number of k-means clusters: the gap statistic and average
silhouette widths across `k`.

**Silhouette** (Rousseeuw 1987, *J. Comput. Appl. Math.* 20, 53–65): for
point `i` in cluster `A`, `a(i)` is its mean Euclidean distance to the
other members of `A` and `b(i)` the smallest mean distance to the members
of another cluster; `s(i) = (b − a) / max(a, b)`, and `s(i) = 0` in a
cluster of one. Widths near 1 mean well-separated clusters; the `k` with
the largest average width is suggested.

**Gap statistic** (Tibshirani, Walther & Hastie 2001, *J. R. Stat. Soc. B*
63, 411–423): with `W_k` the pooled within-cluster sum of squares of the
k-means solution, `Gap(k) = E*[log W_k] − log W_k`, the expectation
estimated from `B` reference data sets drawn uniformly over the box
spanned by the data (or by its principal components, which follows the
data's shape), each clustered the same way. `s_k = sd(log W*_k) √(1 + 1/B)`
(the standard deviation with divisor `B − 1`), and the suggested `k` is
the smallest with `Gap(k) ≥ Gap(k+1) − s_{k+1}`.

- `struct Silhouette`: Silhouette widths of a clustering.
- `fn silhouette`: Silhouette widths of `assignments` (cluster `0..k` of each point) with Euclidean distances.
- `enum GapReference`: The box reference data are drawn from.
- `struct GapOptions`: Options for [`choose_cluster_number`].
- `struct ClusterNumberRow`: Gap and silhouette at one `k`.
- `struct ClusterNumber`: Gap statistic and silhouettes for `k = 1, …, max_k`.
- `fn gap_from_reference`: Gap statistics from observed `log_w` (index `k − 1`) and reference `reference_log_w[b][k − 1]`: `(E*[log W], Gap, s)` for each `k`.
- `fn gap_rule`: Tibshirani et al.'s rule: the smallest `k` (1-based) with `Gap(k) ≥ Gap(k+1) − s_{k+1}`, or the largest `k` examined.
- `fn choose_cluster_number`: Gap statistic and average silhouette width of k-means solutions for `k = 1, …, max_k` (see the module documentation).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/correlations.rs`

Correlation matrices of several continuous variables.

For every pair of variables the routine reports

* **Pearson's r** with its t test of ρ = 0 (`t = r √((n−2)/(1−r²))` on
  `n − 2` df) and Fisher's z interval `tanh(atanh r ± z_{1−γ/2}/√(n−3))`
  (Fisher 1921), computed by [`stat_core::correlation::pearson`];
* **Spearman's ρₛ** (Pearson's r of average ranks), with the same t test
  and interval ([`stat_core::correlation::spearman`]);
* the **covariance** (divisor `n − 1`).

Missing values (NaN) are handled one of two ways:

* **pairwise** — each pair uses every row that has both values, so pairs
  can rest on different rows and counts;
* **listwise** — only rows complete in every variable are used, so every
  pair shares one set of rows.

**Partial correlations** — each pair's correlation with every other
variable held fixed — always use the complete rows. With `P = R⁻¹` the
inverse of their correlation matrix, `r_{ij·rest} = −P_{ij}/√(P_{ii}P_{jj})`
(Whittaker, *Graphical Models in Applied Multivariate Statistics*, 1990,
§5.7). Its t test has `n − p` degrees of freedom: `n − 2` less one for each
of the `p − 2` variables partialled out (Anderson, *An Introduction to
Multivariate Statistical Analysis*, 3rd ed., §4.3).

- `enum MissingRows`: Which rows a pair of variables uses when values are missing.
- `struct PairCorrelation`: Statistics of one pair of variables.
- `struct PartialCorrelations`: Partial correlations of every pair given all the other variables.
- `struct CorrelationMatrix`: Per-variable summaries and every pair's correlations.
- `fn correlation_matrix`: Correlations of the variables in `columns` (equal lengths; NaN marks a missing value) with intervals at confidence `level`.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/correspondence.rs`

Simple correspondence analysis of a two-way table of counts.

For an `r × c` table `N` with total `n`, correspondence matrix `P = N/n`,
row masses `rᵢ` and column masses `cⱼ`, the standardized residuals

```text
S = D_r^{-1/2} (P − r cᵀ) D_c^{-1/2}
```

have the SVD `S = U Σ Vᵀ` ([`stat_core::svd()`]). The **principal inertias**
are `λₖ = σₖ²`; they sum to the total inertia `χ²/n`, where `χ²` is
Pearson's statistic for independence. Row and column **principal
coordinates** are `F = D_r^{-1/2} U Σ` and `G = D_c^{-1/2} V Σ`; rows (or
columns) with similar profiles lie close together, and a symmetric map plots
both on the first two dimensions (Greenacre, *Correspondence Analysis in
Practice*, 3rd ed., chs. 4–8; Benzécri 1973). At most `min(r, c) − 1`
dimensions carry inertia. Each dimension's sign is chosen so that the
largest-magnitude column coordinate is positive.

- `struct CorrespondenceAnalysis`: Result of a correspondence analysis.
- `fn correspondence_analysis`: Correspondence analysis of `counts[i][j]` (rows × columns).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/discriminant.rs`

Normal-theory discriminant analysis: linear and quadratic classification
rules with prior probabilities, and Fisher's canonical discriminant
functions.

#### Classification
With `g` groups of sizes `n_k`, means `x̄_k`, priors `π_k` and, for each
group, a multivariate normal density, an observation `x` is assigned the
posterior probabilities
`P(k | x) = π_k f_k(x) / Σ_j π_j f_j(x)` (Anderson, *An Introduction to
Multivariate Statistical Analysis*, 3rd ed., 2003, §6.4–6.6; Rencher &
Christensen, *Methods of Multivariate Analysis*, 3rd ed., 2012, ch. 9):

* **linear** rule: every group shares the pooled within-group covariance
  `S_w = W / (n − g)`, `W = Σ_k Σ_{i∈k} (xᵢ − x̄_k)(xᵢ − x̄_k)ᵀ`, so
  `ln π_k f_k(x) = ln π_k − ½ (x − x̄_k)ᵀ S_w⁻¹ (x − x̄_k) + const`;
* **quadratic** rule: each group has its own covariance `S_k` (divisor
  `n_k − 1`), adding `−½ ln|S_k|`.

The most probable group is the predicted one.

#### Canonical discriminant functions
Fisher's linear combinations `vᵀx` that best separate the group means
relative to the within-group variation solve the generalized eigenproblem
`B v = λ W v`, with `B = Σ_k n_k (x̄_k − x̄)(x̄_k − x̄)ᵀ` (Fisher 1936,
"The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems", *Annals of
Eugenics* 7; Rao 1948). There are `r = min(p, g − 1)` functions:

* eigenvalues `λ_k` of `W⁻¹B` and their shares of `Σλ`;
* canonical correlations `√(λ_k / (1 + λ_k))`;
* Wilks' `Λ_k = Π_{j≥k} 1/(1 + λ_j)` testing that functions `k, …, r` are
  all zero, with Bartlett's approximation
  `−(n − 1 − (p + g)/2) ln Λ_k ~ χ²` on `(p − k + 1)(g − k)` degrees of
  freedom (`k` counted from 1; Bartlett 1947);
* **raw** coefficients `v` scaled so that the scores have unit pooled
  within-group variance (`vᵀ S_w v = 1`), with scores centred at the
  grand mean, `(x − x̄)ᵀ v`;
* **standardized** coefficients `vⱼ √(S_w)ⱼⱼ` (for variables in pooled
  within-group standard deviations);
* **structure** correlations: pooled within-group correlations of each
  variable with each function, `(S_w v)ⱼ / √(S_w)ⱼⱼ`.

Each function's sign makes its largest-magnitude raw coefficient positive.

- `enum DiscriminantRule`: Which covariance model classifies.
- `struct WilksTest`: Wilks' Λ test of the canonical functions from one onwards.
- `struct CanonicalFunctions`: Fisher's canonical discriminant functions.
- `struct DiscriminantFit`: A fitted discriminant analysis.
- `fn fit_discriminant`: Fit a discriminant analysis to observations `x` (rows of `p` values) in groups `groups` (`0..n_groups`), with `priors` (one per group, positive; rescaled to sum to 1).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/distance.rs`

Distance (dissimilarity) matrices between rows of a data set.

For rows `x` and `y` over `p` variables:

* **Euclidean** — `√Σₖ (xₖ − yₖ)²`.
* **Manhattan** (city block) — `Σₖ |xₖ − yₖ|`.
* **Bray–Curtis** — `Σₖ |xₖ − yₖ| / Σₖ (xₖ + yₖ)` for non-negative data
  such as abundances (Bray & Curtis 1957, *Ecological Monographs* 27;
  Legendre & Legendre 2012, *Numerical Ecology*, 3rd ed., §7.4,
  coefficient D14). Two rows that are both entirely zero are at
  distance 0.
* **Jaccard** — on presence/absence (a nonzero value is “present”),
  `1 − a / (a + b + c)` with `a` the variables present in both rows and
  `b`, `c` those present in only one (Jaccard 1901; Legendre & Legendre
  §7.3, coefficient S7). Double absences are ignored; two rows with
  nothing present are at distance 0.
* **Hamming** — the *number* of variables on which the rows differ.
* **Simple matching** — the *proportion* of variables on which the rows
  differ, `1 − m / p`, one minus Sokal and Michener's matching
  coefficient (Legendre & Legendre §7.3, coefficient S1).
* **Gower** — the general coefficient for mixed variable types (Gower
  1971, “A general coefficient of similarity and some of its
  properties”, *Biometrics* 27): `d(x, y) = Σₖ wₖ δₖ / Σₖ wₖ`, where
  for a numeric or ordinal variable `δₖ = |xₖ − yₖ| / Rₖ` with `Rₖ`
  the range of the variable over all rows (ordinal level codes are used
  as ranks, as R's `cluster::daisy` does; Kaufman & Rousseeuw 1990,
  *Finding Groups in Data*, ch. 1), for a nominal variable `δₖ` is 0
  when the levels agree and 1 otherwise, and for an asymmetric binary
  variable (nonzero = present) `δₖ` is the mismatch indicator but the
  variable is skipped (`wₖ = 0`) when both rows are absent. A variable
  missing in either row is skipped as well, so the average runs over
  the variables available for that pair. A variable with zero range
  contributes 0.

Gower (1966, “Some distance properties of latent root and vector
methods used in multivariate analysis”, *Biometrika* 53) showed which of
these give Euclidean configurations; see [`crate::pcoa`] for principal
coordinates of any of them.

- `enum DistanceMetric`: How the distance between two rows is measured.
- `enum VariableKind`: How a variable enters Gower's coefficient.
- `struct DistanceColumn`: One variable: its values for every row and its kind.
- `struct DistanceMatrix`: A symmetric `n × n` matrix of non-negative distances with a zero diagonal, stored row-major.
- `fn distance_matrix`: Distances between every pair of rows of `columns` under `metric`.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/embedding.rs`

Shared pieces of the dimension-reduction methods ([`crate::mds`],
[`crate::tsne`], [`crate::umap`]): the dissimilarities between objects
(Euclidean distances between data rows, or a given distance matrix),
exact nearest neighbours, and the trustworthiness of an embedding.

- `enum Proximity`: The dissimilarities an embedding preserves.
- `fn trustworthiness`: Trustworthiness of an embedding (Venna & Kaski 2001, "Neighborhood preservation in nonlinear projection methods: an experimental study", *ICANN*): with `r(i, j)` the rank of `j` among the neighbours of `i` in the original space (1 = nearest) and `Uₖ(i)` the objects among the `k` nearest of `i` in…
- `fn standardize_columns`: Standardize columns of row vectors to mean 0 and SD 1 (divisor `n − 1`).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/factor.rs`

Exploratory factor analysis of a correlation or covariance matrix.

#### Model
The common factor model writes the `p × p` covariance (or correlation)
matrix of the variables as `Σ = Λ Φ Λᵀ + Ψ`: `Λ` (`p × m`) holds the
loadings of the variables on `m` common factors, `Φ` the correlations of
the factors (the identity before rotation) and `Ψ` the diagonal matrix of
uniquenesses (variance not shared with the other variables). The
**communality** of variable `j` is `hⱼ = Σₖ λⱼₖ²` (for orthogonal
factors), and `hⱼ + ψⱼ = sⱼⱼ`.

#### Extraction
* **Maximum likelihood** (Lawley & Maxwell, *Factor Analysis as a
  Statistical Method*, 2nd ed., 1971; Jöreskog, "Some contributions to
  maximum likelihood factor analysis", *Psychometrika* 32, 1967). For given
  uniquenesses let `θ₁ ≥ … ≥ θₚ` be the eigenvalues, with unit vectors
  `ωₖ`, of `Ψ^{-1/2} S Ψ^{-1/2}`. The likelihood is maximised over `Λ` by
  `Λ = Ψ^{1/2} Ω_m (Θ_m − I)^{1/2}`, which leaves the discrepancy
  `F(Ψ) = Σ_{k>m} (θₖ − ln θₖ − 1)` (equal to
  `ln|Σ̂| − ln|S| + tr(Σ̂⁻¹S) − p`) to minimise over the uniquenesses. Its
  gradient is `∂F/∂ψⱼ = (Λ̂Λ̂ᵀ + Ψ − S)ⱼⱼ / ψⱼ²`. The minimisation is a
  projected quasi-Newton (BFGS) iteration inside the box
  `0.005 sⱼⱼ ≤ ψⱼ ≤ sⱼⱼ`, started from `ψⱼ = (1 − m/2p) / (S⁻¹)ⱼⱼ`
  (Jöreskog's start). A uniqueness that stops on the lower bound is a
  **Heywood case** (a communality of essentially the whole variance); it is
  flagged rather than allowed to become zero or negative.
* **Principal axis** (iterated principal factors; Harman, *Modern Factor
  Analysis*, 3rd ed., 1976, ch. 8): the diagonal of `S` is replaced by
  communality estimates — first the squared multiple correlations
  `sⱼⱼ − 1/(S⁻¹)ⱼⱼ` — the `m` leading eigenvectors give
  `Λ = V_m Λ_m^{1/2}`, and the row sums of squares of `Λ` become the next
  communalities until they change by less than the tolerance. A
  communality that reaches the variance is held there and flagged as a
  Heywood case: its diagonal entry stays at `sⱼⱼ`, and its row of final
  loadings is scaled to a communality of exactly `sⱼⱼ` (uniqueness 0;
  Bartlett scores are then unavailable).

#### Test of fit (maximum likelihood)
Bartlett's corrected statistic `(n − 1 − (2p + 5)/6 − 2m/3) · F(Ψ̂)` is
referred to χ² with `((p − m)² − p − m)/2` degrees of freedom (Lawley &
Maxwell §4.3). Small p-values mean `m` factors do not reproduce the
correlations.

#### Rotation
* **Varimax** (Kaiser, "The varimax criterion for analytic rotation in
  factor analysis", *Psychometrika* 23, 1958) maximises the variance of
  the squared loadings in each column. With Kaiser normalisation each row
  is divided by `√hⱼ` before rotating and multiplied back afterwards. The
  rotation `T` is found by the singular-value iteration
  `B = Aᵀ(Z³ − Z diag(1ᵀZ²)/p)`, `T = U Vᵀ` for `B = U Σ Vᵀ`, until `Σσ`
  stops increasing.
* **Promax** (Hendrickson & White, "Promax: a quick method for rotation to
  oblique simple structure", *Brit. J. Statist. Psych.* 17, 1964): from the
  varimax loadings `V`, the target `Q = V ∘ |V|^{k−1}` (power `k`, 4 by
  default) is fitted by least squares, `U = (VᵀV)⁻¹VᵀQ`, whose columns are
  rescaled so that `diag((UᵀU)⁻¹) = 1`. The **pattern** loadings are `VU`,
  the factor correlations `Φ = (UᵀU)⁻¹` and the **structure** loadings
  (correlations of variables with factors) `VU Φ`.

Each factor's sign is chosen so that its loadings sum to a positive value.

#### Factor scores
For standardized (correlation) or centred (covariance) data `z`:
regression (Thomson/Thurstone) scores `z S⁻¹ Λ Φ`; Bartlett's weighted
least-squares scores `z Ψ⁻¹ Λ (Λᵀ Ψ⁻¹ Λ)⁻¹` (Bartlett, "The statistical
conception of mental factors", *Brit. J. Psych.* 28, 1937).

- `enum Extraction`: How the factors are extracted.
- `enum Rotation`: Rotation of the extracted loadings.
- `enum ScoreMethod`: How factor scores are computed.
- `struct FactorOptions`: Settings of [`factor_analysis`].
- `struct FitTest`: Bartlett-corrected likelihood-ratio test that `m` factors suffice.
- `struct FactorFit`: A fitted factor model.
- `fn factor_analysis`: Factor analysis of the correlation or covariance matrix `s` of `n_obs` observations.
- `fn varimax`: Varimax rotation of `a` (`p × m`): returns the rotated loadings and the orthogonal rotation `T` (`rotated = a · T`).
- `fn promax`: Promax rotation of `a`: returns the pattern loadings, the rotation `T` (`pattern = a · T`) and the factor correlations `Φ`.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/hierarchical.rs`

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering.

Starting from single points, the two closest clusters are merged
repeatedly until one remains. Cluster distances follow the
Lance–Williams recurrence (Lance & Williams 1967, *Computer Journal* 9):

* **single** linkage — the closest pair of members;
* **complete** — the farthest pair;
* **average** (UPGMA) — the mean of all member distances;
* **Ward** — the increase in within-cluster sum of squares. Distances are
  updated on squared Euclidean distances,
  `d²(k, i∪j) = [(nₖ+nᵢ)d²(k,i) + (nₖ+nⱼ)d²(k,j) − nₖ d²(i,j)] / (nₖ+nᵢ+nⱼ)`,
  and the reported merge height is `√d²` (Ward 1963, *JASA* 58).

[`hierarchical_from_distances`] runs the same updates on a given
distance matrix (Ward on the squared given distances).

The merge list uses the usual convention: points are clusters `0..n`, and
merge `m` creates cluster `n + m`. Ties are broken by the smaller pair of
indices. Each step finds the closest pair from cached nearest neighbours, so
typical cost is `O(n²)` time and memory.

- `enum Linkage`: Linkage criterion.
- `struct Merge`: One merge of two clusters.
- `struct Dendrogram`: The full merge history.
- `const MAX_POINTS`: Largest number of points accepted (the distance matrix needs `n²` memory).
- `fn hierarchical_clustering`: Cluster `points` hierarchically.
- `fn hierarchical_from_distances`: Cluster objects hierarchically from a given distance matrix (for example Gower distances of mixed data; see [`crate::distance`]).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/imputation.rs`

Missing-value imputation for a set of numeric columns.

Data are row vectors (`data[i][j]`, row `i`, column `j`) with `NaN`
marking a missing value. Each method returns the completed matrix, in
which observed values are unchanged.

#### Missing-data patterns
[`missing_patterns`] groups rows by which columns they lack (Little &
Rubin 2019, *Statistical Analysis with Missing Data*, 3rd ed., §1.2), the
basis of the pattern table and of the EM algorithm's E-step.

#### Column centre
[`impute_center`] replaces each missing value by the mean or median of
the column's observed values: the baseline, which keeps the means but
shrinks variances and correlations.

#### Multivariate normal, EM algorithm
[`em_normal`] finds the maximum-likelihood mean `μ` and covariance `Σ`
of a multivariate normal distribution from incomplete rows by the EM
algorithm (Dempster, Laird & Rubin 1977, *JRSS B* 39; Schafer 1997,
*Analysis of Incomplete Multivariate Data*, ch. 5), assuming values are
missing at random. For a row with observed part `O` and missing part `M`
the E-step uses the conditional distribution

```text
E[x_M | x_O] = μ_M + Σ_MO Σ_OO⁻¹ (x_O − μ_O)
Var[x_M | x_O] = Σ_MM − Σ_MO Σ_OO⁻¹ Σ_OM
```

to accumulate the expected sufficient statistics `T₁ = Σ E[x]` and
`T₂ = Σ E[x xᵀ]` (the conditional covariance is added to `T₂`); the
M-step sets `μ = T₁/n` and `Σ = T₂/n − μ μᵀ`. Each iteration does not
decrease the observed-data log-likelihood

```text
ℓ(μ, Σ) = −½ Σᵢ [ pᵢ ln 2π + ln |Σ_OO| + (x_O − μ_O)ᵀ Σ_OO⁻¹ (x_O − μ_O) ],
```

which is recorded at each iteration. The algorithm starts from the
observed means and variances with zero covariances (Schafer 1997, §5.3.2)
and stops when no mean moves by more than `tolerance` standard
deviations and no covariance by more than `tolerance` times the product
of the two standard deviations. Missing values are imputed by their
conditional means at the estimates.

#### Low-rank SVD
[`svd_impute`] fits the matrix by column means plus a rank-`k` term and
iterates: fill the missing cells, recompute the column means and the
singular value decomposition of the centred (and, optionally, scaled)
matrix, refit the missing cells from the leading `k` singular triples,
until the relative change `‖Z_new − Z_old‖²_F / ‖Z_old‖²_F` falls below
`tolerance` (Troyanskaya et al. 2001, "Missing value estimation methods
for DNA microarrays", *Bioinformatics* 17).

Without shrinkage this iteration can drift away (the kept components
chase the values they themselves filled in, and with several components
the imputed cells can grow far outside the data). By default the kept
singular values are therefore shrunk as in the regularized iterative PCA
of Josse & Husson (2012, "Handling missing values in exploratory
multivariate data analysis methods", *J. SFdS* 153(2); Josse, Pagès &
Husson 2009): with `n` rows, `p` columns, rank `k` and singular values
`σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ …` of the centred matrix, the noise variance per cell is

`σ̂² = n p / min(p, n − 1) · Σ_{s>k} σ_s² / n / ((n − 1) p − (n − 1) k − p k + k²)`,

capped at `σ²_{k+1} / n`, and each kept singular value is replaced by
`σ_s − n σ̂² / σ_s` (the eigenvalue `λ_s = σ_s²/n` shrunk to `λ_s − σ̂²`).
When the discarded components hold no variation the fit is unchanged.
Alternatively, with a soft threshold `λ > 0` the singular values become
`max(σ − λ, 0)`, as in the soft-impute algorithm of Mazumder, Hastie &
Tibshirani (2010, *JMLR* 11); a threshold replaces the regularization.
[`choose_rank`] picks `k` by holding out a random share of the
observed cells and comparing their imputed values with the truth.

- `struct MissingPattern`: One missing-data pattern: the columns a set of rows lacks.
- `struct MissingPatterns`: The missing-data patterns of a data matrix.
- `fn missing_patterns`: Group the rows of `data` by their missing-data pattern (`NaN` is missing).
- `enum Center`: Which centre [`impute_center`] fills with.
- `fn impute_center`: Fill each missing value with its column's observed mean or median.
- `struct EmOptions`: Settings of [`em_normal`].
- `struct EmImputation`: Maximum-likelihood multivariate normal estimates from incomplete data, and the data completed by conditional means.
- `fn em_normal`: Estimate a multivariate normal mean and covariance from incomplete rows by the EM algorithm and impute each missing value by its conditional mean (see the [module documentation](self)).
- `struct SvdOptions`: Settings of [`svd_impute`].
- `struct SvdImputation`: Data completed by a low-rank fit.
- `fn svd_impute`: Impute missing values by an iterated rank-`k` fit (see the [module documentation](self)).
- `struct RankChoice`: The held-out comparison behind a chosen rank.
- `fn choose_rank`: Choose the rank of [`svd_impute`] by hiding a random `share` of the observed cells (always leaving each column at least three observed values and each row at least one), imputing them at ranks `1..=max_rank` with `options`, and taking the rank whose imputed values are closest to the hidden ones (…

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/kmeans.rs`

K-means clustering.

Minimizes the total within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances
`W = Σₖ Σ_{i∈k} ‖xᵢ − cₖ‖²` by Lloyd's algorithm (Lloyd 1982, *IEEE Trans.
Inf. Theory* 28): assign every point to its nearest centre, move each centre
to the mean of its points, repeat until no assignment changes. Starting
centres come from k-means++ seeding (Arthur & Vassilvitskii 2007, "k-means++:
the advantages of careful seeding", *SODA*): the first uniformly at random,
each next with probability proportional to its squared distance from the
nearest centre chosen so far. Several seeded starts are run and the solution
with the smallest `W` is kept. An emptied cluster is restarted at the point
farthest from its centre among clusters with more than one point. A point
equally near several centres keeps its current cluster if that is one of
them, else joins the lowest-numbered, so duplicate points cannot flip
between equal centres and the iterations converge.

Starting centres can also be given (Hartigan & Wong 1979, *Appl. Statist.*
28, take them as an input; so does R's `kmeans(x, centers = )`): Lloyd's
iterations then start from exactly those centres, alone or as one more
start beside the seeded ones, the smallest `W` winning (the given start
on a tie).

Clusters are numbered in order of first appearance in the data, so labels do
not depend on the random start.

- `struct KMeansOptions`: Options for [`k_means`].
- `struct KMeans`: A k-means solution.
- `fn k_means`: Cluster `points` (each of the same dimension) into `options.k` groups.
- `fn k_means_from_centers`: Cluster `points` from the given starting `centers` (one per cluster, so `options.k` is ignored): Lloyd's iterations from those centres, and when `also_seeded` also `options.starts` k-means++ starts, keeping the solution with the smallest `W` (the given start on a tie).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/latent_class.rs`

Latent class analysis of categorical items by maximum likelihood (EM),
with model choice across numbers of classes by BIC.

#### Model
Each respondent belongs to one of `K` unobserved classes with prior
probabilities (class sizes) `πₖ > 0`, `Σ πₖ = 1`. Within a class the `J`
items are independent (local independence; Lazarsfeld & Henry 1968,
*Latent Structure Analysis*; Goodman 1974, "Exploratory latent structure
analysis using both identifiable and unidentifiable models", *Biometrika*
61), and item `j` takes its level `r ∈ {1, …, Rⱼ}` with probability
`ρⱼₖᵣ` (`Σᵣ ρⱼₖᵣ = 1`). A response pattern `y` has probability

`P(y) = Σₖ πₖ Πⱼ Πᵣ ρⱼₖᵣ^[yⱼ = r]`.

**Missing responses.** A missing item is left out of the product for that
respondent (its factor is 1), which is the likelihood of the observed
responses when items are missing at random (full-information maximum
likelihood, as poLCA and stepmix do). A respondent with every item
missing carries no information and must be dropped by the caller.

The model has `m = (K − 1) + K Σⱼ (Rⱼ − 1)` free parameters.

#### Estimation
EM as set out by Linzer & Lewis (2011, "poLCA: An R package for
polytomous variable latent class analysis", *Journal of Statistical
Software* 42(10)). The E-step computes posterior class probabilities
`hᵢₖ = πₖ fₖ(yᵢ) / Σₗ πₗ fₗ(yᵢ)` on the log scale; the M-step sets
`πₖ = Σᵢ hᵢₖ / n` and

`ρⱼₖᵣ = (Σᵢ∈Oⱼ hᵢₖ [yᵢⱼ = r] + α) / (Σᵢ∈Oⱼ hᵢₖ + Rⱼ α)`,

with `Oⱼ` the respondents who answered item `j` and `α ≥ 0` an optional
Dirichlet smoothing (pseudo-count per level, `0` by default — plain
maximum likelihood). With `α > 0` the estimates are posterior modes under
a symmetric Dirichlet(`α + 1`) prior on each `ρⱼₖ·`, which keeps them off
the 0/1 boundary; the reported log-likelihood is still the plain one.
Iterations stop when the objective changes by less than
`tolerance · (1 + |ℓ|)`.

**Starts.** EM finds local maxima, so it runs from several random starts
(as in poLCA): each draws every `ρⱼₖ·` uniformly at random and normalizes
it, with equal class sizes. The start with the largest log-likelihood is
kept, and the number of starts that reached it (within `10⁻⁶` relative)
is reported. Everything is reproducible from the seed.

**Class order.** Classes are relabelled from largest to smallest
estimated size, so labels do not depend on the start (label switching).

#### Standard errors
From the observed information of the log-likelihood (the negative
Hessian), computed analytically in the multinomial-logit parameters
`πₖ ∝ exp γₖ`, `ρⱼₖᵣ ∝ exp βⱼₖᵣ` (one baseline per vector — its largest
element — fixed at 0). For one respondent with `gₖ = πₖ fₖ(yᵢ)` and
`aᵢₖ = ∂ log gₖ / ∂θ`,

`∂² ℓᵢ = Σₖ hᵢₖ (∂² log gₖ + aᵢₖ aᵢₖᵀ) − sᵢ sᵢᵀ`, `sᵢ = Σₖ hᵢₖ aᵢₖ`,

where `∂ log gₖ / ∂γ = eₖ − π`, `∂ log gₖ / ∂βⱼₖ = e_{yᵢⱼ} − ρⱼₖ` for each
answered item, and `∂² log gₖ` is the negative multinomial covariance
`−(diag p − p pᵀ)` of each block. The covariance of the logits is the
inverse information; the delta method (`∂p/∂β = diag p − p pᵀ`) carries
it to the probabilities. Linzer & Lewis (2011) use the same delta method
with the outer product of the scores in place of the Hessian; the two
agree asymptotically. A probability on the boundary (below `10⁻⁷`) has
no finite logit: it is held fixed and its standard error is reported as
not available (NaN). If the information is not positive definite (an
unidentified model, Goodman 1974) every standard error is NaN.
The standard errors use the likelihood alone, also with smoothing.

#### Goodness of fit
Over the `C = Πⱼ Rⱼ` response patterns, using the `N` respondents who
answered every item, with observed counts `oₚ` and expected counts
`eₚ = N P(p)`: the likelihood-ratio statistic `G² = 2 Σ oₚ ln(oₚ/eₚ)` and
Pearson's `X² = Σ (oₚ − eₚ)² / eₚ` (patterns never observed contribute
`eₚ` each), each referred to χ² on `C − 1 − m` degrees of freedom. With
many items most patterns are rare and these p-values are unreliable;
compare models by the information criteria instead.

#### Information criteria and classification
`AIC = −2ℓ + 2m`, `BIC = −2ℓ + m ln n` (Schwarz 1978), the
sample-size-adjusted BIC `−2ℓ + m ln((n + 2)/24)` (Sclove 1987), and the
entropy `R² = 1 − Σᵢ Σₖ (−hᵢₖ ln hᵢₖ) / (n ln K)` (Ramaswamy et al. 1993;
1 for perfect separation, defined as 1 for one class).
[`select_latent_classes`] fits each requested number of classes and
chooses the smallest BIC. A number of classes with more parameters than
the `C − 1` the pattern table can identify (`C − 1 − m < 0`) is reported
as not fitted.

- `struct LatentClassOptions`: Settings of one latent class fit.
- `struct PatternFit`: Goodness of fit of a latent class model over the response patterns.
- `struct LatentClassFit`: A fitted latent class model.
- `fn parameters`: Free parameters of `k` classes over items with `levels`.
- `fn fit_latent_classes`: Fit a `K`-class model by EM from `options.starts` random starts, keeping the largest log-likelihood; classes are ordered by size.
- `struct LatentClassCandidate`: One candidate of a [`LatentClassSelection`].
- `struct LatentClassSelection`: Every number of classes tried, and the one with the smallest BIC.
- `fn select_latent_classes`: Fit every number of classes in `ks` with the settings of `base` (in parallel, deterministically) and choose the smallest BIC.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-multivariate

Methods for several variables at once:

* [`pca`] — principal component analysis via the singular value decomposition.
* [`correspondence`] — simple correspondence analysis of a two-way table.
* [`kmeans`] — k-means clustering with k-means++ seeding and several starts.
* [`cluster_number`] — gap statistic and average silhouette widths for
  choosing the number of k-means clusters; silhouette widths of any
  clustering.
* [`distance`] — distance matrices between rows: Euclidean, Manhattan,
  Gower (mixed types, missing values allowed), Jaccard, Bray–Curtis,
  Hamming and simple matching.
* [`hierarchical`] — agglomerative clustering (single, complete, average,
  Ward linkage) of data rows or of a distance matrix, with dendrogram
  cutting and drawing coordinates.
* [`correlations`] — Pearson and Spearman correlation matrices with tests
  and Fisher-z intervals, pairwise or listwise rows, partial correlations.
* [`outliers`] — Mahalanobis, jackknifed Mahalanobis and Hotelling T²
  distances with their beta and F reference limits.
* [`imputation`] — missing-value patterns and imputation: column mean or median,
  multivariate normal by the EM algorithm, and iterative low-rank SVD.
* [`multiple_imputation`] — `m` completed data sets by chained equations
  (predictive mean matching, Bayesian linear, logistic and multinomial
  regression draws) or by data augmentation under a multivariate normal
  model, with convergence traces.
* [`reliability`] — item analysis: Cronbach's alpha (raw and
  standardized) with Feldt's interval and item statistics.
* [`discriminant`] — linear and quadratic discriminant analysis with
  Fisher's canonical discriminant functions.
* [`factor`] — exploratory factor analysis: maximum-likelihood and
  principal-axis extraction, varimax and promax rotation, factor scores.
* [`mixture`] — Gaussian mixture clustering by EM with six covariance
  structures and BIC across structures and numbers of components.
* [`latent_class`] — latent class analysis of categorical items by EM,
  with standard errors, pattern goodness of fit and BIC across numbers
  of classes.
* [`embedding`], [`mds`], [`tsne`], [`umap`] — dimension reduction:
  classical and SMACOF metric scaling, t-SNE (exact or Barnes–Hut) and
  UMAP, with trustworthiness of an embedding.
* [`pcoa`] — principal coordinates analysis of any distance matrix, with
  Lingoes or Cailliez corrections for negative eigenvalues.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/mds.rs`

Multidimensional scaling: classical (Torgerson) scaling and metric
