scaling by SMACOF.

#### Classical scaling
Torgerson (1952, "Multidimensional scaling: I. Theory and method",
*Psychometrika* 17); Gower (1966). From dissimilarities `δᵢⱼ` form
`B = −½ J Δ⁽²⁾ J`, with `Δ⁽²⁾` the squared dissimilarities and
`J = I − 11ᵀ/n` the centring matrix. With eigenvalues `λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ …` and
unit eigenvectors `vₖ` of `B`, the coordinates on dimension `k` are
`√λₖ vₖ`. For Euclidean distances between data rows `B` is the centred
cross-product matrix, so the solution equals the principal component
scores and is computed from the SVD of the centred data instead. The
share of `Σ λₖ⁺` carried by the kept dimensions measures the fit;
negative eigenvalues mean the dissimilarities are not Euclidean.

#### Metric scaling by SMACOF
De Leeuw (1977, "Applications of convex analysis to multidimensional
scaling", in *Recent Developments in Statistics*); Borg & Groenen,
*Modern Multidimensional Scaling* (2005), ch. 8. Minimizes raw stress
`σ(X) = Σ_{i<j} (δᵢⱼ − dᵢⱼ(X))²` over configurations `X` (`n × d`) by
the Guttman transform `X⁺ = n⁻¹ B(X) X`, where `bᵢⱼ = −δᵢⱼ / dᵢⱼ(X)`
for `i ≠ j` (0 when `dᵢⱼ = 0`) and `bᵢᵢ = −Σ_{j≠i} bᵢⱼ`. Each step
cannot raise the stress (majorization); iterations stop when the stress
falls by less than `tolerance` relative to its value. The report's
stress-1 is `√(σ / Σ_{i<j} δᵢⱼ²)` (Kruskal's normalization by the
dissimilarities). The first start is the classical solution; further
starts are seeded random configurations, and the lowest stress is kept.

- `struct ClassicalScaling`: A classical (Torgerson) scaling solution.
- `fn classical_scaling`: Classical scaling of `proximity` into `dims` dimensions.
- `struct SmacofOptions`: Settings of metric SMACOF scaling.
- `struct Smacof`: A metric scaling solution.
- `fn raw_stress`: Raw stress of configuration `x` against dissimilarities `delta`.
- `fn smacof_from`: SMACOF iterations from configuration `init` (`n` rows of `d`).
- `fn metric_scaling`: Metric scaling by SMACOF from the classical solution and from `options.random_starts` seeded random configurations, keeping the lowest stress.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/mixture.rs`

Gaussian mixture clustering by the EM algorithm, with the covariance
structures of Celeux & Govaert (1995) and model choice by BIC (Fraley &
Raftery 2002).

#### Model
Each point `x ∈ ℝᵖ` comes from one of `K` multivariate normal
components: `f(x) = Σₖ πₖ φ(x; μₖ, Σₖ)` with mixing proportions
`πₖ > 0`, `Σ πₖ = 1`. The covariance matrices are constrained by one of six
structures, named by volume, shape and orientation (E = equal across
components, V = varying, I = identity):

| Key | Covariance | Parameters |
|-----|------------|------------|
| EII | `λ I` (spherical, equal volume) | 1 |
| VII | `λₖ I` (spherical, varying volume) | K |
| EEI | `diag(b)` shared (diagonal, equal) | p |
| VVI | `diag(bₖ)` (diagonal, varying) | K p |
| EEE | `Σ` shared (full, equal) | p(p+1)/2 |
| VVV | `Σₖ` (full, varying) | K p(p+1)/2 |

#### Estimation
EM (Dempster, Laird & Rubin 1977). The E-step computes membership
probabilities `zᵢₖ = πₖ φ(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼ φ(xᵢ; μⱼ, Σⱼ)` (on the log
scale with log-sum-exp). The M-step sets `nₖ = Σᵢ zᵢₖ`, `πₖ = nₖ/n`,
`μₖ = Σᵢ zᵢₖ xᵢ / nₖ` and, from the weighted scatter matrices
`Wₖ = Σᵢ zᵢₖ (xᵢ − μₖ)(xᵢ − μₖ)ᵀ` and `W = Σₖ Wₖ`, the closed-form
covariance estimates of Celeux & Govaert (1995): EII `λ = tr W / (n p)`;
VII `λₖ = tr Wₖ / (nₖ p)`; EEI `diag(W)/n`; VVI `diag(Wₖ)/nₖ`; EEE `W/n`;
VVV `Wₖ/nₖ`. An optional ridge is added to every covariance diagonal
(as `reg_covar` in scikit-learn) to keep the estimates positive
definite. Iterations stop when the log-likelihood changes by less than
`tolerance · (1 + |ℓ|)`.

#### Starts
The first start is a hard partition from k-means (k-means++ seeding, ten
starts) or from Ward hierarchical clustering; each further start is a
single seeded k-means++ run. The start with the largest final
log-likelihood is kept. Everything is reproducible from the seed.

#### Choosing a model
`BIC = −2 ℓ + m ln n` (Schwarz 1978), with `m` free parameters:
`K − 1` proportions, `K p` means and the covariance parameters above.
Smaller is better. (Fraley & Raftery report `2ℓ − m ln n`, the same
criterion with the opposite sign.) [`select_gaussian_mixture`] fits every
requested structure and number of components and picks the smallest BIC;
fits that fail (a component collapsing onto too few points, a singular
covariance) are recorded as such, as mclust records them as missing.

Components are numbered by the first row (in data order) whose most
likely component they are, so labels do not depend on the start.

- `enum CovarianceStructure`: Covariance structure of the mixture components (Celeux & Govaert 1995).
- `enum MixtureStart`: How the first EM start partitions the points.
- `struct MixtureOptions`: Settings of one mixture fit.
- `struct GaussianMixture`: A fitted Gaussian mixture.
- `fn fit_gaussian_mixture`: Fit a `K`-component Gaussian mixture by EM from the starts in `options`, keeping the start with the largest log-likelihood.
- `fn fit_gaussian_mixture_from`: Run EM from given membership probabilities `z0` (`n` rows of `K`, e.g.
- `struct MixtureCandidate`: One candidate model of a [`MixtureSelection`].
- `struct MixtureSelection`: Every structure and number of components tried, and the one with the smallest BIC.
- `fn select_gaussian_mixture`: Fit every structure in `structures` with every number of components in `ks`, each with the starts and settings of `base`, and choose the smallest BIC.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/multiple_imputation.rs`

Multiple imputation: `m` completed copies of a data matrix, each with the
missing values drawn from their predictive distribution, so that analyses
repeated on every copy and combined by Rubin's rules
(`stat_inference::pooling`) carry the uncertainty the missing values add.

Data are row vectors (`data[i][j]`) with `NaN` marking a missing value.
A categorical column holds level codes `0, 1, …, L − 1` (see
[`ColumnKind`]). Observed values are never changed.

#### Chained equations
[`chained_equations`] is fully conditional specification (van Buuren &
Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011, "mice: Multivariate imputation by chained
equations in R", *J. Stat. Softw.* 45(3); van Buuren 2018, *Flexible
Imputation of Missing Data*, 2nd ed., §4.5). Each column with missing
values gets its own imputation model given the other columns. Missing
cells start as random draws from their column's observed values; each
iteration then visits the columns in the visit order and redraws the
column's missing cells from its model fitted to the rows where it is
observed, using the current values of its predictors (observed or
imputed). After the last iteration the data are one imputation; `m`
independent chains (seeded `seed`, `seed + 1`, …, run in parallel) give
`m` imputations. Predictors enter the models with an intercept,
continuous columns standardized over the fitting rows and categorical
columns as indicator variables against their first level; predictors
that are constant on the fitting rows are left out.

The models (van Buuren 2018, §3.2–3.6):

* **Bayesian linear regression** ([`bayesian_regression_draw`],
  Algorithm 3.1 of van Buuren 2018; Rubin 1987, p. 167): with
  `V = (XᵀX + κ diag(XᵀX))⁻¹`, `β̂ = V Xᵀy` and residual sum of squares
  `S`, draw `σ̇² = S/g` with `g ~ χ²(n − q)`, then `β̇ = β̂ + σ̇ L z`
  (`V = L Lᵀ`, `z` standard normal), and impute `xβ̇ + σ̇ ε`. As in
  mice, `κ = 0` (plain least squares) unless `XᵀX` is numerically
  singular, when a small ridge is added.
* **Predictive mean matching** (the default for continuous columns;
  Little 1988, "Missing-data adjustments in large surveys", *J. Bus.
  Econ. Stat.* 6; van Buuren 2018, Algorithm 3.3, "type 1" matching):
  draw `β̇` as above; for each missing cell find the `k` observed rows
  (`k = 5` donors by default) whose predicted means `xᵢβ̂` are closest to
  the cell's `xβ̇` ([`pmm_donors`]) and copy the observed value of one
  of them chosen at random. Imputed values are always values that occur
  in the data.
* **Logistic regression** (two-level columns; van Buuren 2018,
  Algorithm 3.4): fit the logistic regression by Newton's method, draw
  `β̇ ~ N(β̂, V)` from its asymptotic covariance, and draw each missing
  level with probability `logit⁻¹(xβ̇)`.
* **Multinomial logit** (three or more levels): the same with a
  baseline-category logit model, drawing `β̇` from its asymptotic normal
  posterior and each level with its fitted probability.

The logistic and multinomial fits add a small ridge penalty (0.001 on
the standardized slopes), which keeps them finite when a predictor
separates the levels perfectly, the problem White, Daniel & Royston
(2010, *Comput. Stat. Data Anal.* 54) solve by augmenting the data.

#### Joint multivariate normal model
[`normal_data_augmentation`] draws from the posterior predictive
distribution of a multivariate normal model by data augmentation
(Tanner & Wong 1987, *JASA* 82; Schafer 1997, *Analysis of Incomplete
Multivariate Data*, §5.4), each chain starting from the maximum
likelihood estimates of the EM algorithm ([`crate::imputation::em_normal`]).
Each iteration alternates

* the I-step: draw every row's missing part from
  `N(μ_M + Σ_MO Σ_OO⁻¹ (x_O − μ_O), Σ_MM − Σ_MO Σ_OO⁻¹ Σ_OM)`, and
* the P-step: with the completed data's mean `x̄` and cross-product
  matrix `A = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(xᵢ − x̄)ᵀ`, draw `Σ ~ W⁻¹(n − 1, A)` and then
  `μ ~ N(x̄, Σ/n)`, the posterior under the noninformative prior
  `π(μ, Σ) ∝ |Σ|^{−(p+1)/2}` (Schafer 1997, §5.4.2). The inverse
  Wishart draw uses Bartlett's decomposition (Smith & Hocking 1972,
  *Appl. Stat.* 21).

The imputation is the I-step after the last iteration.

#### Convergence
Both engines record, for every chain, iteration and column with missing
values, the mean and standard deviation of the column's imputed values
([`Chains`]); chains that mix well wander over the same range with no
trend (van Buuren 2018, §6.5).

- `enum ColumnKind`: What a column holds.
- `enum FcsMethod`: How [`chained_equations`] imputes one column.
- `fn default_methods`: The default method for each column: none without missing values, predictive mean matching for continuous columns, logistic regression for two levels and the multinomial logit for more (van Buuren 2018, §4.5.2).
- `struct FcsOptions`: Settings of [`chained_equations`].
- `struct Chains`: Means and standard deviations of the imputed values of each column, per chain and iteration (`NaN` for columns with no imputed values).
- `struct MultipleImputation`: The result of a multiple imputation.
- `struct RegressionDraw`: The pieces of a Bayesian linear regression draw.
- `fn bayesian_regression_draw`: The Bayesian linear regression draw of van Buuren (2018, Algorithm 3.1) given its random numbers: `chi_square` is the `χ²(n − q)` draw `g` and `z` the `q` standard normal draws.
- `fn pmm_donors`: The `k` observed rows whose predicted means `fitted_observed[i]` are nearest `target` (ties to the earlier row), nearest first.
- `fn chained_equations`: Multiple imputation by chained equations (see the [module documentation](self)).
- `struct DataAugmentationOptions`: Settings of [`normal_data_augmentation`].
- `fn normal_data_augmentation`: Multiple imputation under a multivariate normal model by data augmentation (see the [module documentation](self)).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/outliers.rs`

Multivariate outlier distances of each observation from the centre of
the others.

With mean `x̄` and covariance `S` (divisor `n − 1`) of `n` observations
on `p` variables:

* the **Mahalanobis distance** (Mahalanobis 1936) of row `i` is
  `dᵢ = √((xᵢ − x̄)ᵀ S⁻¹ (xᵢ − x̄))`;
* **Hotelling's T²** of row `i` is `dᵢ²`. For multivariate normal data,
  `n T² / (n − 1)²` follows a Beta(p/2, (n − p − 1)/2) distribution
  (Gnanadesikan & Kettenring, *Biometrics* 28, 1972; Tracy, Young &
  Mason, *J. Quality Technology* 24(2), 1992), so the upper-α reference
  limit is `(n − 1)²/n · B_{1−α}(p/2, (n − p − 1)/2)`, and the
  Mahalanobis limit is its square root;
* the **jackknifed distance** `d₍ᵢ₎` measures row `i` from the mean and
  covariance of the other `n − 1` rows, so an outlier cannot mask itself
  by pulling the estimates towards it. Leaving one row out changes the
  estimates by a rank-one update, which gives the closed form
  `d₍ᵢ₎² = n²(n − 2) dᵢ² / ((n − 1)((n − 1)² − n dᵢ²))`
  (Sherman–Morrison; Penny, *Applied Statistics* 45(1), 1996). Row `i`
  is then a new observation against a sample of `m = n − 1`, so
  `d₍ᵢ₎² ~ p(m + 1)(m − 1)/(m(m − p)) · F(p, m − p)`, and the reference
  limit is the square root of that quantity's upper-α point.

- `struct OutlierDistances`: Distances of every observation.
- `struct DistanceLimits`: Upper reference limits of the three distances at one α.
- `fn outlier_distances`: Distances of the observations `rows` (each `p` finite values).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/pca.rs`

Principal component analysis via the singular value decomposition.

For an `n × p` data matrix the columns are centred (and, for a
correlation-based analysis, divided by their standard deviations) to give
`Z`. With the thin SVD `Z = U Σ Vᵀ` ([`stat_core::svd()`]):

* the **eigenvalues** (component variances) are `λₖ = σₖ² / (n − 1)`, the
  eigenvalues of the covariance or correlation matrix `ZᵀZ / (n − 1)`;
* the **eigenvectors** (loadings, unit length) are the columns of `V`;
* the **scores** are `Z V = U Σ`, uncorrelated with variances `λₖ`;
* the **proportion of variance** is `λₖ / Σλ`.

Working from the SVD of `Z` rather than forming the covariance matrix avoids
squaring its condition number (Jolliffe, *Principal Component Analysis*, 2nd
ed., §3.5). Each eigenvector's sign is chosen so that its largest-magnitude
element is positive. For a correlation analysis, `vⱼₖ √λₖ` is the
correlation between variable `j` and component `k`.

- `struct Pca`: Result of a principal component analysis.
- `fn principal_components`: Principal components of the columns of `x` (`n` observations × `p` variables).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/pcoa.rs`

Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA, metric multidimensional scaling of
any distance matrix; Gower 1966, “Some distance properties of latent
root and vector methods used in multivariate analysis”, *Biometrika* 53).

From distances `dᵢⱼ` form `A = [−½ dᵢⱼ²]` and Gower's centred matrix
`Δ₁ = J A J` with `J = I − 11ᵀ/n`. Its eigenvalues `λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ …` and
unit eigenvectors `vₖ` give the coordinates `√λₖ vₖ` on every axis with
`λₖ > 0`. One eigenvalue always belongs to the constant vector `1` and
is zero; the other `n − 1` are reported. When the distances are not
Euclidean some eigenvalues are negative: the axes they would define are
imaginary and carry no coordinates.

Two classical corrections add a constant to the distances so that every
eigenvalue becomes non-negative (Legendre & Legendre 2012, *Numerical
Ecology*, 3rd ed., §9.3.4; Legendre & Anderson 1999, *Ecological
Monographs* 69):

* **Lingoes** (1971): `d′ᵢⱼ = √(dᵢⱼ² + 2c)` for `i ≠ j`, with
  `c = |λₘᵢₙ|` the magnitude of the most negative eigenvalue of `Δ₁`;
* **Cailliez** (1983, “The analytical solution of the additive constant
  problem”, *Psychometrika* 48): `d′ᵢⱼ = dᵢⱼ + c` for `i ≠ j`, with `c`
  the largest (real) eigenvalue of the `2n × 2n` matrix
  `[[0, 2Δ₁], [−I, −4Δ₂]]`, where `Δ₂ = J [−½ dᵢⱼ] J`.

The corrected matrix is analysed in the same way; its eigenvalues
include one more zero. A correction is only applied when there is a
negative eigenvalue.

Eigenvalues within `10⁻¹⁰ · max |λ|` of zero are set to zero. The
relative eigenvalues are `λₖ / Σ λ⁺` (the sum over positive eigenvalues),
and the broken-stick expectations for `k` positive axes are
`bⱼ = (1/k) Σᵢ₌ⱼᵏ 1/i` (Frontier 1976; Jackson 1993, *Ecology* 74).
Eigenvector signs are arbitrary: each axis is flipped so that its
largest absolute coordinate is positive.

The Cailliez constant needs eigenvalues of a non-symmetric matrix; they
are found by Householder reduction to Hessenberg form and the shifted
double-step QR algorithm (Wilkinson & Reinsch 1971, *Handbook for
Automatic Computation* vol. II, procedures `orthes` and `hqr`, as in the
public-domain JAMA translation).

- `enum NegativeCorrection`: Correction for negative eigenvalues of non-Euclidean distances.
- `struct PrincipalCoordinates`: A principal coordinates solution.
- `fn principal_coordinates`: Principal coordinates of the distances `d`, with an optional correction for negative eigenvalues, keeping at most `max_axes` axes.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/reliability.rs`

Reliability of a multi-item scale (item analysis).

For `k` items scored by `n` respondents, with item variances `sⱼ²`,
total-score variance `s_T²` (the total is the sum of the items) and mean
inter-item correlation `r̄`:

* **Cronbach's alpha** (Cronbach, *Psychometrika* 16, 1951):
  `α = k/(k − 1) · (1 − Σ sⱼ² / s_T²)`;
* **standardized alpha** — alpha of the items rescaled to unit variance:
  `α_std = k r̄ / (1 + (k − 1) r̄)` (the Spearman–Brown form);
* **Feldt's interval** (Feldt, *Psychometrika* 30, 1965): under the
  usual normal model `(1 − α)/(1 − α̂)` follows `F(n − 1, (n − 1)(k − 1))`,
  so a `γ` interval is
  `[1 − (1 − α̂) F_{(1+γ)/2}, 1 − (1 − α̂) F_{(1−γ)/2}]`;
* per item: mean and standard deviation; the **item–total correlation**
  (with the total including the item); the **item–rest correlation**
  (with the total of the other items, the "corrected" item–total
  correlation, which does not count the item's correlation with itself);
  and alpha (raw and standardized) of the scale with that item deleted.

Variances use the divisor `n − 1`; only respondents with every item
answered take part (listwise). Items to be reverse-scored are flipped by
the caller before analysis.

- `struct ItemStatistics`: Statistics of one item.
- `struct ItemAnalysis`: Reliability of a scale.
- `fn feldt_interval`: Feldt's (1965) interval for coefficient alpha `alpha` from `n` respondents and `k` items, at confidence `level`.
- `fn item_analysis`: Item analysis of `rows` (one row per respondent, one value per item).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/spd.rs`

Small dense helpers for symmetric positive-definite matrices (covariance
and correlation matrices of a few dozen variables): sample moments, the
Cholesky factor `A = L Lᵀ`, quadratic forms `dᵀ A⁻¹ d` by one triangular
solve, and the inverse. Matrices are row vectors (`Vec<Vec<f64>>`).

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/sym_eigen.rs`

Eigen-decomposition of a real symmetric matrix by Householder reduction
to tridiagonal form followed by the implicit QL algorithm (Wilkinson &
Reinsch 1971, *Handbook for Automatic Computation* vol. II, procedures
`tred2` and `tql2`; the formulation follows the public-domain JAMA
translation). It costs about `(4/3 + 3) n³` flops regardless of the
spectrum, so classical scaling of a few thousand objects stays quick,
where cyclic Jacobi sweeps would take many times longer.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/tsne.rs`

t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE; van der Maaten &
Hinton 2008, "Visualizing data using t-SNE", *JMLR* 9), with exact
gradients or the Barnes–Hut approximation (van der Maaten 2014,
"Accelerating t-SNE using tree-based algorithms", *JMLR* 15).

#### Affinities
For each object `i`, conditional probabilities
`p_{j|i} = exp(−β_i δᵢⱼ²) / Σ_{k≠i} exp(−β_i δᵢₖ²)` with the precision
`β_i` found by bisection so that the perplexity `2^{H(P_i)}` (equivalently
`exp` of the entropy in nats) equals the requested value. The joint
affinities are `pᵢⱼ = (p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}) / (2n)`. The Barnes–Hut
variant uses only the `⌊3·perplexity⌋` nearest neighbours of each object
(exact search), giving a sparse `P`.

#### Embedding
Low-dimensional similarities use a Student t kernel with one degree of
freedom: `wᵢⱼ = (1 + ‖yᵢ − yⱼ‖²)⁻¹`, `qᵢⱼ = wᵢⱼ / Z`, `Z = Σ_{k≠l} w_{kl}`.
The cost is `KL(P‖Q) = Σ pᵢⱼ ln(pᵢⱼ/qᵢⱼ)` with gradient
`∂C/∂yᵢ = 4 Σⱼ (pᵢⱼ − qᵢⱼ) wᵢⱼ (yᵢ − yⱼ)`. Barnes–Hut splits it into an
attractive part over the sparse `P` and a repulsive part
`Σⱼ wᵢⱼ² (yᵢ − yⱼ) / Z` summarised by a quadtree: a cell of width `r` at
distance `d` whose ratio `r/d` is below `θ` acts as one point at its
centre of mass (two-dimensional embeddings only).

Gradient descent with momentum and per-coordinate adaptive gains
(Jacobs 1988): gains grow by 0.2 when the gradient changes sign against
the previous update and shrink by ×0.8 otherwise (minimum 0.01). The
first iterations multiply `P` by the early exaggeration factor (12) with
momentum 0.5; momentum is 0.8 afterwards. The learning rate defaults to
`max(n / exaggeration / 4, 50)` (Belkina et al. 2019, *Nature
Communications* 10). The start is the principal component (or, for a
distance matrix, classical scaling) layout scaled to standard deviation
10⁻⁴ on its first axis, or seeded N(0, 10⁻⁴) noise. Everything is
reproducible from the seed.

- `enum TsneMethod`: How the gradient is computed.
- `const EXACT_LIMIT`: Largest number of objects for which [`TsneOptions::method`] `None` chooses the exact gradient.
- `struct TsneOptions`: Settings of a t-SNE embedding.
- `struct Tsne`: A t-SNE embedding.
- `type SparseAffinities`: Affinities as sparse symmetric rows `(j, pᵢⱼ)`, summing to 1 overall.
- `fn calibrate`: Conditional probabilities `p_{j|i}` over the given squared distances (the other objects only) with perplexity `perplexity`: the precision β is bisected (on the log scale) until the entropy is within 1e-10 of `ln perplexity`.
- `fn joint_probabilities`: Dense joint affinities `pᵢⱼ` (`n × n`, zero diagonal, summing to 1).
- `fn sparse_joint_probabilities`: Sparse joint affinities from each object's `min(n − 1, ⌊3·perplexity⌋ + 1)` nearest neighbours (as scikit-learn's Barnes–Hut t-SNE), symmetrized and normalized to sum 1.
- `fn exact_gradient`: `KL(P‖Q)` and its exact gradient for affinities `p` (dense) at configuration `y`.
- `fn barnes_hut_gradient`: Barnes–Hut gradient for sparse affinities `p` at the two-dimensional configuration `y`, with the normalization `Z` estimated by the tree.
- `fn tsne`: Embed `proximity` by t-SNE.

### `crates/stat-multivariate/src/umap.rs`

Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP; McInnes, Healy &
Melville 2018, "UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for
Dimension Reduction", arXiv:1802.03426).

#### Fuzzy neighbour graph
Each object's `k` nearest neighbours (counting itself, as the reference
implementation does; exact search) define a local fuzzy set: with `ρᵢ`
the distance to the nearest other object and `σᵢ` chosen by bisection so
that `Σ_{j=1}^{k−1} exp(−max(0, dᵢⱼ − ρᵢ)/σᵢ) = log₂ k`, the membership
of the edge `i → j` is `exp(−max(0, dᵢⱼ − ρᵢ)/σᵢ)` (`σᵢ` is kept above
10⁻³ times the mean neighbour distance). The local sets are combined by
the fuzzy union `W = A + Aᵀ − A ∘ Aᵀ`.

#### Layout
The low-dimensional similarity is `(1 + a‖yᵢ − yⱼ‖^{2b})⁻¹`, with `a`
and `b` fitted by least squares to the curve that is 1 up to `min_dist`
and `exp(−(x − min_dist)/spread)` beyond it (300 points on
`[0, 3·spread]`). The start is the spectral layout: eigenvectors of the
largest non-trivial eigenvalues of `D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}` (the smallest of
the normalized graph Laplacian), scaled to a maximum absolute coordinate
of 10 with N(0, 10⁻⁴²) noise, then rescaled to `[0, 10]` per axis; or
seeded uniform noise on `[−10, 10]`. The cross-entropy between the two
fuzzy sets is minimized by stochastic gradient descent: edge `(i, j)` is
sampled every `max W / wᵢⱼ` epochs (edges below `max W / epochs` are
dropped), pulling the pair together with gradient coefficient
`−2ab d^{2(b−1)} / (1 + a d^{2b})`; each sample also pushes `i` away
from `negative_sample_rate` objects drawn at random, with coefficient
`2b / ((0.001 + d²)(1 + a d^{2b}))`. Gradient components are clipped to
±4 and the learning rate falls linearly from 1 to 0. Reproducible from
the seed (single-threaded SGD).

- `struct UmapOptions`: Settings of a UMAP embedding.
- `struct Umap`: A UMAP embedding.
- `struct FuzzyGraph`: The fuzzy neighbour graph: symmetric sparse rows `(j, wᵢⱼ)` and each object's `ρᵢ` and `σᵢ`.
- `fn smooth_distances`: `ρ` and `σ` of one object from its distances to its `k − 1` nearest other objects (nearest first), so that the memberships sum to `log₂ k`.
- `fn fuzzy_graph`: The fuzzy neighbour graph of `proximity` with neighbourhood size `k` (counting each object itself).
- `fn curve_parameters`: Fit `a`, `b` of `(1 + a x^{2b})⁻¹` to the target curve (Gauss–Newton with step halving from `a = b = 1`).
- `fn umap`: Embed `proximity` by UMAP.

Test files: `latent_class/tests.rs`, `mds/tests.rs`, `mixture/tests.rs`, `multiple_imputation/tests.rs`, `tsne/tests.rs`, `umap/tests.rs`.

Integration tests: `distance_reference.rs`, `imputation_reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-predictive` (`crates/stat-predictive`)

Predictive modelling: Gaussian processes and sequential design by expected improvement, elastic net (lasso and ridge), classification and regression trees, random forests, boosted trees, multivariate adaptive regression splines, partial least squares, support vector machines, neural networks, validation roles and fit measures.

Dependencies: `rayon`, `stat-core`.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/acquisition.rs`

Choosing the next runs of an experiment from Gaussian-process models
([`crate::gaussian_process`]) of its responses: sequential design by
expected improvement or an upper confidence bound.

**Goals.** Each response is maximized, minimized, or brought to a target
`T`. Its *score* is `y`, `−y` or `−|y − T|`, so the best run has the
largest score.

**Expected improvement** (Jones, Schonlau & Welch, "Efficient global
optimization of expensive black-box functions", *J. Global Optimization*
13, 1998, eq. 15). With the predicted mean `μ` and standard deviation `σ`
of the latent response at a point and the best observed value `y*`
(largest when maximizing), `z = (μ − y*)/σ` and

```text
EI = (μ − y*) Φ(z) + σ φ(z)
```

(mirrored when minimizing). For a target, the improvement is
`max(0, b − |Y − T|)` with `b` the smallest observed distance from the
target; integrating it against `Y ~ N(μ, σ²)` over `(T − b, T + b)` gives
a closed form in Φ and φ (see [`expected_improvement`]).

**Upper confidence bound** (Srinivas, Krause, Kakade & Seeger, "Gaussian
process optimization in the bandit setting", *ICML* 2010): the most
optimistic score within `κ` standard deviations, `μ + κσ` when
maximizing, `−(μ − κσ)` when minimizing, `−max(0, |μ − T| − κσ)` for a
target.

**Several responses** are combined by an overall desirability `D(y₁, …)`
supplied by the caller (Derringer & Suich 1980). Its expected improvement
over the best observed `D*` is estimated by Monte Carlo over independent
draws of the responses' predictive distributions, with the same draws at
every point (common random numbers, so the criterion is a smooth
function of the point): the multivariate expected-improvement criterion
of Henkenjohann & Kunert ("An efficient sequential optimization approach
based on the multivariate expected improvement criterion", *Quality
Engineering* 19, 2007). The upper confidence bound uses each response's
most favourable value within `κ` standard deviations (for a target, the
value in `μ ± κσ` nearest it).

**Batches** use the constant liar (Ginsbourger, Le Riche & Carraro,
"Kriging is well-suited to parallelize optimization", 2010): after a
point is chosen, each model is conditioned on a pretend observation
there equal to the response at the best run so far, with the same
hyperparameters, and the next point is chosen; the lie removes the
chosen point's improvement so the next one goes elsewhere. Runs already
in the table but not yet measured (*pending*) are lied about first.

**Search.** Continuous factors live in the unit cube, cut by a
feasibility test (linear constraints); categorical factors take one of
their levels and enter the models as one 0/1 indicator per level. The
criterion is evaluated at Latin-hypercube candidates (rejecting
infeasible ones) with random levels; the best few are polished by
Nelder–Mead in the continuous factors and by trying each other level of
each categorical factor. Where expected improvement underflows to zero
everywhere the point of largest predictive spread is taken.

- `enum Goal`: What to do with a response.
- `fn expected_improvement`: Expected improvement of `Y ~ N(mean, sd²)` over the best observed value `best` (the response value with the best score) for `goal`.
- `fn upper_confidence_bound`: The most optimistic score of `N(mean, sd²)` within `kappa` standard deviations.
- `enum AcquisitionCriterion`: The criterion that ranks candidate runs.
- `enum Objective`: What the runs should achieve.
- `struct Candidate`: A run: continuous settings in `[0, 1]` and a level index per categorical factor.
- `struct SearchSpace`: The factors' space.
- `struct ProposalOptions`: Settings of a proposal.
- `struct Proposal`: A proposed run.
- `fn propose_batch`: Choose the next `options.batch` runs.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/boost.rs`

Gradient-boosted trees.

**Model.** The prediction is a sum of small regression trees fitted one
after another, each to the gradient of the loss at the current fit
(Friedman, "Greedy function approximation: a gradient boosting machine",
*Annals of Statistics* 29, 2001), shrunk by a learning rate ν:
`F_m(x) = F_{m−1}(x) + ν f_m(x)`. A categorical response with two classes
fits one score per row (logistic loss, `p = 1/(1 + e^{−F})`); with K > 2
classes, one score per class (multinomial loss, softmax probabilities)
and one tree per class per round.

**Trees.** Each tree is grown level by level to a maximum depth with
second-order (Newton) split gains and leaf values, regularized by an L2
penalty λ on the leaf values (Chen & Guestrin, "XGBoost", *KDD* 2016):
with G and H the sums of the loss's gradients and Hessians over a node,
a leaf's value is `−G/(H + λ)` and a split's gain
`G_L²/(H_L + λ) + G_R²/(H_R + λ) − G²/(H + λ)`. Continuous predictors
are binned at their training-row quantiles (at most `bins` thresholds),
so each split scans a histogram instead of sorted values; categorical
predictors split into two groups of levels after ordering the levels by
`G/(H + λ)`. Missing values go the way that gains more (or, when a node
has none, the larger side).

**Losses.** Squared error (gradient `F − y`, Hessian 1), absolute error
(gradient `sign(F − y)`; leaf values are then the median residual of
the leaf's rows, as in Friedman's LAD-TreeBoost), logistic and
multinomial (gradient `p − y`, Hessian `p(1 − p)`). The starting score
is the mean, the median, the log-odds or the log class shares.

**Subsampling and early stopping.** Each round may use a random share of
the training rows (stochastic gradient boosting; Friedman,
*Computational Statistics & Data Analysis* 38, 2002). When validation
rows are given, boosting stops once their loss has not improved for a
set number of rounds, and the model keeps the best round.

- `enum RegressionLoss`: Loss minimized for a continuous response.
- `struct BoostOptions`: Boosting settings.
- `enum BoostRule`: How a split sends rows.
- `struct BoostSplit`: A split of a boosted tree's node.
- `struct BoostNode`: A node of a boosted tree.
- `struct BoostTree`: One regression tree of a boosted model.
- `enum BoostLoss`: The loss a model minimizes.
- `struct Boosted`: A fitted boosted model.
- `fn fit_boosted`: Fit a boosted model on the `train` rows; `valid` rows (possibly none) drive early stopping.
- `fn cross_validate_rounds`: Mean held-out loss after each round, averaged over k folds of `train` (each fold's model fitted without early stopping on the other folds), and the round with the smallest loss.
- `fn loss_curve`: Per-round loss of `model` on `rows`, for a curve of a fitted model.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/elastic_net.rs`

Elastic net regression (lasso, ridge and mixtures) by coordinate descent,
with the penalty chosen by k-fold cross-validation.

#### Objective
With predictors standardized to mean 0 and variance 1 (divisor `n`), the
fit minimizes

```text
(1 / 2n) Σ (yᵢ − β₀ − zᵢᵀβ)²  +  λ [ α Σ|βⱼ| + (1 − α)/2 Σ βⱼ² ]
```

— the lasso for `α = 1` (Tibshirani 1996), ridge regression for `α = 0`
(Hoerl & Kennard 1970), and the elastic net in between (Zou & Hastie 2005).
Coefficients are reported on the original scale (`βⱼ / sdⱼ`, intercept
adjusted) and also on the standardized scale, where they are comparable.

#### Algorithm
Cyclic coordinate descent with warm starts along a decreasing path of
`λ` values (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, "Regularization paths for
generalized linear models via coordinate descent", *J. Stat. Software* 33):
each coefficient is updated in turn by
`βⱼ ← S(ρⱼ, λα) / (1 + λ(1 − α))`, `ρⱼ = (1/n) Σ zᵢⱼ rᵢ + βⱼ` (partial
residual correlation), `S` the soft-threshold, until the largest change is
below `10⁻¹⁰` of the response's spread. The path starts at the smallest `λ` that
sets every coefficient to zero, `λ_max = max|zⱼᵀ(y − ȳ)| / (n α)` (with
`α` floored at 0.001 for ridge), and descends log-linearly to
`λ_max · ε` (`ε = 10⁻⁴` if `n > p`, else `10⁻²`).

#### Choosing λ
The rows are split into `k` folds by a seeded shuffle; each fold's
prediction error is computed from a path fitted to the other folds. The
report gives `λ_min` (smallest mean squared error) and `λ_1SE`, the largest
`λ` whose error is within one standard error of the minimum — a simpler
model with comparable accuracy (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, *The Elements
of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., §7.10). A predictor that is constant
within a fold's training rows carries no information there and keeps a
zero coefficient on that fold's path.

- `struct ElasticNetOptions`: Options for [`fit_elastic_net`].
- `struct ElasticNetPath`: The fitted path and cross-validation results.
- `fn fit_elastic_net`: Fit the elastic net path of `y` on the columns of `x`, with cross-validation.
- `fn fit_elastic_net_at`: Fit at a single λ (standardized coefficients, original-scale intercept and coefficients).

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/forest.rs`

Random forests (Breiman, *Machine Learning* 45, 2001): many unpruned
trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample of the rows and choosing each
split from a random subset of the predictors, whose predictions are
averaged (class probabilities for classification, means for regression).

* **Out-of-bag (OOB) estimates.** About 37% of the rows are left out of
  each bootstrap sample. A row's OOB prediction averages only the trees
  that did not see it, so OOB error is an honest estimate of error on new
  data without holding rows back; [`Forest::oob_error_curve`] tracks it as
  trees are added.
* **Permutation importance.** For each tree, the increase in OOB error
  when one predictor's values are shuffled among that tree's OOB rows,
  averaged over trees (Breiman 2001, §10), with its standard error.
* **Impurity importance.** The impurity reduction of every split on the
  predictor, summed over each tree and averaged over trees. It favours
  predictors with many distinct values (Strobl et al., *BMC
  Bioinformatics* 8, 2007), which permutation importance does not.

Trees are grown in parallel. Every tree has its own seed derived from the
forest's, so results do not depend on the number of threads.

- `struct ForestOptions`: Settings of a random forest.
- `struct Forest`: A fitted random forest.
- `fn fit_forest`: Grow a random forest on `rows` (positions in `features` and `target`).

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/gaussian_process.rs`

Gaussian-process regression (Rasmussen & Williams, *Gaussian Processes
for Machine Learning*, 2006, ch. 2 and 5; Santner, Williams & Notz, *The
Design and Analysis of Computer Experiments*, 2nd ed., 2018, ch. 3).

**Model.** The response, standardized to mean 0 and (population)
standard deviation 1, is a zero-mean Gaussian process plus independent
noise:

```text
y = f(x) + ε,   f ~ GP(0, σ_f² r(x, x′)),   ε ~ N(0, σ_n²)
```

with an anisotropic ("automatic relevance") correlation over the scaled
distances `d_j = (x_j − x′_j)² / ℓ_j²`, one length scale `ℓ_j` per input:

* squared exponential: `r = exp(−½ Σ d_j)`;
* Matérn 5/2: with `ρ = √(Σ d_j)`, `r = (1 + √5 ρ + 5ρ²/3) exp(−√5 ρ)`.

The noise variance `σ_n²` (the *nugget*) is estimated, or fixed (a small
fixed nugget makes the fit interpolate a deterministic simulator). A
jitter of 10⁻¹⁰ is always added to the diagonal.

**Fitting.** The hyperparameters `θ = (ln σ_f², ln ℓ_1, …, ln ℓ_d,
ln σ_n²)` maximize the log marginal likelihood (R&W eq. 2.30)

```text
ln p(y | θ) = −½ yᵀ K⁻¹ y − ½ ln |K| − (n/2) ln 2π
```

whose gradient is `½ tr((ααᵀ − K⁻¹) ∂K/∂θ_k)` with `α = K⁻¹ y` (R&W eq.
5.9). Each start runs a projected BFGS search inside the bounds
`σ_f² ∈ [10⁻³, 10³]`, `ℓ_j ∈ [10⁻³, 10³]`, `σ_n² ∈ [10⁻⁸, 10]`; the first
start is `σ_f² = 1`, `ℓ_j = ½`, `σ_n² = 0.01`, the others are spread over
a Latin hypercube of typical values. The best start is kept. The
formulation (standardized response, these bounds) is the one of
scikit-learn's `GaussianProcessRegressor(normalize_y=True)` with a
constant × correlation + white-noise kernel, which the tests check
against. Inputs are best scaled to the unit cube first (the app does).

**Prediction.** At `x*`, with `k*` the covariances with the training
inputs and `K = LLᵀ`, the mean is `k*ᵀ α` and the variance of the latent
`f(x*)` is `σ_f² − |L⁻¹ k*|²` (R&W eq. 2.25–2.26), returned in the
response's units; a new observation's variance adds `σ_n²`.
Leave-one-out predictions come in closed form from `K⁻¹` (R&W eq. 5.12):
`μ₋ᵢ = yᵢ − [K⁻¹y]ᵢ / [K⁻¹]ᵢᵢ`, `σ²₋ᵢ = 1 / [K⁻¹]ᵢᵢ`.

**Failure modes.** Fewer than two rows, inputs of differing lengths,
non-finite values, more than 2,000 rows, or a covariance matrix that is
not positive definite at every start.

- `const MAX_ROWS`: Most training rows (the fit costs O(n³) per likelihood evaluation).
- `const JITTER`: Diagonal jitter added to every covariance matrix.
- `const SIGNAL_BOUNDS`: Bounds of `σ_f²` (standardized response).
- `const LENGTH_BOUNDS`: Bounds of each length scale.
- `const NUGGET_BOUNDS`: Bounds of an estimated nugget `σ_n²` (standardized response).
- `enum CovarianceKernel`: The correlation function of a Gaussian process.
- `enum Nugget`: How the nugget (noise variance) is set.
- `struct GpOptions`: Settings of a fit.
- `struct GpHyperparameters`: Hyperparameters on their natural scale (standardized response).
- `struct GaussianProcess`: A fitted Gaussian process.
- `fn log_marginal_likelihood`: Log marginal likelihood of the standardized response `y` at `θ` (with the nugget fixed at `noise` when `θ` holds none) and its gradient with respect to `θ`, or `None` when `K` is not positive definite.
- `fn fit_gaussian_process`: Fit a Gaussian process to `x` (rows of inputs, best scaled to the unit cube) and `y` by maximum likelihood (see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/lib.rs`

#### stat-predictive

Predictive modelling:

* [`acquisition`]: the next runs of an experiment by expected improvement
  or an upper confidence bound, in batches by the constant liar;
* [`boost`]: gradient-boosted trees (squared, absolute, logistic and
  multinomial losses; histogram splits, Newton leaves, subsampling and
  early stopping);
* [`elastic_net`]: lasso, ridge and elastic net regression by coordinate
  descent along a path of penalties, the penalty chosen by k-fold
  cross-validation;
* [`gaussian_process`]: Gaussian-process regression (squared-exponential
  and Matérn 5/2 kernels with one length scale per input, nugget,
  maximum likelihood from several starts);
* [`mars`]: multivariate adaptive regression splines (forward pass of
  hinge pairs and their products, backward pruning by GCV or held-out
  rows);
* [`neural`]: fully connected neural networks with one or two hidden
  layers (L-BFGS or Adam, weight decay, several random starts);
* [`pls`]: partial least squares regression (NIPALS and SIMPLS) with
  cross-validated PRESS and VIP scores;
* [`svm`]: support vector classification and ε-regression by SMO
  (linear, radial basis and polynomial kernels; one-against-one classes;
  Platt probabilities with pairwise coupling; grid tuning);
* [`tree`]: classification and regression trees with surrogate splits
  and cost-complexity pruning;
* [`forest`]: random forests with out-of-bag error and permutation and
  impurity importance;
* [`validation`]: training / validation / test roles and k-fold
  assignments;
* [`measures`]: fit measures (RMSE, MAE, R², misclassification, log loss,
  AUC, confusion matrix) and ROC curves.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/mars.rs`

Multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS).

**Model** (Friedman, "Multivariate adaptive regression splines",
*Annals of Statistics* 19(1), 1991). The prediction is a linear
combination `ŷ = b₀ + Σ_m b_m B_m(x)` of basis functions, each a product
of factors on distinct predictors:

* a *hinge* `max(0, x − t)` (right) or `max(0, t − x)` (left) with knot
  `t` at an observed value of a continuous predictor;
* a *linear* factor `x`, for predictors declared to enter linearly;
* a *level indicator* `1{x = level}` of a categorical predictor. A
  predictor with `L` levels gives `L − 1` indicators (every level but
  the first; the first is the reference, like treatment contrasts), each
  treated as a candidate variable of its own. Friedman's (1991, §3.7)
  alternative, factors on level *subsets*, is not used: indicators span
  the same functions once enough of them enter, and keep the formula
  readable.

**Forward pass** (Friedman's Algorithm 2). Starting from the intercept,
each step tries every *parent* term `B_p` of degree below the maximum
interaction degree, every variable not already in it, and every allowed
knot `t`, and adds the reflected pair `B_p · max(0, x − t)`,
`B_p · max(0, t − x)` (or the single term `B_p · x` or
`B_p · 1{x = level}`) that most reduces the residual sum of squares.
Since `max(0, x − t) − max(0, t − x) = x − t`, the pair spans the same
space as `B_p · x` and the right hinge, so the reduction for every knot
follows from running sums over the parent's cases sorted by `x`
(Friedman's fast update, eq. 52): `O(n·M)` per parent and variable. A
new term already in the span of the model (for example the left hinge
when the predictor has a pair at another knot) is dropped, so a step
may add one term. The pass stops when
(i) another step would exceed the maximum number of terms (each pair
step counts two, even when one of the pair is dropped; a single-term
step counts one), (ii) the best step raises R² by less than the
threshold (default 0.001), (iii) R² reaches 1 − threshold, (iv) the
generalized R², `1 − GCV/GCV(intercept only)`, falls below −10, or (v)
no step reduces the residual sum of squares.

**Knots.** For a parent with `N_m` nonzero cases among `p` candidate
variables, knots are placed at the sorted values leaving at least
`L_e = ⌊3 − log₂(α/p)⌋` cases at each end (end span, eq. 45) and
every `L = ⌊−log₂(−ln(1 − α)/(p N_m)) / 2.5⌋` cases in between
(minimum span, eq. 43), with `α = 0.05`; both at least 1. Either can be
set instead.

**Backward pass.** From the forward model, terms are deleted one at a
time, each time the one whose removal increases the residual sum of
squares least (the intercept stays), giving the best subset of each
size. The size is chosen by the smallest generalized cross-validation
criterion (Friedman eq. 30, after Craven & Wahba)
`GCV = RSS / (n (1 − C/n)²)`, `C = k + d (k − 1)/2` for `k` terms, so
`d` (default 2 for additive models, 3 with interactions) is charged per
knot (a pair of terms); `GCV = ∞` once `C ≥ n`. Alternatively the size
is chosen on held-out (validation) rows ([`MarsFit::validation_errors`],
[`MarsFit::select`]).

**Variable importance** over the subsets of size 2 up to the selected
size: the number of subsets that use a predictor, and the sums of the
decreases in GCV and in RSS from the subset one term smaller over the
subsets that use it.

Least squares uses a modified Gram–Schmidt basis with
re-orthogonalization (`X = QR` on the fitting rows), so any subset's
fit is a small `M × k` problem in `R` and `Qᵀy`.

- `enum Direction`: Which side of the knot a hinge is nonzero on.
- `enum Factor`: One factor of a basis function.
- `struct BasisFunction`: A basis function: the product of its factors (the intercept has none).
- `struct MarsOptions`: Settings of [`fit_mars`].
- `enum StopReason`: Why the forward pass stopped.
- `struct ForwardStep`: One step of the forward pass.
- `struct Subset`: The best subset of one size found by the backward pass.
- `struct MarsFit`: A fitted MARS model.
- `fn gcv`: The generalized cross-validation criterion of `k` terms with residual sum of squares `rss` on `n` rows and penalty `d` per knot.
- `fn friedman_min_span`: Friedman's minimum span (eq.
- `fn friedman_end_span`: Friedman's end span (eq.
- `fn fit_mars`: Fit a MARS model of `y` on `features` over `rows` (rows missing the response or any predictor are skipped).
- `struct Importance`: Importance of one predictor (see [`MarsFit::importance`]).

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/measures.rs`

Standard measures of how well predictions match observed responses.

**Continuous responses** ([`ContinuousFit`]): root mean square error
`√(Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²/n)`, mean absolute error `Σ|yᵢ − ŷᵢ|/n`, and
`R² = 1 − Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² / Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²` with `ȳ` the mean of the rows
measured (so R² can be negative on held-out rows that the model predicts
worse than their own mean).

**Categorical responses** ([`ClassFit`]): the misclassification rate of
the most probable class, the mean log loss `−Σ ln p̂ᵢ(yᵢ) / n` (with
probabilities clipped at 10⁻¹⁵ so that a confidently wrong prediction
costs a large but finite amount), the confusion matrix, and the area under
the ROC curve ([`auc`]): for two classes, of the second class's
probability; for more, the average of each class against the rest
(Hand & Till, *Machine Learning* 45, 2001, discuss alternatives).

The AUC is computed as the Mann–Whitney statistic: the probability that a
randomly chosen positive scores above a randomly chosen negative, ties
counting one half (Hanley & McNeil, *Radiology* 143, 1982).

- `struct ContinuousFit`: Fit measures for a continuous response.
- `struct ClassFit`: Fit measures for a categorical response.
- `fn most_probable`: Index of the largest probability (the first on ties).
- `fn auc`: Area under the ROC curve of `scores` for the rows marked `positive`: the Mann–Whitney probability that a positive outscores a negative (ties ½).
- `fn roc_curve`: The ROC curve of `scores` for the rows marked `positive`: points (false positive rate, true positive rate) from (0, 0) to (1, 1), one per distinct score, thresholds descending.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/neural.rs`

Neural networks: fully connected feed-forward networks (multilayer
perceptrons) with one or two hidden layers, fitted by penalized maximum
likelihood.

**Model.** Each hidden layer computes `a = h(W a₋ + b)` from the layer
before it, with the activation `h` one of tanh, the logistic function
`1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)`, the rectifier `max(0, z)` or the identity. The output
layer is linear for a continuous response, one logistic unit for two
classes (the probability of the second class) and a softmax over `K`
units for `K > 2` classes (Bishop 1995, *Neural Networks for Pattern
Recognition*, ch. 4 and 6; Ripley 1996, *Pattern Recognition and Neural
Networks*, ch. 5).

**Objective.** With `n` training rows and weights `W` (biases are not
penalized), the network minimizes

```text
E = (1/n) Σᵢ L(yᵢ, f(xᵢ)) + (α / 2n) Σ w²,
```

where `L` is half the squared error `½(y − ŷ)²` for a continuous response,
and the cross-entropy `−Σₖ yₖ ln pₖ` (with probabilities clipped at 10⁻¹⁵)
for classes. These output–loss pairs are canonical, so the error signal at
the output is `ŷ − y` in every case (Bishop 1995, §6.9); gradients follow
by back-propagation (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986). The penalty `α`
is weight decay (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, *The Elements of
Statistical Learning*, §11.5.2).

**Solvers.** Limited-memory BFGS (Liu & Nocedal 1989; two-loop recursion
with ten correction pairs and a backtracking Armijo line search; Nocedal &
Wright 2006, *Numerical Optimization*, alg. 7.4–7.5) on the full training
set, or Adam (Kingma & Ba 2015) on shuffled mini-batches. L-BFGS stops when
the largest gradient component falls below 10⁻⁵ or an iteration lowers
the objective by less than 10⁻⁹ relative to its size; Adam stops when ten
consecutive passes fail to lower the epoch's mean objective by 10⁻⁴.
[`Solver`] `None` picks L-BFGS up to 2,000 rows and Adam above.

**Starts.** The objective has many local minima, so the network is fitted
from several random starts and the start with the smallest final
objective is kept. Starting weights and biases are uniform on
`±√(6 / (fan-in + fan-out))` (Glorot & Bengio 2010), with 2 in place of 6
for the logistic activation. Each start's generator is seeded from the
request's seed and the start's number, and starts run in parallel with
their results combined in a fixed order, so a fit repeats exactly.

**Failure modes.** No hidden layer or more than two, a layer without
nodes, a negative penalty, no rows, inputs of unequal width or with a
missing value, a non-finite target, or a class code outside the classes.

- `enum Activation`: The activation of the hidden nodes.
- `enum NetworkTask`: What the network predicts.
- `enum Output`: The output layer.
- `enum Solver`: The optimizer.
- `struct NetworkOptions`: Network shape and fitting settings.
- `struct Layer`: One fully connected layer: `z = W a + b`.
- `struct Network`: A fitted network.
- `fn fit_network`: Fit a network to rows `x` (one input vector per row) and `task`.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/pls.rs`

Partial least squares (PLS) regression.

**Model.** PLS finds a few latent factors (scores) `t = X r`, linear
combinations of the centred (and usually standardized) predictors chosen
to have large covariance with the responses, and regresses the responses
on them (Wold, Sjöström & Eriksson, "PLS-regression: a basic tool of
chemometrics", *Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems* 58,
2001). With `a` factors, `X ≈ T Pᵀ` and `Y ≈ T Qᵀ`, so the coefficients
are `B = R Qᵀ` with `T = X R`. It suits many correlated predictors and
fewer rows than predictors, where least squares fails.

**Algorithms.**
* *NIPALS*: each factor's weight vector `w` is the dominant direction of
  `Xᵀ Y` on the deflated matrices (`X ← X − t pᵀ`, `Y ← Y − t qᵀ`),
  found by alternating `w ∝ Xᵀu`, `t = Xw`, `q = Yᵀt/tᵀt`, `u = Yq/qᵀq`
  (one step for a single response). The rotations follow from
  `r_a = w_a − Σ_{i<a} r_i (p_iᵀ w_a)`, so `t_a = X₀ r_a`.
* *SIMPLS* (de Jong, *Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems*
  18, 1993): `r` is the dominant left singular vector of the
  cross-product `S = X₀ᵀY₀`, which is deflated by projecting out the
  loadings found so far; `X` itself is never deflated. For a single
  response both algorithms give the same model.

**Summaries.** Variance of `X` and `Y` explained by each factor
(`tᵀt ‖p‖²` and `tᵀt ‖q‖²` over the total sums of squares, scores being
orthogonal); variable importance in projection
`VIP_j = √(p Σ_a SSY_a (w_aj/‖w_a‖)² / Σ_a SSY_a)` (Wold; Chong & Jun,
*Chemometrics and Intelligent Laboratory Systems* 78, 2005), where
values above about 1 mark influential predictors.

- `enum PlsAlgorithm`: How the factors are extracted.
- `struct PlsFit`: A fitted PLS model with every factor extracted; predictions and coefficients may use any number of leading factors.
- `fn fit_pls`: Fit PLS with up to `factors` factors (fewer if the predictors run out of variation), predictors `x` and responses `y` given as columns of the same length.
- `fn cross_validate_pls`: Squared prediction errors (summed over responses, original units) of each row for 0 to `max_factors` factors by k-fold cross-validation: `errors[a][i]` for row `i` with `a` factors, so `Σᵢ errors[a][i]` is the predicted residual sum of squares (PRESS).
- `fn choose_factors`: The fewest factors (at least 1) whose mean held-out squared error is within one standard error of the smallest (the one-standard-error rule; Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2009, §7.10), from per-row errors `errors[a][i]` as [`cross_validate_pls`] returns them.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/svm.rs`

Support vector machines: C-support vector classification and ε-support
vector regression, solved by sequential minimal optimization (SMO).

**Problem.** Both tasks are the dual quadratic program

```text
minimize ½ αᵀQα + pᵀα   subject to yᵀα = 0, 0 ≤ αᵢ ≤ C,
```

with `Qᵢⱼ = yᵢyⱼK(xᵢ, xⱼ)` and `yᵢ = ±1` (Cortes & Vapnik 1995; Vapnik
1998). Classification has one variable per row with `p = −1`; ε-regression
has two per row (`α` and `α*`), with `p = ε ∓ zᵢ` (Smola & Schölkopf 2004).

**Solver.** SMO (Platt 1998) updates two variables at a time, chosen by
the second-order working-set selection of Fan, Chen & Lin (2005): the
first maximally violates the optimality conditions, the second gives the
largest decrease of the objective. It stops when the largest violation
`m(α) − M(α)` is below the tolerance (10⁻³ by default). The offset ρ is
the mean of `yᵢ∇ᵢ` over free variables (the midpoint of its feasible
range when none is free). Kernel rows are computed on demand and cached.

**Several classes.** One machine per pair of classes (one-against-one,
Knerr et al. 1990; Hsu & Lin 2002); the predicted class wins the most
pairwise votes.

**Probabilities.** Each pairwise decision value is mapped to a
probability by Platt's sigmoid `1 / (1 + exp(A f + B))`, fitted to
decision values from an internal 5-fold cross-validation by Newton's
method with backtracking (Platt 1999; Lin, Lin & Weng 2007). Pairwise
probabilities are combined by the coupling method of Wu, Lin & Weng
(2004, method 2).

**Kernels.** Linear `uᵀv`, radial basis `exp(−γ‖u − v‖²)` and polynomial
`(γuᵀv + c₀)ᵈ`.

- `enum Kernel`: A kernel function.
- `struct SvmOptions`: Solver settings.
- `struct SvmMachine`: A fitted machine: `f(x) = Σ coefᵢ K(svᵢ, x) − ρ`.
- `fn fit_svc`: Fit a two-class C-SVC: `positive[i]` is whether point `i` is in the +1 class.
- `fn fit_svr`: Fit an ε-SVR to targets `z`.
- `struct PlattScaling`: Platt's sigmoid `P(+1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A f + B))`.
- `fn fit_platt`: Fit Platt's sigmoid to decision values and labels by Newton's method with backtracking, on the regularized targets `(N₊ + 1)/(N₊ + 2)` and `1/(N₋ + 2)` (Lin, Lin & Weng 2007).
- `fn pairwise_coupling`: Combine pairwise probabilities `r[i][j] = P(i | i or j)` into class probabilities (Wu, Lin & Weng 2004, method 2).
- `struct PairMachine`: One machine of a one-against-one classifier: class `first` is +1.
- `const CONSTANT_DECISION_SPREAD`: Spread of the training decision values below which a machine counts as constant.
- `struct SvmClassifier`: A one-against-one classifier over `classes` classes.
- `fn fit_classifier`: Fit a one-against-one classifier: `class[i] < classes` is point `i`'s class.
- `enum SvmTask`: What a support vector machine predicts.
- `enum TuningSplit`: Held-out rows for tuning.
- `fn tune`: The held-out error of each candidate `(kernel, cost)`: misclassification rate (by vote) or mean squared error, on the validation points or over the folds.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/tree.rs`

Classification and regression trees (Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone,
*Classification and Regression Trees*, 1984; "CART").

**Growing.** Starting from all training rows, each node is split in two
by the single rule that most reduces impurity, until a node is too small
(`min_split` rows), too deep (`max_depth`), pure, or no split leaves
`min_leaf` rows on each side. Impurity is the sum of squared deviations
from the node mean for a continuous response; for a categorical one it is
`n·(1 − Σ pₖ²)` (Gini) or `−n·Σ pₖ ln pₖ` (entropy), with `pₖ` the class
shares in the node. A continuous predictor splits at a midpoint between
adjacent distinct values (`x < t` goes left); a categorical predictor
sends a set of levels left. For a continuous response or two classes the
best set is found among the levels ordered by their mean response
(Breiman et al. 1984, Theorem 4.5); with more classes all subsets are
tried for up to [`TreeOptions::max_exhaustive_levels`] levels (at most
[`EXHAUSTIVE_LEVELS_LIMIT`]), beyond which levels are ordered by the share
of the node's most common class.

**Missing predictor values.** A split is chosen on the rows where its
predictor is present. Rows missing it then follow *surrogate splits*:
rules on other predictors chosen to send rows the same way as the primary
split as often as possible, kept only when they agree more often than
sending everything the majority way (§5.3 of Breiman et al.). A row
missing every surrogate goes the way most rows went.

**Pruning.** A large tree overfits. Cost-complexity pruning (Breiman et
al., ch. 3) orders the subtrees by `R_α(T) = R(T) + α·|leaves(T)|`, with
risk `R` the squared error (continuous) or the number misclassified
(categorical). Repeatedly collapsing the "weakest link", the internal
node `t` with the smallest `g(t) = (R(t) − R(Tₜ)) / (|leaves(Tₜ)| − 1)`,
gives a nested sequence of subtrees, one per [`PruneStep`]; any α selects
one of them. The step is chosen on held-out data: validation rows, or
k-fold cross-validation ([`cross_validate_pruning`]), where trees grown
without each fold are pruned at the geometric midpoints `√(αₖ αₖ₊₁)` and
scored on the fold.

- `enum Feature`: One predictor's values for every row of the data (rows are addressed by their position in these vectors).
- `enum Value`: A predictor value of one row, for routing it down a tree.
- `enum Target`: The response.
- `enum Criterion`: Impurity measure of a classification tree.
- `struct TreeOptions`: Growing limits.
- `const EXHAUSTIVE_LEVELS_LIMIT`: Most levels for which [`TreeOptions::max_exhaustive_levels`] can ask for every subset to be tried: 2¹⁹ − 1 ≈ 5·10⁵ subsets per node.
- `enum Rule`: Which way a split sends a row.
- `struct Surrogate`: A surrogate for a node's split.
- `struct Split`: A node's split.
- `struct Node`: A node.
- `struct PruneStep`: One subtree of the pruning sequence.
- `struct Tree`: A grown tree with its pruning sequence.
- `fn fit_tree`: Grow a tree on `rows` (positions in `features` and `target`) and compute its pruning sequence.
- `struct CrossValidation`: Cross-validated error of each step of a tree's pruning sequence.
- `fn cross_validate_pruning`: `folds`-fold cross-validation of `tree`'s pruning sequence (`tree` was grown on `rows` with `options`).
- `fn choose_step`: The step to keep given each step's held-out `(error, standard error)`: the lowest error, or with `one_se`, the smallest tree (latest step) whose error is within one standard error of the lowest (Breiman et al.

### `crates/stat-predictive/src/validation.rs`

Holding rows back to judge a predictive model honestly.

Each row gets a [`Role`]: **training** rows fit the model, **validation**
rows tune it (choose a tree's size, a penalty, a number of iterations),
and **test** rows are kept out of both so that their error estimates how
the chosen model does on new data (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, *The
Elements of Statistical Learning*, 2nd ed., §7.2). Roles can be drawn at
random ([`random_roles`]), within strata of the response so that every
class is represented in each role ([`stratified_roles`]), or by whole
groups so that related rows (one subject's measurements) never straddle
roles ([`grouped_roles`]). K-fold cross-validation ([`fold_assignment`])
is the alternative when data are too few to hold rows back.

Every assignment is seeded and reproducible: the same seed and inputs
always give the same roles.

- `enum Role`: What a row is used for.
- `fn random_roles`: Random roles for `n` rows: shares `validation` and `test` of the rows (rounded), the rest training.
- `fn stratified_roles`: Random roles drawn separately within each stratum (`strata[i]` is row `i`'s class), so each role holds about the same share of every class.
- `fn grouped_roles`: Random roles given to whole groups (`groups[i]` is row `i`'s group): the shares count groups, and every row of a group gets the group's role.
- `fn fold_assignment`: Fold of each of `n` rows for `folds`-fold cross-validation: a random permutation dealt round-robin, so fold sizes differ by at most one.

Integration tests: `gaussian_process_reference.rs`, `mars_reference.rs`, `neural_reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-quality` (`crates/stat-quality`)

Statistical quality control: Shewhart control charts, Nelson run rules and ANOVA gauge R&R.

Dependencies: `stat-core`, `stat-mixed`, `stat-multivariate`.

### `crates/stat-quality/src/acceptance.rs`

Acceptance sampling: lot-by-lot sampling plans, their operating
characteristics and the plans that meet a producer's and a consumer's risk
point (Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality Control*, ch. 15;
Schilling & Neubauer, *Acceptance Sampling in Quality Control*).

#### Plans

* **Single attribute plan** `(n, c)`: inspect `n` items, accept the lot when
  at most `c` are nonconforming.
* **Double attribute plan** `(n₁, c₁, n₂, c₂)`: inspect `n₁`; accept when
  `d₁ ≤ c₁`, reject when `d₁ > c₂`, otherwise inspect `n₂` more and accept
  when `d₁ + d₂ ≤ c₂`.
* **Variables plan by the k-method** `(n, k)` for one specification limit
  (shown for an upper limit `U`; a lower limit is symmetric): accept when
  `(U − x̄)/σ ≥ k` (σ known) or `(U − x̄)/s ≥ k` (σ unknown). The quality
  characteristic is assumed normal, so the fraction nonconforming `p`
  fixes the distance `z_p = Φ⁻¹(1 − p)` from the mean to the limit in σ units.

#### Probability of acceptance `Pa(p)` (the OC curve)

For attribute plans the number nonconforming in a sample of `n` follows
one of three models ([`OcModel`]): binomial `Bin(n, p)` (type-B OC, a
process or a large lot), hypergeometric with `D = round(pN)` nonconforming
items in the lot of `N` (type-A OC, an isolated lot) or Poisson with mean
`np` (an approximation, or counts of nonconformities). Then

```text
single:  Pa = P(d ≤ c)
double:  Pa = P(d₁ ≤ c₁) + Σ_{j = c₁+1}^{c₂} P(d₁ = j) · P(d₂ ≤ c₂ − j)
```

(for the hypergeometric model the second sample is drawn from the `N − n₁`
items left, with `D − j` nonconforming). For variables plans

```text
σ known:    Pa = Φ(√n (z_p − k))
σ unknown:  Pa = P(T ≥ k√n),  T ~ noncentral t(n − 1, δ = √n z_p)
```

which is exact under normality (the noncentral-t form; Schilling &
Neubauer ch. 7).

#### Rectifying inspection

Rejected lots are screened 100% and nonconforming items replaced. With lot
size `N`:

```text
AOQ(p) = p · Pa · (N − n) / N                              (single, variables)
AOQ(p) = p · [Pa_I (N − n₁) + Pa_II (N − n₁ − n₂)] / N       (double)
ATI(p) = n + (1 − Pa)(N − n)                               (single, variables)
ATI(p) = n₁ Pa_I + (n₁ + n₂) Pa_II + N (1 − Pa)              (double)
ASN(p) = n₁ + n₂ · P(c₁ < d₁ ≤ c₂)                          (double; n otherwise)
```

with `Pa_I` and `Pa_II` the probabilities of accepting on the first and on
the second sample. The average outgoing quality limit (AOQL) is the
maximum of `AOQ(p)` over `p`.

#### Plans from risk points

Given the producer's point `(p₁, 1 − α)` (acceptable quality level) and
the consumer's point `(p₂, β)` (lot tolerance percent defective):

* [`single_plan`]: for `c = 0, 1, 2, …` the smallest `n` with
  `Pa(p₂) ≤ β` is found; the first `c` whose plan also has
  `Pa(p₁) ≥ 1 − α` gives the plan. Because that smallest `n` grows with
  `c`, this is the plan with the smallest sample size meeting both points.
* [`double_plan`]: with `n₂ = r·n₁` for a chosen ratio `r`, every
  `c₁ < c₂` up to a bound is tried with its smallest `n₁` meeting the
  consumer's point; among those that meet the producer's point the plan
  with the smallest average sample number at `p₁` is chosen.
* [`variables_plan`]: with σ known, the classical solution
  `n = ⌈((z_α + z_β)/(z_{p₁} − z_{p₂}))²⌉`,
  `k = (z_{p₁} z_β + z_{p₂} z_α)/(z_α + z_β)`. With σ unknown, the smallest
  `n` for which some `k` meets both points under the exact noncentral-t OC
  curve, and `k` midway between the largest value meeting the producer's
  point and the smallest meeting the consumer's point.

No tables from published sampling standards are used: every plan is
computed from the risk points.

- `const MAX_ACCEPTANCE_NUMBER`: Largest acceptance number tried by the plan searches.
- `const MAX_SAMPLE_SIZE`: Largest sample size the plan searches consider (unless the lot is smaller).
- `enum OcModel`: Distribution of the number nonconforming in a sample.
- `enum SigmaKnowledge`: Whether a variables plan uses a known process σ or the sample SD.
- `enum SamplingPlan`: A lot-by-lot acceptance sampling plan.
- `struct PlanContext`: The lot and OC model a plan is evaluated with.
- `struct RiskPoints`: The producer's and consumer's risk points.
- `struct PlanPoint`: Measures of a plan at one quality level.
- `fn single_plan`: The single attribute plan with the smallest sample size meeting both risk points (see the module docs).
- `fn double_plan`: The double attribute plan with `n₂ = ratio · n₁` meeting both risk points with the smallest average sample number at the producer's quality level (see the module docs).
- `fn variables_plan`: The k-method variables plan meeting both risk points (see the module docs).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/attribute.rs`

Shewhart control charts for attribute data (Montgomery, *Introduction to
Statistical Quality Control*, ch. 7; NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook §6.3.3),
Laney's charts for overdispersed proportions and rates, and the
rare-event g and t charts.

| Chart | Plotted | Centre | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| p  | fraction nonconforming `dᵢ/nᵢ` | `p̄ = Σd/Σn` | `p̄ ± 3√(p̄(1 − p̄)/nᵢ)` |
| np | number nonconforming `dᵢ` (constant `n`) | `n p̄` | `n p̄ ± 3√(n p̄(1 − p̄))` |
| c  | nonconformities `cᵢ` (constant opportunity) | `c̄` | `c̄ ± 3√c̄` |
| u  | nonconformities per unit `cᵢ/nᵢ` | `ū = Σc/Σn` | `ū ± 3√(ū/nᵢ)` |
| p′ | `dᵢ/nᵢ` | `p̄` | `p̄ ± 3 σ_pᵢ σ_z` |
| u′ | `cᵢ/nᵢ` | `ū` | `ū ± 3 σ_uᵢ σ_z` |
| g  | units between events `gᵢ` (counted from 0) | `ḡ` | `ḡ ± 3√(ḡ(ḡ + 1))` |
| t  | time between events `tᵢ` | `x̄^3.6` | `(x̄ ± 3 M̄R/d₂(2))^3.6`, with `xᵢ = tᵢ^(1/3.6)` |

**Laney p′ and u′** (Laney 2002, "Improved control charts for
attributes", *Quality Engineering* 14(4), 531–537): with large subgroups
the binomial or Poisson limits are often far too narrow because the true
rate itself varies from subgroup to subgroup. Each point is standardized,
`zᵢ = (pᵢ − p̄)/σ_pᵢ` with `σ_pᵢ = √(p̄(1 − p̄)/nᵢ)` (u′: `σ_uᵢ = √(ū/nᵢ)`),
and the spread of the `zᵢ` is measured by their moving ranges,
`σ_z = M̄R(z)/d₂(2)`. The limits widen by that factor; `σ_z = 1` gives the
ordinary p or u chart.

**g chart** (Benneyan 2001, "Number-between g-type statistical quality
control charts for monitoring adverse events", *Health Care Management
Science* 4, 305–318): the number of units, cases or days between rare
events follows a geometric distribution with mean `ḡ` and variance
`ḡ(ḡ + 1)` (counting from 0), giving 3σ limits as above.

**t chart** (Nelson 1994, "A control chart for parts-per-million
nonconforming items", *Journal of Quality Technology* 26(3), 239–240):
times between events are roughly exponential; `t^(1/3.6)` is close to
normal, so an individuals chart is built on the transformed times and its
center and limits are transformed back (a negative lower limit becomes 0).
Run rules are applied on the transformed scale, where the zones are
symmetric.

Negative lower limits are set to zero (and the p and p′ upper limits are
capped at one). With unequal subgroup sizes the p, u, p′ and u′ limits vary
from subgroup to subgroup. A subgroup signals when it falls outside its
limits.

- `const T_CHART_POWER`: Power of the t chart's transformation, `x = t^(1/3.6)` (Nelson 1994).
- `enum AttributeChartKind`: Which attribute chart.
- `struct AttributePoint`: One subgroup of an attribute chart.
- `struct AttributeChart`: An attribute control chart.
- `fn attribute_chart`: Build an attribute chart from `counts` (nonconforming units for p/np/p′, nonconformities for c/u/u′, units between events for g, times between events for t) and, for p, np, u, p′ and u′, the subgroup `sizes` (units inspected for p, np and p′; inspection units, which may be fractional, for u and u′).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/attribute_agreement.rs`

Agreement of appraisers who classify parts into categories: an attribute
(categorical) measurement-system study.

Each of `k` appraisers rates each of `n` parts `m` times (trials) into one
of `c` categories; optionally every part has a known standard (reference)
category. The study asks four questions (Fleiss, Levin & Paik,
*Statistical Methods for Rates and Proportions*, 3rd ed., Wiley 2003,
ch. 18; AIAG, *Measurement Systems Analysis*, 4th ed., 2010, ch. III §C):

* **within each appraiser** — does an appraiser repeat their own rating?
  (needs `m ≥ 2`);
* **each appraiser against the standard**;
* **between appraisers** — do all appraisers give the same rating?
  (needs `k ≥ 2`);
* **all appraisers against the standard**.

#### Percent agreement
A part *matches* when every rating in the comparison is the same (and, for
the comparisons with a standard, equals the standard). The percentage of
matched parts `x/n` is given with the exact Clopper–Pearson interval
`[B(α/2; x, n − x + 1), B(1 − α/2; x + 1, n − x)]` (Clopper & Pearson
1934, *Biometrika* 26).

#### Cohen's kappa (two sets of ratings of the same parts)
With cell proportions `pᵢⱼ` of a `c × c` table, margins `pᵢ.`, `p.ⱼ` and
agreement weights `wᵢⱼ` (`wᵢᵢ = 1`; `wᵢⱼ = 0` off the diagonal for the
unweighted kappa of Cohen 1960, *Educ. Psychol. Meas.* 20, 37–46;
`1 − |i − j|/(c − 1)` linear or `1 − (i − j)²/(c − 1)²` quadratic for the
weighted kappa of Cohen 1968 on ordered categories)

```text
p_o = ΣΣ wᵢⱼ pᵢⱼ      p_e = ΣΣ wᵢⱼ pᵢ. p.ⱼ      κ = (p_o − p_e) / (1 − p_e)
```

The large-sample variances are those of Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt (1969),
*Psychol. Bull.* 72, 323–327, with `w̄ᵢ. = Σⱼ p.ⱼ wᵢⱼ`, `w̄.ⱼ = Σᵢ pᵢ. wᵢⱼ`:

```text
Var(κ)  = [ΣΣ pᵢⱼ (wᵢⱼ − (w̄ᵢ. + w̄.ⱼ)(1 − κ))² − (κ − p_e(1 − κ))²] / (N (1 − p_e)²)
Var₀(κ) = [ΣΣ pᵢ. p.ⱼ (wᵢⱼ − (w̄ᵢ. + w̄.ⱼ))² − p_e²] / (N (1 − p_e)²)
```

`Var₀` holds under no agreement beyond chance and gives the test
`z = κ / √Var₀`; `Var` gives the interval `κ ± z₁₋α/₂ √Var`. A
category-specific kappa collapses the table to that category against all
others (Fleiss, Levin & Paik §18.1).

#### Fleiss' kappa (many ratings of each part)
With `xᵢⱼ` of the `m` ratings of part `i` in category `j`, `pⱼ` the share
of all `nm` ratings in category `j` and `qⱼ = 1 − pⱼ` (Fleiss 1971,
*Psychol. Bull.* 76, 378–382):

```text
κⱼ = 1 − Σᵢ xᵢⱼ (m − xᵢⱼ) / (n m (m − 1) pⱼ qⱼ)
κ  = 1 − (n m² − ΣᵢΣⱼ xᵢⱼ²) / (n m (m − 1) Σⱼ pⱼ qⱼ)
```

with the null standard errors of Fleiss, Nee & Landis (1979),
*Psychol. Bull.* 86, 974–977 (Fleiss, Levin & Paik eq. 18.53–18.54):
`se₀(κⱼ) = √(2 / (n m (m − 1)))` and
`se₀(κ) = √2 · √((Σ pⱼqⱼ)² − Σ pⱼqⱼ(qⱼ − pⱼ)) / (Σ pⱼqⱼ · √(n m (m − 1)))`.
Within an appraiser the `m` trials are the ratings; between appraisers all
`k m` ratings of a part are.

#### Ordinal ratings
When the categories are ordered (scored `1, …, c`), **Kendall's
coefficient of concordance** measures agreement of `J` sets of ratings of
the `n` parts (Kendall & Babington Smith 1939; Siegel & Castellan,
*Nonparametric Statistics for the Behavioral Sciences*, 2nd ed. 1988,
§9.4). Each set is ranked (ties get mid-ranks), `Rᵢ` is part `i`'s rank
sum and `Tⱼ = Σ(t³ − t)` over the tie groups of set `j`:

```text
W = 12 Σ(Rᵢ − R̄)² / (J² (n³ − n) − J Σⱼ Tⱼ)      χ² = J (n − 1) W   on n − 1 df
```

Agreement with the standard is measured by **Kendall's τ_b** between the
ratings and the standard (Kendall, *Rank Correlation Methods*, 4th ed.
1970, ch. 3), with `C` concordant and `D` discordant pairs and `n₁`, `n₂`
the pairs tied in each variable: `τ_b = (C − D)/√((n₀ − n₁)(n₀ − n₂))`,
`n₀ = N(N − 1)/2`; the test is `z = (C − D)/√Var(C − D)` with Kendall's
tie-corrected variance

```text
Var = [v₀ − Σt(t−1)(2t+5) − Σu(u−1)(2u+5)] / 18
      + Σt(t−1) Σu(u−1) / (2N(N−1)) + Σt(t−1)(t−2) Σu(u−1)(u−2) / (9N(N−1)(N−2)),
v₀ = N(N−1)(2N+5).
```

#### Failure modes
Ratings must be balanced (every appraiser rates every part `m` times);
category indices must be in range; at least two parts are needed. Kappa is
undefined (NaN) when chance agreement is complete (every rating in one
category); concordance is undefined when every set ties all parts.

- `struct PercentAgreement`: Percentage of parts on which every rating in a comparison agrees.
- `enum KappaWeights`: Agreement weights of a Cohen kappa.
- `struct KappaEstimate`: A kappa statistic with its standard errors and test of no agreement beyond chance.
- `fn cohen_kappa`: Cohen's kappa of a `c × c` table of counts (rows: first rating, columns: second rating), with the weights `weights`, standard errors of Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt (1969) and an interval at confidence `level`.
- `fn category_kappa`: Cohen's kappa of category `k` against all others: the table collapsed to 2 × 2 (unweighted).
- `struct FleissKappa`: Fleiss' kappa overall and for each category.
- `fn fleiss_kappa`: Fleiss' (1971) kappa of an `n × c` table: `counts[i][j]` of the `m` ratings of part `i` fall in category `j` (every row must sum to the same `m ≥ 2`), with the null standard errors of Fleiss, Nee & Landis (1979).
- `struct Concordance`: Kendall's coefficient of concordance with its chi-square test.
- `fn kendall_w`: Kendall's W of `scores[j][i]`: judge `j`'s score of object `i` (higher scores rank higher; ties get mid-ranks and the tie correction).
- `struct KendallTau`: Kendall's τ_b with its tie-corrected normal test.
- `fn kendall_tau_b`: Kendall's τ_b of paired values `x`, `y`.
- `struct AgreementRatings`: Ratings of an attribute agreement study, indexed by appraiser, part and trial; values are category indices (in category order).
- `struct AgreementOptions`: Settings of [`attribute_agreement`].
- `struct WithinAppraiser`: Repeatability of one appraiser over the trials.
- `struct VersusStandard`: One appraiser (or all appraisers pooled) against the standard.
- `struct PairwiseKappa`: Cohen's kappa of two appraisers, ratings paired by part and trial.
- `struct BetweenAppraisers`: Agreement among all appraisers.
- `struct AttributeAgreement`: A computed attribute agreement study.
- `fn attribute_agreement`: Run an attribute agreement study (see the module documentation for the statistics).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/attribute_capability.rs`

Capability of a process judged by counts: the fraction of defective units
(binomial) or the defects per unit (Poisson), with exact confidence
intervals (Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality Control*,
ch. 7–8; Clopper & Pearson 1934, *Biometrika* 26; Garwood 1936,
*Biometrika* 28).

#### Binomial

With `D = Σdᵢ` defective units among `N = Σnᵢ` inspected, the estimated
fraction defective is `p̂ = D/N`, with the Clopper–Pearson interval at
confidence `1 − α`

```text
lower = B(α/2; D, N − D + 1)        (0 when D = 0)
upper = B(1 − α/2; D + 1, N − D)    (1 when D = N)
```

where `B(q; a, b)` is the beta quantile. The **process Z** is the
standard-normal deviate with the same upper-tail area as the fraction
defective, `Z = Φ⁻¹(1 − p̂)`, and its interval maps the interval for `p`
(`Z` decreases in `p`, so the upper limit for `p` gives the lower limit
for `Z`). It is infinite when no defective unit was seen.

#### Poisson

With `C = Σcᵢ` defects over `U = Σuᵢ` units, the defects per unit are
`λ̂ = C/U`, with Garwood's exact interval

```text
lower = χ²(α/2; 2C) / 2U            (0 when C = 0)
upper = χ²(1 − α/2; 2C + 2) / 2U
```

Both studies assume a stable process: the attribute chart beside them in
the report shows whether that holds.

- `struct BinomialCapability`: Binomial capability: fraction of defective units.
- `struct PoissonCapability`: Poisson capability: defects per unit.
- `fn clopper_pearson`: Clopper–Pearson interval for `d` successes in `n` trials (`n ≥ 1`).
- `fn garwood`: Garwood's exact interval for a Poisson count `c` over exposure `u`, as a rate.
- `fn binomial_capability`: Binomial capability of `defective` units among `inspected` per sample.
- `fn poisson_capability`: Poisson capability of `defects` over `units` per sample (units need not be whole: e.g.

### `crates/stat-quality/src/attribute_gauge.rs`

Bias and repeatability of an attribute (go/no-go) gauge from acceptance
counts at known reference values: the analytic method described in AIAG,
*Measurement Systems Analysis* (4th ed., 2010), ch. III §C ("Attribute
Measurement Systems Study — Analytic Method").

Parts with known reference values `xᵢ` near one specification limit are
each checked `m` times (AIAG: `m = 20`) and the acceptances `aᵢ` counted.
The probability of acceptance is estimated with a half-count adjustment
away from 0 and 1:

```text
P′ᵢ = (aᵢ + 0.5)/m   when aᵢ/m < 0.5 and aᵢ ≠ 0
P′ᵢ = (aᵢ − 0.5)/m   when aᵢ/m > 0.5 and aᵢ ≠ m
P′ᵢ = 0.5            when aᵢ/m = 0.5
```

The gauge performance curve is taken to be a normal distribution
function, so `Φ⁻¹(P′)` is linear in the reference value. The parts with
`0 < aᵢ < m` give the least-squares line `Φ⁻¹(P′) = b₀ + b₁ x`, and
`x(P) = (Φ⁻¹(P) − b₀)/b₁` is the reference value accepted with
probability `P`. Then

```text
bias          = limit − x(0.5)
repeatability = |x(0.995) − x(0.005)| / 1.08
t             = 31.3 · |bias| / repeatability     on m − 1 df
```

with AIAG's adjustment factor 1.08 and constant 31.3 (both stated for
`m = 20` trials). Acceptance that rises with the reference value means the
gauge decides at a lower limit; falling acceptance, an upper limit. The
fitted curve's standard deviation `1/|b₁|` is the gauge's
repeatability standard deviation on the normal model.

AIAG's design calls for at least eight parts: the part farthest inside the
limit accepted every time, the one farthest outside never accepted, and
at least six with `0 < aᵢ < m`; [`AttributeGaugeStudy::design_notes`]
reports which of these the data miss.

#### Failure modes
A reference value given twice, fewer than two reference values with `0 < aᵢ < m`, counts
outside `0 … m`, unequal numbers of trials, fewer than two trials, a flat
fit (`b₁ = 0`) or non-finite input.

- `const REPEATABILITY_ADJUSTMENT`: AIAG's adjustment factor for the repeatability (for 20 trials).
- `const BIAS_T_CONSTANT`: AIAG's constant of the bias t statistic (for 20 trials).
- `struct AcceptancePoint`: Acceptances of one reference value.
- `struct AcceptanceEstimate`: One reference value of the analysed study.
- `enum LimitSide`: Which specification limit the gauge decides at.
- `struct AttributeGaugeStudy`: The analysed attribute gauge study.
- `fn adjusted_acceptance`: Adjusted probability of acceptance `P′` of `a` acceptances in `m` trials.
- `fn attribute_gauge_study`: Analyse acceptance counts at reference values against `limit` by the AIAG analytic method (see the module documentation).

### `crates/stat-quality/src/between_within.rs`

Between/within capability: a process made of several subgroups — batches
in time order, or parallel streams such as mould cavities or filling
heads — whose means differ, so that neither the within-subgroup σ nor the
overall σ alone describes it (Bothe, *Measuring Process Capability*,
1997; Wheeler, *Advanced Topics in Statistical Process Control*, 1995;
