initial states (§2.6.1: a 2×m moving average over the first cycles for
the seasonal indices, then a straight line through the first ten
seasonally adjusted values for level and slope). Parameters are kept in
the usual region `0 < β < α < 1`, `0 < γ < 1 − α`, `0.8 ≤ φ ≤ 0.98` (by
default `[10⁻⁴, 0.9999]` for α, β and γ) and, for seasonal models, in the
admissible (forecastable) region where every eigenvalue of the discount
matrix `D = F − g w′` of the linear (additive-error, additive-season)
form lies in the closed unit disc (Hyndman et al. 2008, ch. 10; the unit
eigenvalue that every unnormalised seasonal model has is allowed). The
seasonal initial states are normalised to sum to 0 (additive) or `m`
(multiplicative), so `m − 1` of them are free.

**Forecasts** ([`EtsFit::forecast`]): point forecasts follow the
recursion with zero future errors. For the linear models (additive or
no trend, additive or no seasonality) these are the forecast means and
the forecast variances are analytic (Hyndman et al. 2008, ch. 6, classes
1 and 2): with `c_j = w′Fʲ⁻¹g`, additive errors give
`v_h = σ²(1 + Σ_{j<h} c_j²)`, and multiplicative errors give
`v_h = (1 + σ²) θ_h − μ_h²` with `θ_h = μ_h² + σ² Σ_{j<h} c_j² θ_{h−j}`.
Intervals are `μ_h ± z σ_h`. Multiplicative-seasonal models have no
closed form; their intervals are quantiles of seeded simulated sample
paths ([`stat_core::rng::Rng`]).

**Model selection** ([`select_ets`]) fits every allowed model and keeps
the one with the smallest AICc. Models with additive errors and
multiplicative seasonality are excluded by default because their
forecast distributions can have infinite variance (Hyndman et al. 2008,
ch. 6); multiplicative components need a strictly positive series, and
seasonal models need at least two full cycles.

**Reporting conventions.** The log-likelihood is the full Gaussian one at
the maximum-likelihood variance, `ℓ = −(n/2)(ln(2π SSE/n) + 1) − Σ ln|μ_t|`
(SSE the sum of squared innovations). Information criteria count the
estimated parameters `p` (smoothing parameters and initial states) plus
one for σ²: `AIC = −2ℓ + 2(p+1)`, `AICc = AIC + 2(p+1)(p+2)/(n−p−2)`,
`BIC = −2ℓ + (p+1) ln n`. The reported residual variance (also used for
forecast intervals) is `σ² = SSE/(n − p)`.

### `crates/stat-timeseries/src/smoothing/recursion.rs`

The state recursion of the innovations state-space models.

### `crates/stat-timeseries/src/spectral.rs`

Periodogram and smoothed spectral density estimates.

#### Method
The series `x₁, …, xₙ` is optionally detrended (mean removed, or the least
squares line on `t = 1, …, n` removed) and multiplied by a split cosine
bell taper that tapers a proportion `p` of the observations at each end
(`m = ⌊n p⌋` weights `½(1 − cos(π(2i − 1)/(2m)))`, `i = 1, …, m`, at the
start and mirrored at the end; Bloomfield 1976, *Fourier Analysis of Time
Series: An Introduction*, Wiley, §5.2). The raw periodogram at the Fourier
frequencies `ωⱼ = j/n` (cycles per observation), `j = 1, …, ⌊n/2⌋`, is

```text
I(ωⱼ) = |Σₜ xₜ e^{−2πi ωⱼ t}|² / (n · U₂),   U₂ = 1 − (5/4) p,
```

where `U₂` corrects for the power the taper removes. The scaling makes
`I` an estimate of the spectral density `f(ω)` with
`∫_{−½}^{½} f(ω) dω = var(x)` (a white-noise series of variance σ² has
`f ≡ σ²`). Frequencies are in cycles per observation; for a series with
`s` observations per unit of time (e.g. `s = 12` for monthly data and a
frequency in cycles per year) multiply the frequencies and the bandwidth
by `s` and divide the density and its limits by `s`.

The smoothed estimate applies a symmetric kernel `{k₋M, …, k_M}`
circularly to the periodogram at all frequencies `j/n`, `j = 0, …, n − 1`
(the value at frequency zero, which the mean removal makes uninformative,
is first replaced by the mean of its two neighbours). The kernel is a
modified Daniell kernel or the convolution of several, one per entry of
`spans`: span `s` gives `m = ⌊s/2⌋` and weights `1/(2m)` for `|i| < m`
and `1/(4m)` at `|i| = m` (Bloomfield 1976, §7.3; Brockwell & Davis 1991,
*Time Series: Theory and Methods*, 2nd ed., Springer, §10.4).

#### Confidence limits
The estimate is approximately `f(ω) χ²_ν / ν` with equivalent degrees of
freedom `ν = 2 / (Σ kᵢ² · U₄/U₂²)`, `U₄ = 1 − (93/64) p` (2 for the raw,
untapered periodogram), so a `1 − α` interval is
`[ν f̂/χ²_ν(1 − α/2), ν f̂/χ²_ν(α/2)]`. The bandwidth (Bloomfield 1976)
is `√(Σ (1/12 + i²) kᵢ) / n` in cycles per observation.

- `enum Detrend`: Trend removal before the periodogram.
- `struct SpectrumOptions`: Settings of [`spectral_density`].
- `struct Spectrum`: A spectral density estimate at the Fourier frequencies.
- `fn modified_daniell_kernel`: Weights `k₋M, …, k_M` of the convolution of modified Daniell kernels with the given spans (see the module documentation).
- `fn split_cosine_taper`: Multiply `x` in place by the split cosine bell tapering a proportion `p` at each end.
- `fn spectral_density`: Periodogram (empty `spans`) or kernel-smoothed spectral density of `y` with confidence limits (see the module documentation).

### `crates/stat-timeseries/src/transform.rs`

Differencing and Box–Cox transformation of a series.

#### Differencing

With the backshift operator `B y_t = y_{t−1}`, `d` regular and `D`
seasonal differences at period `m` apply

```text
w_t = (1 − B)^d (1 − B^m)^D y_t,
```

defined for `t = d + mD, …, n − 1`, so `n − d − mD` values remain (Box,
Jenkins & Reinsel, *Time Series Analysis*, §4.1 and §9.1). Expanding the
operator as `1 + Σ_{j=1}^{K} a_j B^j` (`K = d + mD`) gives the inverse
recursion `y_t = w_t − Σ_j a_j y_{t−j}`, which rebuilds the series from its
first `K` values or extends it with forecasts of `w`.

#### Box–Cox

The transform `(y^λ − 1)/λ` (`log y` at `λ = 0`) of Box & Cox (1964,
*JRSS B* 26:211) is shared with [`stat_core::box_cox`]. For a seasonal
series Guerrero (1993, *J. Forecasting* 12:37) chooses λ to stabilise the
variance across seasonal cycles: split the series into consecutive
subseries of length `R` (the period, or 2 for a non-seasonal series), with
means `ȳ_h` and standard deviations `s_h`, and minimise the coefficient of
variation of `s_h / ȳ_h^{1−λ}` over `λ ∈ [−1, 2]`.

- `struct Differencing`: Regular and seasonal differencing orders.
- `fn difference`: `d` lag-1 and `D` lag-`m` differences of `y`; see [`Differencing::apply`].
- `fn box_cox`: Box–Cox transform of every value: `(y^λ − 1)/λ`, `log y` at `λ = 0`.
- `fn inverse_box_cox`: Inverse Box–Cox transform `(λz + 1)^{1/λ}` (`exp z` at `λ = 0`); NaN where `λz + 1 ≤ 0`, which lies outside the transform's range.
- `fn inverse_box_cox_clipped`: Inverse Box–Cox transform of prediction limits, clipped to the range of the transform first: for `λ > 0` the transformed values are bounded below by `−1/λ`, so a lower value below it is moved to `−1/λ` and comes back as 0; for `λ < 0` they are bounded above by `−1/λ`, so a value above it comes ba…
- `fn guerrero_lambda`: Guerrero's (1993) choice of the Box–Cox λ in `[lower, upper]` (normally `[−1, 2]`): the λ minimising the coefficient of variation (sample sd over mean) of `s_h / ȳ_h^{1−λ}` across consecutive non-overlapping subseries of length `R = max(period, 2)` ending at the last observation (an incomplete le…

### `crates/stat-timeseries/src/trend.rs`

Trend models of a series against time, moving-average forecasts and
forecast accuracy measures.

#### Trend models
Each model regresses the series `y₁, …, yₙ` on the time index
`t = 1, …, n` (the textbook convention: the first observation is at
`t = 1`, so the intercept is the level one period before the series
starts; forecasts are at `t = n + 1, n + 2, …`). See Montgomery, Jennings &
Kulahci (2015), *Introduction to Time Series Analysis and Forecasting*,
2nd ed., Wiley, chapter 3.

* **Linear** `y = β₀ + β₁ t + ε` and **quadratic** `y = β₀ + β₁ t + β₂ t² + ε`
  by ordinary least squares (pivoted Householder QR). Forecasts carry
  prediction intervals `ŷ(t₀) ± t_{n−p, 1−α/2} · s · √(1 + x₀ᵀ (XᵀX)⁻¹ x₀)`
  with `s² = SSE/(n − p)`.
* **Exponential growth** `y = b₀ · b₁ᵗ`, fitted by least squares on the log
  scale, `ln y = ln b₀ + t ln b₁ + ε` (the classical linearisation; it
  minimises relative rather than absolute squared error, so the curve is
  not the least-squares fit on the original scale). Requires `y > 0`.
  Fitted values and forecasts are `exp` of the log-scale fit (the median,
  not the mean, of a log-normal error model); prediction intervals are the
  log-scale intervals transformed back with `exp`.
* **Logistic (Pearl–Reed) S-curve** `y = c / (1 + a·e^{−b t})`, by
  nonlinear least squares on the original scale (Levenberg–Marquardt,
  [`stat_core::optimize::levenberg_marquardt`]; Seber & Wild (1989),
  *Nonlinear Regression*, Wiley, §7.3.4). `c` is the upper asymptote, the
  curve's midpoint is at `t = ln(a)/b` and its scale is `1/b`. Starting
  values come from the linearisation `ln(c/y − 1) = ln a − b t` for several
  trial asymptotes above `max y`; the best converged fit is kept. Requires
  `y > 0`. No prediction intervals are given for this model.

#### Accuracy measures
For actual values `yₜ` and fitted (one-step or in-sample) values `ŷₜ`
with errors `eₜ = yₜ − ŷₜ` over the `m` periods that have a fitted value:
mean error `ME = Σe/m`, mean absolute deviation `MAD = Σ|e|/m` (also
called MAE), mean squared deviation `MSD = Σe²/m` (MSE with divisor `m`),
`RMSE = √MSD`, and mean absolute percentage error
`MAPE = 100 · Σ|e/y|/m` (undefined when some `yₜ = 0`).

#### Moving-average forecasts
The single moving average of span `k` forecasts every future period by the
mean of the last `k` observations; its in-sample one-step forecasts are
`ŷₜ = (y_{t−1} + … + y_{t−k})/k` for `t = k + 1, …, n`, and the accuracy
measures use those `n − k` errors (Montgomery, Jennings & Kulahci 2015,
§4.2).

- `struct AccuracyMeasures`: Forecast accuracy measures of fitted values against actual values (see the module documentation for the formulas).
- `fn accuracy`: Accuracy measures of `fitted` against `actual` (equal lengths, at least one pair).
- `enum TrendModel`: The trend curve fitted by [`fit_trend`].
- `struct TrendFit`: A fitted trend model (see the module documentation).
- `struct TrendForecast`: Forecasts of a trend model.
- `fn fit_trend`: Fit a trend model to `y` on `t = 1, …, n`.
- `struct MovingAverageForecast`: Single moving-average forecasts (see the module documentation).
- `fn moving_average_forecast`: Single moving-average forecasts of span `span` for `y`.

### `crates/stat-timeseries/src/unit_root.rs`

Unit-root and stationarity tests: KPSS and augmented Dickey–Fuller.

#### KPSS (Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt & Shin 1992)
"Testing the null hypothesis of stationarity against the alternative of a
unit root", *Journal of Econometrics* 54, 159–178. With `eₜ` the residuals
of `y` on a constant (level stationarity) or on a constant and the time
index (trend stationarity), partial sums `Sₜ = e₁ + … + eₜ` and the
Bartlett-window long-run variance with truncation lag `l`

```text
s²(l) = (1/n) Σₜ eₜ² + (2/n) Σ_{s=1}^{l} (1 − s/(l+1)) Σ_{t=s+1}^{n} eₜ e_{t−s},
η = Σₜ Sₜ² / (n² s²(l)).
```

Large `η` rejects stationarity. The p-value is interpolated linearly in the
paper's table of asymptotic upper-tail critical values (level: 0.347,
0.463, 0.574, 0.739; trend: 0.119, 0.146, 0.176, 0.216 at 10, 5, 2.5 and
1 %), and clipped to `[0.01, 0.10]` outside the table.
The default lag is the "short" rule `l = ⌊4 (n/100)^{1/4}⌋`; the "long"
rule `⌊12 (n/100)^{1/4}⌋` is available through [`kpss_lag`] (both from
Schwert 1989, *J. Business & Economic Statistics* 7, used in the paper).

#### Augmented Dickey–Fuller
Dickey & Fuller (1979), "Distribution of the estimators for autoregressive
time series with a unit root", *JASA* 74, 427–431; Said & Dickey (1984),
"Testing for unit roots in autoregressive-moving average models of
unknown order", *Biometrika* 71, 599–607. The regression

```text
Δyₜ = [α] + [β t] + γ y_{t−1} + Σ_{i=1}^{k} δᵢ Δy_{t−i} + εₜ
```

is fitted by least squares and the test statistic is `τ = γ̂ / se(γ̂)`
(a unit root means `γ = 0`; large negative `τ` rejects it). The number of
lagged differences `k` is fixed or chosen to minimise AIC
(`m ln(RSS/m) + 2p`) or BIC (`m ln(RSS/m) + p ln m`) over `k = 0, …, K` (or from a
given smallest lag),
every candidate fitted on the same (common) sample, the observations
available with `K` lags. The chosen regression is then reported either on
that common sample or refitted on all observations its `k` allows
([`AdfSample`]).

p-values use MacKinnon's approximate asymptotic distribution functions
(MacKinnon 1994, "Approximate asymptotic distribution functions for
unit-root and cointegration tests", *J. Business & Economic Statistics* 12,
167–176; the approach of MacKinnon 1996, *J. Applied Econometrics* 11,
601–618): `p = Φ(γ₀ + γ₁τ + γ₂τ²)` for `τ ≤ τ*` and
`p = Φ(γ₀ + γ₁τ + γ₂τ² + γ₃τ³)` above, 0 below `τ_min` and 1 above
`τ_max`. Critical values use the finite-sample response surfaces of
MacKinnon (2010), "Critical values for cointegration tests", Queen's
Economics Department Working Paper 1227, Tables 2–3 (`N = 1`):
`C(T) = β∞ + β₁/T + β₂/T² + β₃/T³` with `T` the number of observations in
the regression.

- `enum KpssNull`: Null hypothesis of the KPSS test.
- `enum KpssLagRule`: Rule for the Bartlett truncation lag of the KPSS long-run variance.
- `fn kpss_lag`: Truncation lag of `rule` for a series of length `n`.
- `struct KpssTest`: Result of a KPSS test (Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt & Shin 1992).
- `fn kpss`: KPSS test of `y` for level or trend stationarity (see the module documentation).
- `enum AdfDeterministic`: Deterministic terms of the Dickey–Fuller regression.
- `enum AdfLags`: How the number of lagged differences is chosen.
- `enum AdfSample`: Sample on which the selected Dickey–Fuller regression is reported.
- `struct AdfOptions`: Settings of [`adf`].
- `struct AdfTest`: Result of an augmented Dickey–Fuller test.
- `fn adf`: Augmented Dickey–Fuller test of `y` (see the module documentation).
- `fn mackinnon_p_value`: MacKinnon's approximate asymptotic p-value of a Dickey–Fuller τ statistic (see the module documentation).
- `fn mackinnon_critical_value`: Dickey–Fuller τ critical value at significance `level` (0.01, 0.05 or 0.10) for a regression with `nobs` observations (`None`: asymptotic), from MacKinnon's (2010) response surfaces.

Test files: `arima/tests.rs`, `smoothing/tests.rs`.

Integration tests: `arima_reference.rs`, `decompose_reference.rs`, `extreme_values.rs`, `smoothing_reference.rs`, `spectral_reference.rs`, `transfer_reference.rs`, `trend_reference.rs`, `unit_root_reference.rs`.

## Crate `stat-viz` (`crates/stat-viz`)

Graph canvas engine: variable encodings, faceting, axis scales and composable chart elements (points, fit lines, smoothers, box plots), with optional egui_plot rendering.

Dependencies: `ab_glyph`, `egui`, `egui_plot`, `miniz_oxide`, `png`, `stat-core`, `stat-data`, `stat-inference`, `stat-linear`, `stat-multivariate`, `stat-quality`, `tiny-skia`.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/axes.rs`

A graph's own axis settings: titles typed by the user (read as math
markup, [`crate::math_text`]), axis breaks on continuous axes, and a
second vertical axis on the right of each panel.

**Axis breaks.** A break `[a, b]` removes that stretch of a continuous
axis: values up to `a` are drawn where they were, values from `b` on are
drawn `b − a` lower, so the two pieces meet at `a`, and the spine there
carries the usual pair of slanted break marks (Cleveland, *The Elements
of Graphing Data*, rev. ed., 1994, §2.4, on showing a scale break).
Points inside the removed stretch cannot be placed and are left out (a
note says how many); lines run on across the break, and areas (bars,
bands) are cut at its edges. The break is given in data units and placed
on the axis's scale (on a log axis, `[a, b]` is removed between `log a`
and `log b`). Statistics are computed from the data before the break is
applied, so they do not change. An axis can have several breaks, and
each piece between them a scale and a share of the axis of its own
([`crate::axis_breaks`], which builds the piecewise map).

**Right axis.** Columns on the right-axis shelf are drawn in every panel
against a scale of their own, shown on the right side (spine, ticks,
title). The layers are built exactly as for the left axis (one frame per
right-axis column, aligned panel by panel with the main frame) and then
drawn through the linear map that takes the right range onto the left
one. So that the axis a series belongs to is never told by color alone,
right-axis lines are dashed, ungrouped right-axis markers take the next
palette color *and* shape, grouped ones are drawn hollow, and every key
entry for them ends in "(right axis)".

- `struct AxisBreak`: A stretch of a continuous axis that is left out, in data units.
- `fn break_map`: Drawn position of `v` with the stretch `(lo, hi)` removed: unchanged up to `lo`, `hi − lo` lower from `hi` on, NaN inside.
- `fn break_clamp`: [`break_map`] for areas: values inside the break go to its edge.
- `fn break_unmap`: The value drawn at position `u` of a broken axis (the inverse of [`break_map`]; the break point itself reads as its lower end).
- `struct GraphAxes`: Titles, breaks, markup and the plot style of a graph (what its Plot settings set).
- `type Gap`: The map of a broken axis ([`crate::axis_breaks::BrokenAxis`]).
- `struct RightAxis`: Everything drawn against the right axis.
- `fn right_style`: Marker color and shape of the `k`-th right-axis column when the panels are not split by groups: the palette's style after the left column's.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/axis_breaks.rs`

Broken axes: several stretches left out of one continuous axis, each
remaining segment with a scale and a share of the axis of its own.

**Settings.** [`AxisBreaks`] holds what the user sets on one axis: the
stretches left out (data units, [`AxisBreak`]), one [`AxisSegment`] per
remaining piece (its scale, or the axis's own; its share of the axis
length, or automatic) and the style of the marks drawn where the axis is
cut ([`BreakMark`]).

**The axis map.** [`BrokenAxis`] is the piecewise map those settings give
from an axis's drawn units (its own scale applied, as layers are built)
to the broken axis's drawn units. Piece `k` of the axis lies between the
end of break `k − 1` and the start of break `k`; inside it a value `v` is
drawn at `u = c_k + s_k · g_k(v)`, where `g_k` is the piece's scale. The
offsets `c_k` make the pieces meet: the end of one piece and the start of
the next are drawn at the same place, where the break marks go
(Cleveland, *The Elements of Graphing Data*, rev. ed., 1994, §2.4, on
showing scale breaks; a full-scale break between two panels is the
alternative he prefers when the pieces differ much).

* Without segment scales or shares every slope `s_k` is 1, so the axis is
  the unbroken axis with each removed stretch closed up: values below the
  first break are drawn where they were, and nothing depends on the data.
* With shares, or a segment drawn on another scale (a log segment below a
  linear one, say), piece `k` is given `share_k / Σ share` of the data's
  extent on the axis: its slope is chosen so that the part of the data's
  range inside it takes that fraction of the length. Pieces without a
  share split the rest equally. The first piece that holds data keeps
  slope 1, so its values are drawn in its own units (the default range's
  "never below zero" rule still sees them). Without a data extent (no
  points on the axis) the slopes stay 1.

Points inside a removed stretch are not drawn; areas are cut at its
edge. Statistics are computed before the map, so they do not change.
Straight lines between two vertices stay straight in the broken drawing,
so a fit drawn across a segment of another scale bends only where its
vertices are (fits are sampled finely, so this does not show).

- `enum BreakMark`: How the place where an axis is cut is marked on the spine.
- `struct AxisSegment`: One piece of a broken axis, between two breaks (or a break and an end).
- `struct AxisBreaks`: Everything the user sets about the breaks of one axis.
- `struct BrokenAxis`: The piecewise map of a broken axis (see the module documentation): from the axis's drawn units to the broken drawing's, and back.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/axis_settings.rs`

User settings for plot axes, and the tick positions and labels they imply.

Each axis has a major tick interval (automatic "nice" steps of 1, 2 or 5 ×
10ᵏ, or a fixed interval from a chosen origin), minor ticks (none,
automatic, a number of subdivisions per major interval, or a fixed
interval), grid lines, tick marks, a label format, a title, and the side of
the plot it is drawn on. [`axis_ticks`] turns the settings and the visible
range into tick positions; labels are thinned so they never crowd
together, and [`format_tick`] formats them.

The look of the axis line and its marks is set here too: tick marks
pointing into the plot, out of it or across the axis line, their length
and thickness, an axis line moved away from the data area by an offset,
ranges widened to the nearest major ticks, ranges typed by the user, and
tick labels written by the user (a label in math markup at any value,
replacing the number there or adding a tick of its own).

- `enum MajorTicks`: Major tick spacing.
- `enum MinorTicks`: Minor tick spacing.
- `enum GridLines`: Which grid lines are drawn across the plot.
- `enum TickFormat`: How tick labels are written.
- `enum AxisSide`: The side of the plot an axis is drawn on.
- `enum TickDirection`: Which way tick marks point from the axis line.
- `struct TickMarkSize`: Length and line thickness of tick marks, in screen points (exports use the same values scaled like the rest of the figure).
- `struct CustomTick`: A tick label written by the user: `label` (read as math markup, so `\pi` reads π) at `value`.
- `const MAX_AXIS_OFFSET`: Largest offset of an axis line from the data area, in points.
- `struct AxisSettings`: Settings of one axis.
- `struct PlotAxes`: Settings of both axes and of the plot area.
- `fn split_title`: Split a section heading such as `"Survival Curves (steps: Kaplan–Meier; …)"` into a plot title (`"Survival Curves"`) and a subtitle from the trailing parenthesis (`"steps: Kaplan–Meier; …"`).
- `enum TickKind`: Kind of a tick.
- `struct Tick`: One tick.
- `struct AxisTicks`: Ticks of an axis and the steps they were built from.
- `fn time_label`: The label of the tick at `value` on a date-time axis, from [`AxisTicks::time_labels`] (empty if `value` is not a labelled tick).
- `fn nice_step`: The smallest 1, 2, 2.5 or 5 × 10ᵏ that is at least `raw` (> 0), so ticks fall on round values (…, 10, 20, 25, 50, 100, …).
- `const MAX_TICKS`: Most ticks ever produced for one axis (guards against tiny intervals).
- `fn axis_ticks`: Ticks for the visible range `[lo, hi]` of an axis that is `units_per_point` data units per screen point.
- `fn custom_tolerance`: How close (data units) a tick must be to a user's label to carry it, for majors `major_step` apart.
- `fn extended_to_ticks`: The range `[lo, hi]` widened to the major ticks just outside it, as [`axis_ticks`] would place them on an axis `length` points long (only for linear numeric axes: date-time axes keep their range).
- `fn format_tick`: Label of the tick at `value` for an axis whose major interval is `major_step`.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/bitmap.rs`

Bitmaps inside figures: an image plot's picture is a grid of coloured
cells, placed in a page rectangle and drawn cell for cell (no smoothing).
The figure writers embed it in their own way — PNG data in SVG, an image
XObject in PDF, an inline `image` in EPS — so these are the encodings they
share: PNG files, Base64 (SVG data URIs, figure drawings), ASCII85 (PDF and
PostScript streams) and zlib-compressed bytes (PDF `FlateDecode`).

- `struct Bitmap`: A picture of `width` × `height` cells as straight (not premultiplied) RGBA bytes, row by row from the top.
- `fn base64_encode`: `bytes` in Base64 (RFC 4648, with `=` padding, no line breaks).
- `fn base64_decode`: The bytes of Base64 text written by [`base64_encode`]; `None` when the text is not Base64.
- `fn ascii85_encode`: `bytes` in ASCII85 (the PostScript and PDF `ASCII85Decode` form): groups of four bytes as five characters `!`–`u`, an all-zero group as `z`, lines of at most 75 characters, ending with `~>`.
- `fn zlib_compress`: `bytes` compressed in the zlib format (what PDF's `FlateDecode` reads).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/category_labels.rs`

How category labels under a horizontal axis are set: level, slanted at
45° or upright, chosen automatically from the room between categories.

Rotating crowded tick labels rather than thinning them follows the usual
advice for categorical axes (Cleveland, *The Elements of Graphing Data*,
1994, on keeping every label legible; Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data
Visualization*, 2019, ch. 24, which prefers level text and turns labels
only when they would otherwise overlap). The screen and every exported
figure use the same rule, each with its own text measurements.

- `enum CategoryLabels`: The Plot settings choice for category labels along the horizontal axis.
- `enum LabelTurn`: How the labels are actually drawn.
- `struct CategoryLayout`: The labels' turn and which of them are drawn: every `step`-th, starting with the first (1 draws every label).
- `const LEVEL_GAP`: Room needed beside a level label (in the same units as the widths).
- `const TURNED_GAP`: Room needed between turned labels.
- `fn category_layout`: The layout for labels at most `widest` wide and `line` high whose categories lie `spacing` apart (all in the same units, such as screen points).
- `fn label_depth`: How far below the axis labels at most `widest` wide and `line` high reach when turned `turn`.
- `fn least_spacing`: The smallest distance between neighbouring positions (`f64::INFINITY` for fewer than two distinct ones).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/cluster_map.rs`

The clustered heat map: a data matrix (rows of the table down, numeric
columns across) shaded by value, with its rows and columns reordered by
agglomerative hierarchical clustering and the two dendrograms drawn
beside it (Eisen, Spellman, Brown & Botstein, "Cluster analysis and
display of genome-wide expression patterns", *PNAS* 95(25), 1998;
clustering by `stat_multivariate::hierarchical_clustering`, Lance &
Williams 1967).

* Columns: the numeric columns on the horizontal-axis shelf, in order
  (categorical ones are left out with a note). Rows: the shown rows that
  are not excluded, inside the graph's filter and complete in those
  columns, up to [`MAX_ROWS`].
* Values are drawn as they are or standardized per column,
  `z = (x − x̄) / s` with `s` the sample standard deviation (divisor
  `n − 1`; a constant column gives 0), so columns on different scales
  compare.
* Rows are clustered on their (standardized) values by Euclidean
  distance, and columns on their values across the rows, with single,
  complete, average (UPGMA) or Ward linkage. The leaves are drawn in the
  dendrogram's order (no crossing branches): the leaf order of
  `Dendrogram::leaf_order`, left (lower-numbered) branch first.
* Cell `(i, j)` (display order) spans `x ∈ [j, j + 1]`, `y ∈ [R − i − 1,
  R − i]` for `R` rows, so the first row is at the top. The row
  dendrogram grows to the left of the cells and the column dendrogram
  above them, each a quarter of the matrix's size, scaled so the root's
  height fills it. Row labels (the point-label column, or row numbers)
  are written to the right, column names below.
* The color ramp is the sequential palette ramp from the smallest to the
  largest value (shown as the graph's key). Each cell is a region:
  clicking it selects its row; selected rows are outlined.

- `const MAX_ROWS`: Most rows a clustered heat map draws.
- `const MAX_ROW_LABELS`: Most rows that get a label beside the matrix.
- `struct ClusterMapSettings`: Settings of a clustered heat map.
- `const LINKAGES`: Every linkage, in menu order.
- `fn linkage_key`: Short name of a linkage for saving.
- `fn linkage_from_key`: The linkage with this [`linkage_key`].
- `struct ClusterMapGeometry`: What a clustered heat map panel draws.
- `fn build_cluster_map_frame`: The frame of a clustered heat map: one panel holding a [`ClusterMapGeometry`]; each row's points sit at its cells' centres (for box selection).
- `struct ClusterMapElement`: Draws a clustered heat map panel: cells, dendrograms, labels and the key.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/contour.rs`

Filled and lined contour maps of a function sampled over a triangle mesh.

The surface is taken as linear over each triangle of a
[`ContourField`]: a rectangular grid is split into four triangles per
cell around the cell's centre (whose value is the mean of the four
corners, which settles the saddle cells of marching squares the same
way), and a ternary (simplex) plot is covered by the regular triangular
lattice of its barycentric grid. On a linear triangle every contour
level is a straight chord and every band between two levels is a convex
polygon, so:

* **Lines** ([`ContourField::isolines`]) are marching triangles: the
  chords of each triangle joined into polylines through the shared edge
  crossings.
* **Bands** ([`ContourField::isobands`]) are the isoband construction of
  d3-contour and the `contour` crate, done on triangles: each triangle's
  piece of each band is the convex polygon of its corners inside the band
  and the band's level crossings on its edges, walked round in order.
  The pieces tile the band exactly (they fill on screen as one mesh);
  their edges shared by two pieces cancel, and the edges left over join
  into the band's outline rings (outer edges and holes), filled with the
  even–odd rule in vector files so a band is one shape with no hairline
  seams.

Lines and band edges are computed from the same crossing points, so the
lines lie exactly on the edges of the fills. Triangles with a missing
(non-finite) corner are left out: maps end at holes in the data.

[`draw_contours`] turns a field and a [`ContourStyle`] into what a plot
draws: coloured bands, lines, their labels and the colour-bar key.

- `struct ContourField`: A function sampled at the vertices of a triangle mesh, ready for contouring.
- `struct Isoband`: One band of a filled contour map: values in `[lower, upper)` (no lower bound for the first band, no upper bound for the last).
- `fn nice_levels`: About `n` contour levels at round values (steps of 1, 2, 2.5 or 5 × 10ᵏ) strictly inside `(lo, hi)`, and the step.
- `struct ContourStyle`: How a contour map is drawn: filled bands and their colour scale, level lines and labels, and the levels.
- `struct ColorBar`: A colour-bar key: the bands' colours from low to high and the level values between them.
- `struct ContourDrawing`: Everything a contour map draws, in plot coordinates.
- `fn draw_contours`: What `field` draws in `style`: about `default_levels` levels (unless the style sets a number) at round values over the surface's range or the style's fixed range, filled bands coloured at their middle values (the outer bands at the middle between the range's end and the nearest level), lines and …

### `crates/stat-viz/src/density.rs`

Density estimates for graph layers: one- and two-dimensional Gaussian
kernel density estimates, highest-density contour levels and contour lines
(marching squares), and normal-theory density ellipses.

* Kernel density: `f̂(x) = Σ wᵢ K((x − xᵢ)/h) / (h Σ wᵢ)` with the Gaussian
  kernel (Silverman, *Density Estimation for Statistics and Data
  Analysis*, 1986). The default bandwidth is Silverman's rule of thumb
  `0.9 · min(s, IQR/1.34) · n^(−1/5)`; two-dimensional estimates use a
  product kernel with each axis's own bandwidth (Scott's `n^(−1/6)` rate).
* Contour levels enclose given fractions of the estimated probability mass
  (highest-density regions; Hyndman, "Computing and Graphing Highest
  Density Regions", *American Statistician* 50(2), 1996).
* Contour lines by marching squares with linear interpolation along cell
  edges; saddle cells are resolved by the cell's mean.
* Density ellipses: the contour of the bivariate normal with the data's
  mean and covariance that holds probability `p`, i.e. Mahalanobis radius
  `√χ²₂(p) = √(−2 ln(1 − p))`.

Every function is total: degenerate input gives `None` or empty output.

- `fn silverman_bandwidth`: Silverman's rule-of-thumb bandwidth `0.9 · min(s, IQR/1.34) · n^(−1/5)` for values with frequencies (an empty `freq` means 1 each).
- `fn kde_1d`: Gaussian kernel density of `values` (with frequencies `freq`) at `points` evenly spaced x from `lo` to `hi`, as `[x, density]`.
- `struct Grid`: Values of a function on a regular grid: `z[j * xs.len() + i]` at `(xs[i], ys[j])`.
- `fn kde_2d`: Two-dimensional Gaussian product-kernel density of the points `(x, y)` with weights, on an `nx × ny` grid spanning the data plus three bandwidths on each side.
- `fn mass_thresholds`: Density thresholds whose superlevel sets hold the given fractions of the grid's total mass (each in (0, 1)), in the order given.
- `fn contour_segments`: Line segments of the contour `z = level` by marching squares.
- `fn mean_and_covariance`: Weighted mean vector and covariance matrix `[sxx, sxy, syy]` of the finite points, with divisor `Σw − 1` (frequency weights).
- `fn density_ellipse`: The bivariate-normal density ellipse holding probability `level` for the points' mean and covariance, as a closed outline of `points` vertices (the last repeats the first), with the sample correlation.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/aggregate.rs`

Aggregation layers: bar charts, line charts and heat maps.

- `enum BarLayout`: How the bars of several subgroups share a position.
- `struct BarElement`: Bars of a statistic of the vertical variable (or of the count of rows, when there is no vertical column) at each horizontal position, per subgroup: side by side, stacked, or stacked to 100%.
- `enum LineConnect`: What a line chart connects.
- `struct LineElement`: Lines per subgroup joining rows in table order (a run chart), rows in order of x, or a statistic at each horizontal position (with markers).
- `struct HeatmapElement`: A heat map: one cell per pair of categories across and up, shaded light to dark by the number of rows (frequency-weighted) or, with a continuous color column, by a statistic of its values; optionally labelled.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/annotation.rs`

Annotations: text, arrows, lines and rectangles the user places on a
plot, kept in the plot's style ([`crate::plot_style::AnnotationLook`]).

An annotation is anchored either to the data (its positions are data
values, so it moves with the axes and follows a change of scale) or to
the plot frame (its positions are fractions of the visible view, 0–1
across from the left and up from the bottom, so it stays put while the
axes move). Text is read as math markup ([`crate::math_text`]).

- `enum AnnotationShape`: What an annotation draws.
- `enum AnnotationAnchor`: What an annotation's positions are measured in.
- `struct Annotation`: One annotation.
- `const ANNOTATION_WIDTH`: Width of annotation lines, in screen points.
- `const ANNOTATION_INK`: The color annotations are drawn in (dark ink, light in the dark appearance: see [`crate::palette::for_dark`]).
- `struct PanelPlace`: How a panel's positions map to plot coordinates: its axes (for the scale of data values), axis breaks in drawn units and the visible view in drawn units (after breaks).
- `fn annotation_layer`: The layer drawing the annotations of panel `panel` from `annotations`, in their order (later ones on top).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/bivariate.rs`

Bivariate density layers: normal density ellipses, kernel-density
contours and binned counts (rectangles or hexagons).

- `struct EllipseElement`: Bivariate-normal density ellipses per subgroup at one or more probability levels (e.g.
- `struct ContourElement`: Kernel-density contours per subgroup: lines bounding the smallest regions that hold the given fractions of the estimated density (e.g.
- `struct BinElement`: Counts of rows (frequency-weighted) in a grid of rectangles or hexagons over the panel, each cell shaded on a sequential ramp from few to many — a density view for large data where points overlap (Carr et al., "Scatterplot Matrix Techniques for Large N", *JASA* 82(398), 1987).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/brackets.rs`

Significance brackets between compared categories.

- `enum BracketTest`: The multiple-comparison procedure behind the brackets (all from `stat_inference`).
- `enum BracketLabel`: What each bracket says.
- `const STAR_THRESHOLDS`: The usual star thresholds: `*` below 0.05, `**` below 0.01, `***` below 0.001, `****` below 0.0001.
- `fn stars`: Stars for an adjusted p-value: `****` below 0.0001, `***` below 0.001, `**` below 0.01, `*` below 0.05, otherwise `ns` (not significant).
- `fn stars_with`: Stars for `p` against `thresholds` (one star below the first, two below the second, …), `ns` when `p` is at or above the first.
- `const STAR_KEY`: The key to the stars, as written under a graph with brackets.
- `fn star_key`: The key to the stars for `thresholds`.
- `struct BracketComparison`: One comparison of two categories.
- `fn bracket_tiers`: The tier (0 = lowest) of each interval `(lo, hi)` so that intervals in one tier never overlap or touch: intervals are taken shortest first (ties left to right), each into the lowest tier where it meets no interval already there.
- `struct BracketElement`: Significance brackets: for categories across and a continuous column up, compares the categories' means with a multiple-comparison procedure ([`BracketTest`]: Tukey–Kramer by default, Games–Howell, Holm-adjusted t, or Dunnett against the first category) and draws a bracket above the data between …
- `fn place_brackets`: Heights of brackets over spans `(first, second)` whose data reach `tops` (the tallest point under each span): each sits `gap` above its own top, and is raised to `step` above every bracket already placed over a span it overlaps or touches, so it arches over them.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/distribution.rs`

Distributions per category: Tukey box plots (optionally notched) and
violin plots.

- `struct BoxPlotElement`: Tukey box plots of the vertical variable at each level of a categorical horizontal axis (or of the whole panel when there is no horizontal variable), one per subgroup side by side: a box from Q1 to Q3 with the median, whiskers to the furthest points within the fences, and the points beyond them a…
- `struct ViolinElement`: Violin plots: the kernel density of the vertical variable at each level of a categorical horizontal axis, mirrored about the slot centre, each scaled to the slot's width (so shapes compare, not areas).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/fit.rs`

Least-squares polynomial fits.

- `struct FitLabels`: Which fit statistics are written at the end of each fitted line.
- `struct FitLineElement`: Weighted least-squares polynomial (degree 1 to 5) per subgroup, with a shaded pointwise confidence band for the mean, dashed prediction limits for a new observation, and fit statistics labelled at the line's right end.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/function.rs`

Curves `y = f(x)` typed as formulas, drawn over the data.

- `struct FunctionElement`: One dotted curve per formula in `x` (see [`crate::expr`] for the syntax), in data units: x positions across the panel's data are taken back to data values through the horizontal scale, the formula is evaluated, and the result drawn through the vertical scale.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/histogram.rs`

Distributions of one continuous column across: histograms, Wilkinson dot
plots and probability plots against a fitted distribution.

All three use the horizontal variable only; the vertical axis shows
counts (or density), stacked dots, or standard quantiles, so they need no
vertical column.

- `enum HistogramBins`: How histogram bins are chosen.
- `struct HistogramElement`: A histogram of the horizontal variable: rows counted (with their frequencies) in equal-width bins on the horizontal axis's scale, per subgroup overlaid (translucent) or stacked.
- `struct DotPlotElement`: A Wilkinson dot plot (Wilkinson 1999, "Dot plots", *American Statistician* 53(3)): one dot per row (frequencies repeat it), stacked where values fall within a bin width of each other.
- `struct ProbabilityPlotElement`: A probability plot of the horizontal variable against a distribution fitted to it by maximum likelihood ([`stat_core::distribution_fit`]), one per subgroup: each ordered value `x₍ᵢ₎` at the standard quantile of its median-rank plotting position `(i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4)` (Benard & Bos-Levenbach 1953),…

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/hull.rs`

Convex hulls around the points of each subgroup.

- `fn convex_hull`: The convex hull of `points` (non-finite points ignored), counter-clockwise from the lowest-leftmost vertex, without repeated or collinear vertices.
- `struct HullElement`: Convex hulls: the smallest convex polygon around the drawn points of each subgroup (color or subgroup column), outlined in the subgroup's color with its own line pattern (solid, dashed, dotted in turn), optionally with a light fill.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/points.rs`

Raw data points.

- `struct PointsElement`: Raw data points: jittered along categorical axes, colored, shaped and sized by the encoding; excluded rows as gray crosses; rows outside the graph's filter (when drawn) hollow; selected rows ringed; optionally, while anything is selected, unselected points are drawn lighter (still clearly visible…
- `const MAX_POINT_LABELS`: Most point labels drawn for all rows (beyond this only selected rows).
- `const FADED_ALPHA`: Opacity of unselected points while some rows are selected.
- `const SWARM_PANEL`: The plot area (width, height in screen points) a swarm is laid out for: the layer does not know the size of the window it is drawn in, so the swarm assumes a panel about this size (the canvas's default) and markers just touch there; in a much smaller panel they overlap a little, in a larger one s…

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/reference.rs`

Reference lines and shaded bands added by the user.

A reference line is a straight line right across a plot at one value of
an axis: horizontal at a value of the vertical axis, or vertical at a
value of the horizontal axis. Its value is typed ([`ReferenceValue::Fixed`])
or computed from the plotted data on that axis
([`ReferenceValue::Statistic`]: mean, median, a quantile, mean ± k standard
deviations, or the centre line and 3-sigma limits of an individuals
control chart), and is recomputed whenever the data or the row states
change. A shaded band fills the stretch between two such values, behind
the data. Lines and bands have a key entry and a label written along
them, so their color is never the only cue.

Statistics are of the data values (on a transformed axis they are
computed before the transformation, then drawn on the scale), of the rows
that take part in analyses, with frequencies and weights used as in
[`crate::summary`]:

* mean `Σ fwx / Σ fw`; median and quantiles by the frequency-weighted
  quantile of [`crate::stats::weighted_quantile`];
* mean ± k·s with `s` the frequency-weighted standard deviation (divisor
  `Σf − 1`);
* individuals chart (Montgomery, *Introduction to Statistical Quality
  Control*, §6.4): centre `x̄`, limits `x̄ ± 3·MR̄/d₂` with `MR̄` the mean
  moving range of span 2 of the values in row order and `d₂ = 2/√π ≈ 1.128`,
  computed by `stat_quality::charts::individuals_chart` (frequencies and
  weights are not used: each row is one observation in time order).

A line's statistic is of the whole graph (every panel's rows together),
of each panel, or of each subgroup of each panel ([`ReferenceScope`]).

- `enum ReferenceOrientation`: Which way a reference line runs.
- `enum ReferenceStat`: A statistic of the plotted data that places a reference line.
- `enum ReferenceValue`: Where a reference line sits: a typed value or a statistic of the data.
- `enum ReferenceScope`: Which rows a statistic of a reference line or band is computed from.
- `struct ReferenceLine`: One reference line.
- `struct ReferenceBand`: One shaded band between two values of an axis.
- `struct ReferenceLook`: The reference lines and bands of one plot.
- `struct ValueSet`: Plotted data values (data units, rows in order) of one set of rows.
- `struct ReferenceData`: The data a plot's reference statistics are computed from.
- `struct ReferenceAxes`: How the plot's axes are drawn: their scales and whether they are categorical.
- `struct ReferenceLayers`: The reference marks of a plot.
- `fn reference_layers`: The marks of `look` for a plot with axes `axes` showing `data`: the bands (with their edge lines and labels) in [`ReferenceLayers::back`], the lines in [`ReferenceLayers::front`], each with one key entry.
- `fn widen_range`: `range` widened to show `extent` too: a side that has to move goes past the extent by 6% of the new span (the default padding); a range already showing it is returned unchanged.
- `fn panel_reference_data`: The reference data of `panel` within `frame`: the rows that take part in analyses, in row order, in data units; subgroups by the panel's groups.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/smoother.rs`

Smoothing curves: the cubic smoothing spline and LOESS.

- `enum SmoothMethod`: How a smoother is computed.
- `struct SmootherElement`: A smooth curve per subgroup, dashed, with an optional shaded confidence band: a cubic smoothing spline ([`SmoothingSpline`]; `lambda` is the relative penalty, larger is smoother) or LOESS ([`loess`]; `span` is the fraction of rows in each local fit and `local_degree` its polynomial degree).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element/summaries.rs`

Summary points: one statistic per category (or per distinct x) with
optional error bars.

- `struct SummaryElement`: A statistic of the vertical variable for each horizontal position (each category slot, or each distinct x) and subgroup, drawn as a large diamond in the subgroup's color, with optional error bars around the mean (standard error, confidence interval or standard deviation).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/element.rs`

Chart elements: independent layers drawn in the same panels and
coordinates, so any combination can be active at once (points under a
smoother under box plots, …). Each element turns a [`Panel`] into a
[`Layer`] of toolkit-independent marks and key entries; with the `egui`
feature, `Element::render` draws it straight into an `egui_plot` plot.

* [`PointsElement`] — raw rows, jittered on category axes.
* [`FitLineElement`] — least-squares polynomials with confidence and
  prediction bands and fit statistics.
* [`SmootherElement`] — smoothing spline or LOESS, with a confidence band.
* [`BoxPlotElement`] (optionally notched) and [`ViolinElement`] —
  distributions per category.
* [`SummaryElement`] — a statistic per category or x with error bars.
* [`EllipseElement`], [`ContourElement`], [`BinElement`] — bivariate
  density: normal ellipses, kernel-density contours, binned counts.
* [`FunctionElement`] — curves `y = f(x)` typed as formulas.
* [`BarElement`], [`LineElement`], [`HeatmapElement`] — aggregates: bars
  (side by side, stacked, 100%), line and run charts, category heat maps.
* [`HistogramElement`], [`DotPlotElement`], [`ProbabilityPlotElement`] —
  one continuous column across: histograms, Wilkinson dot plots and
  probability plots against a fitted distribution.
* Whole-panel chart forms ([`crate::forms`]): treemaps, parallel
  coordinates, pie, radar, polar, wind-rose, ternary, waterfall, ridgeline
  and vector-field charts. A scatterplot matrix uses the usual elements, with the
  one-variable ones on its diagonal and the others off it.

- `enum ElementKind`: The kinds of element.
- `trait Element`: A layer of a graph.
- `struct GraphSpec`: A whole graph: encodings, axis options and the active elements with their settings (what a graph canvas saves).
- `enum LegendPlacement`: Where a graph's key is placed.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/encoding.rs`

Variable encodings: which data columns drive which visual channel of a
graph — its position axes, its panel grid, and the color, size and marker
of its points — following the grammar of graphics (Wilkinson, *The Grammar
of Graphics*, 2nd ed., 2005) and its shelf-based specification of views
(Stolte, Tang & Hanrahan, "Polaris", *IEEE TVCG* 8(1), 2002).

- `enum Role`: The visual channel a column can be assigned to.
- `struct EncodingPlan`: The column assigned to each visual channel of a graph.
- `struct ColumnSwitcher`: A column picker: a list of columns the user can step through for one slot of a role (e.g.
- `fn is_continuous`: `true` if `column` of `table` is treated as continuous (numeric or date-time, with the continuous measurement level); everything else is categorical.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/estimation.rs`

Estimation plots: every observation of each group, and the difference of
each group's mean from a reference group's with its confidence interval,
so the size and precision of an effect are read from the graph rather
than from a p-value (Gardner & Altman, "Confidence intervals rather than
P values", *BMJ* 292, 1986; Cumming, *Understanding the New Statistics*,
2012; Ho, Tumkaya, Aryal, Choi & Claridge-Chang, "Moving beyond P values:
data analysis with estimation graphics", *Nature Methods* 16, 2019).

* **Two groups (Gardner–Altman):** one panel. The groups' points sit in
  the first two slots; the third slot holds the mean difference (other
  minus reference) with its interval on a floating axis whose zero is
  level with the reference group's mean, so the difference reads off the
  same units as the data. Dashed lines carry both means across to it.
* **More groups (Cumming):** the groups' points in an upper panel, and in
  a lower panel each group's mean difference from the reference with its
  interval, at the group's own position (the reference shows the zero
  line).

Intervals for `d = ȳ_g − ȳ_ref`:

* **BCa bootstrap** (default): `B` resamples (5000 by default), each
  group resampled with replacement within itself (the stratified
  bootstrap of independent samples), `d*` computed on each; the
  bias-corrected and accelerated interval (Efron 1987) with the
  acceleration from the jackknife deleting one observation at a time
  within each group (`stat_inference::bootstrap`, Efron & Tibshirani
  eq. 15.36) — the interval of Ho et al. and of `scipy.stats.bootstrap`
  with `method="BCa"`. Resamples are seeded (`seed + g` for group `g`), so
  the interval is the same every time. The bootstrap distribution of `d*`
  is drawn as a half violin (Gaussian kernel density, Silverman's
  bandwidth).
* **Welch t:** `d ± t_{1−α/2, ν} · √(s²_g/n_g + s²_ref/n_ref)` with the
  Welch–Satterthwaite `ν` (`stat_inference::means::two_sample_t`).

The analyses use rows that are not excluded, inside the graph's filter,
with a group and a value; a frequency column repeats a row (rounded to a
whole number); weights are not used. The vertical axis is always linear.

- `enum EstimationInterval`: How the interval of a mean difference is computed.
- `struct EstimationSettings`: Settings of an estimation plot.
- `const RESAMPLE_RANGE`: Fewest and most bootstrap resamples accepted.
- `struct GroupEstimate`: One group of an estimation plot.
- `struct MeanDifference`: One group's mean difference from the reference.
- `struct EstimationGeometry`: What an estimation plot's panels draw.
- `fn mean_difference`: The mean difference `mean(other) − mean(reference)` with its interval.
- `fn build_estimation_frame`: The frame of an estimation plot: the first horizontal column gives the groups, the first vertical column the values.
- `struct EstimationElement`: Draws the means, differences, intervals and the floating axis of an estimation plot (its points are the graph's points layer, best laid out as a swarm).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/export.rs`

Vector export of a graph: SVG, PDF and EPS, drawn from the same frame and
layers as the screen, so a saved figure matches what is shown.

The page holds the title, the panel grid (each panel with its frame,
light grid lines, tick labels, axis titles on the outer panels and any
panel headers), the marks clipped to each panel, and the key below. Text
is set in Helvetica, or Times for a serif figure ([`PlotFont`]): PDF and
EPS use the standard fonts without embedding (characters outside their
Latin-1 set are spelled out, e.g. `≤` → `<=`), SVG names the font and its
common stand-ins, and PNG draws the metric-compatible Liberation Sans or
Liberation Serif.

Greek letters go to the standard Symbol font in PDF and EPS. Labels in the
math markup of [`crate::math_text`] are set run by run: scripts smaller
and raised or dropped, fractions stacked over a rule.

PDF output is PDF 1.4 with transparency through graphics-state
dictionaries; EPS (PostScript level 2) has no transparency, so
translucent colors are blended with white.

- `enum VectorFormat`: A figure file format: three vector formats and PNG (drawn by the same code at [`crate::raster::PNG_DPI`] pixels per inch).
- `type PanelView`: The visible range of each panel: `([x_min, x_max], [y_min, y_max])`.
- `fn panel_views`: Each panel's view from shared ranges (with optional overrides by axis name, as set by dragging the axes on screen).
- `fn equal_aspect_view`: `view` widened about its centre along one axis so that a `width` × `height` area shows one unit the same length across and up.
- `fn cmyk`: Device CMYK of an sRGB colour by the simple complement rule (no colour profile): K = 1 − max(R, G, B), and C = (1 − R − K) / (1 − K), likewise M and Y, so black is K alone and white is no ink.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/export_axes.rs`

Axes of exported report figures drawn with the plot's own settings
(`crate::axis_settings`), so a saved figure shows what the screen shows:
the user's tick intervals, minor ticks, number format and tick labels,
grid lines, tick marks pointing in, out or across the axis line with
their length and thickness, axis lines moved away from the data area,
and either axis on its opposite side.

Lengths set in screen points are drawn at [`PT`] page points each, the
scale at which a figure matches the plot's size on screen.

- `const PT`: Page points per screen point (a plot drawn at 96 pixels per inch).
- `struct StyledTick`: One tick of an exported axis.
- `fn styled_ticks`: Ticks of an axis `length` page points long showing `[lo, hi]`, placed and labelled as on screen: the user's intervals and format, labels thinned so they never crowd, and the user's own labels (read as markup).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/expr.rs`

Arithmetic expressions in one variable, for function curves drawn over the
data (e.g. `2.5 + 0.8*x - 0.01*x^2` or `100 * exp(-x / 4)`).

Grammar (usual precedence, `^` right-associative and binding tighter than
unary minus, so `-x^2` is `−(x²)`):

```text
expr    = term   { ("+" | "-") term }
term    = unary  { ("*" | "/") unary }
unary   = ("-" | "+") unary | power
power   = primary [ "^" unary ]
primary = number | "x" | "pi" | "e" | name "(" expr { "," expr } ")" | "(" expr ")"
```

Functions: `sqrt abs exp ln log10 log sin cos tan asin acos atan sinh cosh
tanh floor ceil round min max pow`; `log(v)` is the natural log and
`log(v, b)` the base-`b` log. Numbers accept decimals and exponents
(`1.5e-3`). Names are case-insensitive.

- `enum Expr`: A parsed expression.
- `enum Op`: A binary operator.
- `enum Func`: A built-in function.
- `struct ParseError`: Why an expression could not be read.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/figure_page.rs`

Figure pages: several figures on one page, each in a cell of a grid with
a panel letter, saved as one file (PNG, SVG, PDF or EPS).

A figure is first drawn in the [`VectorFormat::Drawing`] format by any of
the export functions ([`crate::export::export_graph`],
[`crate::export::export_chart`], …), which keeps its drawing operations
as a [`Drawing`] instead of writing a file. [`export_page`] places the
drawings in the cells of [`PageLayout::cells`] (each drawing scaled down,
never up, to fit its cell, and centred in it), writes a letter in the
upper left corner of each cell, and writes the page:

* PNG at a chosen pixel density ([`PageOutput::dpi`], recorded in the
  file);
* PDF and EPS in RGB or device CMYK ([`crate::export::cmyk`]: the simple
  complement rule, no colour profile);
* any format on a white page or a clear (transparent) one. EPS has no
  transparency, so translucent marks are blended with white either way.

Sizes are in points (1/72 inch); [`LengthUnit`] converts millimetres and
inches. Figures drawn at their cell's size keep their text at its usual
point size; a drawing made for a larger cell is shrunk with its text.

- `enum LengthUnit`: A unit for page sizes.
- `enum PanelLetters`: How panels are lettered, in reading order.
- `struct PageLayout`: The page: its size, the grid of cells and the lettering.
- `struct PageOutput`: How a page is written.
- `fn pixel_size`: Size in pixels of a `width` × `height` point page at `dpi`.
- `struct Drawing`: A figure kept as its drawing operations (made by drawing it in the [`VectorFormat::Drawing`] format), so it can be placed on a page.
- `fn export_page`: The page as a file in `output.format`, with panel `i` spanning `spans[i]` columns and showing `drawings[i]` (`None` leaves the cell empty but still lettered).
- `fn export_figure`: One figure on a page of its own, `width` × `height` points: `drawing` scaled (up or down) to fit, keeping its proportions, and centred.
- `fn figure_pixels`: [`export_figure`] drawn into pixels at `dpi` in `font` on white, for previews: `(width, height, RGBA bytes)`.
- `fn look_page_size`: The page size, in points, of a figure drawn with `look` whose own size (on screen) is `natural`: the look's size on paper, else `natural`.
- `fn look_figure`: A figure written as `look` says: on a page of the look's size (else `natural`'s own), laid out by `redraw` on a page [`ExportLook::text_size`] times smaller and enlarged to fit, so text, marks and lines grow together.
- `fn page_pixels`: The page drawn into pixels at `dpi` (as a PNG page would be, on white): `(width, height, RGBA bytes)`, for previews.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/filter.rs`

A graph's own row filter: conditions on columns (chosen levels of a
categorical column, an interval of a continuous one) that restrict what
one graph shows or analyses without changing the shared row states.

What happens to rows outside the filter is chosen separately:
* **show only matching rows** — the others are not drawn;
* **analyse only matching rows** — fits, smoothers and summaries use the
  matching rows only (rows still drawn are marked as left out);
* **select matching rows** — the matching rows become the shared selection,
  so every linked view highlights them (applied by the application when
  the filter changes).

- `enum FilterCondition`: One condition of a filter.
- `fn column_levels`: The distinct non-empty cell texts of `column`, in natural order.
- `struct LocalFilter`: A graph's row filter: all conditions must hold.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/flows.rs`

Flow and network charts drawn from categorical columns: Sankey
(alluvial) diagrams, chord diagrams and node-link networks. Each is a
whole-panel chart form with its own [`Frame`] (one panel, geometry in
[`PanelExtra`]); clicking a flow, ribbon, arc, node or edge selects its
rows, and parts holding selected rows are outlined.

* **Sankey diagram** — two or more columns on the horizontal shelf are
  stages, left to right; each level of a stage is a node whose height is
  its share of the rows (frequency-weighted) or of the sum of the first
  vertical column, and each pair of consecutive stages is joined by flows
  of the rows passing between their levels (Riehmann, Hanfler & Froehlich,
  "Interactive Sankey diagrams", *IEEE InfoVis* 2005). Flows keep the
  color of their level in the first stage (as in alluvial diagrams,
  Rosvall & Bergstrom, *PLoS ONE* 5(1), 2010), so a group can be followed
  across. Nodes are ordered within each stage to reduce crossings by the
  barycentre heuristic (Sugiyama, Tagawa & Toda, *IEEE Trans. SMC* 11(2),
  1981): alternate sweeps left to right and right to left sort each
  stage's nodes by the flow-weighted mean position of their neighbors in
  the stage just swept; the ordering with the fewest weighted crossings
  (`Σ wᵢ wⱼ` over pairs of flows that cross) is kept.
* **Chord diagram** — the first two horizontal columns are "from" and "to"
  (one set of nodes when they share levels, as in an origin–destination
  table). Each node is an arc of a circle whose angle is proportional to
  its flow out plus in; each pair is a ribbon from the "from" node's arc
  to the "to" node's arc, its ends as wide as the flow (Krzywinski et al.,
  "Circos", *Genome Research* 19, 2009). Ribbons take the "from" color.
* **Network** — the first two horizontal columns are the two ends of each
  edge, an optional numeric vertical column its weight (else each row
  counts once); edges between the same pair of nodes are combined. Nodes
  are placed by the force-directed algorithm of Fruchterman & Reingold
  ("Graph drawing by force-directed placement", *Software: Practice and
  Experience* 21(11), 1991): in a unit frame with `k = √(1/n)`, every pair
  of nodes repels with force `k²/d`, the two ends of every edge attract
  with `d²/k`, and each node moves along its net force by at most the
  temperature, which cools linearly from 0.1 to 0 over the iterations.
  Starting positions are seeded, so the layout is the same every time.
  Node size grows with degree; edge width with weight.

- `struct FlowSettings`: Settings of a Sankey or chord diagram.
- `struct NetworkSettings`: Settings of a network.
- `const MAX_NODES`: Most nodes a network lays out.
- `struct FlowNode`: A node of a flow chart.
- `struct FlowLink`: A flow, ribbon or edge.
- `struct FlowGeometry`: What a flow chart panel draws.
- `fn weighted_crossings`: Weighted crossings between consecutive stages: `links[s]` holds `(source position, target position, weight)` between stage `s` and `s + 1`; two links cross when their sources and targets are in opposite orders, adding the product of their weights.
- `fn barycentre_order`: Order the nodes of each stage to reduce crossings (barycentre sweeps).
- `fn build_sankey_frame`: The frame of a Sankey diagram.
- `fn build_chord_frame`: The frame of a chord diagram.
- `fn fruchterman_reingold`: Fruchterman–Reingold positions of `n` nodes joined by `edges` (pairs of node indices; self-loops ignored), in the frame `[−½, ½]²`, from seeded uniform starting positions, over `iterations` steps (see the module notes).
- `fn build_network_frame`: The frame of a node-link network.
- `struct FlowElement`: Draws a Sankey diagram, chord diagram or network panel.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/forms/radial.rs`

Round chart forms drawn in the unit circle, true to shape (one unit the
same length across and up): pie and donut charts, radar (star) charts,
polar charts and wind roses. Angles run clockwise from straight up
("compass" angles), so a pie's first slice and a radar's first spoke start
at twelve o'clock, as is usual (Cleveland, *The Elements of Graphing
Data*, 1985, discusses reading angles and areas; pies are offered for the
familiar share-of-a-whole view, labelled with their shares so the numbers
need not be read from angles).

* **Pie / donut** — slices by the levels of the first horizontal-shelf
  column, sized by row count (frequency-weighted) or by the sum of the
  first vertical-shelf column; slice `k` spans the angle
  `2π · vₖ / Σ v`. A donut leaves the centre open and writes the total
  there.
* **Radar** — one spoke per numeric column on the axis shelves, each
  scaled from its minimum (near the centre) to its maximum (the rim), as
  in parallel coordinates; one polygon per row, or per group the
  frequency × weight–weighted mean (Chambers, Cleveland, Kleiner & Tukey,
  *Graphical Methods for Data Analysis*, 1983, §5.6, "star plots").
* **Polar** — points at angle θ (the horizontal column, in compass
  degrees, mathematical degrees or radians) and radius r (the vertical
  column, r ≥ 0) at `(r sin θ_c, r cos θ_c)` where θ_c is the compass
  angle; optionally joined in row order.
* **Wind rose** — rows counted by direction sector (sector `k` of `S`
  centred on `k · 360°/S`, so the first is centred on north) and by bins of
  the vertical column (round bin edges 1, 2, 2.5 or 5 × 10ⁿ apart, or the
  levels of a categorical column), the bins stacked outward from the
  lowest; the radius is linear in the count or the percentage of rows.

- `fn compass_point`: Point at radius `r` and compass angle `theta` (radians clockwise from straight up).
- `const DONUT_HOLE`: Radius of a donut's hole (the rim is at 1).
- `struct PieSettings`: Settings of a pie chart.
- `struct PieSlice`: One slice of a pie.
- `struct PieGeometry`: The slices of a pie panel.
- `fn build_pie_frame`: The frame of a pie or donut chart: one slice per level of the first horizontal-shelf column, with area (angle) proportional to its rows' frequency-weighted count, or to the sum of frequency × the first vertical column.
- `struct PieElement`: Draws the slices of a pie panel: each filled in its level's colour with its marker shape at the rim (so slices are told apart without colour), its share and value written beside it, slices holding selected rows ringed.
- `const RADAR_HOLE`: Radius of a spoke's minimum (its maximum is at the rim, 1), so polygons through minima stay visible.
- `fn radar_radius`: Radius of the scaled value `t` (0 at a spoke's minimum, 1 at its maximum).
- `struct RadarSettings`: Settings of a radar chart.
- `struct RadarPolygon`: One polygon of a radar chart.
- `struct RadarGeometry`: Spokes and polygons of a radar panel.
- `fn build_radar_frame`: The frame of a radar chart: one spoke per continuous column on the axis shelves (horizontal, then vertical; each once), each scaled from its minimum to its maximum over the rows shown.
- `struct RadarElement`: Draws a radar panel: rings at 0, ¼, ½, ¾ and all of each spoke's range, the spokes with their names and ranges, and the polygons, each in its colour, marker shape and line pattern (by subgroup).
- `enum AngleUnit`: How a polar chart reads its angle column.
- `struct PolarSettings`: Settings of a polar chart.
- `struct PolarGeometry`: Rings and spokes of a polar panel.
- `fn build_polar_frame`: The frame of a polar chart: each row at the compass angle of the first horizontal column (read in `settings.angle`) and the radius of the first vertical column, the rim at a round radius at or above the largest.
- `struct PolarElement`: Draws the rings and spokes of a polar panel (the points layer draws the rows), and, when asked, each subgroup's points joined in row order in its colour and line pattern.
- `struct WindRoseSettings`: Settings of a wind rose.
- `struct WindPiece`: One stacked piece of a wind rose: rows of one magnitude bin in one sector.
- `struct WindRoseGeometry`: The pieces, bins and rings of a wind-rose panel.
- `fn build_wind_rose_frame`: The frame of a wind rose: rows counted (frequency-weighted) by direction sector (the first horizontal column, in compass degrees, any whole turn) and by magnitude bin (the first vertical column binned at round edges from zero, its levels if categorical, or one bin without a vertical column), stac…
- `struct WindRoseElement`: Draws a wind rose: rings with their counts or percentages, compass spokes and labels, and the stacked pieces in a sequential ramp from the lowest magnitude bin outward (named in the key); pieces holding selected rows are ringed, and clicking one selects its rows.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/forms/ridgeline.rs`

Ridgeline plot (joy plot): the distribution of one continuous column in
each group as a Gaussian kernel density (the same estimator as the violin
layer, [`crate::density::kde_1d`] with Silverman's bandwidth per group),
the groups stacked one above another on a shared horizontal axis and
overlapping slightly so many groups fit (Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data
Visualization*, 2019, ch. 9 "Visualizing many distributions at once").

All ridges share one height scale (the tallest peak reaches the chosen
height in category slots), so their areas are equal and their heights
compare directly. The rows themselves are drawn as a rug of ticks under
each ridge.

- `struct RidgelineSettings`: Settings of a ridgeline plot.
- `struct Ridge`: One ridge.
- `struct RidgelineGeometry`: The ridges of a ridgeline panel.
- `fn build_ridgeline_frame`: The frame of a ridgeline plot: the first horizontal column (continuous, on the horizontal scale) for each level of the grouping column — the first vertical column if categorical, else the subgroup column, else a categorical colour column, else one ridge for all rows.
- `struct RidgelineElement`: Draws the ridges of a ridgeline panel from the top down (so lower ridges overlap the ones behind them), each filled in its level's colour with its outline, and the rug: a tick per row, the selected rows' ticks in the selection colour on top.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/forms/ternary.rs`

Ternary plot of data: three non-negative component columns, each row
divided by its total so the components sum to 1 (closure), drawn in an
equilateral triangle true to shape (Aitchison, *The Statistical Analysis
of Compositional Data*, 1986, ch. 1; Howarth, "Sources for a history of
the ternary diagram", *British Journal for the History of Science* 29,
1996).

The first component's corner is at the lower left `(0, 0)`, the second's at
the lower right `(1, 0)` and the third's at the top `(½, √3/2)`, so the
composition `(a, b, c)` sits at `(b + c/2, c·√3/2)` — the same layout as
the ternary contour plots of mixture experiments. Gridlines join points
of equal share of a component every 0.1; each component's shares are
labelled along one edge, rising towards its corner.

- `const TERNARY_HEIGHT`: Height of the unit equilateral triangle, `√3/2`.
- `fn ternary_position`: Position of the composition `p` (shares summing to 1) in the triangle: `(p₁ + p₂/2, p₂·√3/2)` with corners `(0, 0)`, `(1, 0)` and `(½, √3/2)` for the first, second and third component.
- `struct TernaryGeometry`: What a ternary panel needs besides its points.
- `fn build_ternary_frame`: The frame of a ternary plot: the first three continuous columns on the axis shelves (horizontal, then vertical; each once) as components.
- `struct TernaryElement`: Draws the triangle of a ternary panel with gridlines every 0.1, share labels every 0.2 along the edges and the component names at the corners (the points layer draws the rows).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/forms/vector.rs`

Vector-field (quiver) plot: an arrow per row from its position `(x, y)`
to `(x + s·u, y + s·v)`, where `u` and `v` are the row's horizontal and
vertical components and `s` one scale for every arrow, so lengths compare
(the "quiver" display of fluid mechanics and meteorology; e.g. Tufte,
*Envisioning Information*, 1990, on small multiples of direction).

The scale is chosen so the longest arrow is 0.9 × the typical spacing of
the points, `√(width · height / n)` of the data's bounding box (the side of
the square each of `n` evenly spread points would occupy), times the
chosen percentage. Arrows are drawn in the axes' units: with both axes in
one unit, Plot settings ▸ Equal scale makes their angles true.

- `struct VectorSettings`: Settings of a vector-field plot.
- `struct Arrow`: One arrow, in drawn (scaled) coordinates.
- `struct VectorGeometry`: The arrows of a vector-field panel.
- `fn build_vector_frame`: The frame of a vector-field plot: the first horizontal and vertical columns place each row; the second column on each shelf gives its horizontal and vertical component.
- `struct VectorElement`: Draws the arrows of a vector-field panel in each row's colour (the points layer marks the tails); while rows are selected, theirs are drawn on top in the selection colour and thicker.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/forms/waterfall.rs`

Waterfall (bridge) chart: how signed contributions build a total. Each
category of the horizontal column contributes `vₖ = Σ fᵢyᵢ` (frequency ×
the vertical column over its rows); its bar floats from the running total
before it, `Sₖ₋₁ = v₁ + … + vₖ₋₁`, to `Sₖ`, and an optional last bar
stands from zero to the grand total. Categories keep the order in which
they first appear in the table (the order a bridge is usually written
in). Increases and decreases differ in colour, decreases are also hatched,
and every bar can carry its signed value (`+12`, `−5`), so the direction
never rests on colour alone.

- `struct WaterfallSettings`: Settings of a waterfall chart.
- `enum StepKind`: What a waterfall bar shows.
- `struct WaterfallBar`: One bar of a waterfall chart.
- `struct WaterfallGeometry`: The bars of a waterfall panel.
- `fn build_waterfall_frame`: The frame of a waterfall chart: a categorical horizontal axis with one slot per category of the first horizontal column (in order of first appearance), then a "Total" slot, and the running total up.
- `struct WaterfallElement`: Draws the bars of a waterfall panel with dashed connectors from each bar's end to the next bar's start; the selected share of a bar is shaded dark with the selection outline.

### `crates/stat-viz/src/forms.rs`

Whole-panel chart forms that do not use the usual axes: treemaps and
parallel coordinates. Each builds its own [`Frame`] (one panel, with its
geometry in [`PanelExtra`]) and draws with its own element; points can
still be shown on top, and box and click selection work as usual.

* **Treemap** — nested rectangles, one level per column on the
  horizontal-axis shelf (in order), with areas proportional to the number
  of rows (frequency-weighted) or to the sum of the first vertical column.
  Rectangles are laid out by the squarified algorithm (Bruls, Huizing & van
  Wijk, "Squarified Treemaps", *Data Visualization 2000*), which keeps
  aspect ratios near 1.
* **Parallel coordinates** — one vertical axis per column (horizontal
  shelf, then vertical shelf), each scaled from its minimum (bottom) to
  maximum (top), every row a line across them (Inselberg, "The Plane with
  Parallel Coordinates", *The Visual Computer* 1(2), 1985; Wegman,
  *JASA* 85(411), 1990).
* **Multi-vari chart** — the first vertical column against one to four
  factors on the horizontal shelf (outermost first; Seder, "Diagnosis with
  diagrams", *Industrial Quality Control* 6, 1950): every row at its
  innermost cell, each factor's level means marked and joined within each
  level of the factor above, the outermost factor's levels as labelled
  sections.
* **Scatterplot matrix** — every pair of the continuous columns on the
  axis shelves in a square grid of panels (Chambers, Cleveland, Kleiner &
  Tukey, *Graphical Methods for Data Analysis*, 1983, §5.4): the panel in
  row `i`, column `j` plots column `i` up against column `j` across, with
  the graph's layers (points, density ellipses, fits, …); the diagonal
  panels show each column's histogram (or the dot plot or probability plot
  layer when one is on). Brushing any panel selects the rows everywhere.
* **Pie and donut charts, radar charts, polar charts and wind roses**
  ([`radial`]) — round forms drawn true to shape.
* **Ternary plot** ([`ternary`]) — three components normalised to sum 1.
* **Waterfall chart** ([`waterfall`]), **ridgeline plot** ([`ridgeline`])
  and **vector field** ([`vector`]).

- `struct TreemapSettings`: Settings of a treemap.
- `enum GraphForm`: The form of a graph.
- `fn squarify`: Lay out `values` (all positive) in `rect` (`[x0, y0, x1, y1]`) by the squarified algorithm, in the given order (callers sort descending).
- `fn build_treemap_frame`: The frame of a treemap: one panel whose tiles nest the levels of the horizontal-shelf columns; each row's point sits at the centre of its innermost tile (for selection).
- `struct TreemapElement`: Draws the tiles of a treemap panel.
- `fn build_parallel_frame`: The frame of a parallel-coordinates chart: one panel with an axis per column at x = 1, 2, … and one point per row and axis at the row's scaled value (0 at the axis minimum, 1 at its maximum; categories evenly spaced).
- `struct ParallelElement`: Draws the lines and axes of a parallel-coordinates panel.
- `struct MultiVariGeometry`: The means and joins of a multi-vari panel.
- `fn build_multivari_frame`: The frame of a multi-vari chart: one panel whose horizontal axis has a slot per innermost cell (combination of the factors' levels that occurs), with an empty slot between levels of the outer factors; every row's point sits at its cell.
- `struct MultiVariElement`: Draws the means, joins and sections of a multi-vari panel: each factor's means in its own colour and marker shape (named in the key), joined within each level of the factor above.
- `fn build_scatter_matrix_frame`: The frame of a scatterplot matrix: the continuous columns of the horizontal then vertical shelves (each once), crossed in an `m × m` grid (row `i` plots column `i` up, column `j` plots column `j` across).

### `crates/stat-viz/src/frame.rs`

From data and an [`EncodingPlan`] to panels: each row's position on the
axes (on their scales), its marker style, its subgroup, and its panel in
a grid of small multiples (trellis displays: Becker, Cleveland & Shyu,
"The Visual Design and Control of Trellis Display", *JCGS* 5(2), 1996).

* Several horizontal columns give several panel columns, several vertical
  columns several panel rows (each panel pairs one of each).
* `group_x` / `group_y` split every panel column / row by level; `wrap`
  instead lays one panel per level into a near-square grid.
* A categorical axis places level `k` (in natural order) at position
  `k + 1`; a missing horizontal axis is one unnamed category, a missing
  vertical axis a numeric axis with every row at 0.
* `page` shows one level at a time (the frame's current page); axes and
  styles are shared by every page so pages compare directly.
* Hidden rows are left out; excluded rows are kept (drawn differently and
  left out of fits); values outside an axis scale's domain are dropped and
  counted in the frame's notes.
* The graph's own [`LocalFilter`] can drop rows outside it or keep them
  drawn but out of the analyses.
* Frequency and weight columns travel with each point for the elements'
  statistics.

- `enum AxisKind`: What an axis shows.
- `struct AxisSpec`: One axis of a panel.
- `struct PanelPoint`: A row drawn in a panel.
- `struct GroupStyle`: Name, color and shape of a subgroup.
- `struct Panel`: One panel of the grid.
- `struct Tile`: A rectangle of a treemap: `[x0, y0, x1, y1]` in the unit square.
- `struct ParallelAxis`: One vertical axis of a parallel-coordinates panel.
- `enum PanelExtra`: Extra geometry a panel carries for whole-panel chart forms.
- `enum ColorKey`: What the color channel shows.
- `struct Legend`: The key of a graph.
- `struct Frame`: Every panel of a graph with its layout and key.
- `struct FrameOptions`: Axis scales, page and row filter of a frame.
- `const DEFAULT_RADIUS`: Default marker radius in screen points.
- `struct MarkerStyle`: Marker appearance chosen by the user: size, the color and shape of ungrouped markers (and lines), and colors, shapes and sizes for particular levels of the color, subgroup and shape columns (keyed by `column` and `level`, see [`MarkerStyle::key`]).
- `const MAX_PANELS`: Largest number of panels drawn (levels beyond this are left out).
